en: The *Ṛjuvimalāpañcikā*,
composed by Śālikanāthamiśra.
We pay homage to the Sun, who destroys the night of ignorance created [by us], who is a day consisting of the removal of bondage, and who has dispelled the dullness of the world. (Bṛhatīvyākhyā 1)
I pay homage to Aparājita, who always maintains a right vision consisting of light, while his left vision brings heat [to the passions] like the moon.
I am composing this *Pañcikā* (Commentary) which will clearly elucidate the intention of the teacher Prabhākara, whose speech is exceedingly profound. (3)
This exposition of the ancient commentators has been refuted by Vyāsa through both presentation and rejection; thus, I have not sought to disparage it.

The Vārttikakāra has explained the Bhāṣya beginning with "In the world" (*loke*) and ending with "there would result an excessive burden of effort" (*yatnagauravaṃ prasajyeta*) as being intended merely to restate the appropriateness [of the objection] for the purpose of refuting the word *atha*. Considering that such an explanation serves little purpose, the Ṭīkākāra demonstrates its actual purpose by saying "of the Bhāṣya beginning with 'In the world,'" and so forth.
Having created [this work] which has as its object every word found in all the sūtras—
[the reading "ujjāsita" is adopted here from the verse seen at the beginning of the Nyāyakośa].
In this passage, the reading "ujjhāsita" is seen in some places;
it appears to be a scribal error.
2. *bhāvam* (existence), *mita-* (measured).
3. *pañjikā* (commentary).

And this is said: by that, there is no contradiction with the plural number. Since they are the subject under discussion and are the points of dispute, the purpose of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* alone is the removal of the suspicion regarding a non-worldly (alaukika) meaning. "When possible" means when the worldly meaning is possible.
This is the meaning. Why is this so?

For if a worldly meaning is possible, how can there be room for the suspicion of a non-worldly meaning? And if such [a worldly meaning] is impossible, how is this purpose established? The answer is: "from the study of one's own Vedic recitation" (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).

The impossibility [of the definition] arises from fallacious arguments (*nyāyābhāsa*); however, by refuting those, its very possibility is established. But how can there even be a suspicion that it was not intended to be expressed?

The sense is that, because there is a loss of understanding regarding the action useful for the person who has seen [the result], it is not logical for heaven—or even a fruit mentioned in an *arthavāda*—to be the result.

Now, in order to state the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he sets forth the seed of doubt: "Because no qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard in the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*)."
Nor is the qualification for teaching heard of even with respect to study, because it is not an auxiliary part [of it].
Furthermore, because [study] is impelled by the injunction for the production of the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*),
that [impulsion] is the first to occur.
The intention is that the very accomplishment of that [Veda] is the purpose of the injunction for study, and not the subsequent comprehension of ritual acts.
But how can one injunction be impelled by another?
If there is no relationship of being a subordinate part (*aṅga*), how [can this be]?
Is there an application of one injunction by means of another injunction? If it is argued that it is "like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth," this means:

if it is like the injunction for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. For in those cases, application is appropriate because there is no difference in the respective scopes of authority (*adhikāra*), as they are directly heard [in the text] to be connected with them.

In the proximity of an injunction regarding a qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*) whose status as a goal (*sādhya-bhāva*) is established through its connection with a result (*phala*), injunctions do not initially present themselves as goals in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which lack such a qualification; rather, they are merely the essential forms of actions (*karma-svarūpa*) intended for the sake of establishing that qualification. However, for things that are momentary, such a purposefulness is not possible by virtue of their own nature.
1. pravṛtta- ga. 2. -śaṅkā asambhavaś cet. ga. 3. vedādhyayana- ka.
4. *tatprayuktatā* (being prompted by that).
Ga. 5. *vidheḥ* (of the injunction). Ga. 6. The meaning is: "if it be argued that it is like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Ga.

Furthermore, the injunctions [of the subsidiaries] are modified by virtue of being things to be accomplished (*sādhya*); therefore, it is logical that these injunctions, being constituent parts (*aṅga*), are applied even when there is a difference [in the primary acts]. "In this case as well" refers to this.

If it is argued that the qualifying factor (*adhikārāṃśa*) for the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) and the injunction regarding study (*adhyayanavidhi*) does not differ, we say no; because there is no relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) [between them].
This is due to direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), and so forth.

For that which makes known the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅga*)—in its absence, it is not logical to imply something that is not a subsidiary and is unrelated. Thus far, the application [of the mantra] has been refuted on the grounds that there is no subsidiariness. Now, while conceding the application, he refutes the lack of subsidiariness: "But how is it that there is no subsidiariness, if there is application? [The answer is: Application is not the cause for subsidiariness.
Immediately thereafter,
he addresses the objection with the words "nanu" (is it not the case).

Since there is a distinction between being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) and being a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*), [the status of] being a subordinate member does not arise from the mere operation of an injunction (*vidhi*) in the form of its inclusion.
The objection regarding falsity is as follows: "It is not so.
Even in the case of identity, there is a resolution. Regarding "in the arising of another," it is just as in the case of a substance and a deity.
[It is] such as that. Regarding "the effect":
for example, the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, as well as the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for the sacrificer. How then [is it] with respect to the singularity of the animal and so forth?
It is thought that being a constituent part (aṅgatā) exists even from mere material cause (upādāna); yet even that is not produced by application (prayukti).
Herein lies the intention: first, the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha) is applied by means of the case-ending (vibhakti).

And that [number] must be employed when it has been assigned; moreover, the employment of something unqualified is not possible. Therefore, when there is a requirement for a qualifier (*avacchedaka*), precisely that which has already been grasped as a qualifier—such as singularity and so forth—is taken as its qualifier.

Consequently, that number and so forth which previously existed merely as the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) while it was unassigned, becomes assigned through that very act of employment.
1. *ācāryavidhyadhyayana* (ga);
2. *-aṅgasambandhasyā-* (ga);
3. Omits "ca".
ga.
4. Having apprehended the specific qualification. ga.

[The quality] residing in the animal and so forth is established. Its application (viniyoga), however, occurs precisely by virtue of its location therein, just as the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth are subsidiary parts of the sacrifice because they reside in the *juhū* ladle and other implements which are themselves applied to the sacrifice.

In that case, the fact that the *juhū* and other implements reside in [the sacrifice] is due to their inseparable connection with the sacrifice, established by the direct statement of the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita-śruti*); here, however, the distinction is that it is established through the act of material procurement (*upādāna*).
It is precisely that which has been enjoined by the injunctions (viniyukta) that is expressed by the case-endings (vibhakti) as having oneness and so forth;

the meaning is "of that thing" which is enjoined by direct statement (śruti) and the rest. For this very reason, there is syntactic unity (ekavākyatva) between the injunction of number and the injunction of the case-ending.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth":

since oneness and other [numbers] belong only to the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) by virtue of the operation of the material cause (*upādāna*), the following meaning is established: when oneness and so forth reside in a grammatical factor such as the instrument (*karaṇa*), the singular and other case-endings, such as the third case, are employed.
"They come to be. But how is it that [the object] is indeed unassigned and unrelated?
To resolve the first objection, it is reminded:
"The assignment itself is not the cause for the implication; what then? It is the effect."

The point here is this: in the injunction for the act of initiation (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), the act of leading near (*upanayana*) is presented as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by virtue of the scriptural mention of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), even though it is situated at a distance [from the main action]. And that [act], by its very nature, resides in the one being led near (*upaneyaniṣṭha*) and renders assistance through the proximity of the one being led near. In that context, if the boy (*māṇavaka*) who is being brought near were to be of no consequence—

At that time, the act of approaching [the teacher] (āsādana) is useless; and when approaching is useless, the initiation (upanayana) is also useless. Therefore, since there is a requirement for an object to be approached, the study (adhyayana) which is heard in the context of initiation is understood to have the initiated person as its agent and [initiation] as its object. Thus, the injunction for the production of the status of a teacher (ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi), by implying the initiation which is its own constituent part, implies the study.

Furthermore, the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), once established through the performance of study as implied by that [injunction], does not require any other qualification (*adhikāra*) for its own fulfillment.
As for what was said— that "that which is not enjoined cannot be an auxiliary (*aṅga*)"—
when something is an auxiliary, it is [established] by means of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth, through the [force of the] injunction...
[The status of being an auxiliary] to that very [principal action], with respect to its effect, is based on the operation of the *niyoga* (the mandate),
rather than on the direct verbal expression (*padaśruti*) of the word, nor on the sequence of actions (*karmaprakrama*).

It demonstrates that being a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) is not established solely by the act of injunction (*niyoga*) independently of application (*viniyoga*). Furthermore, the function of an injunction, characterized as "comprehension" (*grāhaka*), is established through the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*). Nor is there, through the study [of the Veda], an expression of related meaning with the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*).

There is the expression [of meaning], because the accomplishment of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related) occurs through the very injunction for study by virtue of the hearing of its own words. For there is the phrase "of that which is desired" (*kāmyasya*), which means "of that which is to be desired. Therefore, both are established: the state of being prompted (*prayojyatva*) and the state of not being a subordinate member (*anaṅgatva*).
Thus he says: "Because it is to be employed and because it is not a constituent part.
[The opponent asks: "Does being to be employed imply that they have a single effect?"

The meaning is that, because it occurs first, the injunction for the appointment of the teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*) alone is the motivator. Or rather, because it is not an auxiliary part (*anaṅga*), its purpose is distinct. Even though it occurs later, it is not proper to abandon the purpose inherent in that agent.

The meaning is that if [the mantra] were subsidiary to the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*), it would be impossible to state a purpose residing in another person, because of the contradiction between being enjoined and being subsequently enjoined. Nor by this [phrase].
If the two words had been recited after stating the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [then the objection would not arise].

In that case, there would be no suspicion regarding its being a non-worldly (alaukika) matter; it should be understood as a worldly matter solely for the purpose of refuting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), since otherwise it would have no connection with that *pūrvapakṣa*. However, considering that even when the *pūrvapakṣa* has not been explicitly stated, there is still a suspicion that it might be a non-worldly matter, the Commentator [Śabara] has stated this in order to refute such a hidden *pūrvapakṣa*, by the force of logical reasoning.
1. -ṅgavihitapuruṣā- ga. 2. antaḥsthita- ga. 3. manyamāno. ga-
He says:
"Furthermore, it is not only for him. "In this way, the Vedic sentences themselves..."

Thus he explains the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Its meaning is as follows: if one accepts the worldly sense [of words], then only Vedic sentences are to be explained; otherwise, if they possessed a non-worldly (transcendental) meaning, even Vedic sentences would not be worth explaining, as they would be merely technical or non-worldly (*pāribhāṣikālaukika*).
Furthermore, one would have to provide explanations for the words of its own sūtras, which would entail excessive effort; yet such a consequence does not arise.
Therefore, we understand that these are indeed words with worldly meanings, and thus it reveals the suspicion that they do not possess non-worldly (transcendental) meanings.

In that regard, this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) had not been previously described in the commentary beginning with "In the world" (loka); he shows this [now] in order to clarify it. For the context and other factors are to be sought for the sake of establishing what is heard [in scripture]; why?
Because if that which is heard were to be otherwise than its true meaning, the mere fact of being heard would not be the reason [for its authority].
For in whatever subject matter there is a word that has been heard,
its sentences must be explained;
yet [the opposite] is not applicable.
3. Therefore, having considered this, it was stated by Laugākṣi; this is not shown in the Bhāṣya. [p. 007] ga. 4. [This is not shown in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the state of having a specific meaning (*tātparya*), in that case, the mere fact of being heard (*śrutatva*) is not the sole cause for the comprehension of the meaning. What then? Context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth are also [causes].
And all of that—context and so forth—is present here. Now, as for the phrase "not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣita*): first of all—

The logical principle regarding the intended twofold meaning has already been stated. If, however, because of the absence of technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) and the like in the [grammatical] treatise, and because of the investigation into the meaning of the Veda, one were to maintain that—by resorting to worldly meanings—one must perform the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) following the study of the Veda, and that this is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then there would be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This, however, is not for the sake of an unseen result.

For if it were said that [the Veda] has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), then, because it would terminate in mere knowledge and desire, there would be no manifold investigation (*vicāra*) of Vedic sentences; yet in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), such a term indicates that it culminates in investigation. Now, one might object: "But [if it were so], it would not be intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*)."
1. Because the reasoning has not been stated; 2. because of the lack of intention to express it—thus [it is] in Ga.
3. Regarding the expression of the reasoning: (a) [p. 008] the latent tendency certainly exists; or (b) it exists when one intends to speak of it.

The doubt regarding the pointlessness of the sūtra: the meaning is that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not something to be taught, because it is already established, just like the study of the Veda. Furthermore, "this being so" refers to when the study of the Veda [is already established].

Since its own intended meaning is thus [established], even the immediate succession following the study of the Veda need not be enjoined. It was stated "api ca" (furthermore) with the view that this is an argument made while conceding the injunction of two prior matters. For this very reason, there is no suspicion of the [sūtra] having an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*), because that would entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). If so, for what purpose is the sūtra?

Regarding the non-enjoining of both: [this refers to] the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*). The meaning is that this is intended to refute the lack of intentionality (*avivakṣā*) regarding the matter raised in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). "If it is thus..."
"In that case, even the study of the Veda might occur prior to the inquiry into Dharma";

[the author] completes the Bhāṣya by inserting the word "immediately" (anantaram), stating that there is no immediate succession, as in the rule: "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath."

This is what is meant: the authors of the Smṛtis, by stating "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna)," thus prescribe through the injunction for study itself that one should depart from the teacher’s house immediately after the study of the Veda, which is taught as culminating in the recitation [of the text].

1. Regarding the term “-deśyam”: Ga. 2. By the phrase “having studied the Veda,” this is what is meant: the word “having studied this” refers to that which the authors of the Smṛtis [Ga. p. 009] have taught.

[Objection: But one should not construe the Bhāṣya in this way—namely, that "having studied the Veda, one should bathe" means "they conclude [the study] in this manner"—because the word *samāmnāya* does not occur in the Smṛtis. Nor is this statement of the Smṛti unreasonable.

Because the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*) has as its object that which is already enjoined [elsewhere], and because the comprehension of meaning is preceded by that [recitation];
why then do the injunctions for ritual action not themselves require the study of the Veda for their own accomplishment, by way of providing assistance through the comprehension of meaning?
Anticipating the objection that [the injunction] "one should apply oneself" [is superfluous], he says: "because its object has already been assigned.

Initiation (*upanayana*) has been assigned as the object within the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpana*), due to the scriptural indication of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); and the injunction for study (*adhyayana*) has that [initiation] as its scope; for [the injunction for study] has as its object the act of studying performed by one who has been initiated.

It has been stated that because the eyes enter into the object [of instruction], the "bringing near" (*upanayana*) is the subject matter of the injunction for study. This being the case, the impulsion (*prayukti*) of the injunction for becoming a teacher occurs by way of its subsidiary parts (*aṅga*), whereas the impulsion of ritual injunctions occurs merely through their providing assistance.
We shall explain in the section on *āmikṣā* that whatever possesses the status of an impeller by way of its subsidiary parts is indeed the impeller.
Furthermore, since the comprehension of meaning occurs at a time subsequent to the study, the injunctions regarding ritual acts cannot be motivated by means of that comprehension.

For this very reason, even though the comprehension of meaning is a visible result, it is not accepted as a qualification for the person entitled to perform the rite—just as in the case of the rules governing the acquisition of wealth—because the comprehension of meaning is preceded by the study, and thus no desire for it can arise prior to the study; and precisely because it occurs only at a later time...

Nor is the comprehension of meaning accepted as a further purpose [of the injunction]. By whom was it said? [It was not said] because of the absence of the designation "Samāmnāya" (the Vedic corpus) for the injunction of private study (*svādhyāyavidhi*). Nor [does it refer to] the well-known injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*).
3. —The procedure for the appointment of a teacher—;
4. —Because it is untenable otherwise—.
"This is the purpose" refers to the accomplishment of becoming a teacher. What then is the purpose? For its visible purpose is the comprehension of ritual action (*karma*).

Why, then, is it said that the mere accomplishment of the teacher's function (*ācāryakaraṇa*) is not the primary purpose? For the general rule (*utsarga*) is that the fruit of whatever injunction belongs to the person who performs it, and is thus useful only to that person. However, where that [direct utility] is not observed, there the fruit—even if residing in another person—is accepted. This is indeed observed.

And since the understanding of ritual action occurs subsequently here, that alone is the purpose, not the accomplishment of teaching directed toward another person. And it has been stated: "The study of one's own Veda is exhaustive, because no specific qualification for it is heard."
For if one were heard as being qualified for the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), then study would be solely for that purpose;

and the mass of syllables denoted by the term *svādhyāya* would be intended merely for the accomplishment of the act of study. Consequently, even if a meaning were perceived from a word whose primary intent lies elsewhere, it would not be intended to be conveyed. The Commentator states this very point: "because no qualification [for such an injunction] is heard."
“And it is not there. And even regarding that which they seem to recite, [it applies] “to substances, preparatory rites, and ritual acts. 1. This is stated in the *Bhava*. (Ga.)
2. And its purpose is this:
3. even though it occurs later;
4. one is entitled to both the ritual act and the study.
5. Because the word [of the Veda] is dependent on another [source], and because there is no etymological derivation, it has no meaning.
[Page 012] Now, is study a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*)? It is said: because it is enjoined as something not previously commenced, it is to be accomplished by the injunction itself.

This [study] is indeed a primary action (*pradhānakarma*). Furthermore, there is no application (*viniyoga*) of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) anywhere else, by means of which there could be a recognition of another injunction (*vidhyantara*), as is the case with the *parṇamayī* [ladle] and similar instances. Consequently, it must be accomplished solely through another injunction. Moreover, just like the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and others, the visible refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the syllables is observed; and on that basis, it is not tenable that the comprehension of meaning—which would be a human goal—is the purpose. If, however, this...

It is not seen; rather, the injunction alone would be that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Nor can a fruit be inferred through connection with an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because the injunction possesses its own purpose simply through the fulfillment of the injunction’s meaning. Furthermore, even though there is no possibility of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the direct knowledge arising from the Veda—since it has no other means [of attainment]—it is not purposeless. As it has been said: "Since the purpose of the mandate (*niyoga*) is fulfilled, what other purpose could there be for any injunction?"
[The word] "nāma" [is used].

And because it accepts that its purpose is the comprehension of objects useful to the person (puruṣa), and because it thus serves the human goal (puruṣārtha), the characteristic of sovereignty is established even within the context of the qualification (adhikāra). But [one might object]: "Is it not the case that this is not so here?"

For if there were a contradiction with Smṛti, then a Sūtra would have been composed for the purpose of resolving it; but this is not the case. Furthermore, the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*) of Vedic study would be undermined by [interpreting] immediate succession (*ānantarya*). That is to say, the visible purpose of study would be contradicted if the suffix *-ktvā* were accepted as having the meaning of immediate succession; therefore—

The sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not the meaning of the suffix *ktvā*. This is what is meant: although [immediate succession] is expressed by the suffix *ktvā*, it is not [the primary meaning], just as in the case of the injunction regarding the preparation of the sacrificial vessel (*parṇatā-vidhi*), or as in the case of the Vedic meaning.

3. Because the purpose of the injunction is accomplished, a specific sense of "prior time" is expressed; nevertheless, due to the contradiction with the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), only the mere fact of prior time is accepted as the meaning.

Thus it may be so. For if the Smṛti rule "having studied the Veda, one should bathe" were merely an injunction for bathing characterized by the time following the study of the Veda, then one would have to postulate another source (mūla) for that Smṛti as well.

It might be so; however, when [the injunction] serves the purpose of terminating the restrictive rules—such as the prohibition against bathing—that follow immediately after Vedic study, then, because it is rooted in the logic of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), there can be no inference of another unseen basis (*adṛṣṭa*), since the postulation of an unseen purpose is impossible in that case. When the visible [purpose] is established as being rooted in the logic of the *pūrvapakṣa*, the Smṛti must indeed have that as its root; and if it has that as its root, there is a contradiction, for in the *pūrvapakṣa* it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The purpose of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) ends precisely with the completion of the Veda; once that is accomplished, all the restrictive observances (*niyama*), such as the prohibition against bathing, which were prompted by it, cease.

Therefore, the departure from the teacher’s house occurs immediately after the study of the Veda. For this reason also, it is established that the Sūtra exists to show that the Smṛti is rooted in reasoning (*nyāyamūla*). It is not for the purpose of saying, "One should not return from the teacher’s house," nor to avoid the charge of having an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*).

Regarding the commentary [on the phrase] "as in the case of wealth," it was previously stated that because its source has been observed, one should not postulate another source. Now, he shows that even for the sake of avoiding the view that the rule for bathing has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), another source must not be postulated. He explains that: "another source..."

"Regarding *ratve ca* and *evaṃ ceti*: if this sūtra is intended for the purpose of subverting [the rule of] memory (*smṛtibādha*), then it does not serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), provided that the logical principle (*nyāya*) applies. (Ga.)
2. Withdrawal from family life (kulānnivṛtti).
014] However, this is for the purpose of indicating an improper method; nor is it for the sake of a visible purpose.

Nor is it for the purpose of establishing a principle accepted by all, because the author of the *Smṛti* is himself in disagreement [with that view]. We do not say that the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) should not be undertaken immediately after any other action whatsoever.

Thus he refutes the view that [the study of the Veda] has an invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārthatā). By the words "But having studied the Veda," he rejects the claim that the author of the Smṛti’s purpose is one agreed upon by all disputants, on the grounds of their disagreement.

Regarding the Bhāṣya statement, "The word 'ataḥ' indicates what has preceded by way of a reason," for which preceding factor does it indicate the status of being a reason? It is for the study of the Veda.

The meaning is that the study of the Vedas alone is the cause for the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), which occurs immediately after such study; for it is observed that the comprehension of the meaning follows immediately upon study.
In this regard, it is as follows:

Regarding the description of the meaning of the Sūtra: "Therefore, for the reason that one has studied the Veda, there is the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*); it must be undertaken immediately after study (*adhyayanānantaram eva*). [The author] demonstrates this point, which is accepted by all disputants, as being the cause.

Because the reason is established, a delay is untenable. How is study the cause of immediate succession? Because the comprehension of the meaning occurs immediately after study, therefore study is the cause; thus, by the word "atha" (then), the immediate succession of the cause is expressed.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of understanding the state of being a cause":

since the understanding of the state of being a cause cannot be established without that which possesses the cause, it is appropriate to explain the word *artha* as "that which possesses the cause. For indeed, one who has not studied the Veda would be unable to investigate the Vedic sentences for the sake of [understanding] Dharma.

The Commentator states that the study of the Veda is the cause [of the inquiry], because without the study of the Veda, one lacks the capacity to investigate its meaning. By stating this, the Commentator refutes the view that one is entitled to the study of the Veda out of a desire for the comprehension of its meaning—since such comprehension cannot occur without Vedic study and thus the desire itself would be impossible. He says this with the following [verse]: "By this..."
"Empty of causal agency" means that this is the concluding statement;
the sense is that it is precisely the summary statement.
1. Because of what follows immediately—ga.

Furthermore, this is the case even in everyday usage.

Regarding the process of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*): although words indeed denote only that which is connected to an action (*kārya*), nevertheless, the acquisition of meaning does not occur through the denotation of what is connected to an action; rather, it occurs precisely through the denotation of what is connected to another object (*arthāntara*). For whoever desires the denotation of what is connected to a specific [action], he necessarily desires the denotation of what is connected to another object. And since the application and comprehension of language are established by that much alone, [the theory of *kāryānvita* is unnecessary].

It is not possible to assume that [the Vedic words] denote things endowed with specificities; for in common worldly usage, most sentences are seen to have already established meanings, such as "Are you well? or "I am well," and so forth. Furthermore, even that which is called an "action to be accomplished" (kārya) is defined as that which has its means required; therefore, it is understood from those [Vedic texts] intent upon the action that the status of actions as having their means required is indeed already established.

Even in the case of a statement in the present tense, such as "he cooks with wood" (*kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati*), the linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) that occurs is such that it conforms to a connection with another element associated with an action (*kārya*); thus, it pertains exclusively to that which is connected to an action. One observes sentences that induce activity or cessation even without a connection to a [specific] purpose, such as: "This ground is possessed of treasure," or "This path is beset by robbers.

For when the presence of treasure is made known by a sentence, one who desires to acquire it engages there; and when the presence of robbers is made known, one who wishes to avoid them desists. To this we reply: first, in cases where—

Engagement and withdrawal do exist, and in that regard, there is an understanding of an effect which serves as their cause; for these two do not occur without it. Furthermore, because it follows immediately after the word, an observer standing by infers that this [understanding] was produced by the word itself. Nor does the fact that a word expressing an effect is not explicitly heard mean that the word is not the cause, since [the meaning] may also be obtained through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and other such means.

Because there is no contradiction with its denotative capacity, and because the understanding of specific elements to be supplied is established through a particular fitness (*yogyatā*). Nor can it be maintained that the word is indifferent toward the cognition of the action (*kārya*) on the grounds that such cognition can be achieved by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since activity is observed immediately upon hearing the word; thus, it is understood that the word itself is the cause therein due to its immediate proximity. [The word is] the means of knowledge—

Since that meaning can be obtained even without it, the word may well be a restatement (*anuvāda*); yet it is not for no reason. Furthermore, being a restatement is not a defect in the words of human beings. And because, whether directly through explicit hearing (*śruti*), through ellipsis (*vākya-śeṣa*), or through syntactic supply (*adhyāhāra*), there is an invariable concomitance with a purposeful action (*kārya*) in all worldly sentences, the denotation of meanings connected to that [action] occurs—excluding [the case of] the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth.

It is established that [words] such as the optative (*liṅ*) and others denote only the task (*kārya*). Therefore, all words indeed express an object as connected with a task. [It is] produced by a causal complex of sense faculties and so forth that is free from defects; however, [in this case, it is] arisen from a circle of cognitive instruments whose power has been impaired by defects.

Since its fruit is the killing of an enemy desired by the person, the injunction (*niyoga*) regarding the hawk-sacrifice (*śyena*) would not be an evil. The injunction (niyoga) is understood as being the effect; it does not, however, impel one toward the action itself. We shall explain this in the section on the *apūrva*. The cause (*kāraṇa*); that which serves as the material cause (*upādāna-hetu*) becomes the cause in its specific context (*adhikāra*). Having accepted and intended the *nimitta* (the causal occasion) as the performance of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), it was stated: "For that is indeed violence, and that is prohibited.

A prohibition would be subservient to the sacrifice only if it pertained to the undertaking [of the act], because the activity to be prohibited is dependent upon the activity toward the sacrifice, and thus has a connection with the sacrifice.

It does not fall within the scope of [the prohibition], because its engagement therein is independent. Now, one might ask: why then is the violence involved in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice and the like not also prohibited? And if that were so, then just as the *śyena* and other such rites lack the nature of *dharma* because they are connected with results that are prohibited and harmful (*anartha*), so too would the *jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices lack it because they are connected with prohibited subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). To this, he replies: "One must not harm living beings."

Furthermore, this prohibition pertains to the qualified person (*adhikārin*) and concerns independent activity, not the activity pertaining to the constituent parts (*upādāna*). For activity regarding the constituent parts is derivative (*aupādānikī*), since there is no independent activity toward them beforehand; whereas activity toward the result is independent, because one engages with the primary rite out of a desire for the result, and engages with the constituent parts by way of their being auxiliaries to that primary rite. Thus, activity toward the constituent parts occurs through the activity toward the primary rite; therefore, the constituent parts exist for the sake of the primary rite.

[This is] an engagement. Therefore, because this [prohibition] is connected with the sacrifice (*kratu*), the prohibition is also for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); and yet, this is also for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).

To this, the answer is: it is not possible for a single injunction to have the character of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) when it serves the purpose of the person, while simultaneously lacking the character of being a motivator when it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, because of the contradiction. Why is it not so? The answer to this is as follows: between being the motivator (*prayojaka*) and not being the motivator (*aprayojaka*), being the motivator is what is directly expressed by the verbal suffix (*śrauta*), because it is understood without dependence on anything else; for the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. first convey the task (*kārya*), and that [task] is what impels one to performance.

On the other hand, not being the motivator is to be understood through a consideration of another sentence (*vākya*). When the injunction of qualification (*adhikāravidhi*) is proximate, [the relationship is determined by] the sentence—

The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth occurring within [the *śyena* injunction] are merely reiterative of that [injunction]. Nor is there any comprehension from another sentence such as "one should not harm living beings," because it is an unattached injunction (*anāramyavidhi*). Therefore, this prohibition pertains only to the qualification (*adhikāra*), not to the material cause (*upādāna*). And the injunction regarding the *śyena* sacrifice and the like is indeed characterized by a Vedic impulsion (*codanālakṣaṇa*), because it is its object and because it is an object of valid cognition.

Regarding the injunction for the Śyena sacrifice: since the Śyena sacrifice has as its result the prohibited act of malevolent magic (abhicāra), it is established that it is an evil (anartha). Thus, the counter-example is proven. Therefore, the introductory commentary—that "both are indicated here by the injunctive word" (codanā)—is logically consistent.

Now, the Bhāṣya beginning with "But this [sūtra] is incapable" (nanvaśaktam) objects to the sūtra on the grounds of the fault of syntactical split (vākyabheda); and that is untenable, because for human words, since their purpose is to convey meanings already known through other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), faults such as syntactical split do not even arise by virtue of those other means of cognition. This [following passage] justifies that very Bhāṣya: "But this sūtra is incapable."
"This is for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between worldly (*laukika*) and Vedic (*vaidika*) sentences.

Its meaning is as follows: that which [is the case] regarding these two, worldly and Vedic sentences—due to their dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) and their independence [from such], [respectively] by virtue of other means of knowledge...

And the capacity to convey meaning independently—that very point is stated by the Bhāṣya following the objection. Alternatively, the Bhāṣya phrase "of that which exists and is characterized by injunction" expresses syntactic unity [with the preceding]; however, that too is untenable, because even under this view, there would result a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) consisting of a qualified reference (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*). On this point, the author of the Ṭīkā offers a rebuttal: "Now..."

The phrase "of an existing object" (*vārthasya sataḥ*) is intended to demonstrate that even according to the literal wording of the sentence, a single meaning is possible. The intention here is as follows: there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) characterized by the repetition of an injunction (*vidhi*), but rather there is simply a difference in the mode of connection (*anvaya*).

Because it is the cause of establishment for an object that has become the domain of cognition; for the employment of sentences by persons is preceded by an object already cognized. This is indeed true; nevertheless, independence, never before observed in the world, cannot be postulated.

It is said: First of all, words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) convey an object that is a *kārya* (a task to be accomplished), which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, other words as well—because the *kārya* has no other purpose—denote their own meanings as being solely directed toward that [kārya]. And those meanings associated with it are likewise not objects of other means of valid cognition. Therefore, by considering the very nature of these objects, there is first of all no dependence [on other means of knowledge].

But surely, since linguistic usage in the world has as its object things already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth with respect to an action that is not within the scope of any other [means of knowledge]? This is indeed true in the case of human speech; however, in the Veda, it is determined that the optative suffix and the like denote an action to be accomplished (*kārya*). And because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), one cannot ask: "How does it express an object that is not within the scope of any other [means of knowledge]?"

But surely, if [the word] has no other range of application, how can there be a grasping of its relationship [with the meaning]? And if the relationship is not grasped, how can it possess denotative power? To this it is replied: after hearing a sentence containing an optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, an observer standing nearby infers—by means of the activity [of the listener]—that the elder who was prompted has attained a comprehension that arises upon the existence of that [sentence]. He [concludes]: "By this word, from this [sentence], a meaning has been understood by him as the cause of his activity."
He infers: "It is well-known. Furthermore, the state of being a cause for engagement is observed to result from the understanding of something as an effect (*kārya*);

for everyone indeed does not engage as long as they do not understand, "This is my task (*kārya*). [Objection: But engagement arises from the understanding that a means is desired (*apekṣitopāya*). [Reply: Not so; even if a means is desired, one does not engage as long as it is not determined to be a task (*kārya*).

Is it not the case that being an effect (*kāryatā*) is simply being a means sought after (*apekṣitopāyatā*)? No; for being an effect is being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*), whereas being a means sought after is being an instrument (*sādhanatā*).

Indeed, being an instrument is one thing, and being an end to be accomplished (*sādhyatā*) is another; however, in common worldly experience, an action is understood as an effect by virtue of its being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥsādhanatā*).
And it is in that form [as a means to the good] that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others denote the effect. This is so only in the case of human speech.

In a sentence, there is the capacity to convey an action that requires further expectation; moreover, it is precisely the action—which serves as the means to the highest good—that is understood through other means of knowledge as being the "thing to be done" (*kāryatā*).

Therefore, in common worldly usage, it is only action that is denoted by the word as the "thing to be done"; however, in the Veda, [it is so] for those such as "one who desires heaven. This is thus. (Ga.)

By asserting that *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding matters to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*), it is the means of valid knowledge itself that is proposed as the subject of investigation. Otherwise, since [the validity of injunctions] is already established by worldly consensus, what would be the purpose of proposing a means of valid knowledge? Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras intended the proposal of a means of valid knowledge for a specific purpose: namely, that Dharma is something to be accomplished (*kārya*). This is because he specifies "defined by injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*) once it is established that Dharma is something to be accomplished, and because he states the reason for its validity. What must now be stated is: [The remainder of the passage follows... ...that the means of valid knowledge is not investigated here because it is well-known; rather, it is investigated insofar as it relates to the object to be accomplished. For one who maintains that Dharma is something to be accomplished, the means of valid knowledge is indeed investigated, since the means of valid knowledge is the instrument for accomplishing that which is to be accomplished. The meaning is that another distinct point regarding the three sūtras must be stated again. This is what is being said: for what purpose is another distinct point of the three sūtras stated? For why is this not stated independently, rather than as something obtained through the implication of the meaning of the previously mentioned three sūtras? [The answer is: another distinct point, which serves as the proof for the meaning of the previously mentioned three sūtras, has been stated by this very [sūtra].

Others do not maintain that those things such as universals (*jāti*), which are distinct entities from the individual (*vyakti*), are the objective support (*ālambana*) of conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*); rather, [they maintain] that which is apprehended by the first-arising sensory cognition, which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

The individual (vyakti) is perceived, and that very same [individual] is also apprehended by conceptual cognition (savikalpaka-pratyaya). However, that which apprehends it merely as being associated with universals (jāti) and so forth is nothing but a conceptual construction (vikalpamātra); it does not arise as a delimiting factor for a distinct real entity—this is what has been stated by others.
And by speaking thus, it is understood that falsity (mithyātva) is admitted. Furthermore, that very [conceptual construction] is said to be conventional reality (saṃvṛti).

"And even in this established conclusion" means that even in the established conclusion of the opponents, this suspicion of falsity does not arise; because it is precisely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), as cognized by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*), that is the object of conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka*).

It is accepted that the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists in the ultimate sense; and knowledge whose object is a real thing is true, not false, just like non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*). However, this is the distinction: that which arises together with non-conceptual knowledge is produced by the synthesis, the connection, or the joining of the previously experienced particular characteristic with another object.

Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*); however, non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) does not arise through the recollection of what was previously experienced. In this other established doctrine (*parasiddhānta*), there is the status of being an object of non-conceptual valid cognition (*pramiti*); furthermore, the status of having the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object is the same for the synthetic cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*) as well. And since the objects are the same, it cannot be maintained that conceptual cognition is false while non-conceptual cognition is true.

It is logical that there is an absence of duality; for this duality does not exist for worldly people. Therefore, since there is no suspicion of falsity, the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) does not exist, and thus its refutation is useless.

"But is it not by you yourself?"—
this is the support of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), by means of this distinction, namely, the recollection of genus and so forth.

Regarding the statement "it is born," this has been said by others: that specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the form of an external object which is perceived by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) cannot be the object determined (*paricchedya*) by a conceptual cognition (*vikalpapratyaya*); however, it does serve as its objective support (*ālambana*). This is the intended meaning: for an external entity cannot be joined with universals (*jāti*) and so forth, because it is not connected with conceptual constructions.

[It arises] from contact; however, even though they do not grasp that [object], conceptual constructions appear as if they possess the conceit of grasping it, and in accordance with that conceit, they are said to have that as their objective support (*ālambana*). In ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), however, they are indeed without any objective support. Thus, its falsity has already been stated by others. Therefore, they do not accept that this synthesizing cognition (*anusandhāna-pratyaya*) possesses the capacity for determination (*paricchedakatva*), just like memory.

They say it is "knowledge of the conceptualized" (*kalpajñāna*). Just as the knowledge of memory does not grasp an external object because it appears indistinctly, whereas the external object possesses a distinct form; and yet, there is no difference in the clarity or lack of clarity of the appearance based on a difference in the causal complex of the grasper (*grāhakasāmagrī*), because there is no difference in the object to be known (*vedya*); therefore, even in the absence of an external appearance, [the cognition] arises by way of determining that [external object].
Recollection and cognition appear as if they have that [object] as their objective support; the same is true for conceptual cognition as well. As it was stated by Kīrti himself:

"It is indeed the investigators of the treatises who analyze in this way, not the practitioners. But the latter, having conflated the perceived object and the conceptualized object, proceed while regarding [the object] as being truly external."

Thus, in this established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)— the final doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas— it is accepted that even conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, for others who maintain that [subsequent] reflective awareness consists of mere conceptualization, these two factors— the presence of a defect in the cause and the nature of the object— are not subverting causes for ordinary people.

It is established for everyone that [the object] exists directly. Therefore, since the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is possible, the author of the Bhāṣya—who wishes to maintain the validity of this conceptual cognition—has made this restriction: “That very [cognition] is an incorrect cognition.”
1. [p. 054] For those who take pride in its qualities (tadguṇābhimānin), how then do they consider conceptual construction (kalpanā) to be a synthetic cognition (anusandhānapratyaya)?

The intention here is as follows: since universals (*jāti*) and so forth do indeed exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) apprehended as qualified by them is itself ultimately real; therefore, the cognition of a real object is not a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). However, the opponent says: because there is no difference between the universal and that which possesses the universal (*jātimatorabhedāt*)— [...the opponent continues... ...it is not a conceptual construction. But the proponent replies: even if there were no difference between the universal and the possessor of the universal, the cognition of the particular characteristic as qualified by the universal would still be a conceptual construction, because it involves the superimposition of the form of the universal upon the particular characteristic. Furthermore, since the universal is eternal and the particular characteristic is momentary, their identity is impossible; thus, the cognition of the particular characteristic as qualified by the universal is necessarily a conceptual construction. Therefore, the claim that it is a perception is untenable. Thus ends the section on the definition of perception. Now begins the examination of inference (*anumāna*). Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Of these, inference for oneself is defined as "the cognition of an object through a sign (*liṅga*) that is known, [which is] connected [to the object], and has the three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Here, "known" means perceived or inferred. "Connected" means related through concomitance (*anvaya*) or exclusion (*vyatireka*). "Three characteristics" refers to the three forms of the sign. What are these three? They are: (1) presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) presence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and (3) absence in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*). Among these, "presence in the subject" means that the sign resides in the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmin*). "Presence in similar instances" means that it exists in all or some of those things that possess the property to be proven. "Absence in dissimilar instances" means that it does not exist in any of those things that lack the property to be proven. For example, when one infers fire from smoke, the sign is smoke; its presence in the subject is its being perceived on the mountain; its presence in similar instances is its being perceived in a kitchen or elsewhere where fire is known to exist; and its absence in dissimilar instances is its non-perception in a lake or elsewhere where fire is absent. When such a sign, possessing these three characteristics, is perceived, the resulting cognition of the object is inference for oneself. As for inference for others, it consists of the verbal expression of the three characteristics of the sign for the sake of another person. This is called inference for others because it is the cause of inference for another. It is expressed in the form of a syllogism (*prayoga*). A syllogism is the statement of the three characteristics of the sign. It is of five members: (1) the thesis (*pratijñā*), (2) the reason (*hetu*), (3) the example (*udāharaṇa*), (4) the application (*upanaya*), and (5) the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the thesis is the statement of the property to be proven together with its locus, e.g., "This mountain has fire. The reason is the statement of the sign, e.g., "Because it has smoke. The example is the statement of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), e.g., "Whatever has smoke has fire, like a kitchen. The application is the statement that the sign exists in the subject, e.g., "And this mountain has smoke. The conclusion is the restatement of the thesis, e.g., "Therefore, this mountain has fire. By means of this five-membered syllogism, the three characteristics of the sign are communicated to another, and thus it is called inference for others. Here ends the section on inference. Now begins the examination of analogy (*upamāna*). Analogy is the cognition arising from similarity to a known object. For instance, when a person who has previously seen a cow goes to a forest and sees a gavaya, he remembers the cow and perceives the similarity between the two; the resulting cognition, "This animal is similar to a cow," is analogy. Here ends the section on analogy. Now begins the examination of verbal testimony (*śabda*). Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*). An "authoritative person" (*āpta*) is one who knows the truth and intends to speak of it as it is. The instruction given by such a person is verbal testimony. For example, "There are four noble truths. This is considered a valid means of knowledge because it is based on perception and inference. Here ends the section on verbal testimony. Now begins the examination of presumption (*arthāpatti*). Presumption is the postulation of something else when a fact otherwise established cannot be explained. For example, when Devadatta, who is alive, is not seen in his house, one presumes, "He must be outside," because his being alive is otherwise unaccountable. Here ends the section on presumption. Now begins the examination of non-apprehension (*abhāva*). Non-apprehension is the cognition of the absence of an object due to the non-perception of what is perceptible. For example, when one looks for a jar on the ground and does not perceive it despite the conditions for perception being present, one concludes, "The jar is not here. Here ends the section on non-apprehension. Now begins the examination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The means of knowledge are fourfold: perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony. These alone are the means of knowledge, because they encompass all objects of knowledge. Here ends the examination of the means of knowledge. Now begins the examination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). The objects of knowledge are twofold: the self (*ātman*) and the non-self (*anātman*). The self is characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*). It is eternal, omnipresent, and the substratum of pleasure, pain, and so forth. The non-self is everything other than the self, consisting of the body, the senses, the objects, and the mind (*manas*). Here ends the examination of the object of knowledge. Now begins the examination of error (*viparyaya*). Error is the cognition of something as what it is not. For example, the cognition of a shell as silver. Here ends the examination of error. Now begins the examination of doubt (*saṃśaya*). Doubt is the cognition of an object in multiple ways due to the perception of common properties and the non-perception of distinguishing features. For example, when standing at a distance, seeing the common property of height, and not perceiving whether it is a man or a post, one thinks, "Is this a man or a post? Here ends the examination of doubt. Now begins the examination of dream-cognition (*svapnajñāna*). Dream-cognition is a cognition occurring during sleep. It is considered a type of error because it lacks a real object. Here ends the examination of dream-cognition. Now begins the examination of the result of knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*). The result of knowledge is the cognition of the object as it truly is. Some maintain that the means of knowledge and the result are identical, while others hold that the means is the instrument and the result is the attainment of the object. Here ends the examination of the result of knowledge. Now begins the examination of the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). The fallacies of the reason are fivefold: (1) the unestablished (*asiddha*), (2) the contradictory (*viruddha*), (3) the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), (4) the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and (5) the refuted (*prakaraṇasama*). Here ends the examination of the fallacies of the reason. Now begins the examination of the futile rejoinders (*jāti*). A futile rejoinder is a refutation based on mere similarity or dissimilarity, which does not lead to the negation of the original position. Here ends the examination of the futile rejoinders. Now begins the examination of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). A point of defeat is the failure to understand the meaning of what is said, or the inability to respond when one ought to. Here ends the examination of the points of defeat. Thus ends the *Nyāyapraveśaka*. May this work contribute to the increase of merit and the welfare of all beings. May there be auspiciousness. Just as yellow is a separate substance from blue, so it is not the case that genus and so forth are [separate] from the particulars. Why?

The thumb [is perceived] from the fingers; yet the genus (*jāti*) is not apprehended as distinct from the particulars (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, it is not different.
But surely—in the cognition "this is a cow"—the genus appears as something distinct; to this he replies: "Precisely because..."

Since particulars are apprehended by means of the cognition of the universal, there is no grasping of them as distinct entities; for this very reason, this cognition called "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) is distinct from both valid cognition (pramāṇa) and error (viparyaya).

For this reason, O knower of the subtle, since it does not grasp one object by means of a self that is a different object, it does not fall into error; for this very reason...

The proponents of conceptual construction (vikalpavidaḥ) say: "This cognition called conceptual construction is distinct from valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it apprehends its object otherwise; and it is indeed different from error (viparyaya) as well. By this same reasoning, the postulation of a "quality" (guṇa) is also explained away, since it is not perceived separately [from the cognition itself].

The same reasoning that serves as the cause for rejecting distinct universals (*jāti*) also explains the conceptualization of qualities (*guṇa*). For just as a universal is a conceptual construction because it is not perceived as something separate [from the individual], so too a quality does not appear as distinct from the possessor of the quality; [rather, one perceives] "this is white."
Ordinary people do not perceive it in this way—[thinking], "This is a substance possessing whiteness"—because [the universal] is not perceived separately;

thus the reason must be explained in two ways. When the individual is perceived, at that time the universal is not perceived separately. Likewise, if the universal were distinct [from the individual], then even when the individual is not perceived, [the universal] would sometimes [be perceived].
It would have to be perceived; yet it is not perceived. Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) is not distinct [from the individual].

"No, for even in that case, there is the cognition of non-difference, namely, 'This is Viṣṇumitra.'"

Either difference or non-difference of an entity is possible. [He] concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Therefore, this fivefold conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it arises through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of non-existent universals (*jāti*) and so forth; nor is it a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because neither a subverting cause (*bādhaka-kāraṇa*) nor the cognition of defects (*doṣajñāna*) arises directly [in its case].
With the words "It is said" (*ucyate*), etc., he begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

In this regard, the underlying intention is as follows: these cognitions arise indeed manifesting universals (*jāti*) and so forth; yet a cognition does not make known a form that is non-existent, because it appears as something existing, like the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Sometimes [it is so] by way of having the form of cognition (*jñānākāratayā*). Thus he says: "Conceptual cognition occurs if cognition is to be apprehended through direct perception."
It may be so; however, he will later explain that knowledge is inferential (*ānumānika*).

Now, one might object: in the view that knowledge is not perceptual (*apratyakṣa*), it is untenable for the objective support (*ālambana*) to have one form while the arising of knowledge occurs in quite another way.

This is "being otherwise" (*anyathābhāva*); for mother-of-pearl appears as if it were silver.

And its meaning is as follows: regarding mother-of-pearl, the cognition "this is silver" is a single perceptual cognition produced by the presence or absence of the sense organ; and because there is no external form of silver, that [silver] exists only within the cognition itself.

The meaning of this is as follows: if this is a memory-cognition in the form "this is silver," then because memory is independent of the eyes, it would occur even for a blind person; yet this does not occur for the blind. If it were a cognition of apprehension (*grahaṇajñāna*), then, because it would depend upon the eye, its non-arising in a blind person would occur; rather, its arising would be logically possible only for one who possesses eyes. When a cognition arises regarding a particular object, it is by means of that very [object] and the sense organ—

When a person’s cognition arises from contact with that which is present, that is valid perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*), such as the cognition "this is [silver]"; however, when a cognition arises from contact with something else—such as mother-of-pearl—while having another object as its domain by apprehending silver, that is not perception. Is it not understood that "this [occurs] when there is contact with another [object], and this does not occur when there is contact with another"? For the mother-of-pearl is indeed what is in contact;
therefore, this cognition has the mother-of-pearl as its object, since one designates the mother-of-pearl itself as "silver," and [the cognition] manifests the form of that [silver]. (Ga.)

Whatever form appears in a cognition, that is said to be its objective support (*ālambana*). And a mother-of-pearl does not have the form of silver. Having apprehended another object— namely, the mother-of-pearl which resembles silver— as "this," and failing to perceive the specific qualities of the mother-of-pearl that would cause the realization of its difference from silver due to defects in the sense organs and so forth, one perceives only those common properties present in the mother-of-pearl despite their existence.

The cognition that has arisen becomes the cause of a recollective cognition regarding another similar object for one whose mental faculty has its power impaired by defects, due to the absence of reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) regarding what was experienced—lacking the cognition "I remember. Consequently, the distinction between the perceived and the recollected is not determined. And this consists of two cognitions: "this" [the present perception]...

"Silver" is a recollection, for otherwise the cognition of silver would be impossible. Indeed, it is not produced by the sense organ, because there is no contact with that [silver]; and a sense organ does not produce a cognition regarding what it is not in contact with, since such a cognition does not arise in a blind person. Therefore, this is indeed a recollection. Thus far, [the arguments] regarding mother-of-pearl and the like have been established.
Cognitions of silver and the like are of the nature of memory. But how is it so in the case of dreams and the like regarding non-self objects and so forth?

Since the self and such have never been experienced at any time, their recollection would be impossible; furthermore, in states such as deep sleep, intoxication, and fainting, there is no arousal of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of memory.

"How can there be memory in the absence of a cause for the arousal of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)?"—this is the objection raised in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), pointing out the specific difficulty that in cases such as dreams, memory cannot possibly exist because the causes for the arousal of latent impressions from previous cognitions of silver and so forth are absent. The answer [to this] is stated in the final position (*siddhānta*).

Consequently, while it may be granted that the intellect (*buddhi*) does not exist if it has only a single form, the object—which is perceptible—does not cease to exist. But what is the reason for denying the means of valid cognition specifically, when the denial of the result is common to both?

"But not so for the object of cognition (*prameya*); for both the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition are dependent upon the result, being grounded in the act of valid cognition (*pramiti*).
Do not say so; for while both are indeed dependent upon the result in their *origination*, they are not so in the act of valid cognition itself.

The production of the status of a causal factor (*kārakatva*) for the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), which function as the instrument and the object respectively, is based on the arising of a result. However, the cognition (*pramiti*) of the object of knowledge through perception is independent of a result; whereas, because the means of knowledge is inferential, cognition is dependent upon the result.

Not understanding this point, he asks: "In the arising of what? For when the fruit is indicative (*jñāpaka*), it is the object of cognition (*prameya*) itself that is to be known, not something to be produced (*utpādya*).
By means of the indicative fruit, the object of cognition is merely realized, not produced; for in the case of knowledge, that [object] is indeed—
1. Denial [of the means of knowledge].
Ga. 2. Omitted. Not a denial of the objects of knowledge. Ga.
3. Dependence on the result (phalāyattatvam). [Variants: ka, ga. 4. But there is also the opposite, as far as it is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). [Variant: ga.]

because cognition is inferable, it is dependent upon its result.

This is valid cognition (*pramiti*). Therefore, if one denies the result, one necessarily ends up denying the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself, not the object. Or rather, let the whole [the compound *yasya*] be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) for the two parts, namely the indicator (*liṅga*) and the indicated (*liṅgin*). In this case, the connection is as follows:

"the cognition of a person who has known the relationship. Yet even that is not possible, because no qualifier is seen for the meaning that is being understood. Thus say the venerable authors of the Vārttika:
“Furthermore, no qualification of an object currently being traversed is ever observed,

He summarizes the established point: "Therefore, we do not know whose [it is] that has the known relation. He replies: "It is said: this delusion is based on a lack of thorough knowledge of the relation. But what is it?"

What is the relationship? This is the relationship: inference is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] based on the perception of one part; based on the perception of which part? Based on the perception of that part whose relationship [to the other] is known.
But even in this relation, the status of one part as a subordinate element remains exactly as it was;
and consequently, how [could there be] "this king's man"? (ga.)
2. For there is no non-apprehension of either the person or the collection [of words]. Ga. 3. By which that person is one who has recognized the relationship. Ga.

Ga. 5. *Na ca* is omitted in Ga. 6. A "partial proponent" (*ekadeśin*) is also to be understood [as being included]. Ga.

8. Omitted. *sambandhaḥ*. Ga. [p. 092]:

To this it is replied: regarding a human statement, it has been stated more than once that the resulting split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is not a fault. As for the claim that there is no connection because [the word] is subordinate (*upasarjana*), he says in response: "It is subordinate. This is not a cause for the lack of connection; just as in the case of a subordinate element—

for if it were, the relation would not exist in the absence of that non-subordination. What, then, is the cause? To this he says: "that which is required and capable of fulfilling [the requirement]."
It becomes connected [to the subject].
And in that case, when it is stated "from the perception of one part," an expectancy arises: "Of which one part?"

Therefore, when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), a word whose relation is already known and which is capable of fulfilling that expectancy becomes a qualifier of a specific part [of the object]. He states another reason: "Because perception has the visible object as its primary focus."
Furthermore, in this case, there is no status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjanatva*), because the single part is primary with respect to the perception;
nor does its primacy fail to be established, since the cognition of the other object arises from that [perception of the single part].
It is from the single part alone that the perception—
A cognition of a meaning distinct from the *saṃskṛta* [word] arises. Therefore, the predominant part is connected with another word,

and since even the part that constitutes the meaning of the preceding word is predominant, it is for this very reason that it has been established in various instances that "in this case the meaning of the subsequent word is predominant," and "in this case the meaning of the preceding word is predominant."
Otherwise,
in all cases, there would be only predominance of the meaning of the final member [of the compound]. Since the relationship [of the members] occurs when there is such an expectancy (ākāṅkṣā),
this designation of "subordinate" (upasarjana) is therefore intended solely for the sake of establishing correct usage.

The designation "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*) for a single constituent [of a compound], as stated in the rule "that which is designated first in a compound is the subordinate member," serves solely for the purpose of establishing its placement at the beginning [of the compound] by means of the rule "the subordinate member comes first."

(*kasya gurukulam*).

When it is said "gurukulam" (the teacher’s family), there arises the expectation "whose teacher’s family? "Of what [names]? Of both worldly and Vedic ones.
It is replied: for that which is observed as the pervaded (vyāpya) causes one to infer the pervader (vyāpaka).

Regarding the phrase "of one for whom the relation is known" (*jñātasambandhasya*), this genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not denote the pervaded (*vyāpya*); for grammarians prescribe the genitive from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses merely a relatum (*sambandhin*).
By this, the term "one for whom the relation is known" [is shown to] require [further specification].

He raises this objection: "One cannot specify a single part [of it]. For this *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that of which the relation is known"—is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). And the genitive does not apply only to that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*)—that is, only to the pervaded relative (*pratisambandhin*) whose relation is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*)—such that, by the force of the *bahuvrīhi* in the sense of the genitive, [it would refer] to that which has become the relative...

Only smoke and the like, which do not deviate from their connection with fire and so forth, are called "those whose relation is known. For the genitive case occurs merely by expressing a related term—even for a correlate that is not pervaded—just as in the expression "the king's man.
Indeed, the king does not invariably accompany the man; therefore, by the term *jñātasambandha* ("known relation"), only the pervaded part is meant.

The pervaded (*vyāpya*) alone is the indicator (*gamaka*), not the pervader (*vyāpaka*) as well. Therefore, because it does not provide even a single part of that which is accepted by the world as a known indicator (*jñāpaka*) and exists as a pervaded, the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*) is not a qualifier of a specific part [of the subject]. In the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "of that whose relation is known" (*jñātaḥ sambandho yasya*), the genitive case does not mean that the relation belongs to the pervaded alone. It is said: True.
The genitive case is used for that which is related (*saṃbandhin*); however, only that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*) becomes related.
With this, he provides the rebuttal.
