One who possesses a relation is a "related party" (*sambandhī*); however, one for whom a relation both exists and does not exist is not designated as a "related party," for designation occurs by way of what is unique [to that thing]. Now, is it not observed that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used even for that which is not pervaded? To this he says: Just as the genitive case occurs even with respect to an object that is not pervaded when there is an intention to express it as being pervaded, so too is it in that case.
In this regard, we shall explain the meaning of the genitive case.

For instance, it is designated by worldly people as "this is mine"; since designation occurs by means of what is unique [to a subject], the pervasion of the related entity is expressed by the genitive.

Furthermore, the phrase "of another as well" expresses precisely the state of being pervaded by that which is related to it. Therefore, by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the genitive case, it is established that by the term *jñātasambandha* (known relation), only the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is denoted, not the pervader (*vyāpaka*).
Only this much remains to be stated here: what, then, is intended by "relation" in this context? Regarding that:

In this regard, some have asserted that identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*) alone are the relations that serve as the basis for inference. Among these, [inference] from identity is, for example: "This is a tree, because it is a *śiṃśapā*"; and [inference] from causality is, for example: "There is fire here, because there is smoke.
However, this is untenable, because we observe the inference of color from taste even through a relation characterized by inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*).

It might be thought: "The cause of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is perceived from the flavor itself; and since the cause of the flavor, acting as a cooperative factor in the form of an activated capacity, is the generator of the flavor, there is an inference of such a cause.

Because that [cause] is invariably concomitant with its effect, and because the cause is present in the form of an activated capacity, there is an inference of the object of the flavor from the flavor. This [argument], however, belongs to one whose mind is distracted by the mere defense of a position already accepted.
The analogy of clinging to a blade of *kāśa* or *kuśa* grass is to be disregarded, for the world does not understand it in that way;

and worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be followed by investigators. Furthermore, this inference of an effect from a cause is neither based on an essential identity (*svabhāva-hetu*), because cause and effect are distinct, nor is it based on an effect as a reason (*kārya-hetu*), because it is impossible for a cause to be an effect.
Furthermore, how does the effect (kārya) also make known the cause (kāraṇa)? If it is argued that this is because of its non-deviation (avyabhicāra) from it, then [the following applies]:

ga.

If there were non-deviation even for this [other reason], who could deny its capacity to convey [the object]? Furthermore, we shall explain later that it is not impossible to ascertain non-deviation even for another [reason]. Moreover, the relationship of the signified and the signifier is not tenable in a case of identity (*tādātmya*), because [the two would be] one and the same.

Because it is impossible for something to be both known and unknown at the same time. Furthermore, the example [of smoke and fire] is untenable because of the difference between "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātvā*), which refutes [the opponent's] conceptualization. By this, those who assert that five types of relations—namely, inherence (*samavāya*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*), the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and contradiction (*virodha*)—are the constituent factors of inference, are also refuted; for instance, [the inference] of the rising of Rohiṇī from the rising of Kṛttikā [cannot be based on these relations].

In the case of valid inference, [the other types of relation] are impossible for five reasons. Furthermore, the view held by some—that *vyāpti* (pervasion), which is synonymous with "invariable concomitance" (*niyama*), is a distinct type of relation and the cause of inference—is also not tenable. For there exists no other relation called *vyāpti* apart from relations such as that between owner and owned; rather, it is simply a particular relation, such as that of cause and effect, belonging to something.

The distinction is that [the pervader] is not the indicator of anything [in the same way]. In this regard, that which possesses a relation by virtue of which it is the pervaded—such as smoke—is the indicator; for smoke is pervaded by fire through its being an effect of fire and its being in conjunction with fire.
Fire, however, is not always related to smoke; thus, because its relation is not pervasive, it is not an indicator. Therefore, [the relation of] cause and effect—
In this context, only the three relations (*trairūpya*) are intended as the constituent factors of inference. Now, one might ask: how is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke and the like determined?

The capacity for this does not reside in perception (*pratyakṣa*), because its object is limited solely to things existing in a proximate location at the present time; for pervasion is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), and non-deviation [requires] all...
"Given that it pervades space and time. Nor is inference a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here, because it is itself unestablished.

Nor is verbal testimony, because its scope is restricted solely to effects. Nor is comparison, because its scope is limited to mere similarity. As for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), since it depends upon a previously established non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), it does not apply here. Furthermore, as for [the argument] that someone, by means of speech refined and matured...

As for the statement that "this kind of mental perception arises," that too does not deserve serious consideration; because in all cases, the mind does not function toward external objects independently of auxiliary factors.

And when there is dependence on a specific auxiliary factor, since that very factor is the unique cause, the perception should be designated by that alone, and thus it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is not a fault. For the status of being a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntaratva*) is based on the inclusion of a unique, non-common cause;

otherwise, since the mind operates in all cases, there would be only one kind of perception, namely mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*). Regarding this, those whose intellects are purified by the fragrance of the *Pramāṇamālā* begin their rebuttal: "Whatever object is apprehended by whichever means of valid cognition as qualified by a specific relation—as, for example, by perception..."
Smoke is qualified by its connection with fire; through that very same means of valid cognition, its pervasion (*vyāpyatā*) is also understood when [that] connection is established.
3. Refuted. Ga. 4. Pervaded. Ga. 5. "Time" omitted. Ga.
6. Nor [is it established] by means of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). For instance, you yourself should consider this self-cognition: "This smoke is connected with fire. What is there [in this]?

Only smoke itself, delimited by place and time, is manifested; then its relatedness, too, is manifested as delimited by place and time. In this regard, we observe that the smoke, which constitutes the subject (*dharmin*) of the signified (*liṅgin*), appears as "this" (*idantayā*), characterized by being proximate and present; it does not appear as the property (*dharma*) fire.

The relation as well has its own nature exhausted by being a subordinate qualifier of another. In that case, only the existence of smoke requires another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for its application to other times and places; however, the connection with fire, which is invariably concomitant with smoke alone, is already established. For this very reason, even when the object is already cognized, an effort will be made regarding [the need for] another means of knowledge.

[Objection: If that were the case, then fire too would be a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it is related to smoke. [Reply: It would not be so, because it also possesses a non-relation to that [smoke]. [Objection: What is the proof here that this will not be the case for smoke? Therefore, even smoke might have a doubtful pervasion (*vyāpti*). In that regard, those who have reached the further shore of the investigation of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [state] the distinction—

They argue as follows: for when one perceives something in a certain state, suspicion arises regarding that very thing being in such a state. Furthermore, when there is a connection between something and a particular condition (*upādhi*), as in the case of fire and the like with smoke due to its connection with moist fuel, then upon the removal of that condition, the connection ceases to exist. Yet, the connection of smoke with fire is not conditional (*aupādhika*). How, then, is this distinction to be made?

If it is asked how this is to be investigated, it is by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For when the status of something as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is suspected in a certain case, if [the effect] is still perceived even upon the removal of that [suspected condition], it is known: "This [effect] does not have that as its limiting condition. And it has been stated that this is due to the power of repeated observation: "Non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), however, is apprehended through repeated observation."
Thus, this direction has been indicated.

And here, by the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*), the over-common (*sādhāraṇa*), and the contradictory (*viruddha*) reasons are excluded. Among these, the uncommon [reason] is: "Earth is eternal because it possesses odor. For this [reason] exists only in earth.

Furthermore, since its property (*dharma*) called "eternality"—which is intended to be proven—is unestablished, it is impossible to determine its relation with the related entity; thus, it does not possess a "known relation. As for the common (*sādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive reason], such as: "Sound is eternal because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*):
this property characterized as "knowability" has a relation with eternality, yet there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Because there is no sense of a genitive relation (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*) in the phrase "that whose relation is known by it," it does not possess the quality of being a "known-relation" (*jñātasambandhatva*). Furthermore, as for the contradictory [reason]:
1. it is perceived as excluded; 2. it is perceived. (ga)
3. ...by virtue of being its very self.
ka. 4. Precisely from that. ga. 5. And of smoke, it will be. ga.

6. Smoke might also be [present] through a connection based on pervasion (sambandhanyāptika). 7. But [its status as a valid reason is established] by its positive and negative concomitance (anvayavyatireka) with that [fire].
8. And by "unestablished" (asiddha).
097] "The pot is eternal because it is produced"—in this case, there is no relation at all; thus, it is "unestablished due to the relation being unknown" (ajñātasambandhatā).

By the phrase "from the observation of a part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*), the status of that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) as a logical reason (*hetu*) is refuted; for example, [the argument] "action is perceptible because it possesses color" (*pratyakṣaṃ karma rūpavattvāt*).

For color is not a property of action. Of what, then? Of substance (*dravya*). Likewise, by the inclusion of the term "observation," the status of that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) as a logical reason is refuted. Thus, when the nature of the logical reason—consisting of the relation (*sambandha*), pervasion (*vyāpti*), and being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*)—is determined, [the inference proceeds].
The established position is that [the reason] is a constituent of pride (*māna*).
By the words "that, moreover, is of two kinds," he challenges the commentary: what is this twofold nature?
First of all, there is no twofold nature in terms of definition, because [the definition] states: "from the perception of one part."
—Thus, because the definition is one:
"from the perception of a part" is a single definition, and "of one whose connection is known" is a qualification; and that [definition] is one for both as well.
Now, having accepted the twofold nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), this twofoldness is stated.
And he demonstrates the twofoldness of the objects of knowledge:
in one case, a particular is understood through a particular.

From smoke having the form of smoke, by means of the cognition of the concomitance (vyāpti) with fire as characterized by its fiery form, a specific feature possessing the fiery form is understood; whereas in other cases, such as the sun, from the mere reaching of another location—which is a generality—only the cause thereof is inferred. Thus, due to the distinction between these two types of that which possesses a cause, the reason (hetu) is also twofold: the specific and...
Because it has the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*). Here [the opponent] asks: "What, then, is the purpose of stating the difference between these two?
The meaning is: "None at all. Furthermore, by the statement of their definitions, non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*) is established.

And this effort, consisting of the definition, is for that purpose— that is, for the sake of ensuring non-deviation (avyabhicāritva). Whether there be a twofold distinction between cause and effect or not, it matters not.

In this regard, some who consider themselves experts in policy—failing to ascertain the specific characteristics [of things] and ignorant of their individual internal distinctions—[speak] regarding: 1. the relation; 2. the nature of the logical reason (*hetu*). (Note: *ga* manuscript reads "relation" and "nature of the reason").
3. And that [attainment] belongs to these two.
Ga. 4. Attainment occurs from mere movement.
They maintain that nothing unperceived as a related entity is ever grasped by inference in a general way, that is, in its universal form; to dispel this misconception, it is said:

"From conjunction and effort, action arises in the hand"—thus [it is said].

Furthermore, a conjunction initiates its effect only within that which possesses the conjunction, just as the conjunction of parts initiates its effect in the whole (avayavin). Moreover, conjunction and disjunction do not [reside] in the substratum alone...

[The two] are conjoined, because they are conjoined even in a location that is not their substrate. Therefore, another action is inferred, distinct from the conjunction with the self. Thus, even though it is to be inferred, there is no fault whatsoever. This is what is meant: in every instance involving a conscious being...

Whether in the case of sentient beings or insentient objects, motion alone is the cause for reaching another location; therefore, there exists inference that culminates in the mere universal [of motion]. And it has been demonstrated that Devadatta’s [arrival] was preceded by motion.

And what is the distinction here?

For it is ignorance regarding the object of valid cognition that must be dispelled; and as for this ignorance, when it is said to be either inferential or non-inferential, he says: "For even those [who hold] that action and so forth are inferential..."

They also maintain that knowledge is non-inferential; for they indeed subvert inference itself—specifically, they subvert inference from its form as it is commonly established in the world. Therefore, that [position] too must be rejected. Consequently, even in this case, the purpose of stating a definition is precisely the exclusion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, there is also confusion and lack of distinction regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*); that too is removed by means of the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Some maintain that smoke observed in places such as kitchen hearths is not capable of establishing the fire located on a mountain.
When the connection of one thing has been apprehended, another thing is not to be expressed; rather, it is that which is to be stated. Here, however, he states the intention of the objection.

Because it is a cause [of cognition]. Others hold that only particulars are apprehended, since the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is untenable due to the absence of a graspable relation (*sambandha*). Still others maintain that it is merely memory (*smṛti*).

Because it is already grasped by the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through its relation (*sambandhin*), since there is thus a confusion [of the two], he therefore qualifies one "part" (*ekadeśa*) as "that whose relation is known";
and he qualifies the other "part" as "not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) with respect to the other part. What is the purpose of this qualification?

Is it refuted? First of all, recollection is refuted by the statement "that which is not in contact [with the senses]"; for it is precisely because it is not in contact that another part [of the object] is cognized. Non-apprehension is also refuted by the mention of the arising of cognition;

“The treatise states: ‘Cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arises from the cognition of a word.
What does this phrase ‘from the cognition of a word’ mean?”

Is "cognition of sound" intended to mean a cognition whose object is a meaning [derived] from a sound, or is it a cognition regarding a sound? If, first of all, "cognition of sound" means a cognition regarding a sound— that is, one having sound as its objective support— then in that case:
He states the fault in the opposing position: "That is incorrect, for from that [the Veda] no instruction (śāsana) is understood.
Instruction is a command (preraṇa); and that from which instruction is understood is a scripture (śāstra). A scripture is so called because of its instructive nature—this is the worldly etymology."

Because [that would lead to] over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the understanding of the teaching derived from a cognition that has the word as its objective support (*ālambana*); rather, it is the understanding of the task (*kārya*).

For it is from the understanding of the task that the understanding of the impulsion (*preraṇā*) arises. Therefore, the definition that "the scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of the object arising from the cognition that has the word as its objective support" is incorrect. Alternatively, if the cognition of the object that arises from the word is the "cognition of the word," then it is the cognition of the task.
Therefore, that cognition which arises regarding an object not present to the senses when there is an instigation [to act] is scripture (*śāstra*). True, this definition is thus established;

however, the cause for understanding the specific [meaning] must be stated, or rather, the reason for adopting the analysis as a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*)—rather than a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), which is also possible—must be explained in order to understand the specific distinction. To this, he replies: "And it has been said: 'scripture'."

And it has been said that the scripture (*śāstra*) is the cause for the comprehension of specific distinctions; for the description of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) must conform to the object to be defined (*lakṣya*). Here, moreover, the scripture is the object to be defined; therefore, a definition corresponding to it must be stated. [The opponent says: "Let it be so; nevertheless, what [follows]? He replies:

4. And it has been said thus. Ga. 5. But. Ga. 6. This is the corresponding object to be characterized. Ga.
For a treatise (*śāstra*) is so called because it instructs (*śāsana*).
And that [instruction] occurs only when there is cognition whose object is the meaning; thus, in the expression "cognition of the word" (*śabdavijñāna*), the fifth case [is used].

When understood by resorting to a compound, [the definition] is applicable, but not when referring to the mere nature of the word itself. Therefore, it is determined that this is a *pañcamī* (ablative) compound. Even in the second alternative, even if it were a *saptamī* (locative) compound, the definition of the science (*śāstra*) is established because the cognition based on the word—even though separated by the cognition of the grammatical operation—serves as the cause for the cognition of the injunction (*preraṇā*). Thus, the definition of the science is proven.

The point is that, by virtue of the authoritative treatises (*śāstra*), one must rely upon a causal relationship through a traditional lineage (*pāramparya*) in accordance with the observed instances (*lakṣya*).
But surely even a pseudo-word (*śabdābhāsa*) is seen, such as "this son of a barren woman goes," and so forth?

That too is understood from the word itself. By this, he points out a defect in the definition due to its being over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), because the definition exists even in the case of a pseudo-word (*śabdābhāsa*); for in that case as well, the cognition of the object arises solely from the cognition of the word. He asks: "Why? and replies:

For we do not perceive any cause here for [the cognition] being like that of vapor and so forth, as is the case with a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) in a fallacious inference. Even in that case, because it arises from the presence of the word, the word itself is the cause. To this, the resolution is: this has already been answered by the statement, "If that [is from] a trustworthy person."

Thus, the meaning is this: a human statement, acting as a logical mark (*liṅga*), conveys its object by means of presenting another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this [cognition] arises from what is merely a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).

This has been explained in the Bhāṣya by the words "if that [is obtained] from a trustworthy person. Furthermore, this very instance of deviation (vyabhicāra) is refuted by the statement of the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
Those who maintain that even the knowledge arising from human speech is verbal (śābda) have also been refuted; for it has been stated that such [knowledge] is actually inference (anumāna).
Thus ends the section on the treatise.

3. Over-extension of the definition (ativyāpti-lakṣaṇa). 4. Manifestation (bhāsa) due to some other cause (kiñcit-kāraṇāntara).
5. Because it is not produced by the existence or non-existence of the essence of sound (śabdatattva-bhāvābhāvitvāt).
6. This is its meaning.
7. For the purpose of [attaining] those respective marks (liṅga).
8. Also, the arising (samutthāna). Ga.

Comparison (*upamāna*) also produces cognition regarding an object not present to the senses by means of similarity; for example, the sight of a *gavaya* [produces the cognition] of the recollection of a cow.

On this point, the experts in categories (padārthavidaḥ) say: "There is no such thing as similarity (sādṛśya); it is not something distinct from substance, quality, action, generality, inherence, and particularity, nor is it included within them, because it is not enumerated among them in their compendium. To this it is replied: indeed, that which is called "similarity" is similarity.
The meaning of this is as follows:
"Similarity" refers to that wherein there is cognition; and this cognition exists; it is based upon that [similarity].

And [this concerns] the determination of the object. Therefore, by that power of cognition, one must admit a similarity that is either distinct from the qualities and so forth, or inherent within them. The statement in the Bhāṣya, "of the recollection of the cow," is inappropriate, for no cognition arises from recollection itself; to this he replies: "of the recollection of the cow" means "of a person who has previously experienced the cow."

Regarding "gosmaraṇasya": it is either a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom there is remembrance of a cow," or [it is derived from] "he remembers a cow" (*gāṃ smarati*), with the suffix *-lyuṭ* applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "from roots such as *nand*, etc. (*nandy-ādibhyo lyuḥ*);
or it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) meaning "the remembrance of a cow" (*goḥ smaraṇaḥ gosmaraṇaḥ*). But what, then, distinguishes this from inference? For here too—

Similarity, when its relation has been previously known, produces the cognition of a cow upon seeing it in a gavaya; for the similarity residing in the gavaya has a relationship of concomitance that is already known through the similarity residing in the cow. This is the distinction from smoke and the like: namely, that the signified and the signifier are properties belonging to two different substrata; for in inference, when smoke and so forth are seen in a certain place, the cognition is produced therein.
[The word] *dayati*; and this has been expressed by the word *antara* in the phrase "in another part" (*ekadeśāntare*), whereas similarity (*sādṛśya*) [is mentioned] elsewhere.
1. Regarding "similarity": what is similarity? Ga.
2. Omitted. ca. ga. 3. Omitted. vā. ga. 4.
"He remembers the cows," so [it says]. ga.

5. In the case of a distinct property (*bhinnadharma*), that which has become the property-possessor (*dharmibhūta*) is the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*). For inference is indeed [this]. Ga.
108] But is it not the case that the state of having a known relation (*jñātasambandhitā*) is the same [in both cases]?

[This refers] to similarity and to smoke and so forth. And that [similarity] is also the defining characteristic here in inference. Whether it occurs there [in the subject] or elsewhere, what does this matter? It matters greatly; for "the perception of one part" is indeed the defining characteristic there.
Because one part is the primary factor. The phrase "of that whose relation is known" is a qualification of the single part.
He concludes: therefore, the similarity residing in the gavaya does not constitute a single part of the cow.

Of what kind of cow? It means that in which there is the cognition "similar" (*sadṛśa-avagati*); that is to say, of the subject (*pakṣībhūta*) whose property one desires to know. Furthermore, the cause of inference is indeed a relationship perceived repeatedly.

When the related object is apprehended as being without limiting conditions (*nirupādhika*), it possesses the status of a logical reason (*hetutā*); and it has been stated that this state of being without limiting conditions is to be understood through repeated observation. However, similarity (*sādṛśya*) does not have its relation [to the object] already known, because cognition arises even upon the first observation. Likewise, there is no requirement for repeated observation, since it is indicative even when observed only once. [This applies to] the exclusion from what is of a different class (*asajātīyavyāvṛtti*).
And it is dependent;
that is, it is dependent upon the exclusion of smoke from non-congeneric things, namely, from those that are not fire. Thus says the author of the Vārttika:

“As long as there is even a one-hundredth part of a doubt regarding the non-exclusion [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa), how can the power of the reason to produce cognition exist? Thus [it is said].

In this case, however, exclusion from what is not of the same class (*asajātīya-vyāvṛtti*) is not required; thus, this is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), namely comparison (*upamāna*).
What, then, is the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) here, for the purpose of whose removal this definition is intended? Is it anything other than the appearance of similarity (*sādṛśyābhāsa*)?

The observation of deviation: it has been shown that the cognition "it is similar" which occurs when there is a mere appearance of similarity does not constitute *upamāna* (analogy), because similarity is not established in that case. For indeed, that which...
1. Omitted. api. ka. 2. Added. *bhṛśam upayujyate*. ga. 3. *dharmiṇā* iti. ga.
4. But similarity is known by that [perception]. Ga. 5. It is [the cause of] error. Ga. 6. The power of comprehension, Vācaspatimiśra.

That which has no similar counterpart is nevertheless said to be "similar" to it; for example, upon seeing a heap of straw, one forms the cognition, "The elephant is like this," which thus has as its object a semblance of similarity.

It has already been stated that similarity exists as something graspable by the cognition of resemblance. Now, in order to distinguish whether this is simply a universal (*sāmānya*) or something else, he presents the view of others: "In this regard, some have declared that similarity is nothing but a universal."

It is precisely the universal (sāmānya) residing in another substratum—such as qualities, parts, or actions—that, when being cognized, is called similarity (*sādṛśya*). As it has been said: "Similarity is said to be the manifestation of many universals belonging to qualities, parts, and actions, made distinct by a primary universal."
To this he replies: "That is not similarity.
Similarity is distinct; for the similarity in a cow is indeed something other [than that in a gavaya].

Similarity; and furthermore, the similarity of a gavaya to a cow; as for [the universal] "quality-ness" and so forth, it is that very same [universal] in another substrate, because "cowness" and so on are one; and since there is no distinction in "ear-ness" and so forth, they too are indeed one.
Now, one might object: "But in this case, there is no object of cognition (prameya) at all."

For some maintain that for one who has previously seen a cow, its similarity to a gavaya appears [to him], and that for such a person who has seen the cow, there is no further object of knowledge (*prameya*) remaining; to this, he replies: "That is incorrect, because even what has been experienced may be understood through other means."

It has already been stated that [this] is indeed a valid object of cognition (*prameya*) in the case of inference. Here, however, the similarity of a cow to a *gavaya*, which had not previously been experienced, is now experienced through another cause—namely, the similarity of the *gavaya* to the cow as it is currently being perceived; therefore, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is all the more certain.

This is correct. As for the essential nature of comparison (*upamāna*): "That cognition which, arising with respect to a correlate (*pratiyogin*) from something perceived due to similarity, has similarity as its object—that is called comparison."
Thus concludes the section on analogy (upamāna). [Note:
1. "tatū" is omitted in manuscript *ga*. 2. "karmādikam" is read as "karmādi" in manuscript *ka*.]
3. [The properties of] being an ear and so forth. Ga. 4. Validity has been stated. Ga. [p.

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also the postulation of a fact because a perceived or heard fact cannot otherwise be accounted for; for example, the postulation of the unperceived presence outside of the living Devadatta upon seeing his absence from home. This is to be explained as follows.

By the passage beginning with "What is this so-called *anyathānupapatti*? [the author] states that since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference, a separate definition for it need not be formulated: "If, first of all, its existence is not possible without this [other thing]," then this is simply the inference of a cause from an effect in terms of its objective reality; it is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For by the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*), which denotes a mode of being distinct from the mode under discussion, the non-existence of the object to be postulated is expressed; and by the phrase "it is not possible" (*nopapadyate*), its non-existence is likewise stated. Thus, the following meaning is established: having understood that this object does not exist in the absence of the postulated entity—

[The objection: "It is the postulation of another object. And thus, this results in an inference of the cause from the effect; for it is understood that an effect is not possible without a cause, and being so understood, it leads to the inference of that cause. Now, this is said: the definition of inference is "for one who has known the relation"; yet here the relation is unknown. Therefore, [it is not] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
1. Separate mention. Ga.
2. For the sake of the purpose [of the effect]. Ga.
3. In all cases, the cause is another factor (gaṇa). [p. 111] Thus it is said.

The intention here is this: although the "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti) is equal [in both cases], nevertheless, there is no inference because of the absence of knowledge of the relationship. That is incorrect; for how can one who does not know the relationship be able to understand that "this is not possible without that"?
To the question "Why is it not possible?", he says: "For *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise) is not apprehended through perception.
For if *anyathānupapatti* were apprehended by means of perception, then...

This [inference] is determined even without knowledge of a relationship, nor is it apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is it the case that "presumption through the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) is a means of comprehension only when it remains undetermined; for the Commentator has stated: "It is not possible otherwise."

Thus [it is said]. In common usage, the word *iti* is observed to be primarily used for the indication of knowledge (*jñāna*). Furthermore, there is no cause for the apprehension of a qualified object when the impossibility (*anupapatti*) has not been ascertained. Therefore, it is the ascertained impossibility itself that is the cause. However, that [impossibility] is indeed to be understood through its non-deviation from the effect. For the effect, by virtue of its non-deviation from the cause, is thus understood.
It is understood that an effect is not possible without a cause. Furthermore, this invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) is preceded by repeated observation.
For it is through repeated observation that the natural connection between an effect and its cause is ascertained.

The ascertainment of the connection with an intrinsic cause is the ascertainment of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Therefore, whether perceived or unperceived, only that which has its relationship known is understood through *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise).
Thus, "perceived" means perceived by way of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that which is...

Inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is that which is not observed through its specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇataḥ*). That [inference] is understood precisely as one whose relation is already known (*jñātasambandha*), by way of its being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*); it is not, however, [understood] when the relation is unknown. Therefore, since this comprehension of an object arises from a known relation, it is nothing but inference; any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is merely a mirage. This is true, provided that [the object] is [established] by that [means].
Without [it], [something] is not possible; that very thing would be the means of comprehension.

The meaning of this is: if for something there is an impossibility without another, and if that [other] were the means of comprehending it, then this would be an inference (*anumāna*). But here, that which is not possible—[that is what is being considered].
1. Nor should this be stated otherwise. (ga) 2. And the word is the indicator.
(ka) 3. Therefore, it is not indeed understood. (ga)
4. Omitted. *yat svalakṣaṇa-ga*. 5. *tadanyathā. ga*. 6. Omitted. *vinā. ga*.
7. Omitted. That which is indeed to be understood. [p. 112] ga. va. avagamyam.

When the proponent has spoken thus, the opponent says—in a single passage: "What here is not tenable? Since one observes the absence [of a person] from his house while he is alive, his absence elsewhere is not tenable. Even for one who is alive...

When his absence from home is observed, his absence elsewhere is not logically possible, because that would entail the consequence of his death. When asked "What follows from this?", he reveals his intention: "It is not the absence [of the person] that is being cognized here; rather, it is his presence [elsewhere]. And that [presence] is not established by the observation of his absence from home."
The existence [of the person] outside is understood. As it has been said:
"The postulation of an external existence that has not been perceived.
Nor is there any inconsistency in that [existence] given the absence from the house.

On the contrary, it is precisely the occurrence [of something] that [is required]; and for that non-existence which is impossible, there can be no object of cognition. Therefore, it is illogical to say that "that which is impossible is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Now, if it is argued: "It is true that when the absence from the house is perceived, there is no impossibility of its existence elsewhere; however, even without the perception of the absence from the house, the impossibility [of its non-existence] certainly arises."

[The opponent claims: "The word *anyathā* (otherwise) expresses the very meaning of the word *vinā* (without); therefore, the existence outside [the house] is impossible (*anupapatti*) without the perception of Devadatta’s absence from the house. This is not so; for that [existence outside] is not impossible without the perception of his absence from the house. For even one who does not perceive the absence from the house of Devadatta or others still perceives his mere existence outside.

In perception, there is no appearance of impossibility; therefore, this mode also is not tenable. "Certainly it is not tenable," says the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin). Here, the underlying intention is as follows: it is not by the perception of the absence from the house...
"Non-occurrence in the absence [of something]" is what is being stated; however, it means that by the observation of the absence from the house, existence outside is not logically possible.
Therefore, the observation of the absence from the house is the cause for the non-occurrence of existence when the connection with the external location has not been cognized;

and this "non-occurrence" is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). When there is the observation of the absence from the house, yet the connection with the external location remains uncognized—
Even life, which is established by means of valid cognition—how could it not exist here? Or, if one were to doubt whether he lives or not, what [doubt] would there be in this case?
For [he is] indeed living.
3. Furthermore, the arising of non-existence is necessarily [the case]. (ga) 4. And there is no [arising] of that [non-existence]. (ga) 5. For existence is otherwise. (ga)
6. And that [absence] is not [established] even by the perception of the absence [of the person] in the house. Ga. 7. And here, "being outside" [is what is meant].
Ga. 8. For indeed. Ga.
9. Comprehension of the truths through vision. 10. Doubtful cognition.

It is understood as being connected with the external region; therefore, it is established that it is precisely that [external] state which is logically untenable here, and it is precisely that which is understood. For indeed, the existence outside is not possible without the observation of absence from the house.

The meaning of the text is that, by observing the absence from the house, existence outside is not possible without [the person being present elsewhere]. By the word *bāḍham*, it is stated that the impossibility (*anupapatti*) is extreme.
Now, one might object: "A thing seen or heard is not otherwise possible."
Thus, he demonstrates that it is the impossibility of the indicator (*gamaka*) occurring otherwise [than in relation to the indicated] that is shown,
not [the impossibility of] the indicated (*gamya*). For the object has been seen otherwise.
The intended meaning is that the connection [of the words] appears as "it is not possible. [The phrase] "the beloved of the gods (devānāṃ priyaḥ) is one who does not know the text" is used;
regarding this insult, there is no elision of the genitive case-ending, as it is stated: "An addition should be made for the expression 'the beloved of the gods' when used as an insult."
Thus [he says]. He shows the ultimate truth (paramārtha): "The conceptualization of an object as something seen or heard."
What is this "conceptualization of an object"?

It means that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible. The meaning is that an object, whether perceived or heard, serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another object.
The intention here is that the word "kalpanā" (conceptual construction) refers to valid cognition (*pramiti*).
With what, then, is the phrase "it is not otherwise possible" (*anyathā nopapadyate*) connected?
If it is not stated that this is connected with the words "seen" or "heard," then with what is it connected? We reply: it is connected with "cognition" (pramiti).

We say that it is connected with that valid cognition which is designated as *arthāpatti* (presumption). Regarding this, he states the formulation of the statement: "It makes known another object by bringing about the state of being otherwise inexplicable.
Otherwise, how...
1. There is no connection with this word "veti. With what? Ga. 2. It is "saṃjñikā. Ga. [p. 114]

When there is no conceptualization of this [absence], and when the external connection has not been cognized, one might urge that the absence from the house— by way of establishing an inconsistency or a contradiction with another means of knowledge— indicates the existence outside as a distinct object (*arthāntara*). Is it not the case here that the requirement of a known relation (*jñātasambandhitā*) is simply not required?

This, however, is further questioned. Its meaning is as follows: as long as it is not understood that lifelong existence is necessarily connected with a specific location, then for one who does not perceive the absence from the house, there is no logical inconsistency in not cognizing his presence outside. Therefore, because it depends upon the cognition of a related term (*sambandhi*), this is indeed inference (*anumāna*). It is required.
For there is only the cognition of a relation, not the state of being related.
True; what is required is the relation of living with a place, but not the state of being related between the indicator—the absence from the house—and the state of being outside.

Therefore, in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the mere knowledge of the connection between living and a location is the factor that brings about comprehension; however, in the case of inference,
it is stated that "for one who knows the relationship," the genitive case indicates that the state of being related itself is what brings about comprehension.

The genitive case used in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), "of whom the relation is known," indicates that it is only a part of the related entity (*sambandhin*)— namely, the perceived [part]— that serves as the indicator (*gamaka*). Therefore, it is the living person whose connection with a particular place is understood who is indicated.

There is no such thing as [independent] suggestiveness; and for that which possesses suggestiveness, there is no dependence upon the knowledge of a relation. Thus, it is established that this is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). On this point, there are these verses:
"Without conceptual construction, the meaning leads to an inconsistency..."
That other object which is postulated is the domain of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

Just as existence within the house [is established] by means of non-existence [therein], so too, when [existence] outside is being postulated, its lack of logical consistency is brought forward without any conceptual construction; for it is only when it is being postulated that it appears as such.

In this context, the impossibility of the object to be known— characterized by the occurrence of doubt due to contradiction with other means of valid cognition— is established without recourse to conceptual construction.
For an entity is never observed without its location;
therefore, even when [the absence] in the house is established, it still falls into doubt.
The postulation that proceeds for the purpose of removing that doubt is known as presumption (arthāpatti), arising from an object that gives rise to doubt.
In inference, however, the indicator (gamaka) is characterized by its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa);
its impossibility [to exist there] is understood without the object to be inferred (gamya).
1. Omitted. *saha* ga. 2. *mavagamakamiṣyate*. ga. 3. *kalpanātaḥ*. ga.
4. The arising of doubt. Ka. 5. And that is the definition. Ga. 6. It would be understood. Ga.

“It is certain that these two means of valid cognition, known as presumption (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*), are distinct from one another due to the difference in their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).”
Thus:
Is the mention of "seen" or "heard" intended for the purpose of excluding other causes?

By the term "seen," that which is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is grasped; by the term "heard," however, that which is understood through verbal testimony (*śabda*) is grasped. If...

However, if "perceived" (*upalabdha*) were expressed by the term "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), then the term "heard" (*śruta*) would be redundant. Therefore, the phrase "seen or heard" was stated in order to include both types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and to exclude other forms of valid cognition;
such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
[The opponent] objects: "In that case, presumption (*arthāpatti*) preceded by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not be included. This is the criticism held in mind.

The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), however, says: "We say 'no'"; it is not for the purpose of excluding other means of valid cognition. What then? It is [to indicate] what is observed...

"Or 'heard'?"—the meaning is "an object that has been perceived. Consequently, by including merely what is perceived, there is a subsumption of all means of valid cognition; this is the meaning. Now, for what purpose is the inclusion of the term "heard"? Should one not simply say "seen"?
Because by the very use of the term "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), which denotes that which has been perceived, what has been heard (*śruta*) is also included. Now,
although what has been heard is indeed perceived, nevertheless, [in the case] of that which is preceded by what has been heard...
The term "heard" (*śruta*) is employed to indicate the distinction [of presumption] as being a grasper of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagrāhin*).

Now, one might object: even in the case of presumption from what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), it is the heard absence of eating during the day—which, being untenable given the fact of fatness, becomes untenable without eating at night—that leads to the postulation of eating at night, not the word itself. For indeed...
The non-apprehension of the object is not due to the absence of the word, but rather to the absence of the object itself. This is true;

however, presumption (*arthāpatti*), which is engaged in postulating the object, results in the word itself being the first thing encountered, because that object is grasped by a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) and is thus perceived as preceded by the word; it does not reach the object itself. Rather, it is the word alone that is understood as the object.
1. Added. *pramāṇāntara-ga*. 2. *upalabdhimātra*. *ga*. 3. Omitted. *pīnatvasya*. *ga*.

[He] establishes [this]. But if that were so, would not even in the case of perception and the other means of knowledge, conceptual cognitions fail to grasp the object and instead terminate only in the word? For in the cognitions of animals and the like, which are devoid of words, the sense organ [grasps] the object itself.

Since [the capacity] has been determined to reside in the word, it must therefore exist in that very place even during the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*); it cannot exist elsewhere, because the postulation of a separate capacity would be redundant. Furthermore, the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) never occurs for animals, because it is dependent upon the acquisition of linguistic usage (*śabdavyutpatti*); for one who has not acquired such usage does not understand the meaning of a sentence preceded by words. Now, as for the presumption based on what is seen (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*)...

Thus far, it has been established that the capacity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) resides solely in its object; here too, it ought to be the same. It is true that the capacity is observed to reside in the object itself, but only insofar as it serves as a means of justification (*upapādaka*); for even an object is not perceived in its own right, but rather by way of being a justification. And that which is the justifier is that upon the cognition of which the inconsistency (*anupapatti*) is resolved. This is the case with words as well.
Since the contradiction is resolved when the word is directly uttered, it is the word itself, encountered first, that performs the function of *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).
Thus the venerable author of the Vārttika said:
"And this second object is not understood again through the [first] object."
But because it is graspable by conceptual cognition, it is concealed.
Fire is not apprehended as "fire" solely through its sense organ and inferential marks;
likewise, it is perceived by animals as well through its very nature as an object.
However, the cognition resulting from presumptive testimony (śrutārthāpatti) never occurs for animals;
for this cognition arising from the understanding of words is considered to be born from the acquisition of linguistic convention.
Through its cognition, this [mental construction] does not apprehend the object itself as distinct from other words;
therefore, it is necessarily directed first toward the domain of the sentence.

In conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*), a word is perceived as having the form of a delimiter of the object; and by virtue of being a designator (*vācaka*), the word delimits the object. Therefore, in the cognition "cow," the object is understood in this manner: "this is what is denoted by the word 'cow'."

It is grasped [as such], yet a word does not express its own status as being denotable by that word. Therefore, in this context, the word is not a communicator of the object; rather, through its denotative capacity as understood from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), it brings forth the denoted object.

It shines forth as something distinguished. Therefore, because it does not bring about the presence of an object (*arthānupasthāpakatva*), even though it occurs first, it is not capable of pacifying the logical inconsistency; thus, it cannot be considered an object of knowledge through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Consequently, this [cognition] also has only the object as its domain.

The mention of "scripture" (*śruta*) is not even for the purpose of indicating a distinction. As for those who think that in sacrifices such as the *viśvajit*, the word itself is untenable because it is incomplete, and who therefore claim that the word which supplies that [meaning] must be inferred—
they, speaking with the confusion born of their own arbitrary imagination, deserve to be ignored, yet they are treated by fools as if they were authorities.
Thus, for the sake of instructing the ignorant, something is said.

What, then, is this "inconsistency of the word" that is distinct from the "inconsistency of the meaning"? If it is incompleteness, what indeed is the incompleteness of the word? For it is the meaning itself that becomes incomplete when lacking some portion of its referent.

If it is argued that because the meaning is incomplete, the word is also incomplete, let it be so; for one must accept the validity of that very [meaning] upon which its [the word's] non-validity depends. Otherwise, the incompleteness of the word would remain exactly as it was. Therefore, even if the word is incomplete, it is the meaning alone that must be postulated. And not the meaning—

The application of the term "word" is untenable [in this context], because of the difference between the word and its object. Now, if it were argued that—given the untenability of the object and the absence of a cognizable thing—the status of the word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is likewise untenable—even so, it would be the status of being a means of valid cognition that is untenable, not the word itself. Furthermore, the status of being a means of valid cognition is not untenable independently, but rather precisely through the untenability of the object; if this is the case, then the root—

Let it be that the non-occurrence of the actual fact itself is what brings presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) to mind. Furthermore, the status of a means of valid cognition is itself untenable due to the suspicion that its object of cognition might not exist, even in the absence of some [other] object; it is not due to the absence of the word [itself], which would lead one to postulate the word. Enough with this excessive deliberation;
we have wandered far afield—let us return to the subject at hand.
The answer to this is as follows: this [term "perceived"] is merely another designation for "apprehension.
Its meaning is this: the inclusion of everything is not achieved by the word *dṛṣṭa* alone, but rather by it together with the word *śruta*; therefore, the mention of *śruta* is not purposeless.

But how is it that by the word *dṛṣṭa* (seen), used in conjunction with the apprehension of what is heard (*śruta*), the apprehended is expressed? Listen: although the word *dṛṣṭa* denotes merely that which is apprehended, nevertheless, due to the proximity of the word *śruta*, it denotes that which is distinct from what is known through verbal testimony, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Now, what is the purpose of resorting to this *gobalīvardanyāya*? It is said:

We are worldly people, and we see that even the world engages in such conventional usage. Furthermore, there is no room for questioning in the world, because it is beginningless. Therefore, this was said: this is merely another synonym, well-known in the world, which expresses "apprehension."
Thus ends the section on presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

“Non-existence, too, is the absence of a means of valid cognition, regarding the object ‘it does not exist,’ which is not in contact with the senses.”
"Non-existence also is the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva). What, then, is this definition of a means of valid cognition?
This is the question of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin). And here, the intended meaning is as follows:

If this is the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is untenable because of the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*). If, on the other hand, it is not the definition of a means of valid cognition, then there is a contradiction with the established consensus that there are six means of valid cognition. In that case, this treatise would be incoherent and purposeless. Regarding this, a teacher-like scholar says: "It is said, 'Yes' (*om*)."

The meaning is that this definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is accepted. And the intention therein is as follows: first of all, the absence of jars and so forth in places such as the ground is perceived—namely, "there is no jar on the ground. This perception does not have the bare ground alone as its objective support.
For even if the jar were present, [the cognition] would result in an absurdity. Nor is it without an objective support (*nirālambana*), because it itself establishes an objective support.

Therefore, this [cognition] takes non-existence itself as its object. Furthermore, it is not invalid (*apramāṇa*), because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) and because it consists of a definitive ascertainment (*niścaya*).

For this very reason, since it appears within this cognition which is of the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that [non-existence] also possesses the status of an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*).

This is correct. Furthermore, if non-existence were not perceived, there would be no such practical activity as placing one's foot upon the ground and so forth; for this [activity] does not arise from the mere determination of the bare ground, since it occurs even when thorns and the like are present, nor from the apprehension of a "ground-only" [in isolation], because if non-existence were not an object of cognition, its isolation (kaivalya) could not be determined. Isolation...

For the property of the ground is not other than non-existence; nor [is it established] by the mere apprehension of a nature unassociated with anything else. For if the ground associated with subtle thorns and the like were apprehended merely in its own nature, there would be the undesirable consequence of purposeful activity [toward it], since an inquiry preceded by effort would be impossible. Likewise, if non-existence were not an object of cognition (*aprameya*), then even things such as a hare’s horn would be subject to inference.

[Otherwise] it would follow [absurdly] that there is no obstruction. Therefore, non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of cognition (*prameya*). Nor is this cognition of non-existence perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it does not arise from the contact of the sense organs (*indriya-saṃprayoga*). If it is asked, "Is the fact that [the cognition of absence] arises when that [object] is absent not established otherwise? What is the proof for this?"—it is because we observe the apprehension of absence even in one who has grasped the mere nature of the object, whose sensory activity has ceased, who has gone to another place, and who has developed a desire to know through other causes.

Nor is this a case of inference, because the apprehension of the relation [between the mark and the probandum] is impossible; for [inference] does not occur when the related term has not been apprehended.

The determination of the relation is easy to understand; however, there is no apprehension of a related object that is non-existent. Therefore, this other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva) has been defined by this commentary.

Consequently, it follows that what is called "it does not exist" is its object of cognition (prameya). This being the case, that which is not cognized would be an object of cognition; thus, there would be the status of being an object of cognition for that which is not being cognized. There is a means of valid cognition (*pramiti*) for that [object]; otherwise, there would be only the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*). Therefore, the claim that there is validity (*prāmāṇya*) for what is not cognized appears almost as something non-worldly.

The non-apprehension of that object by the self consists precisely in the self’s being associated with an experience that is unconnected to that object; and that state of the self is indeed self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*). Therefore, no further object of knowledge remains. Furthermore, even for one who asserts that non-existence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the cause for the arising of the cognition thereof is simply the self’s association with an experience unconnected to it; and this [non-existence] is not unknown, unlike the eyes and other sense organs.

It produces knowledge by its mere existence (*sattāmātreṇa*); for even when something currently visible on the ground or elsewhere is not being perceived, the cognition "this was previously here" is observed even in the absence of that perception. Therefore, the present cognition of non-existence arises necessarily from the previous perception alone, which has now ascended into memory.

This must be accepted. Therefore, let non-existence be defined simply as "perception alone" (kevalopalambha); what is the point of adopting a separate entity? Furthermore, that quality of being associated with perception alone belongs to the self [the cognizer] either due to the deficiency of the causal complex for perception in some cases, or due to its completeness in others. It is precisely this [quality] which initiates the conventional usage of non-existence regarding a certain object.
For one who reflects upon such a state [of affairs], the linguistic convention "there is no jar on the surface of the earth" proceeds.

Nor is there any over-extension here—namely, that the linguistic convention of non-existence would apply even to what is in contact [with the locus]—because the perception of the bare locus is distinct from the perception of the object in contact. Furthermore, even an inquiry preceded by effort [is required] regarding subtle thorns and the like on the ground.

What inconsistency is there in seeking to establish that "this state exists" even when the entire causal complex for the perception of objects such as a pot is present? Otherwise, due to the suspicion that this state belongs to the self because of its subtlety, the conventional usage of non-existence could not proceed without hesitation;
and only when this very state, which serves as the counter-position and consists of non-existence, is established, can inference regarding [non-existent things] such as a rabbit's horn [proceed].

Since [cognition] does not arise with respect to things such as the horns of a donkey, it is established that non-existence is not a separate object of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, the definition [of non-apprehension], namely "the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*), characterizes it precisely as not being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it is the absence of a means of valid cognition—

When it is said that "it is an entity" (bhāvaḥ), it is understood that it is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); for indeed, one cannot say that "the means of valid cognition is the absence of a means of valid cognition. Therefore, this is not a definition of a means of valid cognition. Now, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says:
there is indeed this well-known tradition among the Mīmāṃsakas that this is, as it were, a sixth means of valid cognition. Nor is this [known] from the text...

The meaning is that the nature (*svarūpa*) which is not determined by the previously mentioned characteristics is determined by this [text]. How so? He says:
"This treatise is the supplement to the statements naming all particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). But what, then, is named by this [particular characteristic]?

Regarding the point that [the status of being a means of valid cognition] is established by the subsequent portion of the text, he says: "For the status of a cognition as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its object is not determined merely from its arising;
for it is not the case that simply because a cognition has arisen, [its validity] regarding its own object [is thereby established]."

The validity of knowledge, which has become a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is ascertained; for, even when its being produced by contact with that [object] and so forth is perceived, [the ascertainment follows].

"For this determination that 'it is this very thing' regarding a given object does not occur without the concomitant cognition of the absence of other things."

that which is this absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-viraha)..."
"that non-existence [of the object] also pertains to the domain of the means of valid cognition"—
by this, it is understood that the very nature of the means of valid cognition is defined by the previously stated definition itself, extending even to its culmination in ascertainment; for—

The exclusion of another object (*arthāntaravyavaccheda*), when the totality of the causal complex for perception is present, is characterized solely by the perception [of that object] and consists precisely in the non-arising of its corresponding means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore—because the effect [of the cognition] has ceased, meaning because the consciousness of the effect of the means of valid cognition does not arise due to the perception of the object alone—the conventional expression "it does not exist" occurs; for this reason, the previously stated definition of the means of valid cognition is indeed correct.

It is said: For if non-existence (*abhāva*) were indeed something entirely different from existence (*bhāva*), then all the previously stated definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be incorrect; because non-existence would not be cognized by that [perception] alone, there would be no determination of the object preceded by it, and since it is untenable for that which results in non-determination to be a means of valid cognition, the definition of a "means of valid cognition" that is itself not a means of valid cognition is nothing but the babbling of a child.

It might be so. But what, then, is this "commonly recognized" (*prasiddhi*)? This is a further inquiry regarding *prasiddhi* in order to provide an answer:
"Common recognition is like the commonly recognized [existence] of a yakṣa in a banyan tree."
This means that this conventional usage is preceded by delusion. If they consider there to be a difference in causes because of a difference in worldly practice, then what can we do?
There is the conventional usage of existence (*bhāva*).

The conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) occurs even without the consideration of the non-perception of a perceptible object; rather, it arises from the consideration of mere perception even when that object is perceptible. Since there is this very difference in conventional usage, if some Mīmāṃsakas consider the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to be distinct [in these two cases], what can we do? Thus, one should maintain equanimity toward them. To this he says: "For the establishment of a distinction between means of valid cognition does not follow from a distinction in conventional practice. Regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*)—

For the difference between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs precisely through the difference between the cognitions themselves; it is not the case that a difference in the objects of cognition (*prameya*) constitutes a difference in the means of valid cognition merely by virtue of a difference in conventional usage.
Therefore, this is not a separate means of valid cognition. He concludes: "Therefore, this has the very same definition as those.
This [definition] belongs to those very means of valid cognition.

This is its definition; it is not the definition of some other independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And this alone is the definition of that non-existence (*abhāva*); it is not something else, such as the claim that "non-existence" is a property of a real entity (*vastu-dharma*). How there is no other definition has already been stated. Therefore, because it is well-known, the cause [of its cognition] need not be further examined.
The introductory section of the root text is concluded.

That which is not perceived as an object of perception does not exist, just like the horn of a rabbit. And the instruments of perception are the senses of animals and the like; yet, after the sacrifice for those desiring cattle, cattle are not perceived. Therefore, the sacrifice does not have cattle as its fruit. Let other means of knowledge such as perception and the rest exist, but verbal testimony (śabda) is not a means of knowledge.
What is the intended meaning?

The sense of this question is as follows: how can the cognition arising from a word regarding its object be invalid? This is the intended meaning: [it refers to] that which was stated [by the opponent], namely, "because it is independent" of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

That which makes known an object not otherwise accessible is merely false (*mṛṣā*).

The statement made—that by the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "because of independence" (anapekṣatvāt), the word makes known and establishes an object not apprehended by other means of knowledge—is false. Why?
Because this object is yet to come into being (bhaviṣyan).

Thus, by means of this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the independent authority (*svātantryeṇa prāmāṇyam*) of the word and its meaning—since they are to be brought into being (*bhāvyatayā*) as effects (*kāryatayā*) and are not cognizable through any other means of knowledge—is stated; however, that is not possible in the case of the *citrā* sacrifice and the like. But how is it impossible?

Is there a sentence devoid of an injunction (*niyoga*)—that is, one lacking the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, which by etymology means "that by which one is enjoined"—such that [the objection of] impossibility would apply? For indeed, every sentence whatsoever possesses an injunction. This being the case, since it denotes an action to be accomplished (*kārya*), [the possibility of its being a source of knowledge] certainly exists.

Regarding its authority: the answer to this is as follows—what will the injunctive force (*niyoga*) expressed by words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) accomplish here? The point is that it does not make known an object independently. For we observe such [injunctive] forms as *liṅ* even in cases where the object is dependent on another and is already cognizable through other means of knowledge, as in the case of traditional texts (*smṛti*) and the like. What is meant is this: the fact that the meaning of the optative suffix and others is dependent on something else is beyond dispute.

Furthermore, absolute independence (svātantrya) is never observed anywhere, and it is logical for a conceptual construction to follow what is observed. Therefore, having considered that very relationship between the sacrifice of the Citrā and the cattle— which is understood through the mutual connection of the group of words expressing the meanings as grasped by the *niyoga*— the *liṅ* [suffix] [expresses] the *niyoga*.

The scope of this must be stated. What is meant is this: the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth express the "task-to-be-done" (*kāryatā*) of the sacrifice precisely as being based on its being a means to a result. Indeed, when this is accepted, the independence of the word that has not been observed will not be postulated, and its dependence that has been observed will not be abandoned.
