1. This is false. Ka. 2. Omitted. It causes [the object] to be cognized. Ga. 3. Not denoting an injunction. Ga.
4. Now, the subsequent [section]. Ka. 5. In the state of dependence. Ga. 6. Added: *tāvat*. Ga.

[Page 126] That which consists of a collection of words expressing positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has as its object only that which is currently perceived; for it, the perception of what is currently perceived is the cause of apprehension.
That relationship of the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between the sacrifice and the cattle, which possesses another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), is that which is currently...

That whose object is not perceived [as such] is perceived only as having a perceivable object, as in the case of "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," and so forth. It is precisely this state of being an effect (*kāryatā*), based on its being the means to a result, that is expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like.
What here is meant by "perception of what is present"? It is the state of the fruit arising immediately after the action;
that is, the nature of the fruit to come into being immediately following the action. And this is because rain and so forth have perceptible results.

When rice and other crops are withering, rain and the like, being desired, are understood precisely as having their results occurring immediately thereafter; by this reasoning as well, immediate succession is logical. Furthermore, it is possible to state—on the basis of another means of knowledge—that an action has its result immediately following it, since this entity consisting of the relationship between the means and the end is accessible through such a means.

By this reasoning, since it is possible for [the Veda] to have as its object the necessity of performing a sacrifice based on a result—provided that it falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition—who indeed in the world is capable of postulating an unseen independence for the word? Therefore, *niyoga* (an injunction) is exactly equivalent in meaning to *praiṣa* (a command) and the like; just as there is *niyoga* in worldly commands and in Vedic ones, and that is a means of valid cognition—
It should be understood that this [reasoning] applies equally to that which falls within the scope of an injunction; thus, what we have stated is the answer to the question "From where?"— namely,
"Because [the object] is perceived while existing."
Thus the answer has been given in the Bhāṣya. But if the text is explained in this manner, then the passage beginning with "animals are not perceived" would be meaningless.

Whether the objects [of perception] are apprehended or not apprehended, the point to be proven is simply this: that verbal cognition is dependent upon other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and that is already established. For what purpose, then, is the subsequent argument regarding the non-perception of a result (*phalānupalabdhi*) put forward?
1. And because of the fruit—ga.
2. It is desired—ga.
3. Herein lies the probandum—ga.
4. Furthermore, he states the rebuttal: "This much is indeed to be proven; and by whom was it said that anything else is to be proven?"
By which [reason] there would be a refutation? Here, another says: "In that case, the presentation of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is not tenable, because it is purposeless."

Thus it has been said. As for the objection raised regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*), it is not the case that it is untenable; rather, it is indeed tenable. For this reason, the text is intended to show that validity must be asserted through an investigation into the existence of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
The meaning of this is as follows:
this statement of validity based on the non-perception of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is intended to demonstrate dependence upon other means of knowledge;
for the validity of that which is independent is indeed established even when other means of knowledge are not perceived, by virtue of its own autonomy.

And for that which is dependent [on something else], its validity is contingent upon another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). That other means of knowledge would exist only if the result followed immediately after the action; in the absence of such a result, this matter cannot be understood through another means of knowledge.
Therefore, it is indeed logical that what depends on such [another means] lacks validity. Consequently, if the purpose of this [text] is to demonstrate dependence upon another means of knowledge...

There is nothing inconsistent in this treatise. Now, one might ask: even if there is dependence on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why would it be invalid due to the absence of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others? To that, he says: "And that other means of valid cognition is seen here. By the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), perception is intended here.
The [passage] beginning with "kṣādi" is stated. But how, then, is there an understanding of perception here?
The meaning is: how is it understood that perception alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this case? Because the result occurs immediately after the action.

Because whatever is a result occurs immediately after the action; and the status of being a means (sādhanatva) for that which exists immediately after the action is indeed cognizable through the means of perception (dṛṣṭapramāṇa). How then is this the case with agriculture and the like?

If every result occurs immediately after the action, then how is it that in agriculture and similar activities, the result is not obtained immediately, but is instead realized after a lapse of time? To this, the answer is: Is it not observed that the result of agriculture and so forth does indeed follow immediately?

Because you speak thus, he says in a single passage: "Is it that the fruit of action is not understood, or [is it] the non-attainment of the intermediate fruit? Another says: "Or [is it] that... [The word] "tat" is omitted; [the reading] "uta" is in manuscript *ga*.

[Page 128] Regarding "the fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*), he speaks again in a single passage: first, the splitting of the constituent parts of the earth is the fruit of action (*kriyāphala*).
It is not understood that [the result] follows immediately;

for even in the case of agriculture and the like, the fruit does not follow immediately. However, the production of rice is the purpose (*prayojana*), because human activity is directed toward that end. And thus, the definition of purpose as stated by Akṣapāda is: "That with reference to which an action is performed..."
"That which proceeds is the purpose. Furthermore, it is not said that [the purpose] is unseen simply because its purpose is not perceived.

For if we were to say that a purpose is "unseen" by us simply because it is not perceived immediately following [the action], meaning it is devoid of any observed means of valid cognition—as in the case of painting and the like—then we would be subject to reproach whenever we state that a purpose exists only immediately after an action, as in the question:

"How then is it so in the case of agriculture and the like? However, we do not say this based on the mere non-perception of a result; rather, we say it because there is no deviation [between the action and its result] in those cases.

"But surely, even in this case, cattle might be obtained at a later time, just as grain is obtained; to this he replies: for here, it is understood that the purpose and the result are indeed the cattle themselves, since no other result is observed.
But is there not a modification of the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*) and so forth?"

Regarding this, he says: "And whatever sacrificial oblation (havis) or modification thereof is perceived, that cannot—unlike the [grinding] of flour and so forth—be said to be the cause of the animal for the production of rice and the like, because it is not observed.
The meaning of this is: although it is seen in this way, nevertheless...

It must be stated that the animals themselves arise immediately [after the sacrifice], because their production at a later time is impossible— given that the ritual action has perished and the modification of the oblation is not conducive to their production; just as plowing is the cause for the growth of grain,
and from that alone its production occurs, therefore, since the fruit arises immediately and the animals constitute that fruit.

In this regard, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) has been observed; therefore, it is established that in its absence, there is a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). He concludes the point already proven:

"Therefore, those who desire to know *dharma* must investigate only other means of valid cognition here, and not derive the understanding of *dharma* from Vedic study alone. But how can there be the perception of something presently existing in [injunctions] such as "one who desires heaven"?
Regarding heaven:
1. "That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose (prayojana)"—this is the reading of the printed Nyāyasūtra.

2. Omitted. It is not possible [to say] that it does not exist, because the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is to be understood through means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that have not yet been perceived; and consequently, regarding the injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), etc., [it follows that they are authoritative].

[The opponent argues: "Validity [of the Veda] would exist independently. To this, the reply is as follows: First of all, the very nature of an injunction (*niyoga*) has been subverted in the case of animals and so forth; and it is an established principle that this single injunction is differentiated according to the differences in its constituent elements (*anubandha*).
Therefore, it follows that in every instance, [the injunction] is dependent upon something else.
The meaning of this is as follows: First of all, the mandate (*niyoga*) does not possess the quality of being an instigator (*niyojakatva*).

Since it is precisely the fact that actions are means to a result—cognizable through other means of knowledge—that acts as the instigator of action, and since the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth merely restate that [fact], when it was stated regarding animals and the like, then because the mandate is one and the same in the case of heaven and so forth as well, there would be no distinction in the entitlement (*adhikāra*).
1. *sthitam*. (ga) 2. *janakatvaṃ nāsti*; *tena*. (ga) [p. 130]

A word that is differentiated merely by its connection with an object does not possess the power to enjoin [an action] everywhere; therefore, because it is dependent even in that case, it follows that "every word is dependent. Consequently, where another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) exists, let it be so in that instance.

Furthermore, it lacks validity because it is merely reiterative. Where there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), let there be no suchness (*tathātva*) either; how much less, then, can there be validity? Therefore, it was rightly said: "But the word is not a means of valid cognition."

Thus [it is said], because there is an absence of validity in every respect. Here, the fundamental reasoning is that dependence is established by the observation of reliance on another; however, the fact of apprehending what is already present is merely an additional argument for that very dependence.
It is established that even in the case of the injunction for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), there is a lack of authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*) because of its dependence [on other factors].
1. *mātre* is read as *bhinnasya* in manuscript Ga.

Having recited the commentary beginning with "And some Vedic [passage] contradicts perception" and ending with "Thus, a statement of this kind that is contradicted by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not authoritative," he raises an objection: "But how is this contradicted by the means of valid cognition? It is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)."

This is so; furthermore, all contradictions with valid means of knowledge found in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have been explained as being figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*), according to the principle: "But it is a figurative description."

Thus, by means of the Sūtra. Now, if the intention is that "the explanatory passages (arthavādas) have not yet been explained by resorting to figurative interpretation (guṇavāda)," this is the talk of a fool; for it is not the case that the meaning already stated, or that which is being stated now, [is different from what was previously stated].

And this is merely an illustration of what is about to be stated: it is logical to raise an objection against that which is established and supported by reasoning; yet, if that [established position] were already settled, then the statement in the Bhāṣya—that even the figurative praise (guṇavāda) is established—would be untenable, because no specific distinction has been stated elsewhere.

However, when there is a specific statement, an implication for the sake of that very specific statement is appropriate; here, that is not the case. For if a specific distinction between what has been said and what is being said were intended, everything would become unstable, as everything would be useful in every context where it is about to be stated.

Because it would result in the impossibility of the designation [of the self as non-existent]. Therefore, since [the self] is established, its very establishment is the reason for whether something is expressible or inexpressible. Furthermore, regarding the contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that was raised here and which has been resolved by resorting to figurative description (*guṇavāda*), [it remains as follows:]

Furthermore, in that section concerning the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), the presentation [of the objection] beginning with "because of contradiction with scripture and what is seen" (*śāstradṛṣṭavirodhāt*) is not appropriate. The resolution is:
1. *syānyathopapannasya* (it would be for that which is established otherwise). Ga.
2. "iha tat" is omitted in Ga. 3. "atra" is omitted in Ga. 4. "virodhādyapanyāsaḥ" [is the reading] in Ga.
It is said: while the interpretation of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) remains established, this statement is raised as an objection.

Because here, as stated, that which is expressed by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) does not constitute a mere figurative description (*guṇavāda*). By the word "possessor of sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhī*), the Self itself is denoted through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and regarding its journey to heaven with the intention of [its] qualification, this quality-based description—which consists of secondary indication based on the intention of applying a word for one thing to another—is not possible. Why? Because of the quality...
For [this cognition] does not arise through the power of the apprehension of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
as in the case of "a hamlet on the Ganges. And here,
the apprehension by another means of valid cognition occurs only with respect to the body.
Since there exists nothing whatsoever apart from the body,
because such [a self] is not perceived; that body, being perceptible, is designated by the word "this" and is said to "go."

This is contradicted by the fact that the body is being burned. Therefore, whether through the injunction (*vidhi*) by examining the injunction, or through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) by examining the explanatory passage, it is determined that the statement is indeed not in accordance with reality. By this [is meant] the application of another example—

The person [as the agent] has also been shown. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that while an injunction (*vidhi*) exists, a suspicion of independence might still arise even from the sense of necessity (*niyoga*); however, in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), even that suspicion does not exist: "Nor is there an injunction such as 'he goes'..."
"The word [is the means of knowledge].
The meaning of this is that, according to the view of injunction (*vidhi*), because the mandate (*niyoga*) is not the object of any other means of knowledge, it is independent.

There might even be a suspicion [of untruth] regarding an injunction; however, in the case of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because its object is already established, there is a dependence on other means of knowledge for that which is established—this is due to the intention [of the author].
For qualities (*guṇavāda*) do not arise by virtue of being perceived through other means of knowledge.
3. And that body. Ga. 4. For in the case of the [positive] alternative (vidhipakṣa). Ga. 5. *ca* added. Ga.
Because there is no dispute, even that independence, though it might be suspected, does not exist; thus, "nor does it go."

It is established that the author of the Bhāṣya makes this clear by this [statement]. It is said: "The relation of a word with its meaning is not dependent on another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). What then? It is innate (autpattika).
By this passage, [the author] demonstrates [this point].

He begins to resolve the objection stated previously: For if the relationship between a word and its meaning—the relation of signifier and signified—were dependent upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then in sentences such as "The Citrā sacrifice [is to be performed]," the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth would express a state of being an action (*kāryatā*) based on the fact that the means to a result has been experienced through another means of valid cognition; in that case, there would indeed be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). However, in the case of the innate (*autpattika*)...
However, if the capacity to denote were inherent and independent, then validity would be logical because the determination of the object occurs through its own autonomy.
But surely, in the world, every word is observed to depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Just as it is in the world...

And since there is cognition [of its meaning] in the Veda, its authority is dependent [on other means of knowledge]. This is true regarding conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), but not regarding denotation (*abhidhāna*).

The meaning of this is as follows: in conventional usage, characterized by the employment of words, dependence on other means of knowledge for the object is indeed true; however, [it is not so] in the case of denotation.

Since the world employs words based on [conventional] understanding, there is no dependence [on other means of knowledge] in the act of denotation itself, because the meaning is expressed through the word's own inherent power (*svaśakti*). Nor does such dependence in worldly usage introduce a defect into the Veda, because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*); for it is a person who requires the apprehension of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) before employing a word. In its absence, however, there is no such dependence. How so?

Furthermore, there is no dependence on further verbal expression [to establish meaning]; regarding this, he says: "And just as in the world verbal expression is innate (*autpattika*), so we shall explain in the *Sambandhaparihāra*.
If the relationship were of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), there would be a state of dependence.

When, however, he will state its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*), then its independence (*anapekṣatva*) will be established. [Objection: But has not this entire meaning of the Sūtra already been explained in the very *Autpattika-sūtra*? It is merely restated here.
By this [statement], the redundancy [is avoided];
for when there is the capacity for meaning,
there is dependence upon the expression of that meaning.
[Page 135] He said: "The reply is: 'True, it was restated in order to state a specific distinction. But what specific distinction is stated here?"

He demonstrates this: "But surely there is no relation at all"—having thus raised again the very objection stated previously, he offers a further resolution: "But surely this meaning of the sentence has been refuted because it is perceived as something already existing.
The Mīmāṃsakas, however, maintain that the innate nature (autpattikatva) pertains to the word.

Therefore, the meaning is that because their objects are distinct, the objection and its refutation are unrelated. What is the use of this speculative discourse by one who has not served a teacher and who advocates the theory of "the connection of what is already expressed" (*abhihitānvaya*)? For whatever is cognized from something is the meaning of that thing; and [meaning] is not [cognized] from a word alone by an elder...
In common usage, the comprehension of some meaning is observed; and it is difficult to maintain the claim that there is a relationship with a meaning that is not being comprehended.
By this passage, an objection regarding the subject matter of the sentence is raised, as is the [objection] concerning its innate nature (*autpattikatva*).

The resolution is that [the meaning] pertains exclusively to the sentence; for a single word alone does not produce the cognition of a meaning, because such a capacity is absent in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).

This is because linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) occurs only through the denotation of its own meaning as related to others, and since this relation (*anvaya*) depends on other meanings, it cannot be understood without other words. And since it depends on other words, it is established that the meaning belongs to the sentence alone.

It is the state of being expressive; not that of an isolated word alone. How, then, is this common understanding [of words] established? It is said that the innate relationship (*autpattikatva*) pertains to the word as a whole. Because it has not been studied under a teacher, it is stated to be rooted in error. Therefore, the innate relationship...
The relationship between the sentence and the meaning of the sentence.
1. And because of the non-hearing of another word.
Ga. 2. "Siddham" omitted. Ga. [p. 136]

This might be so: there is no connection whatsoever between a word and its object; how then could it be either human-made (*pauruṣeya*) or not human-made (*apauruṣeya*)? Why? If there were a connection with the object, then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (*kṣura*) and "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), one's mouth would be cut open or filled [respectively]. You, O proponent of established tenets (*siddhavādin*), speak thus with reference to a connection consisting of physical contact (*saṃśleṣa*).

The innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of the relationship is not what is being asserted; for relationships such as cause and effect, signifier and signified, basis and based, or kinship are simply untenable between a word and its meaning.
Having read the Bhāṣya, [the author] says "it exists" (*bhavati*).
Having supplied the word implied by the sense, he explains it: “This might be so,” meaning:
if the relationship were eternal.

By this, he shows that the *bhāṣya* passage "If the relation were eternal" [is introduced by] "This might be so. As for the meaning of the *ṭīkā*: the meaning of the *bhāṣya* sentence "This might be so" is as follows—"If the relation were eternal, then this [consequence] would follow"—thus it means. Now, once again...
1. By the proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin).
ga. 2. *Punaḥ* omitted. ga. [p. 137]
He explains word-for-word the commentary beginning with "It might be argued thus" (*syādetat*): this refers to what was stated in the concluding commentary, namely, "Therefore,
Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction" (*tasmāccodanālakṣaṇo dharmaḥ*).
Thus, why should this not be so? For, by the phrase "syādetadevam—
codanālakṣaṇo dharmaḥ," the word "etad" (this) refers to the proposition "syādetat" (it might be thus).
The meaning is that by hearing the word "iti" in the Bhāṣya, that which was previously introduced— namely, "Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction"—
is recalled. This would be so if [the connection] were with the sense.
By stating, through the passage concerning the utterance of the words "razor" and "sweetmeat," that there is an absence of this relation— which he calls "relation"—
the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates his acceptance of a relation characterized by conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*): "It is said with reference to a relation consisting of conjunction."

By this commentary [the author] states the objection: "By whom has this relation been accepted, such that it is presented here as something to be refuted—since its refutation would entail the absurdity of cutting open and then filling the mouth? He says this in a single continuous passage:
But surely, by the Mīmāṃsakas who maintain the independence of the word, this very relation— namely, that "the object is understood from the word"—
is accepted as the relationship between the signified and the signifier; it is not a physical conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), for such a thing is not admitted.
"Refutation" (*nirākaraṇa*) is a term for blindness;
it means "without prior investigation. He states the resolution:
"It is precisely this that is refuted here, namely, that 'the object is understood from the word.'"
Thus,
this is precisely the relationship between the signified and the signifier,
as stated in the Bhāṣya. (ga)
2. *Saṃśleṣasya* has been added. [p. 138] It is refuted. By what reason is it refuted? This is not tenable; the meaning is: "by this reason."
But how does the refutation of this [notion]—that "the object is understood from the word"—occur through the rejection of the relation of conjunction?
For the intention is that when one thing is rejected, another is not thereby rejected. It does indeed occur.
The reply is as follows: the meaning is that it has been refuted. Why? Because the knowledge of an object from a word is an effect that must have some cause.
In this regard, it cannot be said that this effect arises from the word alone by itself, just as [an effect] does not arise from the eyes and other sense organs alone.
The effect of the eye and so forth arises from the eye and so forth themselves; this [word] is likewise [not the cause]. Why?

Because it is not recognized upon the first hearing. He states this in a single passage: "If that were so, then in this case the very nature (svarūpa) of the word would not be the cause for the cognition of the object, just as the very nature of smoke and so forth is not the cause for the apprehension of fire and so forth."

What then? [The relationship] is characterized by coexistence and so forth. And this [relationship] is not perceived at all in the case of a word prior to the comprehension of its meaning, whereas in the case of smoke and the like, coexistence is perceived even before the inference. Therefore, for this reason—
By refuting other types of relationships between real entities (*bhūta*), the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakatā*), which is itself an effect, is thereby refuted.
If the refutation of the connection (*saṃśleṣa*) were based on its being a cause, then all relationships whatsoever would have to be refuted.
Why, then, is it said that [relationships] such as those of kinship (*yauna*) and so forth are not possible?

Merely demonstrating the non-existence of what has been established does not constitute a refutation. Refutation consists in sublation through reasoning, and that has not been performed regarding [the relationship of] blood-ties and so forth.
(Note: "na" was omitted in manuscript ka.)
2. "They do not exist at all.

For it was precisely the refutation of the *ṣaṣ* (the sixth) that was established as being with reason (*sahetuka*). Now, if this is the intention—that the six [objects], beginning with the female organ (*yoni*), are not perceived—then...

Thus, because they are not to be suspected [of being real], they are not refuted. He refutes this: Is their conjunction actually perceived, such that it could be refuted? For even that is not perceived. And so the commentator himself [says]: "The razor..."

By this passage, "at the utterance of the word *daka*," non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone is presented as the reason. Therefore, we do not understand by what specific distinction this conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) was presented by the author of the Bhāṣya as something to be refuted. Now, perhaps the intention is as follows:

The word possesses the quality of being the signifier (*gamakatva*), and the object possesses the quality of being the signified (*gamyatva*); and this [relationship] is observed elsewhere only between things that are conjoined (*saṃśliṣṭa*). Therefore, it might be suspected here as well that this same [conjunction] is the cause; thus, [the objection] is refuted. That is incorrect, because the relationship of signifier and signified is observed even between cause and effect when they are not conjoined; therefore, conjunction alone is not the absolute cause. Rather, [it arises] from the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
The sense is that those [theories] must also be refuted. Here, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that even the cause and effect, such as the threads and so forth, are in contact.
The meaning of this is: "Contact is pervasive everywhere."

For we observe a close union (*saṃśleṣa*) even between cause and effect—such as between the threads and the cloth, which constitute the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and between the conjunction of the threads, which constitutes the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the cloth. This [union] is not possible in the case of an instrumental cause (*nimitta*);
this state of being closely joined does not exist in the instrumental cause, such as the weaver.

It is possible. Nor is it the case that weavers and the like are not causes, for there is no difference in the fact that the effect exists when they exist. Furthermore, they are to be understood as such because the effect is observed [to arise from them]. Therefore, comprehension does not result exclusively from conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), but rather from other types of relations as well. Consequently, this entire refutation of the relation of mere conjunction appears to be nothing more than a blind path. To this, he states the rebuttal: "It is said."
1. Omitted by the author of the Bhāṣya. (ga) 2. Therefore, it is not even exclusively [the case]. (ga) 3. Omitted "it is said. (ga)
In this regard, some proponents of the theory of the innate connection (*autpattika*) maintain that a word conveys its meaning by superimposing its own essential form (*svarūpa*) upon it.

The grammarians indeed maintain that words themselves, superimposed in the form of objects, are understood from the word; and they have stated the reasoning for this: "The very form of the word is that which appears as the transformation into an object."

This form of the object is the very nature of the word; therefore, the object consists of the superimposition of the word. And the reason for the form of the object being of the nature of the word is precisely the identity of their designations. Consequently, it is for the purpose of refuting that [view] that this refutation of conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is stated. Therefore, according to that position, the relationship between word and meaning is conjunction itself, in the form of identity (*tādātmya*).

This conjunction [of the word and its object] is not tenable because the effect [of such a union] is not perceived; thus it was said: "Upon the utterance of the words 'razor' or 'sweetmeat,' the mouth would be cut or filled.
If there is no identity [between the word and the object], how then can one say, "This is a cow"?
Thus, is the designation of word and meaning identical? To this, he states the resolution: "This designation exists, but it was stated by them [the Grammarians] alone. (Variant reading: *ga.*)
2. Because. Ga. 3. Here is the refutation. Ga. [p.

We shall state the refutation [of the view] that [the application of a word] is produced by superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in the *Ākṛti* section. By the statement, "But relations such as consanguinity (*yauna*) and so forth are untenable for a word," he demonstrates his non-acceptance [of those views].
He does not designate any single relation here that is worthy of being designated.

By stating that the relationship between the signifier (*pratyāyaka*) and the signified (*pratyāyya*) is characterized by the relation of name and named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-lakṣaṇa*), the proponent (*siddhāntin*) further reinforces its innate nature (*autpattikatva*). He asks: "If the word is a signifier, why does it not cause comprehension when heard for the first time?"

Thus says the Bhāṣya; regarding this, the author of the Ṭīkā clarifies the intended meaning: for the activity of all entities occurs by their own nature, just as the eyes and other organs function in the perception of form;
indeed, all entities proceed toward the performance of their respective effects.

The sense organs, such as the eye, function by themselves in the apprehension of form; however, a word does not function by itself upon first hearing because it does not convey meaning at that time. Therefore, it is understood that it must be set in motion after some connection has been established. Consequently, since a word is dependent for the comprehension of its meaning, why would it not convey it when heard for the first time?
This has been stated by the commentary with the words "yatīti" (it goes), namely: "In all cases, our perception is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
[Regarding] natural things, [this applies] by their very nature.
(Note: *ākṛti* was omitted in manuscript *ga*.)
2. "Evam" means non-acceptance.
3. From the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), [it arises] by itself (*svataḥ*). 4.
Having established a connection (*sambandha*) with that which is connected (*sambandhin*), it proceeds (*pravartate*).
[Page 142] Thus,
for those things that produce effects independently of human effort, both dependence and independence are understood through observation alone;
for it is observed that although the eye and other organs possess their own inherent nature, they depend upon light for the perception of form, as in the case of fire.

Furthermore, fire and the like are independent [of human effort]. Therefore, at the first hearing, there might be a sense of mere dependence [on something else] because the meaning is not yet fully established, but it would not be a dependence on human exertion. This is what was stated: “In all cases, our observation is the authority.”

For it is observed that in those cases the effect is independent of human effort because no person [as its agent] is perceived; yet it is dependent [on such effort] because there is no comprehension upon the first hearing, whereas comprehension occurs through a subsequent application. What, then, is the intention of the challenger when he asks: "If it does not cause comprehension when heard for the first time, then is it a product?"
By this, he objects to the commentary. With a single passage, he says:

"If the intended meaning is merely that [the word] is produced and is an effect, and not that it is conventional—i.e., set in motion by human convention—then one is proving what is already established. Why? Because verbal [cognition] is indeed independent of other persons and other cognitions."

For one who speaks of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what is intended is [the status of being a means] as in the case of the eyes and so forth with respect to the apprehension of form; however, [the status of] having an origin (*utpattimattā*) is not accepted [as the definition].

1. [The reading] *kāryakāriṇām anapekṣya* (those which produce an effect without depending [on anything else]) is found in manuscript Ga. 2. [The reading] *tatpuruṣaprayatnānapekṣitvam* (the state of not depending on the effort of that person) is found in manuscript Ga.
3. ...-ness [does not apply] to one who asserts that sound is not a means of valid cognition.
ga. 4. *api* has been added.
For a relation indeed arises, because it has action as its core; and since action is subject to origination, the relation that follows it must also be subject to origination.
He states this very point again in a single passage: "Now, [the relation] is produced, like that between a rope and a jar."

The intention is that [the relation] is produced by human effort. That is incorrect; for even though the eye and other [senses] sometimes fail to produce their effect when light is absent and produce it when light is present, the relation [of the sense organ to its object] does not depend on another person’s cognition or another cause.
Likewise, the relation of the word would also be [independent].
Therefore, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "If it is produced, then... appears as if it were incompetent or powerless in its departure from the established tenet;
yet this is not incompetent. This is its intended meaning:

This hearing of the second [syllable] and so forth is not equal to illumination (*udyotana*) and the like; for even illumination has this as its function, namely, being a benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) corresponding to that [hearing].
1. *tadanurūpa*. ka. [p. 144]

It is indeed to be attained [through inference], because, just as in the case of the eyes and other senses, cognition is preceded by non-cognition and yet the effect [of cognition] is observed. Furthermore, the eyes and so forth do not function as cognizers by being themselves previously known as cognizers; therefore, that is appropriate in their case. But regarding the word, you must state this: "The cognition of meaning is itself preceded by the cognition of meaning," because in linguistic usage one says, "This is its meaning."

Having understood this from the word, one then comprehends the meaning. Furthermore, as long as comprehension has not yet arisen, the cognition "this is its meaning" does not occur. Therefore, you must admit that comprehension is necessarily preceded by comprehension.
This must be explained. However, this is not tenable, because it is precisely the cause of comprehension that is being investigated.

Nor is it logical to claim that comprehension itself is the cause of comprehension, as that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, since another cause must be sought, it is appropriate to conclude that in the case of cows and other such objects, it is the convention (*samaya*)—as observed in the case of Devadatta and others—that is the cause of the cognition of meaning. And thus it has been stated by Kīrti:
“Whatever kind [of effect] is established from whatever [cause], it is understood as distinct from that [cause], like fire and wood;
even though another cause is unperceived, it is recognized as being specific.”

Thus he says this: "Therefore, the comprehension of meaning is preceded by another relation; thus, its dependence is established. By the word *kṛtaka* (produced), either conventionality or the state of being produced is expressed. When this meaning is set forth—
If that which you intend is [the case], then this restriction of usage—namely, "this word is to be employed by me"—is *samaya* (convention);
the relationship between word and meaning established by that is *sāmayika* (conventional). And in that view:
Having perceived the intention to convey a meaning through the employment of a word, one subsequently gains knowledge of its capacity;
this is the convention (saṃketa) of a person, namely that "this is the meaning of this word. It is intended that the relationship is "made" (kṛtaka), being produced by that [person].
In that view, however, the knowledge of the object arises from the word alone. And in both of these views, because they depend upon human effort, [the Veda] is not [eternal].
1. Omitted "na ca. 2. "tasyā nimittā-" (ga).
3. The cause for the comprehension of meaning.
ga. 4. —even by this.

Since the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda is preceded by that [human agency], the Vedas themselves must be of human origin. And since persons communicate a meaning only after having understood it through other means of knowledge, there is a state of dependence. Consequently, the injunction (codanā) lacks authority; such is the established objection.
Thus ends the objection regarding the relationship [between word and meaning].
Now, as for the question "What is the word in the case of 'cow' (gaur)?"—what is the meaning of this question? It implies a state of dependence.

When the opponent has stated that verbal testimony (*śabda*) lacks authority, what is this question? Now, it is the proponent’s turn to establish his own position (*siddhānta*), yet this is not yet the commencement of that final conclusion. For instance: “The venerable Upavarṣa [says] that [the word ‘go’] consists of the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga.”
Thus might be the reply of the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*); but that is untenable.
Therefore, this question is improper. This is the question: if a word makes its meaning known through non-modification (*apariṇati*), then what exactly is intended by the term "word"?

In this regard, the true nature of the matter is as follows: when the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) has been defeated by the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin), the grammarian (vaiyākaraṇa) interrogates the very siddhāntin: "By you, who reject a relationship characterized by conjunction (saṃśleṣa) yet accept the relation of the signifier and the signified (pratyāyyapratyāyakabhāva), it is accepted that a word conveys its meaning through non-modification (apariṇati)."

[Objection: It has been refuted; yet, if you accept this [position], what kind of "word" (*śabda*) do you intend? It cannot be of the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), because the comprehension of meaning from them is impossible. Therefore, a word that is not of the nature of phonemes must be accepted; and its identity with the object is not contradictory. Thus, let a relationship characterized by "fusion" (*saṃśleṣa*) be accepted. And in that case, it would also be innate (*svābhāvika*).

Since the relation is established, its independence is also established. Therefore, let the relation characterized as that between the signified and the signifier be abandoned. Thus, this question is appropriate. He says in a single passage: "That which is delimited by the sense of hearing is intended to be sound."
Now the proponent says: "Om" is uttered.
1. This, Ka.
2. Not when the proponent has been defeated.
(ga) 3. *ca* omitted. (ka) 4. *bhavataḥ* added. (ka)

[Page 146] For if it is accepted, one says "yes" (*om*); that is to say, by that it is accepted. Because in common worldly usage, the word "sound" (*śabda*) is well-known to refer to an object grasped by the sense of hearing; and those [phonemes], the *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya*, are indeed grasped by the sense of hearing.
Therefore, those very [phonemes] are the words. But if this is so, the cognition of meaning is not possible.
Why? Because phonemes occur sequentially.

And because their perceptions are momentary; furthermore, the determination of words and so forth occurs through being perceived, not through mere existence. Therefore, the cognition of meaning is untenable.
The meaning of this is as follows: first, the phonemes...

They establish the object as being merely existence (*sanmātratā*), because, due to its omnipresence and eternity, the cognition of the object occurs everywhere and at all times. However, in the view that [the word] is perceived, there is no capacity to convey the meaning in each individual instance, nor in their collective totality, because perceptions occur sequentially; and sequential perceptions cannot result in a stable, simultaneous perception of the object.

[Page 147] There is no conjunction (*sāhitya*) among them, because they are momentary. Nor is there any other mode of existence distinct from those modes; thus, the cognition of an object is untenable. Now, if the intention is this: even upon the destruction of the perception, through the assistance of its memory—
Regarding the phrase "the comprehension of meaning":

its meaning is this—although cognitions cannot occur simultaneously due to their momentariness, nevertheless, the phonemes, aided by the recollection of them, will bring about comprehension. Furthermore, that recollection does not have all [the phonemes] as its object.
Like the apprehension; for it follows the apprehension.

The meaning of this is: that memory, too, does not have all [the letters] as its single object; just as the apprehension has each individual letter as its object, so too does that [memory], because [it arises] from the apprehension.

An impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced, and from that impression comes memory; therefore, just like perception, memory has each individual phoneme as its object, and thus it does not have all the phonemes as its object. Nor can there be a comprehension of meaning from memories that have each individual phoneme as their object—even if those memories arise simultaneously through the simultaneity of impressions—because this would also occur when the phonemes are uttered in a reversed order.

Furthermore, because there is no distinction in simultaneity regarding the recollection of phonemes through the simultaneous occurrence of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that there is a simultaneous cognition of their respective meanings. For this reason as well, the comprehension of meaning is not possible [through the sequence of phonemes]. Therefore, those learned in the science of words have stated that this very reality of sound (*śabdatattva*) manifests itself as the form of the object (*artharūpatayā vivartate*).

Since the word, which transcends the individual phonemes, is apprehended through its effect, there is no contradiction with experience in the claim that it manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of the object. For if the word were identical in nature to the phonemes, the fact that cows and other objects possess that [unitary] form would contradict direct perception. Alternatively, on the theory of manifestation, the cognition of the word’s own form or of the object would occur independently of the operation of the auditory organ and other senses.
Can it be said [that this is not the case]?

The meaning of this is as follows: even for the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*), it must be admitted that the cognition of either the nature of the word or its object depends upon the operation of the auditory organ and other senses. That [cognition] presents the forms of both the word and the object as if they were distinct. If...

If it were admitted that cognition occurs independently of the operations of the ear and other senses, then indeed there would be illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); however, since such [independence] does not exist, the position of illusory manifestation is also untenable. To this, the reply is: "Certainly;
it can be explained with great clarity."
For sounds and the like, although they are of a single nature, appear as if they were of multiple natures due to the delimitation by the auditory organ and so forth.
The meaning of this is: 1. *sarvavarṇa* (all phonemes), [as found in] manuscript Ga.
2. Because of that consequence.
ga. 3. Omitted. hi. ka. 4. Added. ca. ga.
5. They appear. Ga.
148] Although in the ultimate sense there is no difference, nevertheless, due to the influence of limiting conditions such as the ear and so forth, a cognition of difference arises.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In emeralds, rubies, and so forth, even a single face appears as if it were of many forms;
likewise, it will be so here as well. But surely, in the case of swords and such, there is a single perceiver?
The visual faculty; for swords and the like are merely limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
By virtue of that single [adjunct], one says "one face."

Thus it can be said that [the objects] are distinct, and it can also be said that these distinctions are based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). But in this case, what is the single apprehender of sound and the rest, by virtue of which the distinction created by the limiting adjuncts such as the ear is described as "this is indeed one and the same reality"?

If it is argued that the various sense-faculties, such as the ear and so forth, exist as distinct only by virtue of being mere limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) to a single grasper, and that distinction [among objects] occurs due to their influence—
then the following reply is given: What is this nonsensical claim that a single object exists by virtue of a single grasper?
In this case as well, the face is not one by virtue of a single perceiver; rather, it is one precisely because of its oneness,
since it is perceived as a unity.
[Objection: You [assert] that; therefore, because they are perceived here as a unity, sound, form, and so forth must be one. [Reply: But was it not already stated that unity itself is not perceived?
For the ear and other senses are the causes of perception, and they exist only as distinct entities.
They produce cognitions; when there is a difference in cognition, the statement "this is one and the same object" is difficult to maintain.
How then, in the case of a sword and so forth, does the thought "this is that very same face" arise?
Thus? Can it be said that the distinction [between reflections] is based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) because of the recognition of their form as the original object (*bimba*)?
The meaning of this is: how is there a manifold appearance within the limiting adjuncts?

Even though there is the certainty that "this is that very same face," there would nonetheless be a difference; for if there were recognition of the form of the original object (*bimba*), then one could say that the difference is based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), but not otherwise.
1. *Marataka*. Ka.
149] Reply: In that case, you yourself have stated their identity (*ekatva*).
For by you, in asserting that "on account of recognition there must be oneness," oneness has been stated. Why? Because of recognition, since everywhere there is the cognition, "This very same face.

In that case, given the mutual contradiction between difference and non-difference, and because difference can be accounted for even through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), non-difference alone is the ultimate reality.

It is determined. [Objection: But let this be so in the case of the mouth; how is it so in the case of sound (*śabda*) and the rest? To this he says: "And this oneness exists even in sound and the rest.
From the identical designation of both the genus (*jāti*) and the word (*śabda*) as "this is a cow" (*gaur ayam*), there is the comprehension of their oneness.
In the cases of "this is white" regarding color and sound, or "fragrant sandalwood" regarding odor and substance— both of which are pairs consisting of a quality-word and a substance-word—
it is therefore established that because there is recognition of identity here as well, this distinction is based solely on the auditory organ and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding all words, there is first a single cognition, namely, "word, word," while the difference [perceived] is due to the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*). Because the genus (*jāti*) and other properties of a word are designated identically, there is non-difference; however, difference arises through the influence of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as the auditory organ. Thus, it is logically established.
[The opponent] objects here: "What is the basis for the distinction between the auditory organ and the others?
The intention here is this:

according to your view, the entire world is of a single nature; therefore, how can there be a distinction even among the auditory organ and the rest? [This objection arises from the perception of] a difference in objects.
We say it is due to the binding of the faculties (*pattinibandhana*).
The meaning is that there is a distinction among the ear and the other senses because of the distinction in their functions. What is the basis for the cognition of the distinction between objects?

The meaning is: what is the cause for the cognition of the difference among the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth? It has just been stated that the distinction between the auditory organ and the others is the basis. This being the case, a circular argument (itaretarāśrayatā) is asserted.

And that [objection] is not tenable. Indeed, it has been rightly said: "This mutual dependence is a mere *mātṛkā*. It is like a *mātṛkā* (a mnemonic matrix). For if there were no inconsistency whatsoever, this would be so.
It would be knowledge alone; ignorance (*avidyā*) is that which has an untenable object. For this very reason, it is called "ignorance" by the wise.
Precisely because [it is so], at no time here... (anupapanna).
2. By the Buddhas. Ka. [p.
150] It is established. Therefore, only the theory of evolution (vivarta) is to be relied upon by those who know reality as the cause of comprehension.
Because the *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) theory is logically tenable. Thus, having established his own position and defeated the Mīmāṃsaka, the Grammarian challenges him:
"Therefore, the 'beloved of the gods' (the fool) does not know words, he who [asserts] a relationship between word and meaning that are established as separate entities (*yutasiddha*)."

He considers this to be the cause for the comprehension of meaning: that the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the signifier (*vācaka*).
What, then, is this so-called "impression"? If it is first of all the comprehension of the phonemes themselves, then it is that which is refined (*saṃskriyate*).

[The opponent argues: "By the etymological derivation ‘that by which the nature capable of cognizing an object is produced,’ [the sense-organ is established as the cause]. This has been refuted; for even its status as a cause for the apprehension of an object is not possible, since it was stated that there is no simultaneity. Now, if the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is memory, [it is distinct] because its essence is different from [the cognition]. Thus [it is said]. (ga)
2. pratyāyaka. ga. 3. anayeti. ka. 4. tasyā na. ka.

[Page 151] Here it is said: memory is also exactly like that; just as perception is, so too is memory without a [corresponding external] cause, precisely because they do not occur simultaneously. Now, if...
On the grounds that the occurrence of memory would otherwise be inexplicable, it is postulated that there exists a certain specific entity that persists over time.
Memory occurs only with respect to an object that has been experienced, not one that has not been experienced; therefore, if there were no experience...

If one were not to produce some excellence (*atiśaya*) within oneself, then, because there would be no distinction between what has been experienced and what has not been experienced, memory would arise in both cases alike; yet it does not arise in both cases. Therefore, this memory, arising according to a fixed rule, postulates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience. And if that [impression], like the experience itself, were momentary, then at a later time—

Memory is not otherwise possible. Therefore, it is understood that there exists a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which persists over a period of time; by virtue of its stability, the simultaneity [of the perception of letters] becomes possible. To this, he replies: even that [impression] can be postulated as having each individual letter as its object, because the apprehension has each single letter as its object and because memory follows that [apprehension]. This is its effect.
And because of the [nature of] the mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

The meaning of this is as follows: since a mental impression produces the recollection of phonemes, it would become the cause for the cognition of meaning by bringing about the simultaneous apprehension of the phonemes in memory; yet that [impression] has only each individual phoneme as its object.

It does not have all the phonemes as its object. Why? Because impressions (*saṃskāras*) are deposited by perceptions, and those perceptions have only individual phonemes as their objects; therefore, by way of that cause, the impression has only a single phoneme as its object.
And so too is the effect. Furthermore, that which leads one to infer the existence of the impression also has only individual phonemes as its object.

Because memory follows upon perception; for that which has been perceived is remembered, not that which has not been perceived. And since the letters in their collective form have not been perceived, there can be no memory whose object is the collection of letters. Furthermore, because the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has that [perception] as its cause: "that which has that as its effect" is *tatkārya*; the state of being such is *tatkāryatva*; therefore [the impression arises from the perception]. This is what is meant.

It follows that the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), when postulated on the basis of memory, must be postulated as having each individual phoneme as its object, because it must conform to its effect. Therefore, like the perception of the phonemes themselves, this [impression] also is not the cause [of the cognition of the word].
Now, let it be the cause of memory.

The latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has each individual phoneme as its object; let it be something entirely distinct and unprecedented, produced by each phoneme, and the cause for the cognition of the meaning.
To this, he says:
there is no evidence that a latent impression exists which is devoid of the cognition of memory.

He will state that the effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning is established even through a transformation (*vivarta*). And he demonstrates that the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) has each individual phoneme as its object: "The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes, is the communicator [of the meaning]."

Thus speaking [the author] states that while the preceding phonemes generate the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the final phonemes do not; from this text, it follows that the phonemes acting in combination produce the impression.

It is understood that they do not initiate [an action]. Therefore, what additional capacity does the author of the Bhāṣya consider this [inference] to have in the comprehension of an object beyond perception and memory?
The point is that it possesses no additional capacity. Now, as for how...

The comprehension of meaning is untenable, and likewise, the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* is also untenable; because the *sphoṭa* is not manifested by each individual phoneme or sound (*dhvani*). Nor should it be said that it is not manifested at all, for that would entail the consequence that the cognition of meaning could arise from what has not been manifested. Nor is it manifested by them collectively, because a collective whole is impossible. Nor is it manifested part by part—

[The opponent argues: "Since there is no part [to the word], it is the individual [word] itself; therefore, let the comprehension of meaning arise directly from the phonemes themselves—what is the use of postulating the *sphoṭa*?
To this, he replies: "How could even the proponents of the *sphoṭa* explain how the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* occurs? This remains unanswered."
The proponent [of the final view] says: For the acceptance [of a position] is not the cause for the establishment of a fact. Indeed, that which is untenable remains untenable;
it does not become tenable merely through acceptance. Therefore, this text must be explained [otherwise]. Now...
The distinction lies precisely in its persistence over a period of time.

Perception and memory are momentary, whereas the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) persists for a period of time; therefore, it possesses an additional quality. That is not so; for if there is no mutual connection [between them], what will this persistence accomplish?

Why? Because that [cognition] is the cause of the recollection of each individual phoneme, and since recollections do not occur simultaneously, even its permanence does not serve as a useful factor. Now, if it is argued that the very comprehension of meaning is the cause for [establishing] the relationship;

The comprehension of meaning, being otherwise inexplicable, leads one to postulate a memory that has all the phonemes as its object simultaneously; and this memory, in turn, [depends on] the mutual [activation] of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The understanding of the meaning is itself the cause for the mutual connection of the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) in their collective activity. To this, the reply is:
in this way, a circular dependency (*itaretarāśrayatā*) results;
for only when the understanding of the meaning has been ascertained from the phonemes themselves does the mutual [connection] [occur].

The postulation of a relationship [between sounds and meaning] implies that the cognition of meaning must be asserted to arise from the phonemes themselves through their mutual connection; for the comprehension of meaning can be accounted for even by means of the *sphoṭa*. If it is argued that this mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatā) would not constitute a fault, as in the case of the proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*), we reply: no, such an admission is not tenable when the true nature of reality is being investigated. How then is it explained in cases such as the seed and the sprout?

If it is argued that "the sprout arises from the seed, and the seed from the sprout," and that even in that case there is no mutual dependence because it is observed to be so; [then we reply: 135.14–16. If it is said that this is because it is observed [to be so], then [we ask]: 135.17–18. Is it not the case that in the world, when one sees that a sprout has arisen from a seed, one does not see that the seed arises from that very same sprout? And when one sees that a seed has arisen from a sprout, one does not see that the sprout arises from that very same seed? Therefore, since it is not observed that the seed arises from the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Furthermore, 135.19–20. It is not the case that the seed is perceived as existing simultaneously with the sprout. For the seed is perceived as perishing at the very moment the sprout is arising. Thus, since the seed is not perceived as coexisting with the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Moreover, 135.21–22. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then the seed would be perceived as having the nature of the sprout. But since the seed is not perceived as having the nature of the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Furthermore, 135.23–24. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then the sprout would be perceived as having the nature of the seed. But since the sprout is not perceived as having the nature of the seed, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Finally, 135.25–26. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then both would be perceived as being produced by causes other than themselves. But since they are not perceived as being produced by causes other than themselves, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Therefore, since it is not observed that the seed arises from the sprout, and since the seed is not perceived as existing simultaneously with the sprout, and since the seed is not perceived as having the nature of the sprout, and since the sprout is not perceived as having the nature of the seed, and since both are not perceived as being produced by causes other than themselves, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Thus, it is established that there is no relationship of mutual dependence. 135.27–28. Furthermore, if it is argued that the relationship of mutual dependence exists because it is observed, then [we ask]: Is it not the case that in the world, when one sees that a sprout has arisen from a seed, one does not see that the seed arises from that very same sprout? And when one sees that a seed has arisen from a sprout, one does not see that the sprout arises from that very same seed? Therefore, since it is not observed that the seed arises from the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Furthermore, 135.29–30. It is not the case that the seed is perceived as existing simultaneously with the sprout. For the seed is perceived as perishing at the very moment the sprout is arising. Thus, since the seed is not perceived as coexisting with the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Moreover, 135.31–32. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then the seed would be perceived as having the nature of the sprout. But since the seed is not perceived as having the nature of the sprout, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Furthermore, 135.33–34. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then the sprout would be perceived as having the nature of the seed. But since the sprout is not perceived as having the nature of the seed, how can there be a relationship of mutual dependence? Finally, 135.35–36. If the seed were to exist simultaneously with the sprout, then both would be perceived as being produced by causes other than themselves. Thus, it is established that there
If it should be argued that the sprout is seen to arise from the seed and the seed from the sprout, and that there is no inconsistency in what is observed,
then here too such an observation can be stated:
for the comprehension of meaning is seen to follow the perception of the phonemes.

Therefore, this view is established; the meaning is that because there is the possibility of an alternative theory (vivarta) as a counter-position, and because the comprehension of an object can occur even from such an alternative theory.
For the comprehension of an object establishes the causality of the cause-in-general.
It is the cause-in-general that is the indicator.

However, [the self] does not become the cause for the connection with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). In the case of the seed and the sprout, however, it is logical because a specific causal relationship is observed:
we see that the sprout arises directly from the seed, and the seed arises from the sprout. But here, [in the case of the self], it is not so, because of the non-arising [of the self].
(Note: *utpatteḥ* is the reading in manuscript *ga*).
2. Added *ca*. ga. 3. *pratīti-* ga. 4. *sya* omitted. ga.

Because the formative factor (*saṃskāra*) has color as its object, the perception of a specific cause is not tenable due to its momentariness. Therefore, we consider the theory of transformation (*vivarta*) alone to be more reasonable.
Since the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) alone is more logically consistent, this [following] point is also untenable now.
What is untenable? "Both that [manifestation] and the conceptualization of sound. How is it untenable?
For in the case of illusory manifestation, what indeed is this "conceptualization of sound," given that [the object] possesses distinctions superimposed by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)?

It has been stated that there is a single reality cognizable by all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this claim—that an innate (*autpattika*) relationship is asserted even between two distinct things, namely word and meaning—is simply a lack of understanding of words.
For indeed, between two distinct things, the signified and the signifier—

A relationship characterized by [distinct] definitions must be accepted; yet, according to the reasoning already stated, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) asserts that such a relationship does not exist. To this it is replied: Indeed, even for one who maintains the doctrine of oneness, this distinction cannot be asserted—namely, that "this is the Jyotiṣṭoma" and "these two are the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

To the question "Why?", he says: For if there were unity, it would not be the case that there is stability in the unity of a single sentence alone; rather, all sentences would attain the status of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), just as phonemes [are unified] in a word, or words [are unified] in a sentence. Why? Precisely because of the cognition of unity; for indeed...
In all sentences—the word "word," the word "word"—there is a single cognition.
Therefore, the sentences themselves are indeed non-different.
And just like the sentences, the sentence-meaning does not differ. Regarding all sentence-meanings, there is the cognition: "sentence-meaning, sentence-meaning."
Thus, there is a single cognition; by virtue of that as well, unity is attained. Therefore, all this—namely, the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rituals—is said to be non-different.
(Omitted: ucyate. ga.)
2. It can be understood.
Ga. 3. *vākyārthaḥ* is omitted. Ga. [p. 155]

One would then incur [the fault of] over-extension (*prasaṅga*). And this cannot be accepted; thus he says: "And differences in qualification (*adhikāra*) are seen to be both contradictory and non-contradictory; the contradictory ones have contradictory results, and the non-contradictory ones have non-contradictory results.
In that regard:

The *kṛṣṇala-caru* and *sarvasvāra* sacrifices and others are contradictory, because of the contradiction between their two fruits—longevity and death; whereas the *agnihotra* and others are non-contradictory. And this multiplicity of meaning is not possible if the sentences were a single unity. He provides the solution: "True, this is not possible if there were a single meaning; however, these sentences have distinct meanings."

Because the distinction between the objects is directly perceived. Now, if it is argued that since the sentences are one, their meanings must also be one, he says in response: "And the unity [of the sentences] is for the sake of the comprehension of a single meaning."

Since the comprehension of meaning is impossible without syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), a single sentence is accepted; however, in this case, a single intended meaning is not perceived within these distinct sentences. Therefore, while it may be appropriate to deny the existence of words and phonemes within a single sentence, on what basis is another sentence denied?

Therefore, this objection regarding contradiction and non-contradiction is not tenable; for one who maintains the authority of verbal testimony refers by the word "word" to that which is connected with an object, and not even to the crowing of crows or similar sounds, though they too may be perceived by the ear.
1. And not contradicted by differences in form.
(vi. ga. 2) 2. Those which have different meanings but a single meaning. (ga. 3) 3. "Eka" omitted. (ga.)

4. Nor [is it a property] in non-distinct [things]. Ga. 5. For those who maintain that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition (*śabdapramāṇavādin*), the word is intended as the word itself, which possesses a connection with its object.

Therefore, due to the difference in objects, a difference in the words that convey those objects is logical. But surely, by describing the difference between the ear and other senses as being constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*), it has been stated that all this is born of ignorance. Why is this "half-old woman" argument (*ardhajaratīya*) being put forward—like saying one half is old and the other half is young? [This refers to the rule: "And [the suffix *cha* is added] after a compound whose object is that [ignorance]."

The suffix *cha* is used here in the sense of "as if" (*itivārthe*). In this case, there is indeed a distinction between the sentence and its meaning. To this, he replies: "The beloved of the gods (i.e., the fool) does not understand the intended meaning."
Since this non-difference has been stated in respect to Brahman—that is, in the state of being Brahman—by whom can difference be asserted on the basis of that very nature?

Or by whom can difference be denied on the grounds of its being the meaning of the scriptures, as one might deny the existence of the ears and other senses? The intention is that difference is based on ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is non-difference. He raises an objection again: "True, it is not denied."
There is a distinction made by you; however, ignorance (avidyā) results [as the consequence], whereas knowledge (vidyā) is intended as the Vedic meaning. Otherwise—
How can it be said that prosperity arises from ignorance? For ignorance is indeed the cause of transgression. He replies: True, as you have said; however, transgression is relative.

Even that which is slightly desired is called a transgression (pratyavāya) in relation to something else, just as heaven is [considered such] in relation to liberation because it is finite. Therefore, the entire collection of karma born of action leads only to transgression due to defects such as finitude. And that transgression is the purpose of the injunction (vidhi).

1. And since it is relative, it is established that there is a distinction even from those things which are superficially pleasing yet lead to no higher rebirth (*anabhyudaya*); thus he says: "But rather... [p. 157] *praty-*.
In one case, such as the killing of a Brahmin and so forth, there is only the means; in another case, there is both the means and the end.
This is the distinction regarding the Vedic purpose.
Therefore, no prior statement of non-difference here is contradicted by the subsequent statement of difference based on ignorance.

Now, if there is no identity between sentences and their meanings, then even though there is a distinction between sentences and their meanings, [how can it be reconciled with] the originative injunctions of ritual action such as, "One should offer the Agnihotra"?

The point is this: how can it be said that statements concerning qualities, such as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), are identical in meaning with [the injunctions] such as "he offers," when their meanings are distinct? It has been stated:
even though they are distinct, the accomplishment of a single performance is established.

For by such injunctions as "He offers with curd," a distinct performance is not enjoined in the manner of two separate applications, such as those for the obligatory and the optional Agnihotra. Just as in the case of the optional application of the Agnihotra and other rites...
And for that which is eternal, the accomplishment of a single performance is established. Therefore, everything is logical even in this view.
1. *tasmin*. (ga) [p. 158]
Now he begins the established conclusion (siddhānta): This might be so, if there were a single cognition;
for there is no single cognition here. But surely, in all words, there is a single cognition, namely, "word, word"?
And if there were no single cognition, then in the absence of that single cognition, even the status of being denotable by the word "word" would not apply to all words.

Just as the word "sound" does not apply to visible forms and the like, so too it would not apply to the phonemes *ga* and so forth. To this, he replies: for the state of being denotable by a single word arises from a single cause, and not from actual oneness.

The meaning of this is as follows: there is no single cognition (*ekākārā buddhi*) regarding individual phonemes (*varṇa*); for a single linguistic application (*ekaśabdapravṛtti*) does not occur without a single underlying cause (*nimitta*). And that cause is, in some cases, a universal (*jāti*), an action (*kriyā*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dravya*)—as in the examples "cow," "goer," "white," and "horned"; in other cases, it is simply the oneness of the object itself—as in the case of that very same [object].
Furthermore, regarding the application of the word "space" (ākāśa) to an object, one says "space, space"; yet its oneness is not the sole cause for this.

Therefore, because the application of the single word is not invariably [based on] oneness, a single cognition is not established. Anticipating the objection that—since there is no other cause—the very oneness of the thing's own nature must be the cause for the application of the single word, he says: "And here, the word..."
There is a single basis for the application of the term "sound" (śabda), namely, being perceivable by the auditory organ;

for it is well known in the world that the word "sound" is applied to an object grasped by the ear. Therefore, being perceivable by the auditory organ alone is the basis for the application of the term "sound. Nor is there any deviation [of this definition] due to properties such as "existence" (sattva) or "color-ness" (varṇatva), because existence and the like are not perceivable by the auditory organ; for indeed, existence—
We shall demonstrate immediately hereafter that there exists a universal such as "color-ness" (varṇatva) which is perceptible by the senses.
What, then, is the reason? The meaning is: for what reason? [This is according to the rule] "in the case of nimitta, kāraṇa, and hetu."

Thus, the first or second [case-ending] is used in the sense of the third and so forth. Here, "being perceptible by the ear" alone is taken—that is, accepted—as the cause (*nimitta*), and not, however, "cowness.
(Note: *tadā* and *a. ga.* are omitted).
