Is it accepted that "soundness" (*śabdatva*) alone is the cause? To this, the reply is: ignorance regarding the distinction between the general and the particular is indeed at fault in one who raises such an objection.

By objecting in this manner, it appears that you do not understand either the universal (*sāmānya*) or the particular (*viśeṣa*); for if one understood the universal or the particular, one would not object in such a way.
Furthermore, what kind of knowledge regarding universals and particulars is it that you ask me whether I lack? Regarding that—

He says: That universal (*sāmānya*) is that object regarding which, when a particular thing is perceived, there arises a reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) connected with previous perceptions—just as, for example, when distinct things such as a brindled cow and others are perceived, there occurs a recollection of the form previously seen, namely "cow, cow," and so on;
that universal, such as "cowness" (*gotva*), is that which has this [recollection] as its object. And here, "similar" (*samāna*)...

In order to demonstrate that there is no universal "flame-ness" (*jvālātva*) in flames that exist as a continuous series (*vartikāvartinīṣu jvālāsu*), the qualification "when the object is perceived" (*padārthagrahaṇe sati*) has been employed; for indeed, no differentiator of the flames is apprehended. Furthermore, we shall explain in the section on words (*śabdādhikaraṇa*) that even the cognition of unity in those cases is based on the non-apprehension of difference. Nor is there [unity] among the *ga*-sounds and so forth—
When there is the apprehension of one phoneme, there occurs a recollection of another phoneme;
the meaning is that there is no recollection of a form experienced in a different phoneme, as is the case with words such as *pācaka*.

Just as there is no single uniform cognition regarding many individuals who are cooks, so it is here as well. By this, the universals such as "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth are refuted; for there is no apprehension of a common form among genus, quality, action, and substance, since words such as "existent" (*sat*) function just like words such as "knowable" (*prameya*).
Because of its possibility. But what, then, is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "existent"? It is the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇasaṃbandha*).

[Objection: If that were so, then in the absence of such a connection with a means of valid cognition—that is, in a state where something is not being cognized by a means of knowledge—the cognition permeated by the word "existent" would not occur, as in: "the jar exists," "the jar existed," or "the jar will exist. Certainly not.

When the connection with the act of cooking (*pacikriyā*) is not understood, someone designates [the agent] as "a cook" (*pācaka*). However, even if this designation were to occur only after the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has functioned,
the threefold distinction would still not be tenable in all cases.
Because it has transcended its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be the expression "it was"; however, with respect to the great generality (*mahāsāmānya*) called existence (*sattā*),
because that [existence] has passed away, there is "it was."
Thus it is said: because it exists in the present, it is "existent" (*asti*); or [it is so called] because it is common to what is yet to come.

And because of this, it will come to be.
To this, the following response is given: Even for one for whom the universal is distinct—

If it is argued that even for that [universal], why would it ever waver or cease to exist, given that its substratum—the substance—is either being destroyed or is yet to be produced? What, then, is destruction? If you say it is simply the departure from existence (*sattā*), then this is well said: "the departure from existence results from the departure from existence. Alternatively, if destruction is the departure from one's own nature (*svarūpa*), then likewise for that which is to come...
If it is accepted that even the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) itself possesses the state of being (*bhāvitva*), then the existence of the intrinsic nature of entities also exists.
If that is admitted, then because that very [existence] pertains to the three times, it follows that [entities] "were," "are," and "will be."

Thus, the threefold designation is established. Furthermore, we deny "existence" (sattā) as a great universal (mahāsāmānya), but not even existence as an intrinsic nature (svarūpasattā). By this, the following argument is also refuted: that there could be no doubt regarding the existence of an object when all connections with means of valid cognition have ceased, because such a connection has been rejected and [existence] is defined by it.

Regarding "of existence" (sattāyāḥ): because when all operations of the means of valid cognition have ceased, it is the very nature [of the object] itself that is doubted. However, regarding the application of the word "existent" (sat) to the diverse natures of things, it is said that the cause is simply the fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition;
it is not, however, the actual connection with a means of valid cognition that is denoted by the word "existent," just as [the word "man"] applies to many individuals who are mutually distinct.

It is not untenable that the word "cook" (pācaka) is applied by virtue of the limiting condition (upādhi) of the act of cooking. He concludes the present topic: therefore, this denotability by the word "word" (śabda) is based solely upon action. Of what is this a transformation (vivarta), and of what do the ear and other [senses] become the limiting conditions?

Since a single entity appears as differentiated due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the auditory organ, let it be so postulated; for there exists a single reality. Therefore, this [claim that] "it evolves into the form of objects" is a mere mockery.
Thus [it is said].

However, it is appropriate in the case of the face and so forth, because all cognitions arise through the synthesis of the single form of the face within mirrors and other such objects. Precisely for this reason, there exists no cause for the apprehension of an object that serves as an antidote to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).

Therefore, based on the very effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning—which is otherwise inexplicable—the relationship of the mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) must also be postulated as having the nature of producing a single unified recollection; it does not [belong] to perception and memory, because an infinite regress would be observed.
1. Since all that is measured... (ka. kha.)

[Page 161] Since there is no distinction among the mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) produced by the individual experiences of each phoneme, and since they occur simultaneously, why would the cognition of meaning not arise from a recollection that has as its object all the phonemes combined? Likewise, even in the case of phonemes uttered by various persons, each single...

Is it because there is no difference between the perceptions? To this, first of all, this very answer must be stated: when a concomitance is postulated on the basis of an effect, it is only logical to postulate it exactly according to that effect; however, it is only the phonemes (*varṇa*) as apprehended in a specific sequence that are the cause of the cognition of meaning. It might be thought: [what of] the phonemes, which are by nature eternal and omnipresent?
Since there is an absence of temporal sequence (*kāla-nibandhana*) or spatial sequence (*deśa-nibandhana*), that [sequence] must be accepted as being based on perception (*upalabdhi-nibandhana*);
and since this single cognition consists of the recollection of everything, a sequence based upon it is not logically possible.
This, however, is incorrect; for it has been stated that this cognition consists of recollection. Therefore, its connection with the prior perception—

Considering the sequence of their occurrence, what is inconsistent about [the cognition] "it arises"? [Objection: But how can memory, which occurs in a single moment, manifest a relationship between a limit (avadhi) and that which has a limit (avadhimat)—a relationship that is non-different? [Reply: Because this memory has as its object various phonemes perceived in a sequential order. By this, the perception of a difference between words in cases such as *nadī* and *dīna* is explained, since that is established through the difference in sequence.

And thus, when [phonemes] are uttered with an interval, there is no comprehension of the meaning, because simultaneous recollection is absent. Furthermore, the statement in the Bhāṣya, "The final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes, is the expressive [unit]," is a provisional assertion (*anāsthāvāda*). This is the ultimate truth—

In all classes of words (*sarvavarṇa*), the cognition of meaning occurs only when they have ascended to the state of being remembered; for we shall explain that the theory of the denotation of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*) would otherwise be untenable. As for what was also said—that "it is improper to assume both [the word and its meaning] as conceptual constructs"—there too, it is simply a failure to understand the matter that constitutes the error; for this is what is stated therein:

The conceptualization of an attribute (*upādhi*) belonging to the ultimate reality itself, which is produced by words, is the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of a single entity that does not exist [as such]. This is what is meant by "that [conceptualization] and the conceptualization of words. 1. *dhir iyam*. (ga)
2. paryaṃ paryā-ga. 3. How is it divided? ga. 4. By means of discernment. ga.
5. *na* omitted in *ga*. 6. *tatrāpi-evaṃ* omitted in *ga*. [p. 162]

Thus far, it has been stated that there is no identity between words themselves. Now, he demonstrates the distinction between words and their meanings—stating that "we shall provide the refutation regarding fragrant sandalwood and so forth in the section on *ākṛti* (generic form).
But surely, this common worldly expression, "we understand the meaning from the word," would now be untenable?
The proponent asks: Are *ga* and the other [phonemes] not sounds (*śabda*), such that there would be this inconsistency? Previously—
The bird says: "Those sounds are many, not a single sound; and the singular number in the word 'śabdāt' (from the sound) refers to the individual words."

Furthermore, there is no word distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), and phonemes are many; therefore, it is not tenable to employ the singular number with reference to them. Thus, this apparent inconsistency of worldly speech is established as being logically sound within our final doctrine (*siddhānta*). Accordingly, even the authors of the treatises have presented their arguments with reference to the word itself: "The preceding... [and so forth].
“He expresses a state that has been overcome by means of a verb. Let it be granted that this is not established; for [the opponent argues] even though the meaning is unestablished...
A worldly statement is observed—such as, for example, "those very ten pomegranates are those very six cakes.

Furthermore, because even an illogical worldly statement can occur, it is precisely for the purpose of eliminating such [usage] that grammar and other sciences are undertaken. Thus he says: "And having seen something in the world whose meaning is indeed illogical..."
Grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*) is undertaken for the purpose of restriction (*niyamāya*).

Otherwise, since corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) would not even be applicable [in place of correct ones], grammar need not have been commenced. However, in this case, there is no such inconsistency, because the whole (*samudāya*) is the cause.
Because of that [word's] nature;
and because it is singular, the use of the singular number is appropriate. Here he says: "But surely the word 'śabda' (sound/word) applies to a collection.
[Note: 1. Vyākaraṇa, etc. Ga.
2. For the sake of that restriction:
163] it is not possible, nor does a denotative word exist within a collection of denotative words. Why is this so? From common worldly usage.

If you say "it is so," then understand that it exists [as a single entity], because the singular number would otherwise be inexplicable; moreover, the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) has already been refuted.

Furthermore, since all the phonemes combined convey the meaning, the state of having a single form is established, and thus the singular number is appropriate. As it is said: "And due to the unity of the effect, there is a figurative attribution of oneness. Therefore, the author of the treatise—

The verbal testimony [of the scriptures] is also established by this very reasoning. Furthermore, the designation of "words" and "sentences" is likewise established, such as: "the word 'cow' (gauḥ)," "the word 'horse' (aśvaḥ)," "a worldly sentence," and "a Vedic sentence," and so forth.
Therefore, it is proven that the word is nothing other than the phonemes beginning with *ga*; there exists no word distinct from the phonemes *ga* and the rest.
Thus ends the discussion on *sphoṭa*.
Now, as for the question, "What is the meaning of this word 'cow' (*gauḥ*)?", this question is not tenable.
Now, one might object: "The word has already been defined; now the meaning is being defined. To this, he says: "In that case, it is proper to ask: what is the word in the expression 'cow'?"

As for what was asked: this is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt of the Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) that denotative capacity (*vācakatā*) is not possible in the case of the phonemes (*varṇa*); however, regarding the denoted object (*abhidheya*), there is no difference whatsoever—whether it be the configuration (*ākṛti*) or the quality (*guṇa*).

1. Indeed, whether it be the denotative power (*vācakatva*) or the individual instance (*vyakti*) that is the denoted object, even so, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the relation being innate (*autpattika*).

For it is appropriate here to demonstrate that the relationship is innate (*autpattika*) and conducive to its purpose; furthermore, this position—that the genus (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), and individual (*vyakti*) are the denotata—is not tenable. If the very relation existing here were not intended to apply there as well, [the argument would fail].

Otherwise, the presentation of the signified and the signifier there would be purposeless. One should simply have said: "You do not point out that single relation which is characterized as the name and the named. For this very reason—

In this case as well, the relationship is that very same one; therefore, by the phrase "for that very reason it has been previously established that it is produced," he demonstrates that this is merely a restatement of what was previously said.
Otherwise, the relationship would be something different from the previous one.
The statement, "Who is this other one? is not tenable, given that it was previously established that "he, however, is produced.
Furthermore, what is the purpose of these questions and the presentation of arguments?

The meaning of this is as follows: when an objection has been raised by others in the preceding section ending with the words "If it is produced, then... and so forth, one should provide only a refutation of that objection; one should not, however, introduce further questions or propositions.

This is the reason here: the question is posed by one who considers that, regarding the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), it is impossible to assert the independence of two things established as distinct.
The meaning of this is as follows: having had his own position refuted, the proponent of illusory manifestation addresses the Mīmāṃsaka himself.

He raises an objection: "If the word and its meaning are established as separate entities (*yutasiddha*), then what is their relationship? For in my view, the relationship between word and meaning is established precisely through identity (*tādātmya*). If one were to admit a relationship characterized by the signifier and the signified (*pratyāyya-pratyāyaka*) even between two things that are separate, then the independence [of the word] would not be established. By this, the question is first set forth.
For it is possible to assert the independence of the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) due to its beginninglessness, by means of the method to be explained; thus,
the presentation of that very relationship characterized as the signified and the signifier is made [by the statement] "But that is produced," precisely as previously described.
1. In that very [place]. (ga) 2. As previously stated. (ga) 3.
How [can there be] inseparable establishment (*ayutasiddhi*)? (ga)

[177] It was stated by the grammarian himself with the very same intention expressed in the section on the refutation of the theory of the relation [between word and meaning]. Therefore, we consider that,
according to your own view, some person must have established a relation between words and their meanings in order to engage in linguistic usage.
By stating that "the Vedas were composed," the dependence [of the Vedas upon human agency] has been concluded.

For if the relationship [between word and meaning] were created, then the Vedas, which come into existence after that relationship, would also be created; otherwise, [the relationship] could not apply to those words prior to the convention.

There would be no comprehension of meaning from the Vedas. Furthermore, the observation that the author of the relationship and the composer of the Veda are one and the same is intended to show that, in every respect, the Vedas—being connected to a created relationship—are themselves created. "Now this is being stated:
because the relationship is non-human (apauruṣeya), it is established."
He explains the commentary: this is the presentation of the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
If it is the very beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of elders that is presented here, what is this?
What, then, is the answer to the question? He demonstrates that very point by asking "How?"— that is,
when the reason for the non-human origin of the relationship has been questioned.

The reply, "because there is no person who acts as a connecting link," is not tenable. It should rather be stated thus: "Because the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is beginningless. He states the justification for this: "This [is said] in order to refute the opposing view regarding the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of the elders."
[The opponent] has proposed:
"The existence of a creator of the relationship [between word and meaning] is the counter-argument to the beginninglessness of linguistic usage;
this is what is refuted by this passage. But how does this perception of a creator of the relationship serve as a counter-argument?

Is this doubted? Indeed it is doubted: for even though the comprehension of meaning from words is established through beginningless usage by the elders (*vṛddha*), in cases where an author of the relationship is perceived, there the very fact of having a beginning follows by the force of that perception, as in the case of "vṛddhir ādaic" [Pāṇini 1.1.1].
"Like [the expression] *itivat*.

Its meaning is as follows: although the comprehension of meaning from a word is established by the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), nevertheless, when one observes the direct creation of a convention (*saṅketa*), that beginninglessness cannot be asserted; thus it occurs.
The perception of a person who establishes the relationship is the counter-position. Therefore, the perception of an author must be refuted.
To the question, "How is it that the relationship does not exist? what answer is appropriate? [It is] that of perception.

If it is argued that [the self does not exist] because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because the others are preceded by it, how is this not tenable? For inference and the other [means of knowledge] are also accepted as being valid cognitions.
Therefore, the refutation of perception alone does not entail the non-existence of the one who connects [them].

Now, one might object: "Since perception has been refuted, inference and the other means of knowledge are also refuted by the passage stating that they are preceded by perception.
To this, he replies: "And being preceded by perception is untenable, because it would entail that verbal testimony is dependent [on something else]."

The meaning of this is as follows: if whatever is preceded by perception becomes refuted when that perception is refuted, then it follows that wherever perception operates, [the subsequent cognition] must likewise operate there alone. Since verbal testimony (*śabda*) is also preceded by perception, it too must operate only within the domain of perception; therefore, this [verbal testimony] is dependent upon perception.

[The word] would be [already] obtained; and since actions and the like are not objects of perception, they would fall into the state of being non-inferable. Furthermore, because inference is preceded by perception, it would follow that its operation is necessarily restricted to those very objects [of perception]. Moreover, if the word were dependent [on something else], the effort to establish the innate nature of the relationship between word and meaning would be entirely futile.
Because invalidity is difficult to avoid, this situation arises that is heard in worldly conversations on emptiness: "The horse has been forgotten by you who are mounted upon it.

It is "forgotten" because it has departed from the mind. This form belongs to the verb *smṛ* when its object functions as the agent. [This is said] by one who does not understand the intended meaning.

To this, the following objection may be raised: it is not possible for [the object] to be cognizable solely through inference and scripture when the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), which is beginningless, stands as an adversary.
The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, those two—namely inference and scripture—are "solely" (i.e., independently) devoid of the operation of perception.

[The two] are dependent; therefore, let it be granted that [the word] is not the creator of the relationship (*sambandhṛ*), because inference of a cause from an effect is a mere inference (*kevalānumāna*);

and the cognition of an object from a word is an effect, yet that [cognition] is not uniquely capable of inferring the creator of the relationship, since it is also logically possible through the beginninglessness of the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Likewise, scripture (*āgama*) as an independent authority is likewise not [the creator of the relationship].

In the case of a sentient being, [scripture] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its sole object is the effect [of that being]. If one must speak of it as being preceded by perception and inference, even then, since there is no possibility of an inference that is independent of perception—given that even an inference preceded by another [inference] can only arise through the mediation of beginningless linguistic usage among elders—it is impossible for it to exist without depending on perception. Therefore, scripture and inference are both preceded by perception and have as their objects only those things grasped by perception.
1. Perception as a means of valid cognition.
2. As for those two.

"It is to be refuted. Therefore, the response is established. Now, for what purpose is the plural number used? "Because the others are preceded by that."
Thus:

if [the critique] is directed at the refutation of a possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the refutation of analogy (*upamāna*) is useless, because its object is mere similarity (*sādṛśya-mātra*) and it lacks the possibility of [apprehending] a relatum (*sambandhin*); whereas presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) [does have such a possibility].

Since there is no contradiction for anyone in the absence of a method (*naya*), [the objection] is simply impossible. He states the resolution: "The presentation of what is to be suspected applies to two [cases], but the impossibility applies to all"—thus the plural number is justified.
The meaning of this is as follows:

There is, first of all, an absence of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it is entirely appropriate to say that, because of the non-existence of others [the other means of cognition], there is no relationship. Wherever there is no suspicion, a refutation with reasons is not presented; however, wherever there is a possibility, a refutation with reasons is performed.
He states the lack of proof [for the opponent's position] by saying, "Is it not so because of its having occurred long ago?
By this, he means: "Is it not the case that, because it occurred long ago, it would be beyond the range of perception for those of the present day?"
Thus, he states the purport of the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

By this commentary, the author of the *bhāṣya* asserts that the non-existence of perception is unestablished (*asiddhatā*). How is it unestablished? Because it is possible for [the Veda] to have been an object of perception for ancestors. "For that which has existed for a long time would not fail to be remembered."
Thus, the intention is that even for the ancestors, direct perception (pratyakṣa) regarding this matter is not possible.
If such direct perception had existed for the ancestors, it would have been remembered, just as [the grammar of] Pāṇini is remembered.

by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), lack of application (*anabhiyoga*) is also to be understood. And not [the absence of] the person—

Its validity would follow from the validity of that [source].
Therefore, the intention is that a break in the tradition of recollection is not tenable on the grounds of its being purposeless.

The meaning of this is as follows: when a person who is related [to the convention] is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the meaning must be understood through agreement with that person who established the convention (*saṅketṛ*). For indeed, if there is disagreement among those who establish the convention, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) would not occur, just as between an Ārya and a Dramila regarding the word "kali. Therefore, by that [agreement of the convention-maker]—
For the sake of correct understanding, the person [the author] should be remembered. That this necessity of being remembered is demonstrated by the mention of Pāṇini and Piṅgala—
mention (upanyāsa) meaning an illustration (dṛṣṭānta)— is expressed in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "yadyapi ca," and so forth.
Having recited [the objection], he says in order to refute it: “Even if forgetfulness were possible”—
of what object is this forgetfulness put forward?
If, first of all, that [cognition] has as its object the relatum of the probandum, then, given the existence of that relatum, what is this "that"?

183] The proof is this: namely, the possibility of forgetfulness; for that which is called "forgetfulness" is the state of even a grasped object [being lost].
Non-remembrance arises from some specific cause; it is not merely the absence of remembrance regarding an object that was never apprehended.

And since the apprehension and the existence [of the object] are established precisely through the establishment of non-remembrance, therefore non-remembrance constitutes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been stated in the *Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*: “Non-remembrance, too, is possible.”

Thus, this is the reason for the existence of these Vedic statements. As for what is also said—that just as there may be non-perception of something even though it exists, one cannot on that basis alone assert "the horn of a hare exists" without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that too is incorrect; for if [something] were indeed existing...
Regarding this very non-perception of a rabbit’s horn, by whom could it be said that "the rabbit’s horn does not exist"?
For even in the determination that "this is a non-perception of something previously ascertained as existing," existence itself [is involved].

Because [the existence of a creator] is certain, it cannot be said that he does not exist. Now, if the intention is this: "Even though in other cases—such as the Himalayas, oceans, and groves—the possibility of forgetting the creator has been observed, it cannot be asserted on that basis alone that here too the possibility of forgetting the author of the relationship exists"? This intention is incorrect; for what is certainly and preeminently observed in one place may indeed apply elsewhere.
It is said that [the object] exists. For this very fact—that what is observed in one place exists elsewhere—is indeed the domain of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
If, however, there were a restriction such that what is observed in one place does not exist elsewhere, then inference based on general observation would no longer be possible.
Thus it is said: "it exists. (Note: *bhavatītyucyate* is omitted in the manuscript *ga*.)
[Page 184] Refuted. To this it is replied: neither forgetfulness nor non-perception is being presented here as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, this is presented for the purpose of refuting defects in the cause of an object already perceived.

The meaning of this is as follows: nowhere do we put forward non-remembrance or non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of a real entity; rather, it is that which has been perceived from another source—such as a Vedic sentence [inferred] through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for a memory in the section on memory (*smṛtyadhikaraṇa*)—and its cause...

The following objection might be raised: "If there were a Vedic statement [for this], it would necessarily have been remembered or perceived; therefore, this inference does not possess an unimpaired causal complex. This objection is refuted by the possibility of forgetfulness and non-perception: "Forgetfulness is possible, and non-perception is also possible."

Thus [it is said]. Here, however, you have presented this forgetfulness at a time when the relationship has not been perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it is irrelevant. It was stated that even by refuting the defect in the cause, it does not connect [to the point].
He states the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*: "Just as there is a non-perception of a jar or the like, even though it has been perceived."
One cannot assert the existence of a rabbit's horn on this basis alone. Why it cannot be so asserted is stated here:
the non-perception of an object that is otherwise perceptible requires another cause.

If indeed the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were exactly the same [as before], why is it not perceived as it was previously? Therefore, in the case of its non-perception there, another cause must be stated.
However, regarding the non-perception of things such as a rabbit's horn, the non-perception is simply due to non-perception itself; there is no other cause in that case.
This is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). And by thus explaining the example, he has shown that this same application applies to the subject of the illustration as well.

Even though there is forgetfulness regarding what was perceived elsewhere, we cannot establish a composer merely from the absence of memory without some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this is well said.

[Page 185] “But surely we may understand the author of the relationship through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti),” says the Bhāṣya; he [the opponent] objects to that as follows:

"But surely, why is this designation 'presumption' (arthāpatti) being introduced? "Yes," says the partisan of the prima facie view (ekadeśin). The proponent of the final conclusion (rāddhāntin) refutes him: "But what is it that is 'not possible' here?"
Is it apprehended by this cognition? That which "is not logically possible" in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Thus, that which is apprehended by this cognition is precisely what is to be understood (*gamya*). In that case, if this is an *arthāpatti* (presumption), then here too there must be an object of knowledge (*prameya*) apprehended as being otherwise inexplicable. To this, he asks: "What is that? The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) replies: "Indeed..."
Regarding the phrase "the agent of the relation," the proponent asks: "But how is it that this is not tenable?"
Is it grasped in this way? Again, a certain partisan says: "Because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing.
The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) says: If the meaning is not apprehended upon the first hearing, what has happened to the relationship [between word and meaning]?
[The question is: "Of the agent?

[The answer is: The meaning is that for him, there is never any impossibility [of its existence]. An opponent says: "In that case, even in the example of *arthāpatti* based on what is well-known, if Devadatta is not perceived in the house, what follows?"
Regarding "external existence" (*bahirbhāva*):
even in that case, the meaning is that there is no impossibility regarding the external existence that is to be understood.
The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) states the distinction: we do not say that external existence—an entity qualified by an external location—is untenable.

What then? It is existence, which is established through scripture as in the statement "Devadatta is alive"; that this [existence] would not be possible [if he were not outside] was stated in the definition of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); for it is indeed existence that is [the object of inference] when he is not seen in the house.

This has been explained by Vyāsa: "It is apprehended as being unreal because it is not logically tenable. This very same existence, when apprehended as being untenable, is the cognition that "it exists externally"; therefore, in that case, only the untenable is perceived.
But here, since the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing, what [connection] could there be for the agent?
Is a relationship observed?

For in that case, the observation of Devadatta’s absence from the house is indeed connected to his existence; by means of that, it extends [the inference] regarding the impossibility of that existence. Here, however, because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing, there is no connection with the related term.
Since there is no relationship whatsoever [between the word and its meaning], this does not entail the impossibility of a related entity.

Now, suppose it occurs to the mind: "People do not comprehend [the meaning] from hearing a word for the first time, yet they do comprehend it upon hearing it a second time or thereafter; therefore, another cause besides the word must be sought."
For if sound alone were the cause in this case, then comprehension would occur from the mere sound even upon the first hearing;
yet it does not so occur. Therefore, there must be another cause for the comprehension of meaning. [The author] refutes this:
"In that case, this inference from effect to cause has been presented. Now, having refuted the partial view, [the opponent] asks:
'How then [is it established] by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)?'"
Is this commentary [applicable] even to your own position? The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) justifies it:
the meaning is that there is the occurrence of inference from the sense of the matter (arthāt).
Thus, "presumption from the sense" (arthāpatti) is said to be an occurrence from the sense; "occurrence" (āpatti) means conceptual construction (kalpanā).
It is called *anumānāpatti* because it is both inference (*anumāna*) and a logical consequence (*āpatti*). Why? Because it arises from an effect as its object (*artha*).

This was stated in the very section on the "objection regarding the relation" (*sambandhākṣepa*), where it was said that [the cognition] is characterized by the comprehension of the object. Now, is this not also an inference?

This is not tenable, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the lack of comprehension upon first hearing, since the meaning is understood from a Vedic sentence even when heard for the first time. And here, by the term "inconclusive," one should understand the fallacy of partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddha*). In the Veda...
1. From the meaning, that is, from the effect (*kārya*). Ka. [p.
187] Because it is not established that the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing; nor, moreover, is it intended to be "erroneous" (*savyabhicāra*) or "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). If...

Even if the occurrence [of the reason] were established independently of the existence of its connection with the probandum (*sādhyasambandhin*), it would be subject to deviation (*savyabhicāra*); yet such is not the case, because even the Vedic sentence is included within the category of the probandum. Here, the proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) offers a rebuttal according to his own opinion: "But surely, this inquiry pertains to the word (*pada*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: this is an inquiry into the innate relationship between a word and its referent (*padapadārtha*). Therefore, with reference to the word itself, it is stated that "the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing.
And since no word whatsoever conveys its meaning upon the first hearing, there is no lack of pervasion (*bhāgāsiddhi*) [in the reason].

The proponent refutes [the objection]: "What is this thing called a 'word' (pada), regarding which you are conducting this inquiry? He says: "It is precisely this: well-known words such as 'cow,' 'horse,' and so forth, as in the sentence, 'Devadatta, drive the cow hither.'"

In such sentences as these, the proponent asks: Are [the words] well-known as having a distinct "thing-to-be-done" (kārya) as their meaning, or is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning itself the "thing-to-be-done"?
This is the underlying intention: that the words do not [directly denote] the sentence-meaning.

There is no other effect [of the sentence] than the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; and that comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs even upon the first hearing, for it arises from the sentence as a whole and not from a single word. Nor does the sentence require a second hearing. An adherent of a particular school says: "True, they are well known to have distinct effects."

For, by means of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*), it is determined that the comprehension of the mere meaning of words alone is the task to be accomplished. The proponent asks: "In what [context]?"
The answer is: in common usage (*vyavahāra*).
It is by this that the elders engage in worldly activity;
or, according to the etymology "that by which one is engaged in activity," it is the sentence itself that is denoted by the word *vyavahāra*. Therefore...

Although linguistic usage occurs by means of sentences, the point is that it is not the comprehension of the sentence-meaning alone that constitutes the function of words through insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*). He asks again: "By what means do the elders engage in linguistic usage?"
This is its intended meaning: elders engage in linguistic usage by means of sentences, and in that regard—(1) "And that [sentence] does not exist" (variant *ga*).
(2) "A partisan says" (*ga*).

[Page 188] It is observed that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning alone is the effect, not the comprehension of the isolated word-meanings. Again, with that same intention, he provides the example: "Devadatta, bring the cow, the white one."
By such statements as these, he brings forward the position of the Siddhāntin:
"In that case, linguistic usage proceeds by means of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha); for an object not established through linguistic usage [cannot be accepted]."
It can be understood by way of its distinct function (*kāryāntaratayā*).
And in this sense, the word *hi* is used, meaning "for" or "but not.
Although the power (*śakti*) of words is determined through insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*), nevertheless, it remains exactly as it is in common usage (*yathāvyavahāram eva*).

It is logical [to hold this]; furthermore, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is observed to have only the sentence-meaning as its object; it is therefore appropriate to postulate that the expressive power (*śakti*) of the word also has that [sentence-meaning] as its object. Consequently, because the primary sentence-meaning is connected with multiple individual word-meanings, it is determined through the methods of inclusion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*) that the words function solely as causes for the comprehension of those meanings which serve as its constituents. Thus, [the relationship between word and meaning] is necessarily concomitant (*nāntarīyakī*).

The understanding of the word-meanings [is the result]; however, the result of all words is indeed the understanding of the sentence-meaning. The partisan of the single-school (ekadeśin) states the contradiction with the text: "How then [is it that the Bhāṣya asks] 'Now, what is the meaning of this word *go*?'"
And what is the answer to the claim that "the form (ākṛti) is characterized by the dewlap and so forth," if there is no difference in the effect?
If...

Since the word (*pada*) has no separate function, how can there be a question regarding its function characterized by the comprehension of a specific meaning, and how can there be an answer by demonstrating the function characterized by the comprehension of the word-meaning? The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says:
"Or rather, how is its innate nature (*autpattikatā*) asserted on the basis of the linguistic usage of elders?"

The meaning of this is as follows: just as you consider that this treatise is not consistent with my view, so too, in your own view, it is not consistent to assert that this relationship is innate (*autpattika*) on the basis of the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*); for when the usage of elders is examined, [it is seen that] the meaning of the sentence—

It is the cognition of the syntactical relation itself that appears as the effect, not the mere cognition of the word-meanings; since there is such an apparent inconsistency, this text must be explained in such a way that the proposition and its proof form a single coherent statement.

The thesis is that the relationship [between word and meaning] is innate; the proof is that the linguistic usage of elders is beginningless. Just as these two constitute a single syntactical unity through the relationship of the probandum and the probans, so too is this [the case].

The treatise is to be described. However, that has already been described by the commentator himself in the section on "That Which Has Become That" (*tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*), while stating: "Words convey the meaning of a sentence precisely through the mediation of the cognition of word-meanings. Therefore...

It has been stated that [the word] has the meaning of a generic form (*ākṛti*) which serves as the cause (*nimitta*). This has also been stated by the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) later on. Now, the partisan of a rejected position (*ekadeśin*) challenges the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*): "In that case, what is the resolution of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*)? The reply is:
"It gives"—this is said with the intention of referring to the cause (*nimitta*); one who has not grasped the cause does not comprehend it upon first hearing.
The meaning of this is as follows: the "cause" is spoken of with reference to that which consists of the word-meanings (*padārtha*) in the communication of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

“Why does that which is heard for the first time not convey [the meaning]? This is what is meant: a word heard for the first time does not cause the comprehension of the word-meaning as its signifier (*nimitta*); and one who has not comprehended the signifier [cannot grasp the sentence-meaning] from a word heard for the first time.

Since it does not even convey its own meaning, it is established that even in the case of the Veda, that which is heard for the first time lacks the capacity to convey meaning. Therefore, the intention is that there must be another cause, distinct from the word itself, for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. Now, if all words indeed serve as the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, then the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas) is accepted—that the entire collection of words [is the cause].

Since it brings about the understanding of the sentence-meaning by combining [the parts], the division therein is merely conceptual. With this intention, he asks: "What, then, is the difference between the signifier and its cause?
The answer is: "Precisely for this purpose..."

For indeed, this section on "That Which Has Become" (*bhūtādhikaraṇa*) is commenced precisely for the purpose of stating the distinction [between the two views]. In this regard, it is said: according to the view that [words function as] causes (*nimittapakṣa*), words, while operating upon their own meanings as already connected, produce the comprehension of the sentence-meaning; they do not, however, express the sentence-meaning as something partless and devoid of the division of words. And when it is stated in this manner, [the distinction] has indeed been stated.
The distinction between the denoter and its cause is sufficient; the detailed exposition will occur in the very section concerning "that which has become that" (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa).
190] "No, because the instruction is given as an established fact."

And in this sūtra, the word *upadeśaḥ*, which ends in the nominative case, has been transformed by the author of the Bhāṣya into a form ending in the ablative case, and the word *siddhavat* has been supplied; having done so, he stated this. Its meaning is as follows:

The meaning is that this non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the relationship is established as if it were already proven. Because of "instruction"—that is, instruction from elders—when one elder instructs another elder regarding the performance [of a rite], the understanding of the meaning by a bystander is established through the mere latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of grasping the relationship; thus, the postulation of a creator of the relationship is untenable. Not having understood this very meaning of his [the author's]...
He asks: "What is this 'because of the instruction as if it were already established'? This is what it means:
here, an agent of the relationship cannot be postulated, because the usage of elders is beginningless. Therefore...
It is established that the relationship [between word and meaning] is innate (*autpattika*).

If the linguistic usage of elders were not beginningless, then, due to the absence of a means for the first two elders to grasp the relationship, there would be no application of words and no comprehension of their meanings.

These two would not exist; and due to their absence, if the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha*) were not to proceed, then for others as well, there being no apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning], the application and comprehension [of language] would likewise be severed. However, the linguistic usage of the elders is beginningless, because the birth of one generation of persons is preceded by another generation of persons. For just as the persons of today are indeed preceded by another generation of persons.
"Likewise, [the same applies] to those who hold the prior view.

Regarding this, some— whose intellects have been deceived by an excessive faith arising merely from encountering scriptural passages concerning creation and dissolution found within *arthavādas*, and whose minds are inclined toward the doctrines of Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) and Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama)— [assert that] God is the cause of everything, including the body and the world.

Proclaiming their status as causes, they declare: we observe that everything possessing parts has acquired its existence through the conjunction of parts and is thus of recent origin; and the body, the world, and so forth possess parts;
and the conjunction of parts extends down to the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); and even the dyad, being a composite, must be initiated by the conjunction of two atoms (*paramāṇu*); and as for the two atoms...

The conjunction [of atoms] is produced by mutual action, and this action in the atoms is asserted to arise solely from the conjunction of the soul with that which possesses the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
As it has been said: “The initial action of atoms and of the mind is caused by the unseen force.
And the unseen force is insentient.

Furthermore, that which is insentient cannot accomplish any task whatsoever without being presided over by sentience, just like an axe or similar tools. Nor is it reasonable to suggest that those very hearers (*śrotṛjña*) themselves should be the presiders over their own unseen merits (*adṛṣṭa*), because they are ignorant; for it is observed that one who knows both an object and the capacity of an object is the presider over it, just as a carpenter is.

Or rather: the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls), even though possessing [the qualities] inherent in themselves, are not capable of knowing the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) characterized as merit and demerit, either in its essential nature or in its capacity; therefore, a conscious principle distinct from them is postulated. By that [consciousness], [the soul’s] consciousness— [p.

The Lord is the presiding controller. Since the body, the world, and so forth are understood to have a beginning—being produced through a succession of effects such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) initiated by atoms joined together due to karma arising under the influence of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)—it has been established that everything which possesses origination is subject to destruction.
How then can there be an infinite succession of the linguistic usage of the elders? This [objection] applies even to the level of the opposing position.
The author of the commentary has overlooked this point, stating that "it does not occur [to them] to descend.

For instance—even if this wish were fulfilled, one must still understand how all the composite wholes (*avayavin*) could dissolve simultaneously. Why is it that at this very moment there is the arising of some and the dissolution of others?

Thus, we consider that it is not accepted [as a valid reason] because it follows what is observed (*dṛṣṭānugama*). And who can deny the continuity of the tradition of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*)? Furthermore, if the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are not the presiding agents due to the absence of knowledge, then how could another be the presiding agent, since for him too knowledge is impossible? [This would follow from] the conjunction of the self and the mind...

Because cognitions arise depending on what is perceived, namely through the accompaniment of the respective conjunctions of sense-faculties and their objects, this causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is not possible with respect to unperceived things. If it is argued that there is another cause for that [unperceived], it is not so; for it is illogical to infer another unperceived cause while setting aside a perceived cause. In all cases, inference follows what is perceived.

Even inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) does not occur anywhere by way of subverting what is perceived. But has this not also been observed—that that which is insentient does not function unless presided over by a conscious being? In that case, this [inference] would be abandoned. True; but when both [reasons] are abandoned, which one should be abandoned? In that regard, because it concerns a specific object, our own [position] alone is the cause for the arising of knowledge.

Inference is to be respected; however, for those who maintain the existence of a Lord (Īśvara), it does not have as its object an absolute universal—namely, that "the insentient is presided over by the sentient"—because particular inference (*viśeṣānumāna*) is more powerful. As it was stated by the venerable author of the *Vārttika*:
"That which has well-known constituent parts, or that which is established in a particular [instance]..."
And it is more powerful than the general aspect (sāmānyadṛṣṭa) of the portion to be accomplished by that [planet].
"Just as there is sublation of a general rule by specific scriptural injunctions,
so too is there sublation of one inference by other inferences."

By this, the following view is also refuted: that the intellect (*buddhi*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) is eternal. For whatever is an intellect, it is characterized by origination and is subject to destruction; therefore, the intellect of the Lord must likewise be of such a nature. Furthermore, the purpose of his presiding over [the world] must also be explained; for what kind of [action] is performed by the hand in relation to tools such as an axe?
An abode such as the body is observed [to belong to a conscious being]; therefore, the same should be inferred for those things that are unobserved. But that is not possible.

Likewise, what other activity could there be for the unseen (adṛṣṭa) than the acquisition of its own nature, just as there is for an axe the action of striking and the contact with wood and so forth? Furthermore, the acquisition of its own nature by the unseen is established precisely through the performance of sacrifices and other rites.
Therefore, the doctrine of a creator God has not been refuted by us either. Here, an objection is raised: "How is it that this was introduced in one way and concluded in another? Regarding sound—
The understanding of meaning was the subject under discussion; it was introduced by one who stated that the word is the signifier and the meaning is the signified;
and it was introduced by one who stated that the understanding of meaning depends upon the linguistic usage of elders, [established] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

It has been concluded that the comprehension of meaning arises solely from linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). This [conclusion] is misplaced elsewhere and falls right back where it was set—like a cluster of arrows from an unskilled archer.
For [the understanding of meaning] comes from the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
When the meaning is understood through inference, the meaning is not truly understood from the word itself, as in the case of hand gestures and the like.
He explains the illustration: even hand gestures and so forth are established solely through the linguistic usage of elders.

Even an elderly person employs hand gestures as a convention; however, the intention is that hand gestures and the like are not inherently connected to their referents and thus do not convey meaning on their own. Indeed, it is linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) alone that is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, not the hand gesture itself.
[The suffixes] *daya* and so forth; for these are conditions for etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

The meaning of this is as follows: a hand gesture (*hastasaṃjñā*) is indeed conventionally established (*saṅketyate*) thus: "When this object is intended by me, then this illusory hand (*māyāhasta*) must be moved."

Thus, when he moves his hand again in that very same way, he then recalls his prior training and, having determined the specific intention once more from the hand gesture, understands the object; the hand gesture is merely a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Therefore, the word is a limiting adjunct and not the cause of the comprehension of the object.
The cause is like the striking with whips, goads, and prods;
it is like the striking of horses, elephants, and bulls with whips, goads, and prods.
It is like one fallen [from a vehicle], as if intoxicated with passion.
2. Regarding the category (padārtha).
3. The meaning is that they do not exist.

The goad is the driver’s whip. Precisely because the relationship between word and meaning cannot be established according to the Mīmāṃsaka position, for this very reason it has been stated by the Grammarians, who know the true nature of words: “The theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) alone must be adopted by the proponents of the Veda.”
Thus [it is said]. Here, the proponent of the established view (siddhāntin) offers a rebuttal: "What is the use of this recourse to the theory of illusory manifestation (vivarta)?
This has already been refuted, because no identity is perceived between words and their objects. The proponent of the theory of illusory manifestation replies:

If this is so, then the authority of the Veda is refuted, because a word lacks the capacity to convey meaning. To this it is replied: when a meaning is understood through the linguistic training derived from the usage of elders, what else is there [required] beyond the word?

Do you consider the cause to be something else? Surely we consider linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) itself to be the cause. Not so; for linguistic proficiency concerns the relationship between word and meaning, whereas the comprehension of the word and its meaning does not [arise] from proficiency.
The meaning of this is as follows: for in the linguistic usage of elders, it is established that "by this word,
this meaning [is conveyed]."
The term "learning" (*vyutpatti*) refers precisely to the determination of the relationship between the signifier and the signified between word and meaning— namely,
that "the meaning is understood from the word"— and nothing else; thus, such is the very nature of learning.

Thus, it is linguistic proficiency itself that consists in the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning]; that proficiency has a beginning, but the relationship between the word and its object does not, because that relationship is the very object [of such apprehension]. Just as the cognition of the self has a beginning, [so too does proficiency].
Nor even a self. Therefore, it has been correctly stated: "No, because the instruction is given as an established fact."
Now, in order to refute what has been stated by others— namely, that "whatever kind [of word] is established from whatever [source]"— the author sets forth the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa):
But surely, even if the relationship [between word and meaning] is one of causality (kārya), the acquisition of proficiency through the linguistic usage of elders remains entirely consistent.
[This is] for the sake of the ignorant. How is this presented as an antidote?

The meaning is as follows: just as even though a word such as "Devadatta" is artificial, its conventional usage is mastered through the linguistic practice of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), that very [word] is artificial.

[Objection: "In that case, let it [the understanding] also occur with respect to cows and so forth. [Response: True; however, when the object to be understood is known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), linguistic proficiency arises—just as proficiency arises from grammar and the like—and there is no contradiction. [This applies] to what is to be inferred (*kalpya*).
1. *atha ca*. (ka.)
2. And yet, for whom is that which is produced? Furthermore, how does conceptual construction cease? [p. 195]

The meaning of this is as follows: where the relationship is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be exclusively one of effect (*kārya*), let it be an effect; however, where there is no other means of valid cognition for its being an effect, there the state of being an effect must be inferred, and that [inference] arises from the characteristic of the comprehension of the object.

[The cognition arises] from the effect; and if that effect is established solely through the understanding derived from the linguistic usage of elders—which is as good as perception—then an inference based on its being an effect is not possible, for when another cause is already perceived directly, it cannot be the case that [the elders' usage] alone is the cause in every instance.
(Variant reading: *bhūtārthopagamāt*)
It is not possible to measure [the relationship]; therefore, by the force of the effect, which is the comprehension of meaning, one cannot assert that the relationship is of human origin.
However, where it is directly perceived, it is accepted as such; and here, there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It has been stated that [the relationship] exists. Furthermore, if the relationship were something produced, there would be no purpose for an agent to establish it in inaccessible regions; for the establishment of a relationship is for the sake of practical usage (*saṃvyavahāra*), and practical usage is not possible with those situated in inaccessible places.

The meaning of this is as follows: if a single person alone were to compose the Vedas after establishing a relationship between words and their meanings, then he would have to establish that convention only among those who engage with the Vedas; it could not be established among Mlecchas and others residing in inaccessible regions, because they lack engagement with the Vedas. And yet, [such usage] is observed in the lands of the Mlecchas and others.

The application of the word "cow" occurs even in those [beings] possessing a dewlap and so forth. Nor is this [objection] tenable—that the author of the relationship is indeed someone other than the author of the Veda—because the creation of a relationship would be purposeless; for Pāṇini, Piṅgala, and others establish conventions only for the sake of linguistic usage. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. By this, [the sūtra] "And there is non-difference... [is explained].

Thus, the first explanation has been described. He describes the second: "And the relation, being an effect, is not possible without a word denoting the related entity; if the relation is accepted as having an effect for its purpose,"
"By one who has accomplished the task.
The meaning of this is: "By means of this word, this object is here represented.

The connection should be made in this way: "It is to be understood. However, that cannot be accomplished if it is not admitted that certain words already mastered through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*) serve as the means for those who are to be instructed.
For one who is previously unacquainted with a word is not capable of understanding even the meaning of the sentence used to establish the relationship. If...

If certain [words] already established through the usage of elders are accepted as being among those to be derived, then what further purpose is served by establishing a [new] relationship? Let the usage of elders itself be the means for derivation. Now, he raises an objection regarding the established conclusion: "But even derivation depends upon the status of being an effect (kāryatā)."

"How so? is the question. The answer is: "For one who has not understood the meaning in this way—that 'this [word] is the designator of this [object]'—there is no comprehension of the object from the word."
"It was born as a form" (rūpam apadyata)—this objection is raised for the purpose of establishing parity with one's own position. The refutation, however, is this:
indeed, there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived. For it is observed that the understanding of children arises from mere conventional usage alone.

He concludes: Therefore, since the cause for understanding the meaning of words is perceived through direct perception, and since linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is thus established, it has already been explained previously that the postulation of an author (*kartṛ*) is not tenable.
He explains the meaning of the phrase "when the object is not perceived" as follows: this is another [instance] of a connection that is useless for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), namely,
the assigning of a name to an unperceived object such as a deity when the relationship has been artificially created.
1. Omitted. artha. ga. 2. Of Devadatta and others. ka. [p. 198]

The meaning of this is as follows: a name should be assigned for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), just as a father gives his son the name "Caitra. However, there is no practical usage involving deities. Now, why was it stated in the Bhāṣya that the mere absence of a purpose [is the reason]?
The author of the Bhāṣya has also stated: "Furthermore, since it is impossible to comprehend [the existence of] deities and so forth, it is impossible to establish a relationship with them.
To the question, "Why then is this not explained? he replies: "The incapacity [to do so] has indeed already been described."
In the Bhāṣya, it is not explained by that [reason]. Therefore, it is said: "The fact that naming is performed is a mark of those superior to us."
This is refuted, because the very application of designations such as "deity" and so forth is unestablished. Therefore, since the relationship is innate (*autpattika*),
its independence is established.
Thus concludes the refutation of the [intrinsic] relationship.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya raises an objection with the very words of the Bhāṣya: "Now, as for what was said, 'Word is not the cause [of dharma]'"—that is to say, O Mīmāṃsaka! as for what was stated previously, "Word is not the cause."
"Thus [it has been argued] by us;
what is the rebuttal to that? He raises this objection: "Now, as for what was said—that sound is without cause—"
Why is this objection raised?

For this very point—that the relation lacks a cause—has already been refuted by the statement that the relation is innate (*autpattika*). Now, it might be argued: "By the statement that the relation is innate, something else [is being asserted]..."
It has been refuted; here I ask— of what else could this refutation be understood to apply, since it concerns the doctrine of the innate nature [of words]?
By what means? What is it that [you] ask? Nothing else has been proposed that could be refuted. [It is] the perception of what exists—
For by that very [principle], the absence of other objects for the injunction is demonstrated in such cases as "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā."

The meaning of this is as follows: because it is perceived as something presently existing, the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) and the cattle (*paśu*) is indeed apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the object of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such terms is the "state of being a task" (*kāryatva*) preceded by that relationship of means and end, which is accessible solely through other means of valid cognition; it is not some other kind of object. This was demonstrated previously.
Therefore, the refutation of that very [objection] has been given on the grounds of its being innate (*autpattika*). What else remains as if unrefuted that is being presented?
Here is the resolution: it is true that the refutation of that very [objection] through its innateness has been stated;
however, even regarding the innate relationship, the distinction from other objects appears as if unstated; for the sake of that distinction, this [text] is once again—
The form is set forth.

Its meaning is as follows: for if the relationship [between word and meaning] were of human origin, the fact that the Vedas would necessarily be of human origin—thereby resulting in their being dependent on something else—would be refuted by the assertion of an "intrinsic" (*autpattika*) relationship. However, in the world...

By demonstrating the independence [of the word], the doubt that a word has as its sole object a thing already within the scope of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is refuted. Even though the relationship is innate (*autpattika*), this distinction—that the object of the word is independent [of other means]—seems as if it were not stated; therefore, this objection is raised again in order to clarify that distinction: "Action—"
Having recited the commentary with the words, “because no fruit is seen at the time [of the action], and because the action would be non-existent at another time,” he raises an objection— [p.
[The opponent] replies: But what is the purpose of this commentary (*bhāṣya*) which has been introduced for the sake of distinguishing it from other objects?

For since there is no other object, and because it would be dependent [on something else] by virtue of being the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) was demonstrated in the absence of that [other object].

Since verbal testimony lacks an object that is not already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since it depends upon other means of valid cognition by virtue of having as its object a thing graspable by those other means, its lack of authority in the absence of such other means was demonstrated in the *Citrākṣepa* [section]. Here too, that very same point is stated by this commentary (*bhāṣya*). What, then, is that?
What appears as if it were not stated?
That which is expressed by this commentary. He provides the resolution: "This is that";

for when there is the cognition "this is that" regarding an object within the scope of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is an injunction (*niyoga*). And in that case, [it concerns] what is not yet perceived.

It has already been stated previously that invalidity is indeed manifest; nor can it be imagined that, while this state of affairs exists, the fulfillment of the injunction occurs solely through the injunction itself.

The connection is that "this [point], though not explicitly stated, is expressed by this commentary. Its meaning is as follows: although a result is not established immediately after the ritual action, and yet there is no ritual action at a later time, nevertheless, the result will arise at a later time precisely from the *niyoga* (the mandate).

This is answered by the following: because, in this matter, since it is possible for the object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to exist, it cannot be postulated that the accomplishment of the fruit arises from the injunction (*niyoga*) alone; for at that time, the injunction lacks the status of a means of knowledge.
Indeed, the nature of an injunction is such that it is not known through other means of knowledge; how then could a word [that is an injunction] depend upon other means of knowledge?

[The animal sacrifice] would be an object of knowledge? Therefore, because the fruit is not seen immediately after the action, and because the action no longer exists at a later time, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the animal-sacrifice offering. Thus, it is clear that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) lacks authority regarding what is not perceived. This [objection] is now refuted: this would indeed be so, if [the relationship between word and meaning] were innate (*autpattika*).
It would not be so; yet that has been established.
If the relationship were innate, what of it? This [is the consequence].
Therefore, the injunction (niyoga) requires this point: that "this fruit is accomplished by means of this action. Its intention is as follows:
for if the relationship [between word and meaning] were of human origin, then its human origin would necessarily follow by force of logic.

[Otherwise] it would fall under the category of *codanā* (Vedic injunction); and that being the case, since it would then become an object of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), the meaning of the *niyoga* (the mandate) would depend solely upon the relationship between the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). However, once the non-human origin of the connection [between word and meaning] has been established, its independence (*svātantrya*) is not contradicted, and thus it cannot be asserted that it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*). As for what was said—that in common worldly usage independence is not perceived—[that remains to be addressed].

To this, he says: "For even in the case of a worldly object cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not understood that the mandate (*niyoga*) depends on the establishment of a relationship between the end and the means.
The meaning of this is as follows: [it is established] by the observation of activity that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc.)...

In common worldly usage, it is first understood that words serve to convey a purposeful action (*kāryārtha*); thus, those who are proficient [in language] do not require any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the expression of their own meaning. Therefore, even if a speaker intends to express a state of being an action (*kāryatā*) that has already been apprehended through another means of valid cognition, nevertheless, the word conveys that very state by its own inherent capacity alone. Consequently, this is likewise the case in the Veda.

The meaning [of the injunction] is not expressed by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth as preceded by an understanding of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). And here, by the word "niyoga" (the mandate), the optative suffix and so forth are intended. This has been shown in the Bhāṣya: "For it is observed that [one thinks], 'I am acting because I have been impelled by my teacher.'"

"Success does not come for him through this [mere statement]. What is meant is this: since the cognizer, having understood the task (*kārya*), performs it, and not [merely] the relationship between the means and the end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*); therefore, while acting, he says when questioned, "I am impelled by my teacher; having been urged by my teacher after he made me understand the task, I perform it."

Thus it is designated; there is no comprehension of a relationship between means and end. If the cognizer understands the task to be performed independently even from a human-authored sentence, then why is the dependence on a person for the relationship [between word and meaning] rejected? Let the relationship be human-made and let the Vedas be human-made as well; nevertheless, regarding the independent cognition of the object—

Validity will arise by virtue of its being self-sustained. To this, the reply is: it is refuted in order to eliminate the possibility of defects in the cause, but not with respect to self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvitti*).
The meaning of this is: if authorship by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*) were not refuted, [then validity would not be established].

In that case, even though the cognition of the effect has arisen, it might be false due to defects in its cause; for a person communicates to another an object already cognized by themselves through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And in that regard, concerning the human word which is the effect, [the cause is...

[This is] the capacity to indicate [the truth]. And if the Vedas were of human origin, then a person would have to provide the instruction after having understood the meaning of the Veda through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); yet no such other means of valid cognition exists. Thus, even if a cognition were produced, it would be false due to defects in its cause—as in the case of [the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should worship a *caitya*."
It is like the injunction, “One desiring heaven should give food to the Saṅgha”; however, there is no dependence on another for the knower’s own self-realization within his own consciousness.

The notion that [the injunction] exists [independently] is thus refuted. He concludes: "Therefore, the independence of the injunction" (*tasmāt svātantryaṃ niyogasya*)—by this, the distinction is demonstrated.
If the injunction possesses independence, then heaven and sacrifice are not the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

The understanding of the state of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) is perceived; for an injunction (*niyoga*), when it is to be understood as delimited merely by the object and the person to be enjoined, would be like an obligatory duty (*nityādhikāra*). To this, he says: "For one who enjoins a person brings about the understanding of the accomplishment of what is to be achieved."
And this he will explain with supporting arguments in the sixth [chapter]. Thus he says: "He will establish this in the sixth.
Even if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth convey the effect independently, does this mean that the non-perception of an immediate [succession] is thereby refuted?
Does it occur?

For, within the context of desire (*kāma*), the meaning of the sentence extends up to the accomplishment of the result; and since this result is not seen immediately thereafter, does the non-perception of the immediate consequence lead to a lack of authority by contradicting other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Is it refuted? Indeed, it is refuted.
It is not capable of establishing validity. Why? He says: because in this position, the establishment of the probandum does not follow from the determination of the capacity for action. What [then]?
Then [how is it established]? By virtue of the meaning of the *niyoga* (the injunction).

This is its meaning: for if the accomplishment of the goal were due to the determination of the power of the action (*kriyāśakti*), then the meaning of the scripture would be that the fruit must necessarily occur immediately thereafter; and this is not the case here.

In the view that the action is denoted independently (*svātantryeṇa kāryābhidhānapakṣe*), the accomplishment of the goal to be achieved (*sādhyasiddhi*) occurs after having ascertained the capacity of the action in this manner: "Since this action is capable of accomplishing the result, therefore the attainment of the result of the action follows from this. What, then, [is the case]?
Since the desirous person is prompted toward an action (*kārya*), therefore the action is the result (*phala*). And an action that is momentary in its destruction [cannot be the result].
(1) [Omitted *na*. ka. ga.

Since one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is unable to understand that the sacrifice is to be performed as the means for attaining heaven—which is to be experienced in another fixed body—the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. cause one to understand the *apūrva* as the task to be accomplished, because it is capable of producing a result that persists until another time. Thus, due to its enduring nature, there is no contradiction in its being the means to the result even at a later time; therefore, from the sacrifice, the *apūrva* is established.
