It is understood merely that the accomplishment of the result occurs through an intervention; it is not specified whether this is immediate or mediated. And that independence has been established from the outset.
That which brings about its own validity is the principle: "By this, this is accomplished."

This is the meaning of "independence from [external] objects," and that has been established thoroughly by demonstrating the lack of authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*). What is this [statement]: "If there were only five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)..."?
Thus,
the presentation of five means of knowledge distinct from verbal testimony is not tenable, because [you] accept only five means of knowledge. "This is that very thing."
It is not unreasonable to proclaim the number five. Again, the objector says: "But was it not stated that even non-existence (abhāva) is the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva)?"

It has been stated that "non-existence is the absence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*). Therefore, because there is a restriction to five means of valid cognition, this [definition] is not tenable. The defender, providing a firm rebuttal, asks: "What follows from this if it is so? The objector himself says: "This follows from it—[that there are] five..."
"It is not tenable to say 'the means of valid cognition' [are four]. The respondent says: "Or rather, it is possible to say that they do not exist by means of the four."

He says, with a tone of irony (*kāku*), that this is not possible: "It is not possible to initiate the linguistic practice consisting of the employment of the word 'it does not exist' by means of the four instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) other than verbal testimony. The objector says: "In that case, non-existence (*abhāva*) is itself an instrument of knowledge."
Here, the respondent first states the contradiction with the text: "Can it be said that 'either a means of valid cognition or the absence of a means of valid cognition' [is the case]?
Here too, by means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), it is stated that it cannot be so. If...
"Non-existence (abhāva) would be another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa); how then can the author of the Bhāṣya say it is 'the absence of a means of valid cognition'?
He states that even by reasoning, non-existence is not a separate means of valid cognition: "Regarding the validity of non-existence, [it is subsumed under] perception and so forth—"
[204] "Dependence upon an object" refers to the object.
Its meaning is as follows: if non-existence (*abhāva*) were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then—whether it be perception (*pratyakṣa*) or the others—...
Since no other distinct object beyond the delimited [surface] is possible, non-existence (*abhāva*) would necessarily be dependent [on something else]. To explain:

it is not the case that the bare nature of the ground, which is apprehended by perception when a jar or the like is present, must be understood as "it does not exist"; rather, it is because even though the jar and so forth are visible, they are not perceived in their own nature [there]. Therefore—

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is dependent upon the object to be determined, because there is no other object distinct from that [positive entity]. Furthermore, that which does not present an object independently is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, its definition is stated solely as the delimitation (*avacchedaka*) of an object already cognized by another means of valid cognition.
The definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception and the rest, is their function of delimiting an object— that is, determining it as "this very thing"— and not otherwise.
As a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). By this, the contradiction with the text defining [the means of knowledge] is resolved. Now he addresses the objection:
"But the difference in linguistic usage (*vyavahārānyatva*) is indeed already accepted;
for there is no hesitation in the designation 'it does not exist'."

The distinctness of conventional usage characterized by words is indeed already accepted and agreed upon. Furthermore, this presentation is for the sake of establishing conventional usage, not for the sake of establishing the essential nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Conventional usage must also be carried out by means of words.
This point was introduced for the following purpose: this might be so, if there were only five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, the meaning is this: if there were only five instruments for establishing the conventional usage of valid cognition, whereas in fact even verbal testimony (*śabda*) is an instrument for establishing the conventional usage of valid cognition. However, it is not the very nature of a means of valid cognition that is being established here.
By which [reasoning] it would follow that there is another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) beyond the five. Now, why is it explained in this way?

For the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) might simply refer to the nature of the means of valid cognition itself; let it not be explained with the intention of referring to the instrument for the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of a means of valid cognition; and furthermore, let non-existence (*abhāva*) be accepted as another means of valid cognition. To this, he says: "In the acceptance of another means of valid cognition..."
"What is the fault? He answers: "Indeed, it is not any [sin] such as the killing of a Brahmin; rather, it is invalidity (*apramāṇa*)."

If something is not a means of valid cognition at all, it is said to be "that which is a means of valid cognition"; since, by the logic already stated, non-existence lacks the status of a means of valid cognition, to say that it possesses validity would be the fault of accepting what is untenable.
Furthermore, the *Lakṣaṇagrantha* composed by the author of the *Bhāṣya*— which takes the form "non-existence is the absence of means of valid cognition"— is disregarded;
and the independence of all means of valid cognition is thereby refuted,
as is the [independence] of non-existence with respect to perception and the other [means].

If one were to admit that even a dependent [cognition] possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it might be suspected that yet another means of valid cognition could likewise be dependent. Therefore, since there is no other means of valid cognition, this mention of "five" was made solely with the intention of establishing conventional practice (*vyavahāra*).
He concludes: "Therefore, it is established that the word has a distinct object."

It is established that the subject matter of verbal testimony is distinct from the objects of perception and other means of knowledge, because it conveys its effect independently [of them]. And once that is established, its status as a valid means of knowledge is established.
If the establishment of the authority of verbal testimony (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) alone is the subject to be accomplished here, then for what purpose is the mention of "five" made?
It should have been stated as "four" if [the point were] merely that words serve as a means for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

If [the object] were the probandum (*sādhya*), then this would indeed be appropriate; but when validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself is what is to be proven, then what is the purpose of mentioning the number "five"? He provides the answer: it is for the sake of demonstrating the fivefold linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
[Regarding] the linguistic usage of words—
The mention of "five" is intended to demonstrate the fivefold convention regarding emptiness (*riktavyavahāra*). For if the mention of "five" were not made, another convention would not be shown;
since the cognition of another convention is achieved only through effort and is not easily attained.

Since this is possible, the Naiyāyikas consider that the linguistic usage "the branch is fruitless" is produced by perception alone. Now, if they so consider it, let them do so; to this he replies: "The object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
And this conventional usage arises from exclusion (*apoha*):
"This is that very same thing."

Thus, having delimited the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and having ascertained it through the knowledge that determines the probandum (*sādhya*), the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāvavyavahāra*) proceeds. Now, [an objection]: "In that case, if there is such a delimitation, would this not require another means of valid cognition?
To this, he replies: "And the delimitation of the object of the means of valid cognition cannot be said to be a separate object [of cognition]."

When, even with respect to another perceptible object, there occurs the apprehension of its own nature alone, then the "non-existence" of that other object is simply the delimitation (*avaccheda*) consisting in the very investigation of the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it is not, however, a different ontological nature in reality.

Therefore, there is no lapse into another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But how is it that this conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), which arises from the delimitation of the object of a means of valid cognition, does not occur simply from the comprehension of the nature of the object itself? To this he replies: "And from the comprehension of the mere object, without the delimitation [effected] by the preceding means of valid cognition, the conventional usage 'it does not exist' is not possible."

The linguistic usage consisting of the employment of the word "it does not exist," as well as the practical behavior characterized by moving about without hesitation, does not arise from the mere comprehension of the thing's own nature alone.
Therefore, the difference in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is established. Five conventional usages are based on the comprehension of essential nature (*svarūpa*);
one conventional usage is based on delimitation (*avaccheda*). It is precisely for the sake of knowing this mere conventional usage that this was stated, and not [otherwise].

Furthermore, for the purpose of defining the nature of the means of knowledge called non-existence (*abhāva*), and precisely for the sake of establishing another conventional usage, the number five is introduced at the very time of that usage; it is not the number six that is mentioned at the time of describing the nature of the means of knowledge.

The Paṇḍita says: Therefore, since the number five is introduced here, let your honor understand this—the number five is the differentiator of the conventional usage of "non-existence," not of its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).
For if there were a differentiation of the intrinsic nature—

If it were so intended, the number six would have been presented at the very time of stating the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, by employing the number five at the time of practical application (*vyavahāra*), understand that the distinction exists merely for the sake of conventional usage. As for the common consensus (*prasiddhi*), its answer has already been given.
By stating that [the existence of the self] is equivalent to the well-known case of the "Banyan-tree Yakṣa," it is asserted that the establishment of the six means of valid cognition is rootless.
Thus ends the refutation of the objection regarding the painted image and so forth.
As for the statement presented that contradicts direct perception— namely, "This very sacrificer is equipped with the sacrificial implements"— [it is not so].
"Thus he points to the body as being directly perceived"—here too, [the term] "body" (*śarīraka*) is unestablished. What, then, is pointed out? That of which this is the body.
That is designated as the Self.
But surely this is a designation [of "this"], not [a designation] of "one to whom this belongs."
For if it were thus: "He whose body this is,
that sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world."

If such a designation were possible, then even by way of the soul's own intention (*abhiprāya*), the designation "possessor of sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhin*) would be applicable; however, when it says "this one" (*eṣaḥ*),...

Thus, this designation by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) refers only to that which possesses the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhin*); since the Self is not perceptible to other persons, this [designation] is not tenable even with reference to the Self. In that context, because it conforms to the word *eṣa* ("this"), the term *yajñāyudhī* must refer to the body alone, as is clear therein.

[Objection: There is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). [Response: This designation is based on a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), just as in the expression "the platforms are shouting.
The meaning of this is as follows: by this word, an object perceived by the speaker is denoted; and that which is perceived...
That [the Self] is also clearly existent, yet because the Self's mode of being is not clearly manifest, it is referred to by the word "this" (*eṣaḥ*) through figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*).

Figurative usage is expressed here by the term "metaphorical identification" (*abhedopacāra*). Regarding the statement that "the Supreme is designated by the word 'Supreme' (*para*)," there is the following illustration:
Regarding the expression "the beds cry out," this is a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) based on their being located there [in the beds]. Why is the metaphorical meaning of the word accepted?
The answer is: because it is understood in that way.

Because the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) for the theory of denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) consists in the presentation of meanings capable of being syntactically connected, there arises an understanding [of the literal sense] in that manner; yet, since the body is not capable of going to heaven, one understands it in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*). Indeed, because the words of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have another purpose, the understanding is necessarily figurative.
The word "iti" should also be understood here. Now, it might be argued that only when a difference is perceived can the figurative designation of a *vāhīka* as a "cow" be justified.
When a distinction between a cow and a Vāhīka is perceived, the figurative designation "the Vāhīka is a cow" becomes tenable because a primary sense is otherwise impossible;
yet, in this case, we do not perceive anything other than the body.
Regarding that which is designated by a figurative usage: what is the intention behind the statement "we do not perceive it"?
It is with the thought that it is indeed perceived.
He asks. The answer is: this very intention is that "we do not perceive it. But surely we do perceive it through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, which are its effects?
For an effect that occurs only occasionally must have an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

He measures [the breath]; by that inference, the self (ātman) is cognized. Now, it may be argued that the body itself breathes in and breathes out. The point is that, since the causes of the perceptible body are already present, the inference of another cause is not tenable.
He addresses the objection: "What do you mean by 'body,' O long-lived one?
Thinking that the status of being an effect of the body is not possible for the vital breaths and so forth, he asks about the essential nature of the body. The reply is as follows:

This which is a composite of the four elements—a collection of the four elements—is the position of those who know the meaning of categories here: the body is merely a conjunction of the four elements, not something originated by the four elements [as a whole]; rather, the body is purely earthen, while the watery, fiery, and airy [components] are dependent upon it.
And substances are conjoined. As it has been stated by others: "Conjunction, however, is not precluded among the five [elements] mutually.
For instance, this body is not composed of all five elements, nor is it composed of four elements.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that a substance composed of both visible and invisible substances would itself be invisible, just like the conjunction between wind and a tree. Thus say the Yogins: "That very thing...
Thus: "Because the conjunction of perceptible and imperceptible [elements] is itself imperceptible, that which consists of five elements does not exist.
Nor is it commenced by earth, water, and fire—which are perceptible—possessing respectively non-warm-cold, cold, and warm touch.

Because it would result in a tactile sensation distinct from the three [elemental] contacts; just as a cloth woven from white and black threads possesses a distinct variegated color (*citrarūpa*), so too this body would possess a distinct tactile sensation. Yet, this body has a tactile sensation that is neither hot nor cold;
therefore, it must be composed solely of earthy atoms. As they themselves have said: "The manifestation of another quality..."
"And because of its nature as *rūpa*, it is not even three-fold.
By this reason, it is also not two-fold;
for it is impossible for a scent that is exclusively inherent in a single earthen atom to initiate another scent, and thus [the object] would be odorless.

The body would [otherwise] come to possess [only] smell; and since this [body] possesses smell, it is composed of earth alone. That other things, such as the eyes and so forth, which are conjoined with that [earth], are dependent and are specific effects originated by other elements—this is to be understood from other treatises (*tantrāntara*);
only a mere indication has been given here. Therefore, the aggregate is composed of the four elements. To this, it is said: "In that case, then..."
These are effects of the body, because they do not persist as long as the body exists.

By this, the literal meaning of the commentary passage beginning with "as long as his body" has been shown. And this [literal sense] does not absolutely preclude the possibility of their being effects of the body.

It is capable of being accomplished even through deficiency, because the absence of activity is possible as long as the body exists; moreover, deficiency in a dead body is beyond dispute. Therefore, it is explained otherwise: the meaning is "because it does not exist as long as the elements exist."

If these [qualities] were inherent in substances composed of the elements, then, by virtue of being inherent in an effect-substance, they would necessarily occur in the cause-substance as well; for the production of specific qualities in an effect-substance is preceded by the qualities of the cause, just as the production of color and so forth occurs in a jar; and the specific qualities are cognition and the rest. But [one might object]: even in the case of water, which is a liquid substance...
It is observed that solid transformations such as hailstones and the like arise from insentient cow dung, and from that which is insentient, a sentient scorpion is born.

This is as mistaken as mistaking the sky for something else; for so-called solidity is not a distinct quality, but rather the dense conjunction of parts, and conjunction is not a Vaiśeṣika quality. Furthermore, there is indeed the production of the sentient from the insentient.
1. And alone. Ga. 1.
"Drava" omitted. Ga. [p.

This is now the subject of dispute: that [the qualities] do not exist. In that regard, if cognition and the other [mental qualities] were present even in the causal substance, then the jars and other things produced from it would possess cognition and the rest; yet this is not the case. Thus he says:

"Even though they are elemental, for those [qualities] that are unappropriated—that is, not accepted as constituting a body—they are not specific qualities (vaiśeṣika-guṇa), unlike color and the rest."

The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are perceived. Regarding this, the Blessed Kāśyapa said: "From ignorance of the cause comes ignorance of the effect; from ignorance of the effect comes ignorance of the cause.
This is because of the lack of knowledge—that is, the absence of cognition—regarding the earth and other elements which constitute the causes.

The meaning of these two sūtras is as follows: ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) regarding the body initiated by that [ignorance]; however, ignorance regarding the cause [of the body] arises from the ignorance of other effects, such as a jar. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that pleasure and the like are properties of the elements (*bhūtadharma*);
for the properties of the elements, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are perceivable by the external senses just like the elements themselves, whereas pleasure and the like are not.

Whichever things are elemental properties (*bhūtadharma*) are observed to be perceivable by another's sense-faculties, just as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are [perceivable] by others relative to the elements themselves.

The suffix *-vati* here has the sense of the genitive case. However, pleasure (*sukha*) and the like are not perceivable by another's sense-faculties; therefore, they are not elemental properties. [This applies] to the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*).
It is difficult to maintain that when one thing is not being perceived, the perception of another belongs to it only figuratively.

For those qualities which are perceptible belong to a substance that is perceptible and are perceived together with that substance, as is the case with color and so forth; however, pleasure and other such [qualities], though perceptible, are not perceived as residing in a particular substance. Therefore, we conclude that these must certainly be the qualities of a substance that is imperceptible.

"These" refers to the body, which is perceptible; therefore, these qualities belong to something other [than the body]. Consequently, he to whom this is the effect is designated by way of figurative usage (gauṇyā vṛttyā) as "this very one equipped with sacrificial implements. Let it be that pleasure and the like are not properties of the elements; what proof is there here for something else distinct from them?

[The author] says: "By this [statement], from the Buddhist perspective, he refutes only the Vaiśeṣika who maintains an inferred self and who asserts that consciousness belongs to the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavādin*).

This refutation is offered while accepting the impossibility of [consciousness] being a property of the elements; however, in ultimate reality, these [mental factors] are indeed properties of the elements."

It resides in the heart. For this very reason, at the conclusion [of the Upaniṣad], he will summarize the consciousness of the elements themselves by means of the introduction of the Vedic text: "A mass of consciousness alone, arising from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death. We do not think otherwise. Indeed... [text fragment].
2. Omitted *idam*. ga. [p.
212] "There is perception."

Thus [he says]. The author of the commentary will explain all this underlying intention (*ākūta*). And the statement "let them not be" is made by way of a concession (*abhyupagamya-vāda*). But surely, the very fact that "this effect is not possible without its cause" is the proof (*pramāṇa*) in this case?

In this case, inference from the effect (*kāryānumāna*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of the elements has been refuted, it is established that [consciousness] is a property of something else.
The proponent of the doctrine that consciousness belongs to the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavādin*) objects: "It is not so."
It is established because it is also logically possible through their being mutual effects.
Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: “For it cannot be said that whatever is perceived must necessarily have a related correlate.”
Thus, he objects to that: it appears to be improper; for breath and so forth are observed to have an origin, so how could they not lead one to understand another related entity?
To the question "Why does it cause one to understand?", he says: "For it is established that origination possesses a cause;
whatever is an origination, that possesses a cause, just like [the origination] of jars and so forth. He offers a rebuttal:
1. From the perspective of etymological derivation (vyutpatti). Ga.
This refers to the intention of a dissimilar cause (visabhāga-hetu), and it does not mean that arising is said to be entirely without a cause.
The meaning of this is as follows:
this was stated with the intention of referring to dissimilar causes, not to suggest that there must be no other related factor;
for there certainly exists another cause of the same class. By this, cognition and the other mental factors stand in a mutual relationship of cause and effect.
But how is it understood that this refers to a dissimilar cause? For in the case of "the moon" or "the sun," the word *antara* is heard as referring to another related entity.
For upon hearing the word "antara," a cause characterized by a distinct relationship is understood; and that very [cause] is what is negated.
But surely, the word "antara" is applicable even when there is difference (*anyatva*)?
Even among those of the same genus (*samānajātīya*), there exists a certain difference;
it is with this intention that the term "internal" (*antara*) is indeed appropriate. Therefore, this is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for being of a different genus (*vijātīyatva*).
It is true that [the term] is appropriate, but one cannot conclude that an effect is something other than its cause.
Therefore, since the cause of an effect must necessarily exist, when there is an exclusion of other related entities, it is impossible to exclude a cause that is other than the effect;
rather, it is only a cause of a different genus that is excluded. Let there be a flaw in the text, but this does not constitute a logical fault.
This alone is the reason for understanding another meaning.

If the negation of the mere cause were untenable, then let this text also be considered defective precisely because its meaning is untenable; however, it does not follow from the mere utterance of the word "antara" (other/different) that there must be a connection with something of a different class.
[Objection: An understanding [of the effect] in the interval is not logical. [Reply: No, because the continuum (saṃtāna) is accepted.
By this passage, "in a similar continuum," the continuum is accepted. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: For the continuum is the state of being cause and effect...

The connection [is as follows]: entities established in a cause-and-effect relationship, arising in uninterrupted succession, are what is denoted by the term "continuum" (*santati*). In accepting that, there is at least the acceptance of a cause; and when that is accepted, [the consequence] follows in every respect.
1. Also of the same kind.
(ga) 2. To speak.

The negation of a cause is not tenable. Therefore, the negation is intended with respect to a cause of a different kind. Thus he says: "Therefore, understand that this refers to a cause of a similar kind. He concludes: "Hence, it is a cause for a homogeneous continuum."
"This entire web of effects is indeed [produced] from this [very same cause]; there is no means of valid cognition for the perception of anything dissimilar here"—thus the Commentator concluded:
"When it is possible for homogeneous things, established by perception, to serve as causes, the inference of an entirely unobserved cause is not tenable."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the terms *sabhāga* (homogeneous) and *visabhāga* (heterogeneous), according to the established usage within the Buddhist schools (*svanikāya*), refer to the similar and the dissimilar respectively. Furthermore, if there were no occurrence [of an effect] apart from the heterogeneous, there would be a lack of fixed order (*avyavasthā*).

This is the intended meaning: even that self which is to be inferred is rightly considered momentary alone, because for that which is to be known through its effect, there exists proof only for its existence prior to the effect; this being the case for that [self] as well.

For that which has become an effect, another cause of a different genus would necessarily be momentary; for that [momentary cause] as well, there would be yet another such [cause], resulting in an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*).
However, if one postulates a cause of the same genus, then there is mutual causality, and nothing is untenable.
By this very reasoning, since nothing other than cognition and its like is perceived, and since their mutual causality is logically established—

The meaning of the word "agent" as "one who knows" has already been refuted, along with desire and memory, because nothing else distinct from cognition is observed. For it cannot be said that memory and so forth would not be possible if some other dissimilar entity were not seen; indeed, there is no such thing as the impossible when something is actually perceived.

If there were a perception of something other than consciousness (*jñāna*), then, because these [breaths] would be its cause, their impossibility in the absence of that [consciousness] would be understood; however, since nothing else is perceived, there is no inconsistency whatsoever, for they are perceived precisely as distinct from it. But surely, [this implies] the refutation of the marks such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)?

The Commentator’s [objection] is pointless: if the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are capable of making the Self known, then let there be the cognition of the Self from them as well; if they are not, then it is proper simply to disregard them—why is there this refutation of them?
To this he says: "But what is the reason for setting forth all these as causes for the cognition of the Self?"
"They are cast aside by the author of the Commentary.
He states the purpose: "By these [means], the notion of self in what is not-self arises;
and ignorance must be dispelled in every respect."

The meaning of this is as follows: if these reasons were not refuted, then even for disciples whose intellects have been deluded by hearing the Vaiśeṣika and other systems of philosophy, [the correct understanding] regarding these [matters] would not arise.

There would be no conceit of a self as the cause; and since the determination of the effect depends upon the occurrence of the cause, the aggregate of the elements (*bhūtasanghāta*) itself would be the self according to the power of the cause—thus, there would be a conceit of self only with respect to what is non-self. Furthermore, this refutation is intended so that all forms of ignorance may be removed from the disciples. But how, then, do these causes produce the notion of a self in what is not the self?

What is the objection? He states it in a single summary: as for what was said—"We perceive this [Self] by means of the vital breaths and so forth"—what here is incorrect? For these are not qualities of the elements (*bhūta-guṇa*), because they do not exist as long as the elements exist.

When the view that [the mind] is a property of the elements has been rejected on the grounds that it is not observed in jars and the like, and since things possessing origination cannot arise without an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), it is understood that [the mind] must have another related entity; thus, for the mind, for cognition, and for the object of cognition—

Furthermore, since pleasure and the like arise spontaneously and are dependent [on something], they require another substratum; and while the postulation of such another substratum stands, it is indeed rightly said that "these are qualities of the eternal self, being themselves without a substratum. How so? By this reason.
(This has been explained previously. *Note: This was previously explained.* (ga)

2. [Ga. p. 218] Consciousness cannot be said to have the notion of "self" with respect to itself; therefore, pleasure and the other [feelings], being perceived as dependent, [must likewise be distinct from the self].

Furthermore, because they exist as long as the elements exist, those [qualities] whose dependence on the elements has been discarded have been correctly described by the Vaiśeṣikas and others as being qualities of the self (*ātman*).
To this, it is replied: first of all, it cannot be said that breath (*prāṇa*) and the other [vital functions] exist as long as the elements exist.
Why is this? The answer is: for these, beginning with breath (*prāṇa*), are of the nature of motion; and this is the characteristic property of wind (*vāyu*).
Regarding "motion" (calana): it is not the case that the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth lack the nature of motion within the processes of breathing and the like. Thus he says:
"For in all cases, such as breathing and so forth, only the nature of motion is perceived. Therefore, the claim that [the vital breaths] exist only as long as the elements exist is unproven.

Regarding the vital breaths and so forth: this notion of a self with respect to what is not the self is [false]. As for pleasure and the other qualities that were proposed, they too can be said to be merely qualities of the elements, because they are the causes of modifications in the elements.

He has presented a direct perception [of the self]. For this very reason—that since action is impossible for that which is momentary, there is an absence of agency, and thus the very nature of the self is lost—the proponents of selflessness repeatedly attribute momentariness and inefficacy to the self, saying: "If it were like a piece of leather, it would be impermanent."
"If it were equal to space, it would be equivalent to a non-entity.
Otherwise, the demonstration of momentariness being ineffective would be useless.
It might be so. Therefore, those who know the Self have established that the very capacity to be an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) is the Self, because all agree on this;

since the designation "Self" applies when there is the state of being an enjoyer, it is said figuratively that the capacity to be an enjoyer is the Self. This is logical—that the capacity to be an enjoyer is the Self—but the introduction of agency (*kartṛtva*) is contradictory, because the Self is actionless (*niṣkriya*) and all-pervading (*sarvagata*).
[The soul] is inactive; and its omnipresence is established because happiness is perceived everywhere.
Nor should it be argued that the perception of a property occurs only when [the soul] has arrived; for if there were no arrival, nothing would be contradicted.
1. *sabhṛtyā*. Ka, *satyā*. Ga. [p. 236] thus.

Existence (*sattā*) is established for the self (*ātman*) through the perception of pleasure everywhere; however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this existence is preceded by movement. There is no inconsistency whatsoever even without movement. As for the perception of pleasure and so forth when the body moves, that is accounted for by the localized nature (*prādeśikatva*) of pleasure and the rest. And this localized nature—

Because pleasure and the like arise from the contact of the self with the mind, and because the mind is localized, the very fact that the self is not perceived in a region devoid of the body is due to the localization of cognition itself— namely, that it is perceived only where there is cognition. [The opponent] offers a rebuttal by accepting that action consists of motion.

Inactivity has been stated [with respect to the Self], but not even with respect to the arising of experience (*bhoga*). Experience is perception, which is consciousness; even with respect to the arising of that, there is no inactivity. Consciousness, too, is an action, because it is denotable by a verbal root (*dhātu*); for action is that which is denoted by a verbal root.

[They are] worldly [views]. Otherwise, there would not even be the designation "element" (*dhātu*). Since the self's status as agent and enjoyer is established through reasoning, it is rightly and beautifully stated:
"The self is precisely agency and enjoyment. Thus, being denoted by the word "self" is based upon agency and enjoyment. [This is because of the non-difference between cause and effect—]

And for this reason it is said: "The self is indeed the agent and the enjoyer. Since the self is established as having the nature of being the agent and the enjoyer, this passage—"I saw this"—is appropriately introduced as an argument for the recognition (pratyabhijñā) intended to establish the true nature of the self.

Thus [it is said]. He states another purpose for introducing the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the self: "And the recognition of objects has this as its basis," as is introduced in the section on *śabda* (the word);
"this is that very same [thing]."
1. Regarding the word *gamane*.
In the term *ga*, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is the letter *ga*" is a recognition of a stable cognizer who persists through the states of prior and subsequent experiences.

The term "jñānimitta" (the cause of cognition) introduces the object to be recognized in proximity to the locus of the word, so that recognition of the object may occur once a stable cognizer has been established.
But [one might ask]: "I saw this."

By this much alone, the existence of the self as distinct from the body and so forth is established; why then is it said that "this cognition 'I' occurs with respect to the inner self"? To this, he says:
To what purpose does this [reasoning] apply to the inner self (*pratyagātman*)?
The answer is: for the very sake of establishing its status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). How so? Because enjoyment is observed in the inner self.

Experience is observed in the inner self (pratyagātman) in the form "I experience this"; furthermore, the notion of "I" has the inner self as its object. Therefore, because it has the experiencer as its object, [the notion of "I" refers to the Self].

It establishes the enjoyer. If another [entity] were also to become the object of the notion of "I," then the status of being the enjoyer would be lost; for in that case, the establishment of the status of being the enjoyer could not proceed from the notion of "I. And it has been stated that the nature of being the enjoyer is the Self.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the commentary states for the sake of establishing the Self: "And this occurs with respect to the inner Self. Here follows another portion of the commentary:
Regarding the phrase "not elsewhere":
its meaning is that no recognition occurs elsewhere in the form, "I saw this."

He states that recognition is untenable regarding "otherness" in the sense that "the other is indeed he who was seen on another day. If so, for what purpose is the introduction of the word "I" in the phrase, "where this word 'I' [is used]"?

The point is that one should have stated at the very outset: "In this [self], there is this notion of 'I'"; for if [the opponent] intends only to negate [the self], they might say: "We do not designate the word 'I' as being used in this sense as a logical reason."

Thus, the word "I" (ahaṃ) has been introduced precisely for the purpose of negation. The reply is: not for the sake of negation, but solely for the sake of the cognition of another; for another [is guided] by the use of words in linguistic practice.
It is thus established. Why, then, is there a denial? It is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion that [the self] is a direct cause.
He states this very point: for the opponent, who considers it to be a direct cause, [thinks] that the word "I" exists even with respect to what is not the self.
This has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with, "The word 'I' is also seen used figuratively in reference to others," and so forth. "Not we..."
Thus, it has been made manifest that this was not presented as a direct cause; rather, the underlying point remains in the heart [of the author].

As for the cognition (*pratyaya*) which is the meaning of "cause"—that is, the object in the form of a cause—the employment of words is for the purpose of demonstrating that very cognition. It is indeed cognition itself.

But it is the direct cause. Now, one might object: the statement "I go" cannot be dismissed as being merely an illustration of the meaning of the cause; for here, even the notion of "I" is observed to be indeed subject to deviation.
Because the self is immovable by nature,

and because this cognition has a moving entity as its object, it cannot be said to have the self as its objective support. Therefore, one must consider that it is only the aggregates (skandhas) that become the objective support.
[Objection: This [is the case]; why then is it understood by those who are entirely free from doubt?
[Response: What is there to be doubted here?
Since there is no doubt at all in this matter, it was not raised as a doubt in the Bhāṣya. Why is that? He says: "For this is to be grasped by the notion of 'this' (idam-pratyaya-grāhyam)."

The meaning is: the instrument of action, as well as the object of knowledge and the act of knowing. The aggregates (skandhas) consist of the object of knowledge and the act of knowing; therefore, they are grasped by the notion of "this" (*idam-pratyaya*), which is opposed to the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding an entity graspable by a different notion, there is the support of a contrary notion.
The application [of the term] "cow" is not possible [to a Vāhīka], just as in the case of the statement "the Vāhīka is a cow";
for a Vāhīka is never [a cow].
It becomes the object of the cognition "cow. Now, it is not the case that there is no justification whatsoever; rather, [the primary sense] has been set aside. (ga.

There is no such thing as having a secondary object-condition (*gauṇālambana*). If it is argued that "secondary" refers to what is metaphorically established as a condition, this has already been refuted by you yourself.
For in the case of a secondary usage, there is merely the employment of a word; it does not, however, constitute an actual condition.

For a Vāhīka does not possess the state of being grasped by a cognition that has the form of a "cow. He concludes: Therefore, the "I-cognition" (ahaṃpratyaya) has as its objective support the "this-cognition" (idaṃpratyaya) itself, which is undifferentiated (*asaṃbhinna*).
"Undifferentiated" means unmixed with it.

The meaning is that this very notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is established as the objective support (*ālambana*) for the self (*ātman*), serving as its cause for being posited. That is to say, because it is understood [to apply] only to the aggregates (*skandhas*) which are the objects of the notion of "this" (*idampratyaya*), it is not at all a cause for the establishment of this self. The Brāhmaṇa also restates this same point: [it speaks of] the self's state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) by virtue of its indestructibility; such is the state of being an enjoyer.

The very nature of the self as the self— the Brāhmaṇa also restates this same point regarding the self’s status as the enjoyer by demonstrating its stability in the words, “It is indestructible, for it is not destroyed. And [it contrasts this with] “consciousness is perishable.”
Thus, he establishes that [the object of the notion of "I"] has an objective support distinct from consciousness.
For the notion of "I" has a stable object, whereas consciousness is momentary; therefore, he establishes that the notion of "I" has an objective support distinct from consciousness.

Therefore, it cannot be said that this delusion is the knot of egoism; for "only that cognition whose instrument is defective and which possesses the conviction 'this is false' is an incorrect cognition,
and no other."
Thus, because this matter is established:

if this is the conviction of those who know Brahman—that the state of being an enjoyer which is perceived is unreal, while that absolute liberation (kaivalya) which is not perceived is the reality; [then...]

Salutations to those wise ones; as for the objection that no answer should be given here, this is the resolution. Therefore, this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—“This very sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes straight to the heavenly world”—is not devoid of truth.
[240] He said: "If there is a cognizer other than consciousness, distinct from consciousness,
let it be demonstrated— pointing it out as 'this is it' and 'it is such-and-such'."
When it is asked, "What is this that is being questioned?"—this very thing is what is being questioned. That itself is not known. How is it not known? In this way: not.

It is explained: Is the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) regarding the self endowed with consciousness being presented as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that it is said—"Setting aside consciousness, that [self] must be demonstrated"? For where a cognition has multiple objects as its basis, it is appropriate to say—"Setting this aside, demonstrate that."
In this case, however, the consciousness "I" has the single form of the Self alone;
therefore, it is the Self itself that shines forth here exclusively, and not even cognition. Consequently, it is perceived precisely by setting aside cognition. Thus, this objection does not hold.

"Having set aside consciousness (vijñāna), this [object] must be demonstrated. Therefore, the phrase "this is to be excluded" refers to darkness; the meaning is that it has proceeded without due consideration. To this, it is said: this is his intended meaning.
For if the self were an object of knowledge, it would be impossible to speak of cognition and the cognizer as distinct from it;
nor is it established that consciousness exists apart from these two.
This is the meaning:
For he who asserts that the self is the object of the notion of "I" must state that there is a cognition distinct from the self— which is the object of knowledge—
and that there is a knower, distinct from it, who is the agent. And it is not possible for both of these to be the self.

To speak further: there can be no action devoid of both instrument and agent. Therefore, you—who reject the acceptance of a distinct agent and instrument, yet desire the self to be an object of knowledge—must likewise admit that the self is perceived by setting aside even consciousness as the instrument. If this is so, then for us as well, having set aside consciousness...

"This must be demonstrated as being of such a nature. To this he says: "Therefore, having set aside both the cognition and the cognizer, it must be shown as a distinct object of knowledge"—this is the meaning of the objection. "To this it is replied: It is self-cognizable;
it cannot be seen by another."
Thus [it is asked]: "How is this answer of his tenable?

Why is it not tenable? It is not tenable in this way: for this very thing previously mentioned—the fact that a single cognition has multiple aspects while having a single object—would be what is being admitted.

The meaning of this is as follows: by stating that "it is self-cognizable," it is admitted that the single Self alone is apprehended by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) in the dual form of both agent and object.
"It is said that it is mere conceptual construction (vikalpamātra). This is the fault of non-discrimination; it is not your honor's fault here.
He says this in a single passage: "But surely this notion of 'I' [is such that one thinks], 'I saw this.'"
Thus it has been proposed: "The self is not even to be discarded. [p.
"I saw [it].
This being the case, what is this "manifoldness of forms"?
Therefore:
“Lack of discernment is the abode of supreme calamities.
This is the underlying intention here: the self, while experiencing another object...

It shines, but not in isolation. Thus, in that case, regarding the cognition whose object is another thing (*arthāntara*), the self (*ātman*) is indeed the agent, while the other thing is the object (*karman*). That very same cognition, in producing a perception whose object is the other thing, also illuminates itself. This is the single state of illumination belonging to both the object and the subject.
For an object of knowledge never appears devoid of a knower; otherwise, there would not be the thought, "This has been known by me," but rather,
"This is known."

If this were so, then there would be no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another. Furthermore, the knower does not manifest when there is no cognition of the object to be known, as in deep sleep, intoxication, fainting, and the like.
Therefore, the object and the subject are necessarily perceived together. This being the case, even though...

If the self were not experienced as the object (*karman*) by virtue of its connection with the fruit of the action characterized as the manifestation produced by cognition—just as space is not [experienced as the object] despite its connection with the fruit of conjunction—then, just as in that case the location alone is the object because it possesses the fruit produced by an action residing elsewhere, so too here another entity would be the object. This very point he reveals: "For if the self..."
The state of being knowable (*jñeyatā*) would also have been presented as being denotable by the word "agent" (*kartṛ-śabdavācyatā*).

For if it had been stated that [the agent] is the object (*karman*) denotable by the word "agent," or if, according to the actual state of things, there were an absence of any other object of cognition (*prameyāntara-śūnyatā*), [then the state of being knowable would follow].
In that case, this objection would have arisen:
for if there were no other object of cognition (*prameya*), then in the absence of another action (*karma*), the self itself would be the action—as in "I saw myself. (Ga.)
2. When even that which is known is [itself] to be known. (ga) 3. "Api" was added.
(ga) 4. "Api" was omitted. (ka)
It might be so; however, in this context, consciousness is presented precisely as the cognizer of all that is to be known—
the Self which cognizes every object of knowledge.

Since it manifests solely as the agent, there is no relationship of object and agent; rather, there is only agency itself. Therefore, this is merely a presentation of a thesis and its counter-argument regarding the cognition of multiple forms within a single objective support; how could that very [cognition] be sublated by itself? For that which is to be sublated by something cannot possibly be its sublater.

Therefore, the correct answer is that it is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). For the state of having multiple aspects while having a single object occurs when one accepts that the self is both the object and the agent of its own action. However, when the self does not experience objects but appears as a mere presence, [it is self-cognizable].

In that case, there is no contradiction regarding the occurrence of an action within itself. By this illustration—"just as someone who possesses sight"—it is precisely the negation of any other agent or instrument that is being established. Now, here...
The agent is different [from the object], the instrument is the eye, and both are indeed distinct from the object of cognition, which is color-form (*rūpa*).
Therefore, how can this be an illustration? He provides the answer: "Because of the commonality of the absence of another agent."
The illustration: Just as when a man possessing sight perceives a form for himself, there is no other agent;
this much is the similarity by which it serves as an example. He concludes: "Therefore, [cognitions] free from defects in their cause are non-erroneous.
[Note: 1. nāsti tat. ga.]
2. Kevalaḥ. Ga. 3. Omitted. Ubhayam. Ga. 4.
By this much alone, [it] exists. Ga.
And this is the reason for the existence of the self as consciousness. Whether there be another agent or not,
it exists.
There is consciousness even with respect to the self; therefore, the self exists, even though there is no other agent—this is the sense.
And it has been said: "In whatever way objects are cognized, so they come to be; in whatever way objects are not cognized, so they do not come to be."
In this case as well, regarding the absence of another agent or another instrument, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "when speech has become quiet.
This very [passage] is [cited] because it accords with the meaning of the authoritative source favored by [the author] himself.

He explains: the question is how it is understood that even when the self is occupied with something else external, such as form (*rūpa*), there is an absence of another agent or another instrument (*karaṇa*) acting as the agent. And the mention of speech (*vāk*) in the Brāhmaṇa, accompanied by the word "calm" (*śānta*), is for the purpose of illustrating the absence of other instruments; by the calmness of speech, the absence of other instruments is expressed.

This means up to that point. The meaning of the statement, "The Self is light, O Emperor," is that this very nature of self-cognition has been illuminated by the Brāhmaṇa passage through the sequence of the prima facie and final positions. Thus, when the Self is not grasped by another—so [it is said].

And having established this, the Brāhmaṇa passage, "It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped," is also rendered consistent. But is it not the case that here [the text] speaks only of its being ungraspable?
1. Added. ca. ga.
It has been presented in every respect, but not merely as something graspable by another person. He states the answer: "Have you not heard, O Emperor, that 'the Self is light'?"
Thus [it is said]. For here in this Brāhmaṇa, self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) has been stated;
the sense is that, in accordance with that, only the quality of being perceivable by another (*parāgrāhyatva*), which was required, has been presented. Here, he raises an objection: "This too..."
Have you not heard?

It is called "ungraspability. Between two scriptural statements, the scriptural statement regarding the non-apprehension of this Self—in accordance with that [other] statement and in accordance with its self-luminosity—is explained as being relative, with reference to another person.
Thus, what is the reasoning for not explaining the mention of the "Self" in another way? He provides the answer:
because a figurative description is impossible in the case of the mention of the "self-luminous" (svayaṃjyotis);
its self-luminosity cannot be established through a secondary (gauṇī) mode of signification.
It can be explained that [the self] is ungraspable, for its ungraspability is established by way of relativity;
indeed, ungraspability can be described even with reference to another person. Thus: "The Self is to be known, it is to be reflected upon."
And thus there is no contradiction;
for if non-apprehensibility were not relative, then it would contradict the statement that [the object] is to be known.
And thus, since it is ungraspable in this relative sense, its self-luminosity (svayaṃjyotiṣṭva), which is mentioned in other passages, is also established.

If the Self were indeed only self-cognizable, one might ask: "In that case, how can it be communicated to another? Yet, this undertaking by the authors of the scriptures and the Vedas is for the purpose of producing conviction in others.
For no treatise is composed by anyone for their own sake; likewise, the activity of the Vedas is for the purpose of the understanding of others.
The answer: here, self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) itself functions as the means.

But why is self-awareness alone the means and nothing else? To this he says: because it is experienced by oneself and not by another, for that reason self-awareness alone is the means and nothing else.

Thus, since for all persons there exists a consciousness of the Self that is not cognizable by another, the status of the teachings as "teachings" is established by way of negating the consciousness of another; however, it cannot be said that "this is such-and-such," with this intention [the Upanishads say] "not this, not this."
Thus it was introduced. Here, the Commentator, having stated, "The means for this [self] is the negation of that which another perceives," said:
"Pleasure and the like residing in another are understood by others through their indicative marks (liṅga)."

It has been stated that “they too are not the self”; this [objection] is raised: But surely pleasure and the like, which inhere in themselves, are indeed self-cognized; they too are certainly not cognized by another as residing in another. How, then, can the self be something other than these?

Is it taught by another? Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya stated that because they are understood through indicative marks (*liṅga*), they are indeed understood as being prompted (*preṇā*). That is incorrect, because it would follow [absurdly] for the Self (*ātman*) as well.
For the Self—
It follows that [the body] would be non-self; for even in that case, he himself puts forward an inference based on purposeful activity, since [he says]:
"This too is understood through the activity of a person."

By such commentary, it has been stated that the self is understood through the inference of activities such as beginning and completing what was half-finished; therefore, how can this be written by the learned as being superimposed upon an object already apprehended?
He responds: This objection is raised by one who has not served a teacher. For it is activity that is presented as the means for removing defects in the cause;
that by which a defect in the cause is removed [is what constitutes valid cognition].
The meaning is that it is the removal of the suspicion regarding defects in its cause, which has been presented by means of her existence. This is what is intended:

whatever suspicion there may be regarding defects in the cause within one's own self-consciousness—namely, "Does this self appear due to a defect in its cause even though it does not exist?"—that is removed by the activity residing in another person.
Pleasure and the like, however, are cognizable through the contraction of the eyebrows, the play of the eyes, and so forth;

the meaning is that pleasure and the like are indeed understood by means of the contraction of the eyebrows and such. But what, then, is the distinction between this inference from bodily movement and the inference from the contraction of the eyebrows?

For even in this inference from activity (*ceṣṭā*), it is the consciousness of another that is inferred by means of one's own [consciousness]; likewise, through the inference from the contraction of the eyebrows, there is the consciousness of pleasure and so forth. The answer is: the distinction lies in the fact that [the former] is not an effect (*akāryata*).

For movement is not the effect of the self; therefore, the inference that arises from movement is not [an inference] from an effect. Since frowning and so forth are effects of pleasure and so forth, the inference of those [pleasures] is from an effect. Thus, the self is not cognized through movement; rather, pleasure and so forth are cognized through frowning and so forth. Therefore...

The supreme self (parātmā) is not apprehended by another even through inference, whereas pleasure and so forth are apprehended; this is the distinction. Again, the opponent objects: "But how can one perceive that which is unconnected?"
And how does an unobserved non-contradiction with other persons dispel the suspicion of contradiction regarding oneself?
The meaning of this is as follows: if volitional activity were not an effect of the self, then how could it [be known] by the self?

How can that which is unrelated characterize itself? This statement is made with reference to the universal (sāmānya), and thus the neuter designation "this" (*idam*) is used for "the unrelated. Now, if you think: "We have no need for the self to be characterized; therefore, what is the use of this characterization?"—to that he replies: "And how [could it be] uncharacterized?"

The non-perversion of another person—that is, the non-perversion of another self—is its state of being non-erroneous; does this dispel the suspicion of perversion regarding one's own self? He considers that when the non-erroneous nature of another self is realized, the suspicion of perversion regarding one's own self disappears, and not otherwise. We reply: it is because of the non-perception of perversion.
The meaning is that doubt is dispelled by the mere non-perception of error. When, even upon searching with effort,
no error is perceived in another person, then the doubt regarding error concerning one's own object ceases.

Indeed, through inference from activity, one perceives that the self-apprehension of this [other person] is exactly like one's own; thus a similar apprehension is recognized. Furthermore, since no contrary nature of the self to be apprehended is perceived, doubt is dispelled. And it has already been stated that the state of being a related term is not required for non-apprehension.
1. Added: *svakīya* [means] in one's own self. (ga) 2.
Omitted: *nānyathā*—the suspicion of the opposite. (ga)
Therefore, this statement of Śabara is well-founded. Here, an objection is raised: "Let it not be [the case that the self is inferred] from purposeful action..."

There is no inference of one's own self [from activity], because there is no relationship between activity and the self; but why does the cognition caused by activity not lead to the inference of another's self? [Because] it is a cognition.
"Because of its connection with that which is to be cognized. To this we reply: it has already been stated that the self is defined by being the enjoyer;
that is to say, by being the experiencer. Therefore, [the self] is not something to be inferred as an object of experience.
Because it is not perceived as having the nature of a self, the self is not understood by another through inference. Furthermore, analogy is presented here merely as a means of explanation:
"Or it is taught by means of analogy."
Thus, in the Bhāṣya, [it] is presented as a means of explanation by way of being a secondary [or subordinate] element.
(Note: *nāperaṇa* is corrected to *nāpareṇa*; *tvenopanyastā* is corrected to *tvenopanyastaḥ*).
[Page 250] It is considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"Description" (*kathana*) refers to that by which something is described, namely a sentence; it is itself the comparison (*upamā*), because it brings about the comprehension of similarity.
However, the means of valid cognition in the form of a standard of comparison (*upamāna-pramāṇa*) is not here introduced by the word "comparison"; rather, that which is the description—
Since [the definition] is preceded by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction between the statement of the definition and its practical application (*vyavahāra*).
As for what was also said— "Setting aside consciousness (*vijñāna*), let that [object] be demonstrated"— [it is replied as follows]:
With this, he restates the commentary and raises an objection: "But has this not already been answered by the statement, 'It is self-cognizable'?"

By this commentary, an answer has been given to the objection, "Setting aside consciousness, let that [object] be demonstrated"; and once an answer has been given, the restatement of the question is not tenable. Now, if the intention is as follows—
That which was previously stated is not at all [the answer]; this very response is the immediate reply to this objection.
Now he refutes it: "To whom, then, does that reply belong?
The proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) answers: "If not..."
Regarding someone's response: "Is it by this much that there must be a response to that?
For that is not the response to another;
is it by this much that it becomes a response to that, such that there is a logical justification for its being a response to that?"—this is the meaning.
The proponent of the refutation says: "But surely, because it is mentioned immediately after that, it is understood to be its consequence. The partisan (ekadeśin) says:
"1. The mention of the word [is for the sake of] explaining that. (ga.)
2. Added: *nopamānapūrvakam*. (ga) 3. And of the statement of its definition: *iti tallakṣaṇābhidhānasya ca*. (ga) 4. Omitted: *anena*—of this [phrase]. (ga)

5. This previously mentioned [explanation] is not the answer to this objection; rather, this very [point] is the answer. The meaning is that the reasoning for it being an answer is because [the faults] exist. Ga. 6.
—Understand that because a further question is stated, this is not an answer;

for once an answer has been given, a further question is no longer appropriate. Moreover, sequence (*krama*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, being understood as an answer through the sequence consisting of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), it is [so recognized].
Furthermore, because its lack of being a reply is understood through the mark (liṅga) of the force of the subsequent question, it is sublated;

therefore, that [previous statement] does not constitute a reply to this objection. Now, the final proponent says: "This is as mistaken as mistaking the sky [for something else]; both [statements] are indeed replies to that very same [objection]."

Why? Because even this [statement], "it becomes self-cognizable," is understood as an answer derived from the very same logical mark (*liṅga*). And its capacity to refute that [position] has already been explained.

Therefore, since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) alone is the means of proof for the answer in both cases, both [the *liṅga* and the *śruti*] constitute the answer to that very [question]. Now, having refuted the partisan of a single school (*ekadeśin*), he questions the proponent of the final established doctrine (*paramasiddhāntin*): "For what purpose is the question asked again now?"
The reply:
"Something is clinging" means something is attached. What is that which is clinging?
He shows what is currently clinging: "True."
"It is experienced as 'I am aware of this,' and there is no postulation of another form [of the object]; however, the apprehension of that which is distinct from consciousness would not be possible,
because activity is understood [to belong to the subject]."
If the self is understood as knowing an object, then the apprehension of a self devoid of consciousness is not possible; therefore, there must also be the apprehension of consciousness.
And since no other form [of the self] is perceived upon the comprehension of consciousness, it is once again that very same emptiness; for when consciousness is being apprehended—
It must be apprehended in some form, because there is no apprehension of that which is devoid of form; and in that case, [how could it be] distinct from blue and so forth? Why?
Because [it would be] by means of the cognition of the object, [the self]. (Note: *ga* omits "kutaḥ" and reads "viṣayajñānenātmā".)
Since no other form is perceived, it follows that the very nature of that [object] is blue and so forth; consequently, it follows that cognitions are devoid of an object.
Therefore, when the external object is established as the basis for the apprehension of consciousness, this [notion of] "I" is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
This "knot" is that which is attached to it; therefore, it is mentioned again. What is intended by the respondent when he says, "If you negate the means itself"?
This is what is intended: for it has been stated that apprehension conforms to the object to be apprehended.
There is no conformity with a grasper.

It was stated in the refutation of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) that consciousness possesses the form of the grasped (*grāhya*), not the form of the grasper (*grāhaka*). Therefore, knowledge is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); because it functions as a means during its state of activity—

The state of being engaged (*vyāpṛta*) is mentioned as a means (*upāya*), but not as the actual apprehension through engagement; for when the Self experiences objects, it then appears within the experience related to those objects— how, then, could that which is the goal (*upeya*) be a non-means (*anupāya*)?

"It can be explained. Thus he says: "If you deny the means itself, it is impossible to attain the goal without the means; this very thing is to be understood as the means for those objects that are to be known.
For example: what is called 'white'? That in which whiteness exists."
With the following intention, he raises an objection as to what has been established by this [statement]: "This has been established."
Just as [it is not the case that] there is the aspect of consciousness existing as a grasper (grāhaka) within that very [consciousness]. (ga. 2. Added. ga.
Just as whiteness is not perceived apart from the white object, so too the object of knowledge is not perceived apart from the act of knowing;
and when the object of knowledge is not perceived, the self is not perceived either. Now, he reveals the intention of the objector: "But surely..."

And thus, it has been stated that cognition regarding the white [object] is preceded by the perception of whiteness; therefore, in accordance with this analogy, cognition regarding the object of knowledge (jñeya) is likewise preceded by knowledge (jñāna). In this way, the unintended meaning is established. It is not unintended;
for this much has been said by him: that there can be no status as an "end" (upeya) for ends without a means (upāya).

In that regard, just as something is an instrument for one person, so it is for another; however, it has been stated that even though knowledge is an instrument, the intellect does not necessarily precede it.
He concludes: "Therefore, the status of being an object of all forms of knowledge is established for the self by all means of valid cognition, recollection, and discernment."

The knowability of the self is established by the commentary [statement]: "I perceived this. For here it is said that there is no cognition of an object without a cognition of the self. But if it is thus a knowable object through inferential cognition, does it not follow that it is also an object of inference?
Regarding this, he says: "Even in inference and so forth, there is direct perception.

Because the self appears through direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), it is indeed direct perception even in inference and the like. If the self is perceptible in all cases, then everything [would be perceptible].
1. *ākṣeptāśaya-* (intention of the objector), as in manuscript Ga.
2. *api* is omitted in manuscript Ga. 3. *saṃvido nāsti* (there is no consciousness) is absent in manuscript Ga.

Regarding the claim that it would be perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: for the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from the difference in objects (*viṣaya*), not from the difference in cognizers (*pramātṛ*).
If the distinction between means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were based on the distinction between cognizers (*pramātṛ*), then there would be no other means of valid cognition;
for since the cognizer—the self—is of a single nature due to being perceptible everywhere, everything would be perceptible everywhere.

However, the distinction between means of valid cognition arises from the distinction between objects (*viṣaya*). But why is it that the distinction among the means of valid cognition occurs solely through the distinction of objects?

To the question of why this does not occur even through the differentiation of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), he says: "But the state of being the cognizer in the case of cognition is not to be suspected at all, because it has never been suspected by any proponent. Now, although...

Although this has not been doubted by anyone, [the author] says here: "Why then do we ourselves doubt it?"—it is appropriate that this has not been doubted, because action (*karman*) is characterized by its tendency toward an object; that is to say, because an action possessing an object (*sakarmika*) has the object as its primary element. Consequently, [the result belongs] to the subordinate factor precisely through the distinction of the object upon which the primary [action] depends.

A distinction between knowledge and action is logical. As for what was also stated—that the state of being a knower cannot be understood apart from knowledge—that is because the understanding of that [knower] is dependent upon it;
for the understanding of the knower is dependent upon knowledge. Therefore...
1. Omitted. hi. ga. 2. Omitted. jñānā---gateḥ. ga. [p. 255]
Knowledge must also be known. As it has been said: "There is no perception of another form [of knowledge];
therefore, knowledge itself arises in the form of the knower; thus, there is no knower distinct from knowledge. This too has been refuted:
"Granted that consciousness might be denied, the object is not."
Thus, he concludes the established point: "Therefore, the reality of the Self is proven."
Furthermore, as for the Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "After death, there is no consciousness," which purports to establish that consciousness belongs to the material elements (*bhūta-caitanya*),
that has been explained by the Brāhmaṇa itself through the method of a prima facie argument and its refutation; [it does not support] consciousness consisting of the material elements.
The meaning is that, having presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established by the passage beginning with, “Indeed, this Self is indestructible.
And since the Self is thus established, its status as being for the purpose of an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is indeed appropriate; hence, “nor is this an injunctive word.”
Thus,
that objection which was raised has also been answered. But surely, the phrase "this very one" (sa eṣaḥ) is logically consistent.
1. Omitted. As it has been said. Ga.
"How does one go to the heavenly world? To this, the answer is: it is established because the desires of the qualified person are fulfilled.

This too is established, because it has been settled that the desire of the qualified person for heaven and so forth is accomplished. As it was said: "The notions of 'I' and 'mine' are the conceits of self with respect to what is not the self."
These two notions of "I" and "mine"— the cognitions "I" and "mine"— are [directed] toward what is not the self as if it were the self.
Regarding the phrase "become free from pride": this is to be explained only for those whose impurities have been rubbed away;

that is, it is to be explained only for those whose impurity—namely, passion (*rāga*)—has been rubbed away. It is not for those attached to action (*karmasaṅgin*); thus the discussion concludes. And it has been said:
The venerable Dvaipāyana stated in the section on the secret doctrine: “One should not cause a disturbance of the intellect in the ignorant who are attached to action.
Therefore, the Lord did not explicitly explain that the notions of "I" (ahaṅkāra) and "mine" (mamakāra) have the non-self as their object.
The author of the Bhāṣya states that [the Lord does not act] out of ignorance, in accordance with the words of Dvaipāyana.
Thus ends the section on the doctrine of self (ātmavāda). Regarding this, he says:
"It is not unknown. (Note: *ga* refers to the manuscript reading.)
Some maintain that there is action in that state, because it is observed there.
“It has been stated that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal; that is untenable.”—
What is this untenability?

By this, he raises an objection to the commentary. He resolves it: this very point is the inconsistency; if sound is non-eternal, an eternal relationship that is not produced by human effort is untenable.
For instance, if a relationship were to exist between a non-eternal sound and its meaning, it could not be established as eternal.

Because the relationship itself is non-eternal; for that which is non-eternal must necessarily be produced by human effort—that is to say, it is brought about by convention and so forth. Indeed, it is not possible for a word produced by human effort to have a non-human (apauruṣeya) relationship [to its meaning]; for in that case, its capacity to denote [the object] arises solely from convention.

It might be so; for indeed, in the case of a sound that perishes as soon as it is produced, an innate relationship cannot be established through the usage of elders. If an eternal (non-human) relationship is not possible for something impermanent, how then could it be possible in the case of inherence (*samavāya*)?

Even for an impermanent manifestation (*vyakti*), its relation with the universal (*jāti*), characterized as inherence (*samavāya*), is non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*); likewise is the relation of an action with its factors (*kāraka*s), of a whole with its parts, and of qualities with their possessors. To this, the answer is: the impossibility [of such a relation] between two things established separately (*yutasiddha*).

It is impossible for a relationship between two related entities that are separately established (*pṛthaksiddha*) to be non-human-made (*apauruṣeya*); furthermore, these two are not separately established (*ayutasiddha*).
2. "Produced from the *samaya* and so forth. (ga) 3. "Not [so]. (ga) 4. Omitted. Here follows the reply: this [objection] is preceded by a challenge. (ga)
[Page 258] Individual instances and so forth. What, then, is "separate establishment" (*yutasiddhi*)? It is the state of having separate substrata and the state of having separate movements.
For meanings do not reside in words, nor do words reside in meanings; therefore, they have separate substrata.

And they possess separate movements. Furthermore, among individuals and so forth, universals (*jāti*), actions (*kriyā*), qualities (*guṇa*), and wholes (*avayavin*) do not depend on anything other than the individuals and so forth; whereas individuals, qualities, agents, and parts, although dependent on something else, are nonetheless "possessors of non-separate movement" (*apṛthagatimant*), and thus are "inseparably established" (*ayutasiddha*). What, then, is the reasoning here regarding those that are inseparably established?

Is it not the case that even for impermanent things, the relationship [between word and meaning] is non-human (apauruṣeya)? This is explained as follows: just like their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), their inherence (*samavāya*) also arises from their very causes. We do not, like the Vaiśeṣikas, accept inherence as eternal. However, for words, the connection with their meaning does not arise solely from their own causes, because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing.
[The opponent] says: "Granted that sound is non-eternal, nevertheless the non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) of the relationship [between word and meaning] is still established;
