let it be that the denotative power belongs to 'soundness' (śabdatva) itself as a specific property residing in the individual. Thus, because the denotator is eternal, its non-human origin is indeed established. To this, he replies: "And 'soundness' has already been refuted."
In the section on the refutation of *sphoṭa*: But surely, there exist other [factors] such as *gatva* (the generic property of being a *g*-sound) which have not been rejected;
therefore, let these *gatva*s and so forth themselves be the denoters.

And having gone through the [categories] such as "origination" (*upapanna*) and so forth, [it is argued that] because individuals (*vyakti*), though distinct at each utterance, are perceived as one despite their impermanence, [the word] is like "cowness" (*gotva*) and so on. [The author replies: "That is not so.
The meaning is that what was stated is not [correct]. Why? Because of the particularities of the *ga* [sound]—
Because of non-apprehension.

The meaning of this is as follows: for a universal is admitted only in those cases where there is an apprehension of non-difference accompanied by an apprehension of difference, such as in the case of cows and the like. However, where there is no apprehension of difference, there is no [apprehension of] non-difference.
Since the designation based on non-difference is grounded in error—just like [the case of] mother-of-pearl and silver—the postulation of a universal (sāmānya) is not tenable.

Furthermore, in the view that [the letter *ga*] is non-eternal, there is no perception of any distinction even among those *ga*-sounds which possess inferential difference; thus, this determination of oneness would have to be merely the non-apprehension of difference. By this same reasoning, [the notion of oneness] regarding "flame-ness" and so forth in the case of flames and the like [is explained].

[This is] rejected. For this very reason, the conceit of [the universal] as being the reality in flames and the like is called an error (*bhrānti*); otherwise, because it would have a general property (*sāmānya*) as its object, it would simply not be an error at all. As it has been said:
"The individual, the quality, and the agent are based elsewhere... [ka, ga].
If it is argued that there is recognition even though flames and the like are momentary, that is not so;
for even in that case, what is recognized is the universal, which is indeed eternal.

"But where there is a cognition of difference regarding a certain aspect due to some limiting adjunct (upādhi), there is no recognition, as it is precluded by that very cognition of difference. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, no specific difference in the *ga* sound is perceived here; therefore, this delusion of perceiving identity is caused solely by the non-apprehension of difference, and thus there is no such thing as *gatva* (the universal "g-ness"). If there is no perception of a specific difference in the *ga* sound, how then do we have the perception of difference among parrots, starlings, and humans? Precisely because of the difference between the parrot and so forth...

There is a perception of difference; for this very reason, no intrinsic distinction is perceived therein. Indeed, it is only the parrot, the maina, and the human who constitute the difference in that case. The difference there is based solely on the difference between the speakers, not intrinsically. And thus, when the speaker is the same, there is not even the slightest [difference].

Regarding the term "distinction" (*viśeṣa*): he concludes the present topic—therefore, the eternity of the relationship is not established. Consequently, the eternity of the word must be asserted. This is stated, preceded by an objection: "Some [hold that it is] due to action, because it is observed therein. (*karmaike tatra darśanāt*)
Thus [it was said].

Desiring to introduce the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) because there is no prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: "But if this were so, even a produced (*kṛtaka*) relation would not be tenable."

Because there is no purpose in establishing a relationship for that which perishes as soon as it has arisen; for it is not necessary to employ a relationship created [by convention], since that [object] ceases at that very moment.

Because [the word] has perished, and because another has arisen anew, a connection that is produced (*kṛtaka*) is not possible in the case of an impermanent sound. One who seeks a resolution asks: "What follows from this? The objector says: "In common worldly usage—"
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of worldly transaction" (*vyavahāroccheda*), the respondent speaks again: "What follows from that?"
The objector says: "The thesis of impermanence is not tenable; because it contradicts worldly convention, permanence necessarily follows.
The partial respondent says: "Because it contradicts worldly convention—"
"Let there be no permanence; what follows from the consequence of permanence? The objector refutes this:
"This follows."
"Is it not the case that worldly transaction simply becomes impossible? The respondent says: "True, it would indeed be so, if [the word] were entirely devoid of convention."
"Niṣṭhā" means existence.

The meaning is that there exists a convention (*samaya*) which is the cause of worldly linguistic usage (*lokavyavahāra*). But what is the object of this convention that serves as the cause of linguistic usage? It cannot have sound as its object, because sound is transitory and thus incapable of persisting through the course of conventional usage. To this, he says:
For there is no object that is not within the scope of convention (*samaya*); this convention removes the suffering caused by all logical impossibilities.

The meaning of this is as follows: this illusion of non-difference—which, despite the phonemes being distinct with each utterance, is based on the non-apprehension of their difference—[is established by convention].
The convention has that as its object. Nor is there a discrepancy in practical usage, because there is no discrepancy in intention;
for, having cognized an object by means of another means of valid cognition, persons—due to the superimposition of unity through error—act with the intention of communicating it. (1.
Added. taṃ. ga.)
2. By the force of the element. [ga. *balāt* omitted;
ka. 3. Merely that, because permanence is established.
[ga. 4. He says. [ga.]
5. It occurs.
Ga. [p.
261] They employ words with the conceit that they exist at the time of making a convention; the listener as well, by that very [conceit]—

Through pride—that is, by way of incorporating that [speaker’s] intention—one understands the object; thus, the establishment of the object occurs through the non-deviation of the intention, and from that, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) follows. However, since Vedic usage is based solely on the word, convention (*samaya*) is not the cause there. Thus he says: "Therefore, for those for whom the word is the means of valid cognition, there is no [dependence on] linguistic usage..."
Validity is established by mere perception; therefore, an effort must be made regarding the eternality of the expression,
and this [effort] has now been commenced.

Now, one might ask: even if sound is momentary, why does its validity with respect to meanings not exist independently of persons? Why is it not like the eyes and other sense organs, which, though impermanent, possess intrinsic validity? To this, he says: because the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Regarding the knowledge of the relationship—

And because the comprehension of meaning is preceded by [the knowledge of] that [relation], if [words] were momentary, their status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) would not be established, just as in the case of the eyes and other sense organs.
To the question "Why is there a dependence on the knowledge of the relation?", he says: "Because the meaning is not understood upon the first hearing. "Some say it is an action (*karman*)."
In that context, by the phrase "because it is seen," the produced nature (*kṛtakatva*) of sound is stated; what is this produced nature?
The underlying intention is as follows: if "produced nature" or "artificiality" is asserted with reference to all sounds, then...

The reason (*hetu*) "because it is perceived immediately after an effort" is partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), since it does not apply to things such as the roar of the ocean; furthermore, the subject (*pakṣa*) is contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, on the other hand, one were to take only those things consisting of expression (*abhidhāna*) as the subject and prove that they arise from effort, then the fact that non-expressive things are produced would not have been established—this is the sense. The reply follows:
[Page 262] Arising through human effort is what is called "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Only those things whose nature is that of denotation arise through effort.

The intention is that [the production of sound] is being established. Not having understood this intention, [an opponent] objects: "But surely the production of sound is also seen to be independent of effort, as in the case of echoes and the like. This is not a fault, because the context concerns verbal expression (*abhidhāna*).
For it is the authority of the denotation itself that has been asserted;
therefore, this is stated in order to demonstrate its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeya*). Nor is this denotation seen to be produced without effort;
hence, because it is perceived immediately following an action, we consider that it arises from that very [action].
He objects: "In that case, how is it with roots, water, and so forth?
For roots, water, and the like [are produced] immediately after effort—"
Even when obtained, they are not produced by effort. Herein lies the resolution: because their existence is known from another source.
Since things such as roots and water are understood to exist prior to the exertion [of effort] through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), effort does not produce them.
[Sound] is produced; moreover, in the case of sound, perception occurs only immediately after effort. Therefore, it cannot be said that effort is a manifestor of something already existing.
[Objection: But is it not the case that for sound as well, [perception follows] from effort?
There is this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its prior existence. What is this? It is perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
By means of recognition, one grasps the oneness of the sound; thus, its prior existence is established in relation to the preceding and succeeding moments.

It is established that of two efforts, the subsequent effort is non-productive; and this being established, it follows that the preceding effort [is likewise non-productive], as in the case of water and so forth.
[Page 263, Ga.]

It is established that [the organ] is a manifester, like the subsequent effort; for it cannot be both the producer and the manifester of that very same thing. The proponent asks: how can there be recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) here, since no difference is perceived?
The meaning of this is: where there is a cognition of non-difference preceded by a perception of difference, there recognition occurs.

[The opponent] says: But if otherness is not apprehended, then the error consisting in the determination of oneness is based solely on the non-apprehension of difference. The challenger asks: Does even one who maintains the doctrine of impermanence have an apprehension of otherness?
The meaning of this is: that error consisting in the cognition of oneness is admitted to be based on the non-apprehension of difference only in cases where otherness—
It is not understood; nor is there any perception of difference here even for one who maintains the doctrine of impermanence.

The proponent asks: "Why is there no cognition of difference between that which has been destroyed and that which has arisen? The difference between what is destroyed and what has arisen is manifest. The objector replies: "Because their specific qualities are not perceived."
"Otherness is not apprehended. The proponent asks: "Is recognition based solely on the non-apprehension of a distinction?"
If it is thought that recognition is based solely on the non-apprehension of differences, then it would likewise apply to flames and the like.
The objector asks: "What do you think?"—the meaning is, "Is it exactly so? The defender replies:
"Recognition would then also apply to actions."

The meaning here is that even in that case, it is because the specific distinction is not apprehended. The objector says: "This is said when there is an apprehension of the essential nature [of the object]."

As for the claim that recognition is based on the non-apprehension of specific qualities, that is only possible when the essential nature [of the object] is apprehended; and since action is known through inference,
there is no apprehension of its essential nature in that case.

Even when specific qualities are not apprehended, there is no recognition; however, since the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of sounds is apprehended, it is logical that recognition occurs in their case.
Furthermore, the cognition [of sound] arises from something else.
[Page 264] Recognition. The proponent says: What is the status regarding flames and the like?
For as for flames and so forth...

The essential nature [of the object] is grasped by perception, yet its difference is not apprehended; therefore, do you perhaps intend that there too [in the case of a flame] there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? The proponent, anticipating the opponent's intention, raises an objection: "If the flames and so forth were eternal, it would contradict inference."

If the permanence and stability of flames and the like were admitted, there would be a contradiction with inference; for in a flame, the dispersal of the constituent parts of light is perceived through the expansion of its circle of radiance, and when the parts have dispersed, the whole composed of those parts has perished; yet there is a subsequent perception [of light], which must be another flame.

If it is argued that— because of the inference "it is so because it has arisen [again]," the distinctness of flames and the like is determined, and thus, due to the contradiction with inference, the delusion of a single cognition is based solely on the non-apprehension of difference, and not on recognition— [the author] now refutes this:
"The same applies even when [the reason] is stated, because of the lack of persistence and so forth."

The contradiction with inference here as well is equal [to that in the previous case] due to reasons such as the impossibility of its existence; therefore, how can there be recognition here too? He concludes: "Therefore, even when no distinction is perceived through perception, there is difference based on inference; and since there is difference, its existence prior to effort is not established."

[The opponent argues: "It is established that because they are perceived immediately after effort, there is production through effort. But surely, even for things produced by effort, such as jars and other artifacts, there is no impossibility of practical usage (vyavahāra) due to their persistence over a period of time."

Even for a manifesting cause (*jñāpaka*) such as the eye, which has already arisen, its innate capacity to apprehend form—which does not depend on human effort—is never obstructed; likewise, let it be that even for sound, though produced by effort, its status as a manifesting cause is independent of the person.
This is true in the case of jars and the like; however, this is not the case with sound. Why? Because of its non-abiding nature (*asthāna*).

The meaning is: "because it perishes as soon as it has arisen. Again, he raises an objection: "But even if the eye is not stable, the power to perceive form is not at all impaired in one who opens it at that moment and then closes it; the same would apply to sound as well."
1. Omitted. [In the reading] *jvalāyām*, [the text] is in *ga*.
2. *avagamyate* is in *ga*.
3. Omitted. [The text from] *kṣaṇa* ... *tasmāt* is in *ga*.
If this is argued, the reply is: it has already been answered that [the word] is not understood upon the first hearing,
because it depends upon the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning].

The meaning is that there is no capacity for conveying meaning (*pratyāyakatva*) in that which is momentary. Therefore, this reason—"because of non-abiding" (*asthānāt*)—undermines the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of the relationship [between word and meaning]. If there were persistence over a period of time, then comprehension of the meaning from the word through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) might indeed occur; however, if there is no persistence, then [the comprehension of meaning would depend on] convention (*samaya*).
It has been stated that [this] alone ought to be the refuge, because there is no other basis.

Even worldly usage follows this very same principle. What here is the following of the principle? It is that the root *kṛ* (to do/make) has its primary meaning—[as in] "make a sound," "do not make a sound," or "this boy is a maker of sounds."

Thus, the meaning is that it brings about the manifestation of what has not [previously] existed; this is the primary sense in the case of the position that things are impermanent. The three examples are given to establish the purpose of injunctions, prohibitions, and established facts.

"Furthermore, we perceive sound simultaneously in various locations; this would be impossible for a single, eternal entity. Thus the commentary has been restated. He raises an objection: "What is this impossibility?"
The reply: this is untenable—simultaneous perception of a single person, such as Devadatta, in multiple locations has never been observed; it occurs only sequentially.
But it is indeed seen. If that is so, what follows? The answer is: from that, there is distinctness (*anyatva*).
The simultaneous perception [of a thing] as excluded from one [particular] in multiple locations establishes its distinctness. But has distinctness not already been established?
Therefore, it is as much as to say that this is a redundancy. The reply is: True, [the point] has been established; 1. manifestation. (ga.)
2. Omitted. But the accumulation of causes is now demonstrated. [p. 267] tu. ga. [p. 267] hetupracayastu pradarśyate.
Previously, difference was stated by means of one reason; now, another reason is being stated. What is the benefit?
There is no benefit at all, since the probandum remains undifferentiated even when a collection of reasons is shown.
This is the meaning. The reply is: "Certainly not anyone," because there is no distinction from the probandum (*sādhya*). He objects:
"If there is no one [to be proven], what is the use of a collection of reasons (*hetupracaya*)?"
Response: It is true as you have said; however, this very point contradicts the established tenet (*siddhānta*). This point, being unrefuted, contradicts the tenet.
Someone might have a misconception; therefore, this undertaking is for the purpose of refuting that error.
He explains this as follows: for it is not possible to declare something to be erroneous unless it has been presented; [if it has] not been shown...

And even if it were erroneous, this [text] would not be redundant for someone of dull intellect. Now, one might object: "Surely this error belongs only to those of dull intellect, not to those of sharp intellect; so what is the point of saying this? To this he replies: "And this treatise is for the sake of all, [even] by one of dull capacity."
Thus it has been shown by the author of the Bhāṣya: "In the absence of any distinction, that which is eternal cannot be manifold."
The commentary has been restated. He objects:
"What is this [statement] that 'there is no plurality for the eternal in the absence of a distinction'? [The response is: "In the absence of a distinction, there is no plurality."
Thus it can be said whether [the object] is eternal or non-eternal; we do not perceive the inclusion of the term "eternal.
It can also be stated generally that the inclusion of the term "eternal" is fruitless. If [it refers to] the non-eternal...
1. It is said to be liberated. Ga.
2. By means of demonstration, there is nothing [to be done] for that which is to be proven. Ga.
3. Omitted. eva. ga. 4. Omitted. tasmāt. ga. 5. yo bhaviṣyati. ga.
Even if there were a distinction, there would be a plurality.
It is appropriate that "of the eternal" be a qualification; it is not [appropriate for the non-eternal].

This, however, is the case. Therefore, this treatise must be explained. It is now explained as follows: it is observed that a single entity such as a cow is perceived simultaneously in many places while existing as something eternal.
Therefore, [the reason] is: "and because of simultaneity among other beings."

By this commentary, the possibility that the aforementioned reason is established otherwise has been raised—namely, that even a single entity could be perceived simultaneously in multiple locations if it were eternal; to this, the following reply is given: "provided there is no distinction."
He raises an objection again: "Or rather, does a distinction exist in the case of a cow and so forth? For that too is one and undifferentiated;
for it is not one thing in a brindled cow and another in a black cow."

The meaning of this is as follows: You, who argue for the establishment of the reason, have stated that this observation of a single entity in multiple locations occurs when there is a specific quality (viśeṣa), as in the case of a cow or similar things; yet, no such specific quality exists in the case of sound. Therefore, this [observation] does not [prove] permanence.

[It is] perception; however, it occurs only by virtue of arising in this or that [particular instance]. And in speaking thus, your intention appears to be this: that a distinction exists in the case of cows and so forth. But this intention of yours is untenable, because even in the case of cows and so forth, there is no distinction. Or perhaps your intention is this: that in the absence of a distinction in the substratum...
"There is no distinction in 'cowness' itself, yet when there is a distinction in its substratum, there is also a distinction in 'cowness'";
this intention of yours is likewise untenable, because even in that case, it is only the substratum that is different— what has been gained for the substrate?
For the substratum does not differ because of a difference in its supports, since the two are distinct.
Therefore, it is observed that even a single eternal entity can be perceived simultaneously in multiple locations. Thus, regarding its eternity—

Nor is simultaneous perception a proof of non-difference, since it is established that a single thing can be perceived in multiple places. Now, if this view is held—that perception [occurs] if there is a distinction...
[ga]... (Note: The fragment "darśanaṃ cedviśeṣe. ga. appears to be a textual corruption or a marginal note indicating a variant reading or a specific point regarding the nature of perception.)
2. Omitted. Te. Ga. [p.
269] There is no simultaneous perception of a cow or other such objects in multiple locations; for in that case, it is only the distinct individuals that appear as being in various places.
[Individuals] are apprehended, not "cowness.

With this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) anticipates another intention of the proponent of the justification (samarthanavādin). As for the meaning: now, this justification of yours is the opinion of the proponent of the justification.

This suspected "establishment through other means" (anyathāsiddhi) is refuted precisely by its being unestablished (asiddha): in the absence of a particularity (viśeṣa), there is no plurality for [universals] such as "cowness" (gotva); for universals such as "cowness," there is no particularity. And in the absence of particularity, there is no plurality.
If, moreover, it were perceived simultaneously in multiple locations, then plurality would necessarily follow; and that—

It does not exist. Therefore, there is no perception of "cowness" (gotva) in multiple locations at all; rather, it is only the individuals that are perceived in multiple locations, not the cowness. Consequently, the claim that a single entity can be perceived in multiple locations due to its eternity is nowhere established. Now, [the author] refutes this: "In that case, how is it that the cognition 'cow, cow' arises with respect to all [individuals]?"
The meaning of this is as follows: when "cowness" (*gotva*) is perceived in multiple individuals, it is perceived precisely as occupying multiple locations;

for if cowness were not perceived in multiple individuals, how then could there be the cognition "cow, cow" with respect to all the bodies? For a qualified cognition is necessarily based upon the postulation of a specific [qualifier] and its inherence [in the qualified].
The proponent of the proof says: Precisely because there is the cognition "cow, cow," for that very reason the universal *gotva* (cowness) does not possess multiple locations.
For otherwise, if the individual were perceived as the location of *gotva*, [the universal would likewise be manifold].
‘Cowness is here,’ ‘cowness is here’—
thus it would be.
But this is not the case; therefore, the individual is not perceived as having spatial extension. How then is it said that "inherence is known through the cognition 'here' [in this]"?
The objection is: "How can this utterance of the knowers of categories—that 'inherence [is known] here from perception'—be justified? The answer follows:
1. Omitted. *yugapat*. *ga*. 2. *arthatastu*. *ga*. 3. Added. *ca*. *ga*.
4. The non-distinction of "cowness" and so forth. Ga. 5. Multiplicity.
Ka. 6. Among contradictory things. Ga.
7. Omitted. One here [perceives] "cowness.
Ga. 8. This is the meaning. "One"—Ga.
That [statement] intends the category (*padārtha*) that consists of a single substance; it does not intend individual instances (*vyakti*).
Its meaning is as follows:
"that which is both a single substance and a category"; by the term *ekadravyapadārtha*, the category of action (*karmapadārtha*) is expressed.

The category of action (*karmapadārtha*) alone has a single substance as its substrate; that is, it has only a single substance as its support, and not the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) or the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*). For the category of substance is either without a substrate, such as atoms or space, or it has multiple substances as its substrate, such as a jar and the like. The category of quality, however, has multiple substances as its substrate.

Just as conjunction, disjunction, and number such as duality reside in multiple substances, while color and other qualities reside in a single substance; so too, the category of action (karma) exists in only a single substance. Thus the venerable Kāśyapa said:
"The definition of action is that which resides in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is the independent cause of conjunctions and disjunctions."

Thus, this statement— "inherence [is known] from the cognition 'here' (ihapratyaya)"— is made with reference to a single category (padārtha), not with reference to individual instances (vyakti). Not...
Even in the case of an individual, the cognition "here" (ihapratyaya) depends upon the universal; what, then, is the reasoning here? This is stated:

for the category of action (karma) is inferable, and therefore, when it is not perceived, the substance, having been already apprehended, can at the time of that inference be taken as the objective support by the cognition "here"; however, the universal is not grasped by a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, when a substratum (dharmin) is apprehended, it must necessarily be apprehended as characterized by some attribute (dharma); for every cognition occurs in the form "it is thus" (evam),
and the word "thus" signifies a mode (prakāra), while a mode is an attribute (dharma).

In that case, since the universal (*jāti*) is already included within the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*), the substratum does not require further deliberation regarding the notion of "here" (*ihapratyaya*) with respect to it.

Therefore, the cognition of the universal and the individual occurs only as property (*dharma*) and substratum (*dharmin*), and not as container and contained (*ādhārādheyatā*). Consequently, because there is no other way for [the relation] to be established, simultaneous perception is the reason for their difference, provided that no specific distinction exists.

And thus the commentary is appropriate for the purpose of avoiding the charge of "establishing otherwise" (anyathāsiddhi). Now, one might object: even in the case of something impermanent, there is no difference [in its nature] when no specific distinction exists;
therefore, for what purpose was the term "of the permanent" (nityasya) employed? Certainly, even in the absence of a specific distinction, there is multiplicity [in the case of the impermanent].
1. For that is indeed the intention. (ga) 2. Not accompanied by substance. (ga) 3. Omitted. Guṇa—Kāśyapa. (ga)
4. Even in the case of impermanence. (Objection: How can there be permanence in things such as flames? And that multiplicity of flames and the like is not contradictory, because they are effects.
For an effect, being produced in various instances, can reasonably be manifold; thus he says: "And because it is an effect, there is no contradiction.
However, since that which is eternal is not an effect, its being manifold would be contradictory; therefore, this is a valid reason.
[In the case of] another entity...
And [it is so] because of simultaneity;
moreover, those who know words remember the relationship of original material and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), and this is not [the case here].

It is possible for that which is eternal; therefore, even memory is consistent with the previously stated reason. We also perceive that similarity is consistent [with this], and thus the nature of being an effect is established.

But how can there be magnitude in sound, which is partless? Magnitude belongs to that which has parts; it arises from a multiplicity of causes and from the accumulation of specific causes. Concluding on this point, he says: "Therefore..."
Even for that whose parts are being perceived, an increase in its parts is inferred; a flame serves as the illustration here.
But in that case, the perception is equal. What is this "equal perception"? This is that equal [perception]:
1. because of the specific accumulation of causes.

"Perception"—the reason is the same whether for what is to be done or what is not to be done. How is it the same? By virtue of being common to all (sāṃnyāsikatayā). What is renounced here? This is what is renounced here:
[the claim] that we shall state that [the self] is graspable by perception accompanied by recognition (pratyabhijñā).
If sound were perceivable by a perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),

then its observation immediately following effort would occur because effort serves as its manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*); however, if sound were not perceivable by a perception accompanied by recognition, then effort would be its producer (*kāraka*).

Thus [it is said]. But was it not stated that perception is accompanied by recognition? And has this not been answered: "Just as in the case of a flame and the like, when there is an opposing inference, one cannot assert identity"? True; if...
Recognition would have to be said to be based solely on the non-apprehension of difference; however, it will be demonstrated that it is based on the apprehension of that [identity].
The meaning of this is as follows: if recognition were merely the non-apprehension of difference, then...

The perception [of an object] immediately following an effort would occur only if [the object] were non-existent; however, when there is recognition based on the grasping of that [object], it is possible to postulate an obscuration or the like—even if it is not perceived—by virtue of that [recognition]. Therefore, it is logical that "the perception there is the same."
Thus.
1. Omitted. This is what is set forth here: Ga.
274] “The non-perception of an existing thing is due to the non-arrival of its objects.”

Thus, it has been stated that this non-perception is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But is this not untenable? [For] there is non-perception of that which exists; what [reason] is there for the non-perception of the eternal?
What is the reason? At most, it would be the non-arrival of objects;
yet even that is untenable—this is the sense. He provides the justification: "Let it be then..."
He objects: "That very point is difficult to maintain here. Why is it difficult to maintain?
He states the reason: "For on the view that [sound] is eternal, sound must be something manifested; and sound is one."
And it has space as its object, because its object is space; and space itself is its grasper. What is this "non-comprehension of the object"?
For if there were multiple sounds, then only that which has reached the object would be perceived.
It would be perceived; no other [cause] is possible. Likewise, if there were multiple locations, then it would not be perceived in another location;

moreover, space itself is the perceiver; therefore, since sound is not unattained [by the perceiver], its perception would occur. Consequently, it is logical that only what has been destroyed is non-perceived. By whom was it said that this is not logical? However, in the case of its apprehension...
If this were the case, it would be improper for everyone; therefore it has been said: "If we are able. [1. Omitted. Because there is no scriptural authority regarding the objects.
[ga. 2. But if this were so, it would not be—ga.]
3. "It exists" (asti). Ga.
Now, even if that [object] is apprehended, the postulation of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and so forth does not find a footing here.
Why? Because it contradicts what was previously established. What was established? That space (*ākāśa*) is the sense organ (*indriya*), and that [space] is one;
therefore, if it were the manifester of conjunctions and disjunctions, then all sounds would be manifested by all [organs].

[The word] would result in being perceived [simultaneously]; for all sounds occupy the same location. In that case, upon the manifestation of one, there would be the manifestation of all, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects. Sound resides in space (*ākāśa*); and this space is one.
Since space is the sense-organ (*indriya*), there would be perception by all [senses] due to the manifestation occurring in the sense-organ common to all. Regarding this:
He objects: "It may well be that all [sounds] are perceived; however, it is not logical that all words [be perceived], because the manifestors are distinct just like the causes.
Just as, due to the difference among causes, a certain sound [is produced] by a certain [cause]..."
Just as consciousness is produced, so too is a certain sound manifested by something;

moreover, perception by all [perceivers] is exactly the same even on the view that [sound] is an effect, because the sound arises as residing in all the sense organs. And as for that which belongs to both...

"The fault is the same; it does not constitute a valid objection against that one [position]"—thus has this refutation regarding the word "one" (*eka*) in the context of the agent (*kāraka*) been answered.

Without stating the distinction between the two manifestors, those who maintain the doctrine of non-eternality would certainly not be challenged. Now, the proponent states the distinction: "This is the distinction—does the manifestation belong to the sound or to the sense organ? Regarding the manifestation of the sound, first of all, because all sounds have the same object..."
It cannot be said that the manifestation of [sounds], which have a single object like jars and other things, occurs sequentially,
because such a thing is never observed in the case of well-known manifestors such as lamps and the like;
for they [manifest] all [objects] simultaneously.

Manifestors do not manifest [their objects] all at once, but rather one by one. However, in the case of causes, the inference of a capacity is based on the observation of the effect; it is logical that whatever effect is observed is precisely what is produced.
But surely, in the case of manifestors as well, the inference of a capacity is likewise logical based on the very observation of manifestation?
Just as one infers a specific capacity in causes from the observation of a specific effect, so too,
from the observation that manifestors produce the manifestation of specific sounds, there indeed occurs an inference of a specific capacity in them. [The opponent says:]
He says: It is not possible for it to exist as a counter-position on the side of the "effect" (kārya).

Since the perception of a qualified word is established by virtue of its being an effect, one cannot infer a capacity directed toward a qualified object even if the manifestors (vyañjaka) are distinct.
1. And likewise [the objection] raised by those who maintain that sound is impermanent. Ga. 2. Of lamps.
Ka. 3. Inference from sound. Therein. Ga.
4. For instance, what indeed is the distinction between the manifest (vyañjaka) and the other?
The meaning is: regarding the two positions—that [the effect] is produced or that it is manifested. He states the distinction:

because a capacity directed toward a specific object is observed in well-known causes such as seeds, whereas it is not observed in well-known manifestors such as lamps; and because inference that accords with what is observed is logical, while that which contradicts what is observed is not.
But surely there is a contradiction if they have the same object?

The meaning of this is: if there were only one single object manifested by the conjunctions and disjunctions of lamps and so forth, then there would be an inference of the manifestation of a specific object.
It would contradict what is observed. However, in another case, it is indeed contradictory because of the contradiction [it entails].

For the object of lamps and the like is color (*rūpa*), whereas for conjunctions and disjunctions, it is sound; thus, since there is a difference in the objects, it is not [contradictory] as observed.
There is a contradiction. Not having understood this intention, he says: "True; it is difficult to state that there is a different object here.
Having taken space as the object of sound, this is said. According to his own intention, he says: "No."
Regarding the phrase "difficult to refute":

again, without understanding the underlying intention, he asserts that there is a single object of cognition—because it is accepted that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space (*ākāśa*), and space is non-different; furthermore, all sounds are objects of the auditory organ; therefore, there is a single object of cognition.
Furthermore, there is a contradiction with observed fact due to the identity of the object;

for forms and other qualities that share the same object are not manifested by lamps and such through their differentiation. Now, explaining his own intention in a single passage, he says: "What is this?"
1. The meaning is: "Or who [is there] in the two positions regarding the manifestation of a specific effect? [The word] *viśiṣṭa* [refers to] that which is not established among the causes.
(ga. 2) There is a contradiction; likewise. (ga. [They share] a single object-domain. (ga.)
[Page 278] Is this what is being asserted? Then this follows: "Touched on the ear, one wiggles the hip.
It is the object of manifestation that is being defined, not the word itself; for this [word] is distinct from objects such as a lamp and so forth.
The object of [the inference] is twofold:

by means of lamps and the like, everything is manifested; however, by means of conjunctions and disjunctions, only a certain sound is manifested. Therefore, because it contradicts the case of lamps and the like, the inference regarding a manifester in the case of sound is contradicted.
It has been stated that it cannot be so asserted.

Regarding the inference of the manifestor in the case of sound, it cannot be said that there is a contradiction with what is perceived. Therefore, the inference based on the apprehension of that [sound] is difficult to refute.

Since that [sound] is apprehended through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the word-sound (*śabda*), any inference concerning the manifesting agent (*abhivyañjaka*) whose scope is restricted to a fixed capacity becomes unavoidable. Therefore, it has been stated that non-perception (*adarśana*) is now inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"It is not the case that there is no perception simply because of non-existence;
rather, it is indeed possible even when [the sound] is unmanifest. The opponent says: "But this manifestation has the auditory organ as its object, not the sound as its object."

If sound were an object [of manifestation], it would follow that once sound is manifested, it would be heard by all persons. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "For the ear grasps sound only when it is manifested"—this much is the inference of the capacity in the manifestor; however, it does not [follow] that "it [the manifestor] brings forth this specific sound for this specific person," because there is no...
1. The objectivity of power is certain.
(ga. 2. Omitted. Thus it has been stated. ga. 3. Because of the impossibility. ga.)
4. Furthermore, [the cognition] "this sound" and "that sound," etc., [arises] from the manifestors, such as contact (sparśa). Ga. [p. 279]

The manifestation of the auditory organ does not consist in its being directed toward a specific object, but rather occurs by way of its own essential nature alone; consequently, the auditory organ, once refined, would hear all sounds. As it has been said:
"Once the auditory organ is refined, it should manifest all sounds."
"The eye opened for a jar does not indeed fail to perceive a cloth.
Thus [it is said].
This indeed is your established conclusion as Mīmāṃsakas, namely, that it is the refinement of the auditory organ;
and it has been stated that this is contradicted by inference.
For if the sense organ were manifested, it would [perceive] all objects whatsoever.

One would perceive objects as soon as the eyes are opened. In that case, if the auditory organ were manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions, it would follow that all sounds would be perceived; yet this is not the case. Therefore, since there is no manifestation, only the production of the sound remains; what, then, will its apprehension accomplish here?

Even when that [sound] is perceived, the postulation of it being a manifestor is not obtained; therefore, in this case, the perception of it is itself an error, like [the perception of] a flame and so forth. It is not, however, proper to subvert well-known inference. True, it is improper to subvert well-known inference; yet it is equally improper to subvert well-known perception.

But is it not the case that recognition is not established as being perception, because it is not produced by the sense organs? For a sense organ generates cognition only with respect to an object that is present; yet recognition involves the apprehension of an object characterized by different locations, times, and states.

It is not, however, by virtue of being present in space and time, nor by virtue of possessing a state of existence in the present; therefore, anticipating the objection that for one who has already experienced an object through a sense faculty, there subsequently arises what is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) produced by sensory cognition, he says:
[1. Omitted. *yadi*. *ga*.]
2. Omitted. tat. ga. 3. Without grasping.
And perception, which includes recognition, is established with respect to the self and universals (sāmānya) and so forth;

although this [perception] alone is not sufficient to characterize [the object], nevertheless, it will be produced through the power of the mental impression (bhāvanā) cultivated by previous experience.

Thus, nothing is untenable. With a single passage, he says: since no object whatsoever would be established if both were non-sublated, and since neither the produced effect nor the manifested [object] would be established, it is logical that one of them be sublated; and even in that case, the Naiyāyikas hold that perception is stronger than inference.

Therefore, by the force of that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the inference based on the dissimilarity of the manifesters (*vyañjaka*) is sublated. Now, [it may be argued: "Is not perception subject to error?
Therefore, how can it be more powerful?"

Thus [it is said]. In inference as well, error is no different. He states the specific nature of error even in inference: we do not say that there is no error in inference; rather, because of the non-apprehension of difference here, the cognition of that [object] occurs even with respect to this [other object].

"Like a flame, etc."—we consider that even perception, when accompanied by a possible error, is weak. For this very reason, by having revealed the causes of both manifest and unmanifest error, it has been stated by those learned in logic: "Inference indeed possesses greater force than even perception..."
"...is stronger.
Now, he asks from the perspective of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*): "Is it [the case that] the defectiveness of the cause is already known?"
Has it been presented?
And has that defectiveness of the cause been ascertained? The proponent says: What follows if it has been presented?
Regarding that which has arisen, he says: "But surely, because of the absence of error, it does not exist as such.
[This refers to] inference (anumāna) as well, which is erroneous. He states the distinction. Ga.
2. Therefore, it can be established that [the quality] does not exist in that which is not [its locus]. Ga. [p. 281]
For indeed, no direct cognition of difference exists with respect to the word, by which there could be error. The proponent asks: "Is error alone the cause of falsity?
He says in a single passage:
To the extent that a defect in the cause has indeed been presented as being an improper reason,
therefore falsity arises from the defect in the cause even in the absence of a contrary cognition. But surely, a defect in the cause is [only] perceived through effort—
He was addressed by her.
The proponent says: What is this so-called "effort" (prayatna), which is said not to exist here?
This very thing is that effort—namely, having recognized a defect in the cause elsewhere through its contrary nature, [one acts] precisely because it arises from the presence of that [defect].
One recognizes that "this error is caused by this" in something else; and once that is known, even though the error is no longer present, one thinks, "This was a delusion."

Thus he determines. "Is there anything of this kind here?"—this constitutes a single syntactical unit. For when a subverting cognition has arisen and the state of falsity has been understood, [one asks]: "What..."

Seeking to understand that this falsity has a basis, one determines its causality therein by the fact that it occurs only when a defect in the cause is present; and once that is determined, even in cases where there is no subverting cognition, one concludes the falsity through the knowledge of the defect in the cause which is the ground for that falsity. Such being the case...
"What is there in this? For it does not exist at all, since no sublation (*bādhaka*) is ever observed. The proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) says:

"Certainly, there is an excessive non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgrahaṇa*); for the illusion of silver in mother-of-pearl and similar objects is caused precisely by the non-apprehension of difference. Likewise here too, that illusion [of identity] regarding the flames and so forth is caused precisely by the non-apprehension of difference."
When a direct sublation arises in cases such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it will be understood that the non-apprehension of difference is the cause of falsity. (ga. 1)
2. Its apprehension. What?
282] Even in the absence of a sublation regarding the word, its apprehension will occur based on the non-apprehension of difference. Therefore, it has been well said.
"The apprehension of that [object] is merely the word itself; it is an error.

To this, the proponent himself says: "For one who occasionally has a cognition of an object in a contrary form, it is appropriate to say, 'Because there is no subversion [of that cognition], this is not an error.'"
Thus, according to the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), that which has been grasped must be shown to be non-existent. In that case,
since inference does not apply to an object whose nature has been determined as contrary [to reality], if falsity were established by another perception, [then it would follow that]...

It might be so; however, for one for whom error is based solely on non-apprehension, what power does he have to assert a difference from [the case of] a flame and so forth when there is a contradiction by inference?
For in his view, that which has been apprehended...

It is not that falsity (*mithyātva*) is being asserted; rather, since the non-difference is apprehended, inference indeed arises without contradiction, as in the case of flames and the like. [Objection: But even non-apprehension is determined by subsequent apprehension.
[Response: And here, there is no apprehension of difference at any stage, as in the case of the *saugandhika* flower and crystal.
Just as a crystal, due to its proximity to a colored adjunct (*uparāga*), is not perceived as distinct from a particular ruby (*padmarāga*) or a blue lotus (*saugandhika*),
but is so perceived once the adjunct has been removed— such is not the case here; therefore, how can this be called a non-apprehension of difference?
How is it conceptualized? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "How [is it] in the case of flames and so forth?

The meaning is that even there, the apprehension of difference does not exist through perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is argued that the comprehension of difference arises from inference (*anumāna*), [the response follows].
It has been stated that [this] is an inference based on equal measure.
He concludes: Therefore, perception regarding sound, which involves recognition, is a bond of the noose of hope for the Mīmāṃsaka—
1. Omitted. *tadgrahaṇa*. ka. 2. *mithyātvaṃ*. ka. [p. 283]
Regarding the phrase "of their own": as for what has been stated by others— that even when the object to be refined is the same,
a difference in the result is observed due to the difference in the refining process— just as those whose eyes have been smeared with the fat of a frog see bamboo stalks as if they were snakes.

By this it is said: although the auditory organ is indeed one and the same as that which is to be refined, nevertheless, due to the difference in refinement, it will at times perceive only a particular sound that has reached its range; just as the eye, though one and the same, perceives only a particular form due to the difference in refinement characterized by the application of frog-fat ointment.

He refutes this: that too is merely the manifestation of the snare of hope; for what is called a "refinement" (saṃskāra) is that which produces a capacity for its own effect. And this false apprehension is not the effect of the sense organ;
it has already been established that it is simply non-apprehension (agrahaṇa).

The application of frog-fat ointment is not an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the eye, but rather a mere obstruction of its power; for this very reason, the form of a bamboo is not perceived while the form of a serpent is remembered, as was shown in the discussion on the "loss of memory" (*smṛtipramoṣa*). Therefore, even though there is non-difference (*abheda*) in that which is to be embellished...
Since there is no instance whatsoever among the means of cognition where a difference in the effect follows from a difference in the formative factors (*saṃskāra*), some other example must be shown;
yet that cannot be established. As for the case of the sword, the mirror, and so forth—
When it is said that "the face is manifested otherwise," what is meant?

Is it perceived as distinct due to the difference in the manifesting medium (*abhivyañjaka*), such that a different form of the face is seen when the manifesting medium is a mirror, [and another] when it is a sword?
And what else? He refutes [the objection]: "This coloring (uparāga) is observed in the object of apprehension.

The meaning of this is: even in that case, there is no apprehension due to a difference in the manifestors; rather, only one face is apprehended. However, the object of apprehension—[is it not colored] by the manifestor...
1. *anyathārtha*. ga. 2. *-dudāharaṇīyam*. ka, ga.

Being colored by the mirror of the elements and so forth, it appears as if something else by virtue of that coloring. And this coloring is logical, because even a manifestor can be an object; however, in this case, the auditory organ is not graspable, such that cognition could occur through its coloring.
It may be so; conjunction and disjunction are also ungraspable, and therefore, by their means as well, there is no cognition of difference.
Consequently, this too is merely the manifestation of the snare of hope.
Therefore, the claim that "sound is eternal" is based on faith alone.
It should be understood through the absence of [other] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating the objection, "Why should it be understood through faith alone?", he says:
because the Veda consists of sound, one must not revile the Veda;
for if sound were impermanent, that which consists of sound...

One must also accept that the Veda is non-eternal. He states the fault in censuring its non-eternality: the authors of the Dharmaśāstras have also recited, "That atheist who reviles the Veda is to be cast out by the virtuous."

Since it is impossible to assert the eternity of the word, therefore, in this Vedic usage, its beginninglessness alone is the refuge. Having seen others engaging in practice whose true nature was not yet fully realized, the usage of the Veda is set in motion; by them too, having seen the usage of others, and by those others likewise, [it is thought] "this is the first. Thus, there is no beginning.

It does not exist, because saṃsāra is beginningless. Furthermore, it cannot be logically maintained that the Veda’s authority is independent on the grounds of the eternality of sound. If, however, the world does not function [regarding this] due to its being without a first instance—being like a succession of blind men—then let the world itself be considered as the basis for this.

One who is free from passion and the like, devoid of defects in intention, and speaks of things exactly as they have been perceived; one whose mind is permeated by compassion for the sake of establishing instruction despite being free from passion and the like— because his mind is permeated by compassion distinct from passion and so forth, a mind that seeks the welfare of others and is indifferent to its own interest— he is the giver of instruction to others, being without [self-interest].
One should approach some Blessed One, an excellent sage endowed with the preeminence of Dharma, whose knowledge is unimpeded solely by the power of Dharma.
As they say: "The vision of the Ṛṣis and the vision of the Siddhas arise from the Dharmas."

Thus: as long as such a person has not been postulated by the world, so long will the world’s worldly activity—which is preceded by the ascertainment of meaning—fail to be established from the Veda, which would otherwise be his word. "Let him be postulated" (*kalpyatām*): this is a second *ṇic* suffix applied to the causative (*ṇyanta*) root; [the sense is] "let the world postulate."

"Let it be employed by you, who maintain that the usage of the Veda is sustainable. Now, if the world is unable to postulate such a person because the meaning of the Veda is not the object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then let the view of Bṛhaspati (the Teacher of the Gods) be accepted.

We observe that this very worldly convention, devoid of any unseen purpose (adṛṣṭa-prayojana) and proclaimed by the three Vedas, is maintained by the wise for the sake of accomplishing the course of worldly life— specifically to achieve their own worldly pursuits such as eating and sleeping— as a well-constructed, well-applied, yet essentially hypocritical system. As they say:
“The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff (or sectarian mark), and smearing oneself with ashes—
these, Bṛhaspati says, are merely the livelihood of those devoid of intelligence and manly effort.”

We consider this very view of the Teacher of the Gods (Bṛhaspati) to be logical; for when the purpose of worldly conduct is accomplished through what is perceived, it is not right to postulate something unperceived. Therefore, as for what is said: "If this Veda were merely human in origin and lacked authoritative status, why would the great men of the three higher castes [exert themselves] with such great effort?"

The claim that worldly activity is characterized by the study, retention, and practice of the meaning of the Vedas is rendered otherwise established; for even through deceit toward the upright, one gains a livelihood, which makes the exertion purposeful. Furthermore, this fact is observed by the wise: that the upright are exploited. This is as well-known to those who propound the scriptures—
Even names lack authority because their causes can be discerned, as in such cases as: "They practice the gift of a sacrificial post-elephant," and so forth.

The meaning of this is as follows: even those who accept scripture (*āgama*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) declare its lack of authority in cases such as "they practice the gift of a sacrificial post elephant" (*yūpahastino dānam ācaranti*), because they perceive a motive characterized by greed on the part of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
For instance: a certain most greedy officiating priest (ṛtvij) caused a particular patron (yajamāna), who was preeminent in faith, to give an elephant as a sacrificial gift (yūpahasti-dāna);
upon seeing that, this memory was formed—thus, due to the perception of the cause of the basis, even for two things that are firm...

There is a lack of authority in both memory and custom; likewise here too, because one perceives a motive characterized by livelihood and greed, custom lacks authority. Now, if this is not accepted, then an effort must be made to establish that sound is indeed the object of perception accompanied by recognition. At this point, the respondent asks: "But how [is it known] regarding the flame..."
Can difference be understood through inferential reasoning?
Just as difference can be understood through inference in the case of a flame and so forth, how can difference be understood in the case of sound? The objector says:
"But was it not said that [this is known] from inference? The respondent says: "What is that inference?"
The objector says: "The capacity of manifestors is observed to have multiple objects.
Those which are manifestors possess a capacity directed toward multiple objects, as is the case with a lamp; and conjunctions and disjunctions are indeed manifestors.
"Let it be so," says the respondent. [The opponent objects: "But surely this inference concerns the manifestor;
it establishes the manifestation of multiple objects. With a single sentence, he asks: "How can an inference concerning one object [establish something else]?"
What is the cause for the delimitation of the difference between the object of touch and the object of sound? Again, he says in a single passage:
"For it obstructs the manifesting refinement of the auditory organ.
This is the inference: "The auditory organ [is affected] by the manifester..."
This refutes the idea that "it is being refined," but it does not imply that there is any change in the identity of the word.

The objector says: But has it not been stated that if conjunctions and disjunctions do not produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ—that is, the capacity for perceiving sound—then they must necessarily be the producers of the sound itself? For [if they were not], sound would have to arise [from them].

"And as for the claim that there would be 'otherness' (anyatva): if conjunctions and disjunctions did not refine the auditory organ (*śrotra*), then they would merely be producers of sound; and in the case of production, there would indeed be otherness. The respondent says: "How is the negation of otherness [established]?"
How does it make known its own production?

The meaning is: if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ is negated, how can there be the production of another [namely, the] sound? The objector says: because otherwise the operation would be untenable.

If, once the status of being a *saṃskāraka* (a factor that produces a refinement) has been refuted, it were not the case that they produce sound, then the very operation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) would be untenable. An opponent says: "If they do not effect a refinement..."

"What else could they do other than produce the sound? The respondent says: "Is it necessary that whatever cannot function as a refiner must necessarily be a producer? The objector says: "If it is not a producer,"
It would indeed be devoid of activity.
If it is argued, "Let it be devoid of activity," the author replies to that: "And the purposefulness of conjunction and disjunction is observed."

Therefore, an operation must be admitted; and since its being a purificatory act (*saṃskāraka*) has been refuted, it must have as its object the production of sound. The respondent says: "True, as for those things which are for the sake of [an end], let them be either producers or purificators."
But it is not for the sake of the sound itself, because the sound lacks that purpose.
To the question, "For what purpose, then, are conjunction and disjunction? he says: "And their purpose is established as being for the sake of another's comprehension. Another...

"Let it be understood that sound [is produced]—for this purpose, conjunctions and disjunctions of air are initiated. In that case, let whatever is desired between these two [options], namely being a producer or a manifesting agent, be postulated; however, since there is no relationship with sound as an object in another instance, what basis is there for such a postulation? For indeed, there is no [inherent] connection whatsoever between sound and conjunctions and disjunctions."
"Connection" means, in effect, the connection between conjunction and disjunction on the one hand and the cognition on the other. The author concludes the argument:
"Therefore, how could the Naiyāyikas [possibly maintain] that conjunction and disjunction are the cause of something else?
What do they think? The objector says: They think thus—"If there is no effect in the auditory organ, we perceive the effect in the sound."
The meaning of this is as follows: conjunction and disjunction have the purpose of producing cognition;

and something serves that purpose only when it performs an action, not otherwise. In that regard, since there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of perceiving all sounds simultaneously, when no effect is produced in the auditory organ, then an effect is understood to reside in the sound itself. Furthermore, in that case, manifestation is not the effect.

Because it would follow that all persons, whether near or far, would simultaneously perceive the sound; therefore, production alone constitutes the effect in the case of sound. The respondent says: "Is its being for that purpose [the nature of the word] due to its being an effect? For what reason do you speak thus?"
The objector says: "It is said, 'Yes'.
The respondent says: "In that case, it is established that the effect [of sound] resides in the auditory organ;
the proponents of sound (śabdavidaḥ) maintain that conjunctions and disjunctions are not the objects of the word."

Because they are not perceived within the sound itself, conjunction and disjunction cannot be the meaning of the word. The objector says: "But surely, for those who know the nature of sound, it is not reasonable to say this, because their effect is observed."
Conjunctions and disjunctions do not have sound as their object.

For when there is no effect characterized by a refinement (saṃskāra) due to the undesirable consequence that all sounds would be perceived by the auditory organ, then, by the method of elimination (pāriśeṣya), it is understood that sound itself is the effect; thus, because the effect is observed, conjunctions and disjunctions indeed have sound as their object.
This is the meaning. The respondent says: they claim that there is no observation of an effect at all, because such a [cause] is not perceived in the word.
"That an effect is cognized in the word—this very thing does not exist."

Thus say those who know the science of words. Why? Because that [identity] is not perceived in the word; for since there is the cognition "this is that very same word" regarding the word, its production does not [occur].
[Sound] must be a product, because once its production occurs, its distinctness [from its cause] is inevitable; because it contradicts the cognition that "it is that same [sound]";
and because manifestation is not possible in the case of sound. The objector, who is agreed upon by both disputants, asks:
if conjunctions and disjunctions do not produce the production of sound, then what do they do?

The defender says: "We say that they perform the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory faculty. The objector says: "But surely these [sounds] are [simultaneous] with other refinements of the sense faculties, such as the opening of the eyes, which are the causes for perceiving all forms and so forth existing in the same location?"

It has been stated that it is not tenable for conjunctions and disjunctions—which are accepted as the factors that refine the auditory organ—to possess a character distinct from being the cause for the perception of specific sounds. The respondent says: [This is not so,] because through inference there is an absence of such an effect.

You think thus; we, however, do not accept that production [of sound] occurs through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And it is established that between direct perception and inference, direct perception is more authoritative.
The meaning of this is as follows: [the claim] that "there is no effect in the auditory organ" is—

He thinks that [the production of sound] occurs because of the inference of a commonality among the manifestors; and having understood through inference the absence of an effect in the auditory organ, he postulates the production [of sound] as the cause for its apprehension. We, however, perceiving the oneness of sound through direct perception accompanied by recognition, do not accept its production, but [postulate] the refinement of the auditory organ.
We postulate that the auditory organ has as its object a specific sound, by means of subverting the universal perception that would otherwise follow from the inference of a general manifesting agent.

In this way, your inference regarding the production of sound is preceded by another inference, whereas our postulation of the manifestation of a specific sound by the auditory organ is preceded by direct perception. And between direct perception and inference...

It is established for all disputants that perception is more powerful because it operates more swiftly. In the case of inference, however, the causal complex—characterized by the grasping of the relationship and pervasion (*vyāpti*), the recollection [of that], and the determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)—requires a much greater amount of delay. In perception, by contrast, there is no dependence whatsoever upon the apprehension of another object; thus, it is swifter.

"The determination of an object occurs solely by the force of an active inference"—this is correct, provided that there is a perception [of the object], since conjunction and disjunction produce the manifestation of a specific object. The opponent says: "But surely it was stated that non-perception is the cause of error, as in the case of [the perceived continuity of] flames and the like."

The meaning of this is as follows: if this [perception] were established as being the apprehension of that [object], then the inference based on its power would be stronger; however, just as in the case of flames and the like, where there is a delusion of apprehending them as such due merely to the non-apprehension of their difference even though they are distinct, so too is this [perception] merely a delusion of apprehending that.
"How is it that this inference based on prior [perception] is stronger? The respondent says: "In this case, however, non-apprehension itself is unestablished.
1. *sāmagrībahutā* (the multiplicity of causal complexes). Ka.
2. To be experienced.
(ga) 3. At times. (ka) 4. Error arises from grasping. (ga)
[Page 290] It is not certain here that "this is the non-apprehension of difference"; rather, by the force of cognition, it is established that this is indeed the apprehension of that.
Thus, the strength of the preceding inference is proven. The objector, with the intention of establishing parity, says:

Regarding that, [the opponent asks]: "How is the non-apprehension of difference established in the case of flames and the like? He states the answer as a resolution: "From the inference of the effect.
Because difference is inferred in flames and so forth from the effect characterized by its manifestation, the non-apprehension of difference is established; however, in this case...

That very effect which serves as the basis for the inference of difference remains unestablished even now; and what is unestablished is not sufficient to prove the non-apprehension of difference in the case of words. Perception, however, is established because it is independent. The objector says: "Or rather, what need is there for inference?"
The meaning is that there is no dependence whatsoever. The respondent says: this very thing is the dependence—once inference is established, it must be applied.
There is no effect here established by perception that is equal to [the force of] a command; therefore, the effect must be understood through inference alone.
Therefore, when inference is established, the effect must be known; and when the effect exists, there is inference.
Furthermore, since that inference also depends upon a mark (liṅga), its effect—the mark—must be stated. Therefore:

When an effect exists, one must proceed by means of inference; therefore, because inference depends upon the effect that is to be inferred, it is dependent. And since that effect to be inferred does not exist [in this case], there is no non-apprehension of difference through inference.
In the absence of non-apprehension of difference, it is established that "this is the apprehension of that. However, perception is not like this.
It depends on the apprehension of that [difference].

Just as inference depends on the non-apprehension of difference, perception does not depend on the apprehension of that [difference]; for the apprehension of that [difference] is established through perception itself. This is what is meant: as long as...
This delusion is based on the non-apprehension of difference; thus, perception is not rendered otherwise-established (anyathāsiddha).

An inference that is capable of arising from the force of that [perception] cannot be obstructed. And as long as this [inference] is unobstructed, the inference regarding the production of sound does not find its footing.
Therefore, the inference depends upon the non-apprehension of difference, whereas perception [itself] requires nothing else.
"It depends [on something else]. He states another argument: "Conjunction and disjunction are already established elsewhere as having the ear as their object.
Therefore, they must pertain to that very thing for whose sake conjunction and disjunction are established."
It is logical that they are the producers of mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Why so?
Because they are established as having the ear as their object.
It has been stated, "Because seeing is for the sake of another," according to worldly convention; that is, because the act of seeing— meaning the utterance— is for the sake of another.

Because it is for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of another’s comprehension, specifically for the sake of the listener’s comprehension of the word—it is logical that the effect should reside in the listener alone.
Since the effect cannot reside in the listener [as a whole], it is appropriate that the effect resides in his auditory organ (*śrotra*).
Therefore, given that its purpose is for the sake of another—namely, for the sake of another’s comprehension—the effect must be understood in whatever way it can possibly occur.
It must be postulated; and since that [postulation] is impossible in the hearer, it is stated that it resides in the auditory organ itself.

However, one does not establish the status of being a word-meaning by postulating an effect residing in the word, because it has been stated that "it is not apprehended in the word" (*śabde tadagrahaṇāt*), as no such effect existing in the word is known from any other source.

Thus, he concludes the resolution: "Therefore, there is no proof here for [the non-existence of the cause] otherness, as in the case of flames and the like. He summarizes the subject at hand: "Therefore, it is logical that the non-perception of the existent is inconclusive (anaikāntika)."
The objector says: If [the sound] is an effect in the auditory organ, how then can it be possible to postulate that its manifestation has only a single object?
This is utterly untenable.
"Since all [sounds] are equally present, why does one perceive only a certain sound and not another?

He provides the answer: "Because we observe specific effects; since we observe specific effects characterized by the manifestation of particular sounds, it is logical to postulate a capacity for restricted perception that is not seen elsewhere, but not for that which is already observed."

"It is logical that there should be a denial of the apprehension of that [sound] which resides in the word. Now, if this were so, many conjunctions and disjunctions would have to be admitted as manifestors; otherwise, how could there be the perception of multiple sounds according to their specific distribution? And if those are admitted, there is the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*). To this, he says: "another effect... [kāryāntara-]
However, it is indeed logical to postulate a difference in the cause based on perception;
for when conjunction and disjunction have ceased...

"If it is argued that [the sound] is heard, this is not so; the conjunctions and disjunctions do not indeed cease, since the sound is perceived; for they are not objects of direct perception"—thus the Bhāṣya has been restated.
Regarding the objection raised in the commentary here— “when conjunction and disjunction have ceased”— which two kinds of conjunction and disjunction are intended?

The meaning of the objection is that sound is perceived even when those two have ceased. The answer is: we say that what is intended is the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and other [articulatory organs].
Why is this so?
The answer: because it is heard in the Bhāṣya that "the two have ceased. Now, even if this is what is heard, why are the two belonging to air (*vāyavīya*) not perceived as well? To that he says:
However, the production and cessation of the aerial [atoms] are to be inferred.

The meaning of this is as follows: if this is stated with reference to the aerial [atoms], then, since those two are to be understood through their effects, it is impossible to say that there is cessation when the effect exists.
And he says: "From this we understand that this is stated with the intention of referring to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs.

Therefore, the meaning of this objection in the Bhāṣya is as follows: "The conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs are not the manifestors [of sound], because sound is heard even when those two have ceased. Here, the Bhāṣya provides the resolution: "It is not the case that they certainly cease..."
"Conjunctions and disjunctions.
What is the intention here? Having in mind the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air, this answer is given because [sound] is to be understood through its effects.

The intention is that the conjunctions and disjunctions of air, which are to be understood through their effects, do not cease as long as the effect exists; this reply is intended solely with reference to those [conjunctions and disjunctions] of air,
for "they are not indeed perceptible."

This has been clarified by this commentary: since the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs are indeed perceptible, it was with that intention that he said, "For those conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceptible."
This statement is not tenable; therefore, the refutation is intended solely from the perspective of the air-element (*vāyu*). He objects:
"If this has been made clear in this way, then the subsequent passage is no longer appropriate, [stating]: 'Because that [sound] has space as its object, and because space is one.'"

Thus [it is asked]: how is this not tenable? If the aerial elements were the manifestors, then—just as in the case of the theory that they are produced—the consequence would follow that "wherever they are, there alone must their perception occur," and this is not tenable.

The meaning of this is as follows: for in the Bhāṣya it is said, "If conjunctions and disjunctions manifest sound but do not produce it, then—since that [sound] has space as its locus and since space is one—the very same space that constitutes the auditory organ here must also exist in other places; consequently, what is manifested by those staying in Srughna would be perceived even in Pāṭaliputra."
By this passage,

the objection is raised that if conjunctions and disjunctions were the manifesters of sound, then what is manifested in one place would be perceived everywhere; and that [objection] is not tenable if the manifesters are composed of air, because they manifest [the sound] through contact.
