Because [the sound] is produced [by them]. Therefore, manifestation will occur precisely where they [the conjunctions and disjunctions] exist. However, this objection is appropriate only with reference to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs, because those two [conjunctions and disjunctions] manifest [the sound] without reaching it (*aprāpyābhivyañjakatva*).
The objector himself sets forth the doubt of the respondent: "Now, if this is the intention—that on the theory of manifestation, [the sound is not produced by] the air..."
Sounds do not reside [in the organ]; rather, they reside only in space (*ākāśa*).

Therefore, because space is one and the same everywhere, it is logical that [the sound] is perceived everywhere; thus, the objection applies to the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*). However, for those who...
When those [sounds] are produced, the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to the air become their non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

And when these [qualities] serve as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), then that very substance of air becomes the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for a non-inherent cause is that which is proximate to the inherent cause, just as the conjunctions of threads— which are inherent in the threads acting as the inherent cause— are the non-inherent causes of the cloth inherent in those threads, and just as are the colors of the threads.

Regarding the production of the form of a cloth inherent in its threads: since the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to the air that are in close proximity to the air [are the cause], the air itself is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). And where the inherent cause is located, there alone is the effect perceived;
just as the cloth is perceived only where the threads are—this is the correct position. Now, he refutes this objection:
Even when it is thus established that conjunctions and disjunctions of air are the manifestors [of sound], this objection is not tenable;
for wherever there is a manifestor, there alone is the manifestation, just as wherever there is a cause, there alone is the effect.

However, this objection might indeed apply if the conjunctions and disjunctions of the air-currents produced at the palate and other locations were non-contacting in their operation (*aprāpyakāritva*) regarding imperceptible objects; but that is not the case, since the intention concerning the nature of the air-currents has already been clearly established. Once again, the objector speaks to raise a doubt against the respondent: "Now, you may think that this [property of] being perceived in the location of the cause is appropriate only for an effect."
"Not in the case of manifestation. He refutes this: "That is incorrect; for manifestation itself is indeed an effect.
Therefore, it is logical that manifestation also occurs only in the locus of its cause, and the manifestor is its cause."

Manifestation occurs precisely where there is a manifestor. If manifestation, too, is an effect, then what is the difference between a cause and a manifestor? To this he says: "But that which is manifested has already arisen previously."
Manifestation, though non-existent, is rendered existent;

the object to be manifested has already arisen previously; therefore, manifestation is designated as "manifesting" with reference to the object to be manifested, but with reference to the act of manifesting itself, it is simply a cause. Consequently, perception occurs precisely where there is manifestation in a particular location.
This is equal for both positions. Having raised an objection, he concludes: "Therefore, this text must be explained.
He provides the resolution: "The 'beloved of the gods' (the fool) is ignorant of distinctions; for an effect [occupies] the location of its cause."
It exists;
for its establishment is dependent upon a cause, and in the absence of that [cause], it is absent. Furthermore, that which is not an effect does not depend on another for its location.
Since this is so, therefore let manifestation occur in the location of the manifestor,
because it is an effect; but why should the manifested object itself be in that location, given that it is not produced by it?
Because the manifested object and its location— the space at the location of the sound that is considered to be manifested— are a single part of space,
it is perceived by everyone, even those situated in various different locations. Now, even if it is manifested...
Even so, because manifestation occurs only in specific locations, its perception everywhere would not be logical. It is replied:
the manifestation is not inherent in the manifesting agent (*abhivyañjaka*). What then? It is inherent in the manifested object (*abhivyaṅgya*);
and since the manifested object is manifested without parts and is of a single uniform nature everywhere, its apprehension everywhere is logical.
And thus, the statement "Therefore, let manifestation occur from the location of the manifester" is merely a hypothetical concession (*abhyupagamavāda*).

The objection regarding the conjunctions and disjunctions of air, even though they are known, is indeed appropriate; for since space is one and the same in all locations of the auditory organ, it is entirely logical that this objection should be raised—that because space is unitary, sound, which has space as its object, would be perceived everywhere. He refutes this: "It would be as you say, if the manifestors of sound..."

There would be conjunctions and disjunctions; however, these are merely the manifestors of the auditory organ (*śrotra*). For these are indeed the factors that produce the refinement (*saṃskāra*) [of the organ].
And the location of the auditory organ is precisely the locus of the hearer. But surely, the auditory organ is simply space (*ākāśa*); and that [space] exists elsewhere as well.
This is equivalent to the theory of sound-manifestation (*śabdābhivyakti*). It is replied: True, space (*ākāśa*) is one everywhere;
however, its state as the auditory organ (*śrotra*) exists only in the location of the hearer, because it functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*) through its connection with an agent (*kartṛ*);
for agency resides only in the bodily location by virtue of being the locus of the agent’s experience.
It is not the same as the manifestation of sound.
He concludes: "Therefore, just as in the case of production, so too in the case of manifestation, there would not be perception by all [hearers]. This is not so;
for if [the auxiliaries] assist without reaching [the object], then those situated in near and distant places would perceive the sound simultaneously.
[Page 297] Thus,
having restated the commentary (*bhāṣya*) in order to challenge it, he challenges it: "But surely, on the view that the auditory organ is refined (*saṃskāra*), [the sound] situated at a distance..."
For those who say, "The ear is not embellished," it has been stated that the embellishment occurs only through [the contact] of the [sound] reaching [the sense organ].
But how, then, [is this so]?
Does the statement, "that which is situated at a distance is not refined," imply that refinement occurs only through contact? To this, he replies:
and in the absence of contact, even the designation of "distant" or "near" would not be possible.
The designation "this ear is distant" occurs in relation to a proximate ear; and proximity belongs to that which has reached [the object].

[An effect] occurs [only] for that which has been reached, not for that which has not been reached; therefore, since the designation "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) applies only to those things already reached, what is the point of this passage stating, "If they assist while being unreached"? Here, there is no doubt at all regarding their being unreached, because of the statement, "[The sound] existing at a distance."

By the passage, "The true [sounds] being at a distance do not assist the ear-cavity," it is established that what is situated at a distance is not refined. Therefore, we do not understand how this commentary came to be.
Thus it is said.

He provides the solution: in this way, the following consequence follows—on the view that the auditory organ is refined (*saṃskāra*), because sound is all-pervading (*sarvagata*), wherever the refinement is inferred by its effect, there would be simultaneous perception over that entire extent.

On whatever extent of ground there is the perception of sound, on that same extent there would have to be simultaneous perception according to the view that the auditory organ is prepared (*saṃskāra*),
because sound is all-pervading (*sarvagata*). For if the sound itself were merely localized (*prādeśika*), then it would be encountered sequentially.

Even by the ear, it is perceived only successively; however, because it is omnipresent, it exists everywhere simultaneously, and thus it is not the case that it is not perceived simultaneously due to its being present [everywhere]. 1.

There would be [the flaw of] "attainment" (labdhi). What is the intention? He states it in a single sentence: "But surely, the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air are not capable of refining the auditory organ without reaching it;
and reaching occurs only in a sequence."

Perception occurs in that sequence. To this, he replies: "Indeed, it cannot be said that one conjunction or disjunction initiates another conjunction or disjunction, because that would lead to an infinite regress (ubhayaprasaṅga).
The meaning of this is as follows:

If another conjunction or disjunction were produced by [prior] conjunctions and disjunctions, then conjunctions and disjunctions would possess the property of refining the auditory organ upon reaching it; however, another conjunction or disjunction is not produced by [prior] conjunctions and disjunctions. To the question "Why is it not produced?", he says: "Because of the consequence that both [would have to be produced]."
It would follow that a single [conjunction or disjunction] would possess both the quality of being self-manifesting and the quality of generating another manifesting agent;
therefore, conjunctions and disjunctions are indeed one, while the auditory organs located in various places are what they refine.
Therefore, this is stated [by the opponent]: "If they assist without having reached [the object], then those situated in near and distant locations would perceive the sound simultaneously.
[The author replies: Let there be this undesirable consequence for both sides; what is the fault? To this he says: "For not in one..."
The postulation of two causes for a single effect is logical.
For a single effect called manifestation (*abhivyakti*), there is the postulation of multiple causes;
first, conjunctions and disjunctions are the causes, and furthermore, those produced by them are also [causes]. Conjunctions...
The postulation of two causes based on the contingency of both—that "other divisions" are the cause—is improper.
Why is that? He says: for it is the effect that postulates a cause, and not another effect as well.
For the effect, characterized as the manifestation of sound, leads one to postulate only a cause characterized by conjunction and disjunction;

it does not, however, lead to another further effect characterized by conjunction and disjunction produced by yet other conjunctions and disjunctions, because [the series] would be without foundation.
(Note: *vāyu* is not found in the manuscript *ka*).
2. [The reading] *mabhivyaktyantara* is found in Ka.

Precisely because that effect is appropriate [to arise] from conjunctions and disjunctions, therefore, only the position of its production (*utpatti-pakṣa*) is maintained.
It is possible—namely, that conjunctions and disjunctions initiate their effect according to the momentum [of the cause]—but this is not the case even in the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*).
The meaning of this is as follows: it is only in the theory of the production of sound (*śabdotpatti*) that this [phenomenon] occurs for those who are near and far.
Successive perception is logically possible [only] on the theory of production (*utpatti*), but not even on the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*);

because, according to the theory of production alone, conjunctions and disjunctions initiate the effect characterized as sound for as long as the momentum lasts, and thus sound, being produced successively, is perceived successively. But surely, even on the theory of production, one must postulate another cause for each individual effect?
This is not at all tenable. It is true that it is not tenable.
He states this in a single passage: "The perception of another effect, however, is indeed perceptual, because sound is perceived in succession by those situated far away and those situated nearby."
The point is that, because another effect is observed,
it is logical to postulate another cause. But surely this is the same even in the case of manifestation?
[The opponent argues: "The postulation of another manifestor is justified because another manifestation is observed. [The author] refutes this: "It is not the same;
for one manifestation does not initiate another manifestation, since it is not observed to do so in any case. But as for an effect, [it may produce] another effect—"
There is no contradiction whatsoever in beginning [the process] in the interval; for both effect and cause are relative.
With respect to the root cause, it is an effect; with respect to its own effect, it is a cause. However, this is not the case regarding manifestation—
And [it is] "that which manifests. This is the meaning: it is not the same even regarding manifestation;
because manifestation does not initiate another manifestation anywhere, as this is never observed; whereas an effect, however, necessarily initiates another effect.
Because it is generally observed in the world that [sound arises from contact], therefore the initial conjunctions and disjunctions produce sound; those produced by them [produce further sounds].

ga. 4. Omitted. na—in the world.

It is logical that sounds produce another sound; however, it is never observed anywhere that a manifestation, while producing another manifestation, could itself be a manifestor. Therefore, according to the theory of manifestation, those situated far and near would perceive the sound simultaneously.

Even without reaching [the object], because conjunctions and disjunctions bring about the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) within a certain limited space, and because such refinement is known through its effect, it may well be that there is no refinement of the auditory organ at an extremely distant location; however, within the extent where refinement does occur, it happens simultaneously.

It might be so. Therefore, this objection is valid: "If they [the organs] assist [the word-sound] without having reached it. But surely, even on the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti-pakṣa*), manifestation will occur sequentially; let that very same manifested sound be the manifestor.
And the state of being a manifestor belongs to that which is manifested, just as light from the sun and other sources is the manifestor of the visual organ.
Regarding the claim that a jar or similar object is manifested by the spreading parts of a lamp, he says: "To say that illumination also requires another illumination is the talk of a fool.
By this, he states that the supporting example is unestablished; it is not [the case].
There is no proof for the claim that light requires another light. As for the dependence on the ocular rays, that pertains to its perception, not its manifestation;

for manifestation consists in the production of the capacity for perception, and perception occurs at a time subsequent to that. Indeed, jars and the like are not capable of being perceived by their own nature even when they exist, in the absence of light.
Because it is not seen even by those with wide-open eyes; whereas light, being present for one whose senses are functioning unimpaired, is indeed within the range of perception. As it has been said:
"Fire and other such things are well known as the illuminators of jars and other objects."

"For they do not possess a manifest form, since they have no need for manifestation. Thus, since the example is unestablished (*asiddha*), this [argument]— that the very sound which has been manifested is again [manifested]— is refuted.
"Let it be the manifester," he says. He concludes: "Therefore, let the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to the air originate sound;
and that sound, residing in the air, [is perceived] in the ear by means of the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)."
1. Of those not yet attained. Ga. 2. Omitted. Saṃskā—yadi. Ga. 3. It occurs. Ga.

Let it be perceived through its connection; and let the air, having traveled according to its momentum, gradually come into conjunction with the space of the ear. Or rather, let the established doctrine (rāddhānta) of the Vaiśeṣika followers of Ulūka be accepted: "From conjunction, from disjunction, and from sound..."
This refers to what is stated in the sūtra: "The production of sound. And here is their process:
the first sound is produced from conjunction; for example, from the conjunction of the drum and the stick, aided by the conjunction of the drum and space.

Sound is produced in the ether; having been produced, it initiates another sound, and that one another, in a sequence like the spreading of a series of waves. Thus, when the sound has arisen in the region of the ether within the ear-cavity—which has attained the state of the sense-organ (śrotra) through the influence of merit and demerit—it is perceived by means of the contact characterized as inherence (samavāya). In this manner...

The first sound is produced from disjunction. For example, a sound is produced in space from the disjunction between a bamboo segment and space, which is assisted by the disjunction between the bamboo segments themselves; that [sound] in turn initiates another, and that yet another, as should be applied as before. In this context, the first sound is opposed to its effect; the last is opposed to its cause; and those occurring in between are [opposed to both].

It should be understood that [the cause] is opposed to both the effect and the cause. Here, an objection is raised: "Is this merely because the author of the Bhāṣya has presented the tenet of the Vaiśeṣikas, which was not mentioned here? If it is only intended to show that there is some acquaintance with the Vaiśeṣika system, then this is of no consequence. To this, he says:

"What is this conceit that 'I too have heard this'? This is not conceit; for how could such a thought occur to anyone who is ignorant? This is not the Vaiśeṣika tenet which has been [refuted] by the Blessed One in the Bhāṣya."
[The objection] is of the form: "Is it presented [as a reason] or refuted? To remove that doubt, this is presented:
"By the very presentation of the sound as being composed of air, it is both presented and refuted.
Why? Because the cause is the same.
Regarding both the presentation (*nyāsa*) and the refutation (*nirāsa*):

first, the perception of sound in sequence is the reason for the presentation, and this is equal in both positions; furthermore, the refutation is also equal by virtue of the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For this very reason, [it is said]: "with the wind... (*anuvātam*)...
1. Omitted. *atra ca*. (ga) 2. Omitted. *nāyam abhimānaḥ*. (ga) 3. *sā pakṣadvaye ’pi*. (ka)
"Sound is perceived even from a distance"— this refutation was directed specifically at the Vaiśeṣika position regarding sound carried with the wind.

Because this [argument] is useless under the view that one sound initiates another sound; and even under the Buddhist view, since it relies on the perception of a sound that has not yet reached [the senses], this objection remains unavoidable. Since the positions of the Vaiśeṣika and the author of the *Śikṣā* are thus equal, this passage is intended to demonstrate the difference between the two views: that of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and that of action (*kārya*).
"If they assist [the object] even without reaching it.
In the view that [the effect] is produced (*kāryapakṣa*), perception occurs sequentially; however, this is not the case in the view that [the effect] is merely manifested (*abhivyaktipakṣa*).

This treatise is concerned solely with this much; it does not, however, intend to maintain that even in the view that sound is a product, it must be composed of air alone. Whether it be composed of air or whether it consists of conjunctions and disjunctions—there is no need for excessive insistence on this point.
This is not so; for the air-molecules impelled by a blow [strike] against other stationary air-molecules.

"Striking in all directions and producing conjunctions and disjunctions, they continue to move as long as their momentum lasts"—this is the restatement of the Bhāṣya, intended to be challenged; he challenges it: "But is this not that very same production?"
The nature [of sound] has been stated, and it was asserted that conjunctions and disjunctions are its manifestors.
The meaning of this is:
"For by means of impact..."
By this it is stated: the winds within the chest, being impelled by the impact against internal parts and striking against the stagnant intermediate air, [spread] in all directions.
"Remaining in motion for as long as their momentum lasts without producing conjunctions or disjunctions"— in this regard,

since the objection that "if [the causes] assist without reaching [their object]" has not been resolved, it is stated that they are merely producers (*utpādaka*), and not manifesters (*abhivyañjaka*) through conjunction.
[This refers] to the divisions. Therefore, this response appears entirely irrelevant. The defender asks: "Why, sir? Why is it irrelevant? The objector says: "Because it was already stated."

Because it has been stated that [the cause] possesses the quality of being a producer, this [objection] is therefore irrelevant. Furthermore, in this context, the first word *iti* is intended to indicate the essential nature [of the cause], whereas the second is intended to express the reason; [as in the question] "Why? (*kimiti*).
Thus, the very reason was asked; that same [reason] was stated by means of the word "iti. The respondent said: "You are ignorant of non-manifestation.
The meaning of this is: whatever [is manifested], to whatever extent its manifestation—
One who knows its own nature—how could such a person claim that it is the manifestor of things not yet attained? The objector asks:
"What is this 'knowledge of non-manifestation'?
The respondent replies: "This is what constitutes the knowledge of non-manifestation."
He himself says: "Manifestation (abhivyakti) is indeed the removal of concealment;
it is the movement of the subtle particles of dust by the still air."
The indicators [of sound] are perceived as light as cotton wool and exist by obstructing the auditory organ;

they are removed by the internal air impelled by a forceful impact, just as earth and other obstructions of roots, water, and so forth are removed by digging and similar means—thus, manifestation is simply the removal of obstruction. The objector says:
Who has said that the removal of the obstruction will not be a manifestation? Rather, it was stated that this very removal does not initiate another removal.
This refers to the removal of the obstruction which resides in the vicinity of the ear.
It has been stated that once produced, it does not begin to remove the obstruction situated within the distant range of the sense of hearing; [rather], manifestation occurs. (Note:
*nayāntaram* is a variant reading for *tiraskārāpanayanam*).

"—it does not become a manifester"—so it is stated. Now, one might object: "Granted that one remover may not initiate another removal; however, why should the very same remover not initiate another removal? To this, he says:

For those who remove something act with a single operation upon that which is to be removed, and not for as long as there remains that which is to be removed, just like the light of the sun and so forth.
Those who are removers exert their activity only once regarding the thing to be removed, and not repeatedly for as many things as there may be to be removed.
They would have to operate again to remove that many [objects]; therefore, because their operation is simultaneous, there would be no perception of them in succession.

For this very reason, it must be said that in order to establish successive perception, one removal must produce another removal, yet that does not occur. The defender says: "True; if there were only a single remover..."
If multiple operations were postulated, this fault would indeed arise; however, in this case, there are many manifestors,
because for each individual ear, the conjunctions and disjunctions of the air are distinct, and they possess a temporal sequence.
There are conjunctions and disjunctions, due to the sequential movement of the wind. How is this known?
That there are many conjunctions and disjunctions. The answer is: or, according to your own position on the nature of effects, there must be a multiplicity of causes.

How so? If it is argued that it is because of the multiplicity of effects, then for me as well, there will be a multiplicity of manifestors due to the multiplicity of manifestations. But how can there be a multiplicity of manifestations?
For if the multiplicity of manifestations were established, then there would be a multiplicity of manifestors; but how is that so? 1. Lamps and so forth. (Ga.)
Question: Answer— Just as there is a multiplicity of effects,
in your own view, their establishment follows from their being perceived sequentially.
Likewise, in our view as well, there is a multiplicity of manifestations. To the question, "How then do you ascertain the multiplicity of manifestations?", he says:
"But regarding [the theory of] unity, we shall state that perception is more authoritative.
Therefore, sound is one.
Because of recognition; and in the case of oneness, there is permanence;

and in the case of permanence, there is the state of being a manifester; and in the case of being a manifester, since perception occurs sequentially, there is simply a multiplicity of manifestations, not a multiplicity of effects—this is established.

This must be addressed here: since the removal of the obstructing stagnant air is the same [in all cases], why are not all sounds perceived? This objection is incorrect; for if the removal of the obstruction is postulated as an effect, then those many stagnant airs remain covering the auditory organ, and therein—
This conceptual construction is rooted in observation: that when something is removed, only a certain sound is perceived, and not all sounds.
Therefore, because there is a multiplicity of things to be removed and removers, nothing will be logically untenable, provided that perception accompanied by recognition remains stable.
He recites the sūtra "the supreme of application" (prayogasya param) [as follows]: "of application" (prayogasya).
It stands.
By this principle, the usage "make soundless" (*aśabdaṃ kuru*) is established, just as in the case of cow-dung and similar examples; for instance:
1. *avadhāya*. (Ga.)

Just as the duty regarding cow-dung is expressed by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in reference to the duty regarding its collection, so too the duty regarding words is expressed by way of secondary indication in reference to the duty regarding their application. But how, then, is the description of application [understood] through secondary indication?
To this he replies: because a worldly sentence has as its object that which is already cognized by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Whatever is cognized by another means of valid knowledge, it is precisely that which people employ a sentence to communicate; in that case—
Furthermore, the production of sound by means of another instrument of knowledge is not observed; rather, the production of its application is observed.

Thus, once it is understood that the purport of this sentence is solely to demonstrate the necessity of performing that [application], it is logical to accept figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when such a purport is known—as in the case of the statement:
"Just as of this one existing... [and so forth].
Thus, it produces the illusion of multiplicity;
by this statement,
the meaning of the Bhāṣya— that the perception of multiplicity resulting from the simultaneous apprehension of sound in various locations is an illusion— is restated.
He objects: How, moreover, can it be said that there is error (*bhrānti*) without a misconception (*viparyaya*)?
For a cognition of misconception does not arise in this way—that sound is not perceived in various locations; therefore, [there must be] a subverting [cognition].
If it is asked, "In the absence of a causal condition, how can this be an error? the reply is: "Because one perceives a defect in the cause.
An error also arises from perceiving a defect in the cause. The objector asks: "Which cause here is defective?"
How is this understood?

He states it in a single passage: "In this case, the word as an object is not perceived, because it does not reach the path of the ear, due to its inherence in the auditory organ; for the auditory organ, being manifested, is already refined."
[The perception] exists. Now, if it were postulated that the auditory organ is defective, then in that case, [the fault] would belong to the sound itself.

-pathāpatteḥ. ka, ga.)
3. Because of its inherence in the auditory organ. Ga. 4. Of this very [organ]. Ga. [p.

Apprehension would not occur. For the loss of the power to produce its effect is precisely what constitutes being "impaired"; and the apprehension of sound is the function of the ear. In that case, if it were impaired, how could it apprehend sound? Or, if [it does apprehend] due to its impairment—

It is said that it will not perform any other function; regarding this, he says: "And there is nothing else to be grasped by the sense of hearing apart from sound, wherein defect could exist. The proponent of a partial solution says: "If this is so, if [there were] anything other than sound..."
If there is nothing graspable by the auditory organ, then even on the view that sound is an effect, how could there be an auditory apprehension of its multiplicity?
Since the connection with multiple locations is not a property of the sound itself, there would be no apprehension of plurality by the ear. The objector says:
"That is certainly not auditory."

[The opponent asserts] diversity. For that [cognition] is mental. One who holds a partial view regarding concentration asks: "Is an external object grasped by the mind even when it has not been grasped by the ear?"
If the external object characterized by multiplicity were grasped by the mind even when it has not been grasped by the ear, then this multiplicity would be purely mental;
however, this is not tenable, because the mind is never observed to function with respect to anything that has not been grasped externally. Therefore, it is not [the case].
This diversity belongs to the mental side even in the case of the object. The opponent refutes this:
"Or what external object, distinct from sound, do you intend here, which is not grasped by the ear and yet [is grasped] by the mind?"

"You say it is the object of apprehension. The partisan says: "This which is the plurality of words—that is an external entity distinct from the words; such is the meaning. The objector refutes this: "Or rather, is this distinct from the words?"
[Page 308] Is it a diversity of sounds? He himself conceptualizes this: is it the sound itself, or something other than the sound?

Regarding the phrase "a property of sound": first of all, this is not a property of sound alone, for it is observed even in the case of visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth; for visible forms and the rest are also "various" (*nānā*).
Thus it is apprehended; nor is this [object] merely the word, because we observe a distinction [between them], as expressed in the statement: "There is a multiplicity of words."
Therefore, we do not know which sense organ has the function regarding this multiplicity, whose defect you [the opponents] impute.
A partisan (ekadeśin) says: "In that case, what is this multiplicity? It is simply ungraspable."
"In that case, according to the previously mentioned alternative, is this multiplicity entirely ungraspable? He himself says: "But it is indeed perceived in all objects. Therefore...
Let it not be that this is a property of sound alone; rather, it shall be a property of both sound and other objects.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that this external object which is actually perceived does not exist; what then? It must be stated that it is of the nature of cognition (buddhirūpa). To this, he says: "But its being of the nature of cognition is refuted because cognition is not [itself] graspable."

For if cognition were perceptible, then it would necessarily have the form of cognition; yet it has been stated that it is not perceptible. The objector supports his position: It is said that if something is the object of apprehension for this [cognition], then once that object is apprehended...
Multiplicity is the reflective awareness of distinct objects of apprehension.
The meaning of this is as follows: multiplicity is not something other [than that awareness].
