309] However, when those objects which are distinct by their very nature are apprehended, it is this very distinctness that is reflected upon.

This is plurality (*nānātva*); by that very [perception], plurality is indeed apprehended, because it consists in the form of differentiation (*vailakṣaṇya*). And because they possess this differentiation, entities are not distinct from one another. What then? They are distinct by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). A partisan (*ekadeśin*) says: "If plurality is to be grasped by the ear in the case of the theory of production (*kāryapakṣa*), then likewise, in the case of the theory of eternity (*nityapakṣa*) as well, it must be by the ear alone."

Defectiveness must be postulated. The objector refutes this: "And if there is defectiveness, the apprehension of the word does not occur, because defectiveness obstructs the causal capacity. He himself says: "And when there is no apprehension of the word..."
Whence comes the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of another word?

Precisely because the auditory faculty is not defective. Therefore, since it is by means of this reflective awareness that the object is reflected upon, it is the defectiveness of that reflective awareness which must be postulated, and not a defect in the perception of the sound itself.

Regarding the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*), a certain partisan (*ekadeśin*) says: "In that case, let there be a defect in the mind (*manas*); by means of that [defective mind], even sound is perceived.

Because the ear is not defective while the mind is defective, and because of the non-apprehension of unity, the apprehension of multiplicity occurs. The objector states the refutation: "But surely, it is not possible for the mind itself to be defective..."
To explain:

since sound, which is apprehended by the ear, is grasped according to its true nature, for whatever is apprehended at all, none of it occurs without the mind; therefore, if the mind is unimpaired, then the apprehension of sound itself is accurate.
It would not be so; yet, since there is a correct apprehension of the object in the case of verbal cognition, the mind also is not defective.

How, then, is it understood that there is a correct apprehension of the object in the case of verbal cognition? To this he says: "For indeed, [it is not the case] that one who has not grasped the truth..."
1. Wherein.
Ga. 2. Because of the apprehension of sound by the auditory organ as it truly is.
The reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of that object is possible only for one who has apprehended it;

for there can be no reflective awareness of an object that has not been apprehended—this is the meaning. He concludes: "Therefore, the gods will imagine this error [only] because of the absence of a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇa*)."
And because they are perceived as distinct;
for if they were effects, it would be logical that the cognition of their multiplicity is not an error, and thus their very nature as effects would be established.
To designate a non-erroneous cognition as an "error" is even worse than an actual error. Therefore, this must indeed be explained.

The cause of error has been explained by those who know it. The supreme synthesizer says: this is being stated; for you yourself have said in this passage—"Indeed, for one who has not grasped the correct object, a reflective awareness of that object is not possible"—that the external [object] has not been grasped.
"The object is not grasped by the mind. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Because it is grasped by the sense organ as well;
because it is grasped as 'this is that very same thing,' there is no multiplicity [of the object], according to perception."
It has been established that since multiplicity is not apprehended by the external sense-faculties, it is likewise impossible for multiplicity to be apprehended by the mind as well.
The objector asks: What is the objective support (*ālambana*) for this cognition, and what is the sense faculty (*indriya*) for the apprehension of multiplicity? [He says:
"This is the sense faculty and this is the objective support"—for sounds arising from various locations arrive simultaneously. [End of omitted portion. *tat*. *ga*.
From the statement [arises] delusion.
[The word] "tu" is omitted in manuscript *ga*. Because of the understanding of its being a cause, he provides the resolution. Manuscript *ga* reads "samādhatte."
The auditory organ initiates the embellishment simultaneously, each [sound] being independent of the others; and because it follows that embellishment,
it perceives even a single sound as if it were many.

The meaning of this is as follows: many sounds, independent of one another, produce many latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the auditory faculty; and by virtue of those impressions, various cognitions of distinct sounds arise within the auditory organ. In that case, [the distinction between sounds] is due to the difference in the resulting cognitions.

Even regarding a word that is to be understood, the cognizer engages in the linguistic practice of apprehending difference; he grasps it as if it were manifold. Just as a manifold object, when being grasped, gives rise to manifold linguistic practices, so too does this [word]—the cognition of it.

The meaning is that it brings about the linguistic usage of difference through [the perception of] difference. But why is there a difference in cognition? To this he says: because of the production of a distinct impression for each [object], the visual power—unlike [a single object such as] a finger divided [into parts]—perceives even a single thing as if it were divided.

Since the auditory power is produced by each individual impression (saṃskāra) or sound (dhvani), that power is accordingly differentiated; thus, it perceives even a single object as if it were divided. This is just as the visual power, when affected by fingers, perceives even the undivided moon as if it were divided. He concludes:
Therefore, this error is based on the non-apprehension of a difference in powers.

Not apprehending the difference in powers, one engages in the linguistic usage of various words; for, failing to recognize the distinct power, one fails to conceive of a distinction in the objects of cognition, and thus the object itself remains to be cognized.
He considers [the object] as distinct. But he who considers it to be a difference in capacity knows that it is merely a cognition; [this is] its latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
[It is] produced by that.
3. And the capacity is distinct. Ga. 4. It acts.
It is divided, yet it must be understood as being that very same [single] entity. By this, the apprehension of intervals is also refuted.
As for the doubt that this interrupted apprehension of sound is untenable, [it is addressed by noting that] sound [resides] in the auditory ether (*śrotrākāśa*).
Because [the object] is perceived as being conjoined [with its parts]. To this, it is said: by this [explanation], a response has also been given regarding the perception of intervals;
the meaning is that this too is an illusion. Here, an objection is raised:
how, moreover, is the perception of intervals refuted by this?

In a single passage he says: It is indeed reasonable that the awakening of a capacity occurs by virtue of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); and it is further consistent with this that a distinct capacity, presenting even a single object as if divided, produces the illusion of apprehending many objects due to the non-apprehension of its own internal differentiation. But what is the cause for the apprehension of the intermediate [states]?
"Therefore, state another cause. He replies: "I do not state another cause."
This indeed is the reason. [The opponent] objects: "How is this the reason? [The author] replies:

Sounds arising from various locations, initiating a refinement through their distinctness, produce an awakening of the power [of audition] from its very root. Therefore, although sound resides in the ether of the auditory organ, it is perceived as if situated in those [external] locations, in accordance with the assisting factors [the sounds].

The meaning of this is as follows: those sounds arising from various locations which, as they arrive, produce the awakening of the auditory faculty—these [sounds] "from the root," that is, starting from their origin, are accompanied by the conjunctions and disjunctions that constitute their source; therefore, by virtue of the supporting sounds, [the cognition] resides in the location where the sounds originate.

The word *iva* appears [in the text]; for although, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), sound is perceived as residing in the very space of the auditory organ—since the ear, being an external sense faculty, functions by reaching its object—it nevertheless appears to be situated in various locations due to the influence of the manifesting conditions (*abhivyañjaka*).
1. -deśasthāḥ ga.
2. Omitted. *vibhāga*. Ga. 3. Added. *bhūta*. Ga. 4. *te nānugraha*. Ga.

It should be understood as an error. And this is the established position here: sound is perceived by the auditory organ even though it is devoid of its own location, because the auditory organ resides at the location of the ear and because the sense organs lack the capacity for self-perception; [and] the auditory organ...

However, although it does not apprehend the location independently, nevertheless, by the force of experience, it is postulated that while apprehending the sound, it also apprehends the base location that manifests the sound. In that case, for the sound— which is devoid of location yet requires a location— the connection with that location [is established] by one who does not fail to apprehend its relation with that location.
[The objection is: "There is the conventional usage of 'grasping' [the sound]. But surely it is only the final conjunction and disjunction that produces the impression (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the location of the source of the sound is not the location of the manifestor; nor is there a grasping by the auditory organ of something with which it has no connection.
It was stated, "because it would lead to an over-extension. He offers a rebuttal: "What is this dullness of yours?
Is it not the case that it is not tenable for the final [conjunction] to produce a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) when the preceding conjunctions and disjunctions have not been assisted?
'That by which the preceding conjunctions and disjunctions have not been assisted' is the term *ananugṛhītapūrvasaṃyogavibhāga*. [The word] *anugṛhīta* means assisted."

That which is apprehended as following behind [the sound] by way of assistance is called the "auxiliary" (*sahāya*). This is what is meant: disregarding the preceding conjunctions and disjunctions, the final one manifests [the sound]. The underlying intention here is this: the internal air (*kauṣṭhya-vāyu*), generating conjunctions and disjunctions in the eight locations beginning with the chest (*uraḥ*), gradually proceeds toward the region of the ear.

The ear, subsiding after having previously undergone conjunction and disjunction, becomes refined [as a sense organ], for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-manifestation of specific sounds; for it is only by virtue of the impact upon a particular articulatory location (*sthāna*) that a refinement arises conducive to the perception of a specific phoneme, and not otherwise. Alternatively, a specific wind itself, produced by the force of the impact upon the articulatory location, is what is distinguished...
If it is argued that [the organ] is the cause for the perception of sound, he says in response: "Like its production, [the perception] occurs by virtue of what assists it;
if it is by virtue of what assists it that there is production, then let it be simply an effect (kārya) by virtue of what assists it. For this very reason...
There is a dependence upon the impact of the location; for this very reason, there is the cessation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) following the previous momentum.
That which was previous is [the experience of one's own location]...
[ga].
2. Then, [variant] *ga*.
3. Added. *api*. *ga*. 4. Added. *na hi*. *ka*.
5. By virtue of that assistance.
Ga. [p.
314] The momentum of the winds, which follows that [sound], ceases; or rather, it is the momentum of the *saṃskāras*. Those by which the auditory organ is refined are the *saṃskāras*.

This is the intended meaning: the air that is impelled by a powerful impact acquires a momentum (*vega*) that persists for a long time; from this momentum, known as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), subsequent actions arise within the airs; and when the momentum persists for a long time, the air moves further and further away; however, upon the destruction of that momentum, [the movement of] the airs...

Cessation is characterized by the cutting off of motion. Therefore, conjunctions and disjunctions, by producing an awakening of power corresponding to the self, cause one to perceive an object as if it were divided [into parts] and as if it were situated in another location.
The commentary, “Granted, the regions themselves may be different,” has been restated. [The author] objects:
for what purpose is this presentation made?
For here in the Bhāṣya, it is introduced: "If there is uniformity [of the word], even when there is a difference of location, let it be that only the locations are different, not the word.
And for what purpose is this introduction?

[Objection: But surely this is its purpose: that even when there is a difference in location, the word-sound does not differ. [Reply: It is said—this cannot be its purpose, because a word-sound has no difference of location; every word-sound is perceived as residing precisely in the auditory organ, and not as residing in the location of the manifestor, because the auditory organ functions through direct contact (*prāpyakāritva*). Now, if [it is argued that it resides] in the location of the manifestor...
The word is perceived [only] in this way; that is untenable, because it would entail the position that sound is produced by refinement (*saṃskāra*).
For when there is the perception of sound in the location of its manifestor, the reason for that is precisely this: that the sound has been manifested there.
Indeed, on the view that the auditory organ is manifested, the auditory organ would perceive only the sound inherent within itself. It is not so.
1. Omitted. iti. ga. 2. Omitted. deśa-. ga. [p. 315]
And it should not be said: "Let there be a refinement of the word.

Why? For it is precisely because of that [conjunction and disjunction] that the refinement of the word is obtained and becomes logical; provided that the auditory organ [is affected by] conjunction and disjunction.
It would have to come to the location [of the object].

For only by going to the location of the conjunction does the ear’s functioning as one that reaches its object (*prāpyakāritā*) become possible in that view, and not otherwise. And this is not the case.
The movement of the auditory organ [is not possible], because it has already been refuted in the Bhāṣya itself:
"For the ear-cavity, located in that place, is perceived by direct perception."

Thus it has been said. Therefore, this presentation is purposeless. He provides the resolution: precisely because there is no spatial distinction from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), for that very reason [it is said] "at will" (*kāmam*).
Thus it has been said;
this is for the purpose of demonstrating a position accepted for the sake of argument, even from the perspective of those who hold that there are other sentient beings.
Although sound is perceived in different substances, nevertheless there is no difference [between them],
because of the cognition of their identity— this is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya when he says, "Granted, they may be merely locations."

In this regard, someone objects: "But surely, in the prima facie argument it was stated that a single person is perceived in many places; here, however, many persons are perceived in many places within the sun. Therefore, the example of the sun is not analogous. He replies: "This is the prattle of a fool."

Since the objection regarding the perception of a single object in multiple locations has already been raised and refuted— whether by one person or by many persons— this distinction is not intended to be significant in any way; for how can there be the perception of a single thing in many places?
This was challenged; and since that has been supported by the observation of the sun, nothing is untenable.
1. Because. (ga) 2. Here he raises an objection. (ga) 3. Added. (paricoditā. ga)
4. One [is established] by means of one. Ga.
“A different word is not a modification.”
Thus the Sūtra is recited; here, however, no relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) is taught in the rule "iko yaṇ aci."

[If one were to argue] that this would contradict the instruction of Pāṇini, [the author] says in response to the question "Why is the relationship of original form and modification (*prakṛti-vikārabhāva*) not taught?"— for in common worldly usage, those desiring to employ the phoneme *ya* do not substitute the phoneme *i*.
Nevertheless, he asks "What [follows]? and says:
"And there are instructions regarding that which is established in the world.
That is, the instruction in the Sūtra concerns only that object which is already established in common worldly usage.
This is not an instruction (*upadeśa*). Since this is so, therefore this meaning is prescriptive (*ādeśika*):
when *aci* follows, the letter *ya* should be employed in place of the vowel *i* whenever it occurs; thus, by virtue of Pāṇini’s statement.
The relationship of material cause and modification is not perceived; moreover, similarity is an inconclusive indicator for the existence of such a causal relationship.
Furthermore, the traditional teaching contradicts [this view]. Ga.
2. There is a substitution. Ga.

317] It has been stated in the Bhāṣya that because the relationship of cause and effect (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva) is not observed between *dadhi-piṭaka* and *kunda-piṭaka*, [the rule does not apply]. Therefore—
The status of being a distinct word is established;
it is the letter *y* [that is the substitute], and not that the letter *y* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the vowel *i*.
The sūtra "nādavṛddhiḥ parā" has been recited; it is identical [to the previous one] in its avoidance of differentiation.

The greatness of the phonemes arises from the increase of the sound (*nāda*). He demonstrates this very point: just as in that case, when the distinction [between the phoneme and the sound] is set aside, distinct sounds cause the word to be perceived as if it were distinct; so too here, when they are accumulated, they cause it to be perceived as if it were accumulated and great; and when they abide in their divisions—that is, when they abide with their constituent parts—[they cause it to be perceived accordingly].

That is to say, they possess parts (*sāvayava*); that is, they appear as if divided or as if possessing parts. Consequently, an illusion arises as if they were large or as if they possessed constituent parts.
Herein lies the truth: there are many winds.

Impelled by the same place of articulation (*sthāna*) and the same organ of production (*karaṇa*), and being mutually independent, they reach the entire circumference of the ear-cavity simultaneously; thus, presenting the sound as continuous within the very region of the auditory faculty,
they represent it as a single, large sound, just as trees perceived without intervals appear as one.
1. It arises. Ga. [p.
318] thinks that there is a large whole (*avayavin*). But how is it so? To this he says: "In accordance with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)."
It has been stated that this is the awakening of the capacity (*śakti*).

It has been stated that the awakening of the capacity residing in the auditory organ occurs due to the sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions with air; therefore, by following that [sequence], an error arises. Consequently, this—
Even my [position] holds that this error is based precisely on the non-apprehension of the distinction between mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).
For one who knows the distinction between the impressions understands,
by virtue of that, "many cognitions of sound have arisen simultaneously, and not just one single great sound."
One conceives that "it is perceived"; therefore, this is an error belonging to one who is ignorant of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). He concludes:
"Therefore, since perception accompanied by recognition is established, the previously stated reason for non-eternality is rendered inconclusive."
It has arisen.

Here, by the term "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*), there is a property of cognition consisting in the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) from a prior experience, [expressed as] "this is that very same thing."
Thus, it has been stated that [the means of knowledge] consists in the apprehension of the object, not in cognition itself.
1. Omitted. *anurodha*. ga. 2. *udbodhaka*. ga. 3. *anityatvajñānam*. ga.
[Page 318] Now, it is stated that perception accompanied by recognition has sound as its object;
even in the case of sound as an object—

It is said that perception exists along with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). The sūtra, "But [the self] must be eternal, because seeing is for the sake of another," is recited; [the opponent] objects: "Because seeing is for the sake of another"—of what is this the reason?

The answer: [It is] with respect to the permanence of sound (*śabdanityatā*). The objector says: But surely this property characterized by being for the sake of another (*parārthatva*) is not a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*); for it is the substratum (*dharmin*) whose property one wishes to prove that is denoted by the word "subject" (*pakṣa*). And here, since the property characterized by the permanence of sound is what is intended to be proven, sound is the subject. Yet, sound does not possess the quality of being for the sake of another.
[The opponent asks: "Of what [is it a property]? Of the subject (*dharmin*)? No; rather, of the perception (*darśana*). Nevertheless, why is that? He says:
"The Naiyāyikas maintain that this, being a non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*), lacks the status of a logical reason (*hetu*).
The experts in Nyāya hold this view. The respondent says:
For they have not heard the treatise;

those who think in this way have not studied the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra. To the question "How then is the meaning of the treatise [to be understood]?", he says: here, perception itself is presented for the sake of another.

In this context, the state of being for the sake of another (*parārthatā*) is presented as a qualification of perception (*darśana*). Since there is no perception whatsoever that is devoid of an object, sound (*śabda*) is presented here as its object;
the meaning is that sound, by virtue of being the object, is connected to the perception for the sake of another. From that—
What is it? The answer is: the meaning is that this which is about to be stated arises from that. The reason is its connection with the perception of the object for another.
Thus it is. This is what is meant: "one whose vision is for the sake of another.
He asks [the opponent] right then: "What of him?"
The answer is: permanence. He asks again: Of what, and how?

The reply: We say that it is like every [instance] of smoke and so forth. Therefore, this proof (*sādhana*) should be formulated as follows: "Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "eternal" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Because of its connection with being perceived for the sake of another (*parārthadarśanasambandhitvāt*), whatever is connected with being perceived for the sake of another is eternal, just like smoke and so forth.
Here, he anticipates the objection that the reason is unestablished: "But surely the observation of smoke and so forth is also for the sake of one's own comprehension.
This is the doubt of one who is mistaken, thinking that its being for the sake of others is unestablished. He refutes this: "Let it be for the sake of one's own comprehension."

There is also the purpose of enabling others to understand [the truth]; therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddhi*). But surely, in the Mīmāṃsaka view, there is no such thing as being for the sake of another (*parārthatā*); to this he replies: "And this is not to be rejected, because it is not contradictory.
It is not...

For if the fact that smoke and the like are for the sake of another is accepted, nothing is contradicted; since this being for the sake of another exists in the case of sound as well, if it also occurs in the case of smoke and so forth, what harm is there?

But surely, if permanence (*nityatva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), smoke and the like cannot serve as examples, because they are impermanent? To this, he says: "When it is accepted..."—here he raises an objection. [Page 321] *ga* edition.
The term "eternal" (nitya) denotes the state of persisting through a period of time—that is, persisting beyond the moment of its utterance; it does not denote existence without a cause.
For by its own inherent power, the word "eternal" signifies that which exists without a cause.

"That which exists and is without cause is eternal" is a worldly convention, as in the case of space, the self, and so forth. As the Blessed One Kāśyapa said: "That which exists and is without cause is eternal."
Thus, this is not expressed by the word "eternal" (nitya) in its primary sense;

rather, it refers only to the state of persisting through another time by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Here, an objection is raised: "But surely sound is held to be existent and without cause."

The sense is: why is that very eternality which is established by scripture (*śrauta*) not expressed by the word "eternal" (*nitya*)? He replies: "Certainly it is accepted; however, that [eternality] is established for the vision merely by its being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*)."

For when it is established that the utterance of a word has the purpose of communicating to another because the word persists for a period of time—and not because the word is produced by that utterance—it is proven in this way and need not be established through further effort.
Here, an objection is raised: "If it is indeed accepted that the word is without cause, why [is this so]?"

In that case, it might be argued that even when an eternal word is uttered with effort, what is being established is merely its persistence over time; thus, a distinction is stated [by the opponent]: "Let only eternity itself be established, not persistence over time. He refutes this:
"How indeed could even non-eternal things like smoke serve as examples?"
For if eternal existence itself were to be proven, then things such as smoke could not serve as examples, because they would lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*);

for individual instances of smoke and the like are pervaded by the connection with fire through their general limiting condition (*upādhi*), and thus [they are connected] only to individual instances of fire.

They cause [the object] to be understood. Furthermore, it is not that individual instances of smoke and so forth lack a cause for their existence; rather, they possess a duration extending over a period of time.
Therefore, for the sake of obtaining a valid example, only the state of persisting over a period of time is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Another objects:
"But does this word also not result in being non-eternal (*anitya*), since it is observed in well-known cases such as smoke?"
For in whatever manner a property is observed in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it must exist in that very same manner in the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*);
therefore, by that logic, sound would follow as being impermanent, just like smoke. He refutes this: "Therefore—" [p. 322]
Thus, it is merely the state of persisting for a period of time that is stated as the probandum.
Precisely because impermanence is observed in the example, it is for this very reason that merely the state of persisting for a period of time is stated as the probandum.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of any illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [Objection: Granted that there may be persistence over a period of time, yet its eternality (*nityatā*) would not follow from that alone; to this he says: "And by virtue of persisting over a period of time, the fact that sound is existent and without cause is established."

Therefore, impermanence does not follow as a consequence. To the question, "In that case, how is the state of being existent and causeless established? he says: For it is perception itself that has been suspected by others to be its cause.

Indeed, it was the very act of utterance that was suspected to be the cause [of the cognition of the word]; and since its persistence until another time has been established, that utterance—being for the sake of another, meaning for the purpose of another's comprehension—has ceased to be a cause with respect to the word, but is rather merely a manifestor. Consequently, it is established that even at the first hearing, it is likewise merely a manifestor.

The state of being without a cause. He concludes: "Therefore, since smoke and the like, which are merely connected to the perception of something for another's sake, serve as examples, it is established that sound also lacks the nature of being a cause. Here, he raises an objection: "But surely, the fact that perception is for the sake of another is established by taking its non-difference from its corresponding material cause."

The meaning of this is as follows: if a word perishes immediately upon being uttered, its utterance for the sake of another is not possible, because a word that has been conventionally designated does not exist at the time of usage, and a word that has not been conventionally designated cannot convey meaning. However, when [the word] is conventionally designated...

Even when the sound has perished, another sound arises that is similar to it; those who are deluded by this similarity, taking it as non-different, comprehend the meaning—this is logically consistent. In that case, even the observation of that [sound] would have a purpose for others.
The fact that "it is established" does not, by necessity, allow one to infer its persistence over a period of time. He refutes this:
it is true that it is established; however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being of such a nature. Of this cognition...

First of all, there is no sublating cognition regarding this [Self] as being merely apparent, such as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; nor is there an inferential one, as has been stated in the passage, "The non-perception of the existent beyond [the body].
Therefore, this cognition of it is a delusion.
Thus, it cannot be said [that there is no such thing]. He states the absence of any sublation regarding the phenomenal appearance:
for no living being whatsoever until the end of *saṃsāra*, when pronouncing something similar to what was previously uttered, [there arises the cognition] "this is similar to that."

Thus, the arising of cognition in a listener is observed. By this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—namely, "If it is argued that for someone there will be an artificial relationship [between word and meaning], that has already been stated"—is explained. And by the word "stated" (*ukta*) in the *bhāṣya*, [it refers to] "for whom..."
And it has been stated: "Where the instrument [of cognition] is defective and where there is the conviction that 'this is false,' that alone is an incorrect cognition, and no other.
Therefore, the cognition of an object does not arise through the delusion of non-difference between the word and its artificial connection.
This is what has been stated: because this cognition is non-erroneous, for that very reason they apprehend it without distortion.
For otherwise, if it were erroneous, [the cognition] of the word "hall" would be like [the cognition] of the word "garland."
There would be a misconception arising from a [false] cognition,

just as there is a misconception regarding the object of the word-concept "mālā" (garland) when it concerns the meaning of the word "śālā" (house); that is, from a true cognition whose object is the word "śālā," by which one [perceives] the word "śālā"—
Having apprehended the object "garland" through the cognition of the word "mālā," one subsequently encounters the object "house" upon hearing the word "śālā."

When [the nature of things] is known in its true reality (*tattvataḥ*), the notion of a "garland" ceases; yet here, no such subversion occurs. Therefore, this is not an error (*bhrānti*). But surely, even when there is similarity between two words, once they are understood, no subversion of the cognition of the object is observed—just as, for example, from the word *gāvī*, which is similar to the word *go*, the cognition of the object "cow" arises.

It does not undergo subversion; the meaning is that it should be the same here as well. He refutes this: "But subversion is not observed for those who grasp only that [single instance], nor for those who grasp similarity.
The meaning of this is: those who [use] the word *gāvī* as the only one...
Those who consider [the word] to be the denoter employ it and understand both the word and the object; for them, there is no error.
However, for those who are deluded by the similarity to the word "cow," error certainly occurs. But for those who know the reality, there is simply no arising [of such error].

Regarding words such as *gāvī* and so forth, he asks: "What is meant by 'those who know the truth'? Those who know the truth are those who understand that *gāvī* and other such forms are corruptions (*apabhraṃśa*) of the word *go*. For them, no cognition of the meaning arises even from words like *gāvī*; rather, they comprehend the meaning solely from the word *go*. Thus it has been stated.
By the commentators.
The meaning of this is as follows: all these corrupt forms (apabhraṃśas) have a beginning; therefore, by someone... [added]. ga.
2. Identity. ka.
Therein. ga. [p. 325]

An elder, desiring to utter the word "cow" (go), by mistake uttered "gāvī"; thereupon another elder, having understood his intention through the force of the context and other factors, [perceived that] "he, desiring to utter the word 'cow,' has uttered 'gāvī'."

Thus, one understands the meaning of "cow" from the word *go* alone when it is intended to be uttered, and not from the word *gāvī*. Furthermore, since the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, it is impossible to conceive of any initial word for anything, from which the establishment of linguistic usage could proceed through the adoption of similar forms.

If saṃsāra had a beginning, then it would have to be assumed that the first word possesses meaning by virtue of convention, and that the comprehension of meaning from subsequent words occurs due to their similarity to that first one;
but this is not the case. Therefore, this hypothesis as well is untenable—on account of the similarity to a meaningful [word].
"Thus, there is the comprehension of the object. Therefore, it is established that this worldly transaction is rooted in perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
By observing such transactions, it has been proven that recognition indeed exists for people in the world.

On this point, some raise an objection: that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there is no cause for its arising; for it cannot be produced by the sense faculty alone, since the latter lacks the capacity to take as its object a thing previously experienced. Nor can it be produced by the latent impression (*bhāvanā*) formed by the previous experience—
This [cognition] cannot be produced by the faculty of memory (*smṛtīndriya*), because mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has no operation regarding a present object;

for it is only that which was previously made an object of experience that is remembered through the force of cultivation, and not something entirely new that is apprehended. This is incorrect, for all experience has been established...

The person (*puruṣa*), who is the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) and the sole experiencer of objects, is capable of connecting the preceding and the succeeding when his instruments are operative; he is one whose latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) from previously awakened experiences persist, and thus [perceives] by means of a single [cognition], "This is that."
Through a cognition that carries the reflection of both recollection and perception, one grasps an object that persists over time.

Pure mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause of recollection, while the sense organ alone is the cause of mere perception; however, because they act as mutual auxiliaries, they produce a distinct effect, which is not untenable. As it has been said:
“Recognition of an object is based on this [latent impression].
To this, it must be said here: since manifestation is momentary, how can there be recognition of a sound? For when an object has been perceived, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—
1. Regarding the term "similarity" (sādṛśya), [the text reads] "artha-" [in manuscript *ga*].
2. Regarding "perceptual cognition" (pratyakṣajñāna) [in manuscript *ga*].
3. By way of being merely a form (*ākāramātratayā*). [In manuscript *ga*].

When there is awakening, there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). However, a sound that has not been perceived cannot be recognized by one whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have awakened, because the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) does not persist for that duration of time. It is replied: it is not the grasping of the object...

The awakening of a single latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone is not [the cause], because the causes for its awakening are of various kinds; thus, it is entirely consistent that a latent impression awakened by another cause recognizes the word at the very moment of the first contact.
Here, he raises an objection: "One thing has been established, while something else has been concluded."
Therefore, the opening and the conclusion are mutually contradictory. He states this very point: "The persistence [of the self] over time has been established;
however, it is eternal."
By speaking thus, he has brought forward a perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). One thing was introduced, yet another has arrived;
it is just as when one arrow is shot and another falls upon it—this is exactly like that. He states the resolution:
This very thing is that;
what was introduced is precisely what has been concluded, nothing else. Why? Because it is through recognition alone that persistence over time is established.

This is the intention: there is no contradiction, because it is precisely that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which was established for the sake of proving subsistence over a period of time that has been summarized here.
If subsistence over a period of time is established by recognition alone, why then is it [stated] for the sake of others (*parārtha*)?
Was it stated that the reason is its connection with seeing?

The answer is: precisely because its persistence over a period of time is established by recognition alone, for that very reason it was stated that the reason is its connection with seeing for the sake of another.
For, when the distinctness of each utterance regarding a word has been refuted by means of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the act of perception serves a purpose beyond itself;
otherwise, the utterance would have as its sole purpose the production of the sound. [Objection: But surely there is the observation of non-different meaning—
1. Omitted. *sidhyati*. Ga. 2. *pratyakṣayā*. Ga. 3. Omitted. *darśanasya*. Ga.
[Page 327] This negation of the relation of priority and posteriority in words at each utterance is based on their non-difference, not on recognition;
regarding this, he says: for recognition itself is said to be the perception of an identical object, and nothing else.
Now, one might object: "Granted that recognition has sound as its object, even so, how can it be established on the basis of that [recognition] that perception is for the sake of another?
To this, he replies: because the nature [of the object] is already established by other perceptions, and because recognition is preceded by those [perceptions].
Furthermore, a single effort is not capable of accomplishing both its own purpose and the purpose of another.

The meaning of this is as follows: first, at the initial utterance, the very nature of the word is established by that first utterance itself, according to a different philosophical view [of perception].
It must be said that [the sound] is produced; and based on that [production], there is recognition upon the second utterance.

Since, when such recognition exists, the re-production of a sound-form that has already been produced is impossible, effort serves the purpose of another by way of manifesting the sound. And thus, effort is determined to have a purpose beyond itself.

The word's own meaning cannot be the purpose of its utterance upon the first hearing; rather, like the second hearing, it serves merely as a manifestor. Thus, by means of recognition itself, it is established that the act of utterance is for the sake of another.

"Because [the word] applies simultaneously everywhere. By this, he demonstrates that the word's status as the cause for the comprehension of meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
since the word is employed even with respect to another individual when the class-form (*ākṛti*) is present.
1. *parāparatābhāva*. (ga) 2. Omitted. (*uccāraṇe*—second [time]). (ga) 3. Omitted. (*api*). (ga)
Furthermore, since a word is not applied to that which lacks the form [of the object] when the form is excluded, it is understood that the word denotes the form;
therefore, the fact that a word is the cause for the comprehension of meaning is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). What follows from this being so?

The reply: persistence over a period of time is established; for indeed, there can be no ascertainment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) for that which does not persist over a period of time. Therefore, persistence over a period of time is established.
Even so—
Why is this said? It has been stated that persistence over time is apprehended by perception accompanied by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Therefore, by this method as well, it is established that there exists perception accompanied by recognition regarding sound. How so?
Furthermore, why is its status as a cause for the comprehension of meaning understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
when it could simply be [established] by pointing with a finger,
as in: "This is a cow"?
If this is asked, the answer is: because the generic form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word.
Even if that were so, what follows? He says: moreover, the status of the generic form as the meaning of a word is not something to be understood from a single instance of usage.
Why? Because those things which are dependent on a substance are not perceived independently.
For indeed, those which are dependent on a substance—those [are not perceived independently].
1. Why is this said here?
Ga. 2. Omitted. Of this. Ga. [p. 329]

[Individuals] are perceived independently, like whiteness and other qualities; whereas the form (ākṛti) is dependent upon a substance. Furthermore, because those things not perceived independently are unfit for separate designation, the form cannot be designated as "the denotation of this word. Therefore, the status of the form as the meaning of a word is to be understood solely through linguistic usage.
It is not to be understood through verbal instruction alone;

rather, its status as denoting a form (*ākṛti*) is understood from the linguistic usage of elders. And since linguistic usage arises from positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), one determines its persistence over time by virtue of its capacity for such concomitance, through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
And since there is no certainty that [a thing] persists through a period of time without [the continuity of cognition], recognition is established.
By this sūtra, "Because of the absence of number," that very same perception accompanied by recognition is presented once again.

To the question, "For what purpose, then, is this restated? he replies: "It is for the purpose of showing the accumulation of reasons. It has been restated. Here, an objection is raised: "But in the case of an accumulation, what further additional point is established?"

For that which is to be proven must be established by a reason (*hetu*); and since it is established by even a single reason, there is no further purpose [in citing more], because reasons are independent of other reasons in the establishment of their own object. For if—as much as... mutual...

If they were to establish the probandum only by depending [on other factors], then there would be a purpose for the presentation of another reason (*hetvantara*); but this is not the case. The reply: "Indeed, no one [does so]. [The opponent] asks: "Then it is useless."
[Page 330] Presentation of the accumulation.
He refutes [the objection]: "And it is not purposeless."

He shows the purpose: when there is an accumulation—that is, a multiplicity—of reasons, there arises firmness [of conviction] even for those whose intellects are to be induced (*āhāryadhiyah*), that is, even for those whose intellects require refinement (*saṃskāryadhiyah*).
This effort is for the sake of favoring persons of inducible intellect, not for those whose intellects are already perfected; therefore, it is for those of dull intellect (*mandabuddhi*).
There is a purpose for this awakening. Now, he raises an objection: "But how is this [suffix] *kṛtvasuc* a cause for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)?
The answer: "Because it is seen in the repetition of a single [object]."

Therefore, by the application of the suffix *kṛtvasuc* in the expression “the word ‘cow’ has been uttered eight times,” the repetition of a single word is understood; this is the cognition of oneness.

Let it be that the term *pratyabhijñā* involves the use of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, as it is the cause of recognition. Again, the objector says: "True, [it applies] to the repetition of one thing; however, that [repetition] belongs to an action.
It is when there is a repetition of a single [action] that [the suffix is used], according to the rule: ‘[The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is used] in counting the repetition of an action.’"
Such is the instruction. This is the aphorism of the venerable Pāṇini: "And a word is not an action; rather, it must be either a substance or a quality."

This was stated with a lack of conviction; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, this is indeed a quality (*guṇa*), because otherwise its perception would be impossible. For if sound were a substance (*dravya*) while being eternal, then its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) would have to be admitted, just like space (*ākāśa*); otherwise, it could not be perceived everywhere. And if it were all-pervasive, then—just as in the case of space—[it would follow that...]
Because the ear is an external sense organ, it must be admitted that there is a contact with its object, since external senses function by reaching their objects.

However, no conjunction can exist between two all-pervading substances, because the causes of conjunction are absent; for conjunction arises from the action of one of the two, from the action of both, or from a prior conjunction. But this is not possible for two things that are both omnipresent.
Action exists; yet, even a conjunction produced by conjunction is not possible for partless entities, nor is inherence (samavāya) tenable,
because there is no mutual inherence between two substances that lack the relationship of the originated and the originator, as expressed in the notion "here."

Thus, because cognition does not arise [from it], it is logical that sound, being a quality (*guṇa*), is perceived by the auditory organ, since it inheres (*samaveta*) in the auditory faculty which is of the nature of space (*ākāśa*).

Nor should it be argued that the ear-cavity is composed of earth (*pārthivī*) [and thus cannot perceive sound]. This is because [the auditory faculty] is characterized by its conjunction [with space].
"One perceives sound through contact"—if this were so, it would follow that the auditory organ, being composed of earth, would perceive odor.

Enough, then, with this excessive effort in following other systems. He concludes: "Thus, this enumeration of the repetition of one thing related to an action being predicated of another word follows the maxim of describing a maternal uncle's wealth [to someone else]."
He carries on; he composes himself—here it is said: you are ignorant of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.
To the objection, "But what is the use of knowing the intrinsic nature of things? he replies: for injunctions (*ādeśa*) depend upon the intrinsic nature of things.
Therefore, having understood the intrinsic nature of things, their meaning should be described. To the question "Even so, why?", he says: "And action is cognizable through inference."
This has been demonstrated regarding inference. What follows from this? The answer is:
it has already been stated that the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of that which is accessible through inference is not perceived.

Because that which is observed through general correlation apprehends only "something" [in an indeterminate form], and because action (karman) has an unperceived nature, by what means could its recurrence be established?

Can it be understood? Therefore, repetition of the action is not directly evident. But surely, by the very same means of knowledge by which the existence of the object is apprehended, its repetition will also be apprehended. He himself says: "From the effect."
1. From the foot [of the commentary]. (ga) 2. Omitted. By means of proximity. (ka) 3. Omitted. By that... (anu---tena). (ga)
4. This [existence] is grasped by that;
its existence is understood; let its recurrence also proceed from that very same source.
He refutes this: "Not so;
repetition can be understood from the repetition of the effect, not from the effect itself.
For, by means of the effect, the nature—"

This is the understanding of the measure; therefore, the repetition of the action is to be understood only as the repetition of the effect. And the repetition of an effect as an effect is difficult to achieve.
Furthermore, because it is an effect, there is no repetition of the effect; for that which remains established cannot possess the nature of an effect.
Because it is not logically possible; in that case, there would simply be another effect.

For an effect that is being repeated must indeed be another effect, and not that very same one, because of the difference between what has already been produced and what is currently being produced. Therefore, in the view that [the world] is an effect, it is impossible for it to be produced again and again.

[This is] the position. Furthermore, this counting of the repetition of an action is possible only with respect to that which is to be made known. Now, someone might think that this contradicts the established doctrine;
to him he says: "And it has been stated that the word is what is to be made known by the utterance."
Therefore, from the use of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, what is understood here of the word is its state of being employed again and again;

not its state of being produced. Thus, although the action (*karman*) is by nature transitory, repetition (*āvṛtti*) is spoken of because of the unity of that which is to be made known, and not because of [the action] itself, since the action has the nature of an effect (*kārya*). Nevertheless, as to how it is that there is no repetition by way of its own nature, he says:
The wise, the learned, hold that there is no performing of what has already been performed.

Having accepted a single action as that which is to be cognized by a single [mental] apprehension (*ekajñāpyāvamarśena*), one must resort to the repetition of that action. This, then, is... (Note: The ellipsis indicates a fragmentary text; the translation reflects the available portions.)
1. "Only because of repetition" (āvṛtter eva).
Ga. 2. Omitted. "Of that which has been done"—this is the meaning. Ga. [p. 333]
He summarizes: "Therefore, this suffix *kṛtvasuc* applies precisely to such an object;
that is to say, it relies upon the repetition of the action based on the unity of the effect. Now, one might ask: even so, how is the suffix *kṛtvasuc* the cause [of this]? To this he says:

And it has been stated that the identity of the effect [is established] through recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Therefore, it is logical to present the sense of the suffix *kṛtvasuc* as the reason for its apprehension;
that is to say, in the case of recognition. Those who are deluded by similarity—
"He" is what they will say.
The commentary has been restated. He raises an objection: "What is this?"
"It has been presented.
He replies: "This very thing has been presented;
nothing here is concealed."
"It exists," [the opponent] says. The objector replies: "We do not say that it was not presented; however, we do not understand what has been refuted by this regarding recognition.
He provides the resolution: "This is what is refuted by this."
The meaning is that the capacity of the cognition "that" to establish non-difference has been refuted; for this [cognition] is based on the non-apprehension of difference.
The cognition "that" [arises] with respect to a sound produced at the present moment; even though it is distinct from what was produced previously, it does not apprehend its difference [from that].
Thus: "that."

Thus this designation and this worldly transaction proceed; moreover, the non-apprehension of difference is observed in the case of goats and sheep, as well as in the case of flames and the like, due to extreme similarity. But how, through the non-apprehension of difference, can there be the notion "that [is the same]"?
Regarding the term "designation," he says: "And if difference is not apprehended, otherness cannot be designated; [otherwise] there would be no distinction. (Pūrva-ga) 1.1.15.
And if there is no designation of otherness, what else remains [to be designated] other than the designation "that very thing"?
Therefore, it is the non-apprehension of distinction alone that is at fault here in this delusion; by its power alone, those of dull intellect engage in erroneous practical behavior,
like those devoid of discernment regarding gems, pearls, and the like,
when they have not undergone the examination of jewels.
For those who are weary from their labors, therefore, let resort be taken to solitude;
for "lack of discernment is the abode of supreme calamities."
For those who have become agitated by calamities, solitude alone is the supreme refuge. He confirms this:
"It is true, just as you have said."
The conventional usage of error is based solely on non-discrimination; however,

in this case, there is no cause for the non-apprehension of discrimination— as there is in the case of [the perception of] flames and the like— hence [it is said] "because it is not possible" (*asthānāt*).

This is explained in detail in the Sūtra. It is stated that "because there is no basis" (*asthānāt*), whereas there exists a cause for the certain non-perception of the distinction between flames and so forth, such a cause does not exist here.
In this sūtra, because the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) extends up to its refutation,
[the reason] "because of non-abiding" (asthānāt) is used together with [the sūtra passage]: "The non-perception of that which exists is due to subtlety" (sataḥ paramadarśanam).
Since this constitutes a single sūtra, [the reason] "because of non-abiding" (asthānāt) has already been stated in the passage: "The non-perception of that which exists subsequently."
To this he says: "It has been stated here. It might be argued: "But the intellect and the action are also recognized through recognition; therefore, they too would follow as being eternal."
The commentary has been restated. He objects: "What is this fallacy of the *kūśmāṇḍa*?
Even by the subsequent [passage], the very nature of the *kūśmāṇḍa* is demonstrated: "Now, if it is perceived, it is eternal... [p. 335]
Thus [he says].
By this, he states the reason for this very point: for recognition [serves as proof] of persistence over a period of time.
The reason has been stated.
If that recognition exists with respect to action as well, then let there be persistence over time for action too; what is the point of this objection—that action also persists over time?
For when an action persists over a period of time, it does not follow that the word [denoting it] must also persist over that same period of time.
Now, if the intention is that this would result in the abandonment of one's own tenet,
that is a criticism directed at the subject of the action.

He refutes this: "It is true that we have accepted the impermanence of action—that is, its non-existence at another time—and we have also accepted its inferential nature. Furthermore, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding an object that is merely inferential, because its specific form (*svarūpa*) is not apprehended.
For recognition occurs only in that case where its specific form, its own particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is apprehended; it does not occur otherwise."
Furthermore, there is no apprehension of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of things that are eternally inferable; and action (*karma*) is eternally inferable.

Therefore, this objection is irrelevant, because it lacks the reason for persisting through another period of time as characterized by recognition—that is, if persistence through another period of time were established by recognition, then action too would have persistence through another period of time established by recognition.
[The opponent objects: "He obtains [it]. Now, if this criticism is directed at one who does not even know that action is to be inferred, then he says in response:
"If there is knowledge of our accepted position, let it be in its entirety; why this 'half-old-woman' approach?
If it is understood that the Mīmāṃsaka position is that "action does not persist through another time," then it follows that "it is not recognized [by means of recognition]."

The meaning is that this is also understood. Furthermore, the subsequent statement, "For these are not perceived," is entirely irrelevant; for what ought to be refuted is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and not its perceptibility. If it is argued that recognition itself is refuted by the refutation of its perceptibility, that is not so, because [recognition occurs] even in the case of what is imperceptible.
Because recognition is possible. Furthermore, the claim that "if it were perceptible, it would necessarily be eternal" is untenable;
for even in the case of something perceptible, if recognition does not arise, there is no certainty regarding its persistence over time. It is replied:
If, on the grounds of having a single effect, one expresses the repetition of an action by means of the suffix *kṛtvasuc*, then even the difference in causes is not established;
that is, the difference in the action which serves as the cause is neither established nor perceived. Why?
For there is no cognition of repetition when there is a cognition of difference.
Therefore, you who desire the cognition of repetition must admit that even the action is not cognized as being manifold. And because its unity is being cognized—

Furthermore, because the object being traversed is a single entity, the multiplicity of cognitions is necessarily perceived; consequently, no difference between cognition and action is perceived. This non-perception of difference constitutes recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Therefore, if by means of recognition the persistence of sound over time is established, then it would follow that cognition and action likewise persist; yet this is not the case.

The objection is that the position of the permanence of sound is untenable because it contradicts your own admission that [sound] is produced by you. This has been stated: "For those two—cognition and action—are also recognized [as the same]; they too would consequently be permanent."

By this, the objection (*codyabhāṣya*) has first been refuted; now, providing a refutation of the subsequent commentary (*uttarabhāṣya*) as well, he says: "They might be eternal, if they were perceptible.
The meaning of this is as follows:

For only that which is directly perceived is recognized, and nothing else; neither cognition nor action are directly perceived, therefore they are not recognized. And if they are not recognized, how could there be [recognition of] a different time?

Is it permanent for you? Furthermore, why is there no recognition because of its imperceptibility? To this he says: "For there is no recognition of an object that is imperceptible, because its own nature is not grasped. But surely, recognition consists in the non-apprehension of difference?
And it has been stated that this [recognition] exists even in the case of cognition and action, because those things which are inferable are known through their effects;
furthermore, when the essential nature is not perceived, difference is not perceived; therefore, since recognition is possible even though they are inferable, [it persists] across different times.
[The objection] that [recognition] would result in the non-existence of persistence is raised; [the author] refutes it: "True, if the non-apprehension of difference were recognition;
but the apprehension of that [identity] is recognition.
And that does not exist in the case of an action. Why? Because the effect..."
It produces the cognition merely that "a cause exists," but not that "it is this" or "it is something else.
Recognition, however, is "this is that very same thing."
Thus it is well known in the world:
for as much as is necessary so that an effect is not accomplished, only that much does one conceive as the effect; it does not, however, touch upon whether that [cause] is real or unreal.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), however, is the apprehension of an object as "this is that very same thing" by virtue of its having been previously experienced. Therefore, it has been established in the *Bhāṣya* that there is no recognition of cognition or action, since these two are only accessible through their effects: "For these two... [are not so perceived].
Regarding the phrase "in perception": now, [the meaning is] that it is indeed eternal in perception.
The meaning of this is also as follows: if [there is] recognition—
Therefore, they are known to be indeed eternal; and by the word "perception" (pratyakṣa), what is meant is recognition (*pratyabhijñāyamānatā*).
[Objection: "If it is argued that because yesterday's sound has perished, today's sound is different," [the response follows].
1. Added: yasmāt. ka. 2. -kalpate. ga.
The commentary has been restated; he objects: "What that was not stated here has been stated by the author of the commentary?
He—

Thus he says: "But surely, it was stated that when recognition exists yet there is no perception, another cause must be postulated; and such causes have been postulated as the stagnant air-currents which, by covering the ear, are the reason for the non-perception."
And that perception occurs upon their departure—this is a mere assumption.
That conjunctions and disjunctions of air are the causes for their departure—this too is an assumption. What else remains?
The meaning of this is as follows:

it should not be maintained that there is destruction even during the intermediate period of a sound that was perceived, then no longer perceived, and subsequently recognized again; for its non-perception at that time is possible due to the influence of other causes. If [the sound] were indeed complete...
If, however, non-perception were to occur when the causes for perception are present, then destruction could be postulated;
yet the complete set of causes for the perception of sound is not present, because the removal of stagnant air is also a cause for its perception.
And this [removal] is postulated on the strength of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). This is what is meant by the statement: "The non-perception of that which exists [is due to other causes]."
Thus it has been stated here.

Therefore, what else remains unrefuted that must be refuted again by the author of the Bhāṣya? He provides the answer: this remains: for that which was previously perceived but is no longer perceived is [said to be] "non-existent."
Thus, this cognition attains the status of its object:
that which, having been perceived, is no longer perceived, is precisely what is said to "not exist."

This is the object of this knowledge. The meaning is that it is precisely through the non-apprehension of what was apprehended that "it does not exist" is known and designated. To the question, "Why is it that only the non-apprehension of what was apprehended constitutes 'non-existence'? he says:
1. It has been presented.
Ga. 2. Omitted. Gocara—this very same thing. Ga. [p. 339]

For indeed, the cognition "it does not exist" does not apply to that which is absolutely unperceived. In that case, even if something has been perceived, if it does not come within the range of [the present] perception, then this "it does not exist" is simply without a basis and without an object.
Thus, knowledge is accepted [as having an object]; for if it were devoid of an object, there would be total annihilation. And this has been accepted [in the statement]:
"of the meaning 'it does not exist,' which is not in contact [with the senses]."
Thus, by this passage: therefore, non-existence,
being devoid of an object, must be described as having that very non-apprehension of what was apprehended as its object.
Therefore, since a sound is perceived [at first] and yet is not perceived again in the interim, it must be admitted that it does not exist;

and consequently, it has perished. When the sound has perished, the recognition that occurs—just as in the case of a flame or similar phenomena—is merely a form of non-apprehension of difference; it is not, in the ultimate sense, a true apprehension of that [same] object. Having thus supported the objection in the Bhāṣya, [the author proceeds].

He addresses the objection: "Ah, how indeed this is a lack of discrimination regarding non-apprehension! For just as non-apprehension whose object is absolutely unapprehendable is not desired for the production of the cognition 'it does not exist'..."
The meaning is that it does not become an object [of perception]; likewise, even regarding the object of its apprehension, the meaning is "in the case of an object being recognized.
Therefore, this is merely a non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) which occurs in the interval within the word.
Furthermore, this non-apprehension does not have non-existence as its nature; for precisely because it is not the object of that [non-existent] apprehension, it is not described as non-existence.
And thus, when people have gone out from their house and do not perceive their wife and others who were previously situated within the house, they return to the house again.
1. anupalabdhyavi—ga.
2. Added. punastadgrahaṇāt. ga. [p. 340]
Having entered [the room], when objects are being recognized, they do not understand that "it does not exist" merely because of non-perception.
But how is it understood that they do not understand "it does not exist"? To this, he says: "upon seeing it again, there is confidence..."
Because of perception;
otherwise, there would be no confidence. Therefore, what they say—that although it is recognized, it might nevertheless have perished in the interim—is refuted by non-perception.
Because even non-existence (*mātra*) has the nature of destruction; for it is observed in the world that absolute non-apprehension is what constitutes destruction.
Therefore, in this case, one must state that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) is dependent upon perception accompanied by recognition (*sapratyabhijña*).
Where even recognition does not arise, there is non-existence due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why?
Because non-existence is dependent [upon something else].
Non-existence is the absence of a means of valid cognition; thus, it depends upon that means of valid cognition.

It must be said: recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, non-existence (*abhāva*) must be stated in dependence upon it. Furthermore, because perception (*pratyakṣa*) is independent, perception does not depend upon the non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) of non-existence; for that reason—
Even though there is no perception of an interval, the determination of existence indeed occurs through direct perception in the form of recognition;
and this has been stated in the Bhāṣya in the passage beginning, "This sequence is not established. Furthermore, that which...
— 1. the absence of apprehension. Ga.

It has been stated that inference regarding the non-existence [of all things] has as its object all entities; however, even that is not possible here. That inference regarding the non-existence of all entities which was stated by the Buddhists—that too does not apply here, in the case of the word.
It does not exist. Why? Because "because its destruction is observed at the end" is the reason for that inference;
and yet, there is no destruction of sound at the end.
Therefore, this recognition is not grasped even by that inference;

for it is possible that this recognition [of identity] in the case of jars and the like might cause the inference to waver, since their destruction is observed. However, as will be shown immediately thereafter, recognition cannot be made to waver even in those cases.

We shall explain this: the Buddhist argument, "And because destruction is observed at the end," is to be formulated and refuted as follows—here, entities such as jars and the like are perceived to be subject to destruction; [and since they exist for a time before perishing, they must have arisen from causes].

Regarding these, the inquiry is as follows: do they arise from their own causes as perishable, or is their destruction produced by another cause? In this regard, the destruction of these things does not depend upon another cause; for if it were dependent on another cause, then even when that distinct entity (the destruction) were to occur, the prior state would still be perceived just as before.

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Furthermore, destruction that arises dependent upon another cause cannot be the very nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, because a difference in causes must produce a difference in effects; moreover, it is impossible for that which has already arisen and that which is currently arising to be one and the same.
Therefore, it should be understood that entities are perishable by virtue of their own causes alone. And thus, regarding destruction...
It follows that, independent of anything else, they perish immediately after their arising; therefore, the state of momentary existence is contradicted.
[p. 342] ga. 1. bādhyate.

Dharmas, as entities, obtain their own nature from their respective causes; and they initiate another moment, which is itself another moment. Thus, people who perceive a continuity of similar successions and are subject to delusion, while determining them to be a single reality, engage in conventional discourse. However, when there occurs the intervention of another cause possessing different characteristics, [the sequence is interrupted].
Therefore, they apply the conventional designation of "destruction" upon the arising of a subsequent moment that is dissimilar [to the preceding one].

For [existence] is pervaded by having a cause; in the absence of that [cause], it too would be absent. And sound is without a cause, because the exertion that is presumed is merely a manifester of sound, since [the sound] is recognized (*pratyabhijñāyamāna*) upon a second hearing.
For it is not logical that the very same exertion should be both its producer and its manifester.

He summarizes: This has been commenced; it was stated that the knowledge of word-meanings is innate (*autpattika*) according to the usage of the elders.
That knowledge of meaning which arises from words and so forth is innate.

It has been stated that [the knowledge of meaning] arises independently of human effort and without convention, through the thorough comprehension of a word’s expressive power (*vācakaśakti*) solely from the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), and thus it is produced without dependence on convention. This "usage of elders" is defined as follows: when someone communicates an object cognizable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by means of a sentence, another person understands that object.

When one elder understands an object that can be apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from the speech of another elder, and a subsequent elder understands it in turn, this is called "the linguistic usage of elders" (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Through that understanding—which occurs immediately after hearing the word—even a child comes to know: "This very object was communicated by this very word."
The meaning is that one understands the expressive power (*vācakaśakti*) residing in the word. And the comprehension of the word’s meaning occurs through the cognizer—[the process of] its arising;
thus, the child comes to know it.

The behavior of an elder (*vṛddhavartinī*) is to be inferred from its effects, such as the grasping of objects that serve that purpose; for it is observed that in one's own domain, a child’s acts of avoidance and acquisition are preceded by cognition— thus, having observed the elder’s avoidance and acquisition, the elder’s cognition is inferred.

Furthermore, relinquishment, acquisition, and so forth can only be understood when their objects have been cognized by another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), not when their objects have not been so cognized.
That which is relinquished must have as its object an entity that has been apprehended by another means of valid knowledge.

It is possible to understand that [the relationship] begins with the feet and so forth, but not one whose object has not been cognized by other means of knowledge. Consequently, [it refers to] that which is cognized by another means of knowledge—
From the rejection or acceptance of an object, comprehension is inferred; from comprehension, the capacity of the communicator [to convey it] is inferred;

and from that known capacity of the communicator, the understanding of the word’s meaning occurs. Therefore, only that object which is accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can be understood independently of human convention (*puruṣasamaya*). However, where...
Linguistic usage is preceded by the comprehension of the word; therein, its innate nature (*autpattikatva*) can be understood.

And how, without inferring the elder’s comprehension regarding that object, could he ascertain the word’s expressive power (*śakti*) with respect to that object? Without...
