The inherent nature (*autpattikatva*) of objects is difficult to comprehend; therefore, the laborious effort to establish the inherent power of words based on the linguistic usage of the elders is useless. Proponents of independent scripture (*svatantrāgamavādin*) maintain that this inherent nature is desired for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda.

The Mīmāṃsakas [reply]: Nor can that "intrinsic nature" (*autpattikatva*), which is established through the linguistic usage of elders and concerns objects cognizable by other means of knowledge, be capable of serving as the cause for the cognition of Vedic meanings that are not themselves cognizable by other means of knowledge. Why is it not capable? Because in the linguistic usage of elders, meaning is understood from a collection [of words].

Since the determination of a word's capacity occurs only for that object which has already been understood, and this aggregate [of words] such as "gām ānaya" is not a conventional unit [in the same way].

Such [expressions] are employed in the Veda; therefore, the status of being a cause is not understood [from them]. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the meaning of a sentence is understood—preceded by the meanings of the individual words—from the linguistic usage of elders alone."

The meaning of this is as follows: if the sentence-meaning were conveyed by the collection [of words] alone, then another collection [of words] would not possess the capacity to convey that meaning, because its power [to do so] would be unestablished;
however, when the words themselves convey the sentence-meaning by means of conveying the word-meanings, then...

Since those words also exist in the Veda, the meaning of a sentence can be understood as being preceded by the comprehension of the meanings of the individual words. And how is it known that words convey the meanings of individual words? The answer is: through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He demonstrates these two very methods through insertion and deletion (*āvāpa-uddhāra*): "O Devadatta, drive the cow hither; [drive] the white [cow]; [The text continues: "...[drive] the black [cow]; [drive] the cow [of someone else]; [drive] the white [thing]. By this means, one determines the specific meanings of the words. For instance, when the word *gām* ("cow") is present, the notion of a cow arises; when it is absent, that notion does not arise. Similarly, when the word *śuklām* ("white") is present, the notion of whiteness arises; when it is absent, that notion does not arise. Thus, through the presence and absence of the words, one discerns the meanings of the words. Therefore, it is established that the meaning of a sentence is understood based on the meanings of the constituent words. Consequently, since the meanings of the words are already known from the Veda, the meaning of the Vedic sentences is also understood. Thus, the Veda is indeed a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, because the Veda is eternal, its validity is self-evident (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), unlike other sources of knowledge which require corroboration. Therefore, the Veda is the supreme authority for knowing Dharma. Hence, the inquiry into Dharma must necessarily be undertaken. This concludes the first chapter. Now begins the second chapter. Therein, the author first states the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) regarding the means of knowing Dharma. What is the means of knowing Dharma? It is said: "The means of knowing Dharma is the Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Why so? Because it is the Vedic injunction alone that impels one toward activity for the sake of attaining what is beneficial and avoiding what is harmful. Other means of knowledge, such as perception, do not have the power to impel one toward such activity. Therefore, the Vedic injunction is the means of knowing Dharma. But how is it known that the Vedic injunction is the means of knowing Dharma? It is known because it is the Vedic injunction alone that prompts one to act for the attainment of heaven and the avoidance of hell. Since it is the Vedic injunction that prompts one to act, it is the means of knowing Dharma. However, some argue that even though the Vedic injunction prompts one to act, it cannot be the means of knowing Dharma, because it merely expresses an action to be performed. To this we reply: No, because the Vedic injunction possesses the capacity to express both the action to be performed and the fact that it leads to a desirable result. Just as a lamp has the capacity to illuminate both a jar and its color, so too the Vedic injunction has the capacity to express both the action to be performed and the fact that it leads to a desirable result. Therefore, the Vedic injunction is indeed the means of knowing Dharma. This concludes the first section. Now begins the second section. Therein, the author refutes the objection that the Vedic injunction cannot be the means of knowing Dharma because it lacks a basis in reality. Some say: The Vedic injunction cannot be the means of knowing Dharma, because it is devoid of a real object. For instance, the injunction "one should sacrifice a horse with its head facing east" is impossible, as a horse cannot have its head facing east while being sacrificed. Similarly, the injunction "one should sacrifice a barren cow" is impossible, as a barren cow cannot be sacrificed. Since such injunctions lack a real object, they cannot be the means of knowing Dharma. To this we reply: No, because the Vedic injunction is authoritative precisely because it is independent of human agency. Human statements may be false because they depend on human fallibility, but the Veda is not dependent on humans. Therefore, the Vedic injunction is authoritative. Furthermore, the Veda is eternal and not composed by any person. Since it is not the work of a human author, it is free from error. Thus, the Vedic injunction is the means of knowing Dharma. This concludes the second section. Now begins the third section. Therein, the author addresses the objection that the Veda is not eternal because it is perceived to have an author. Some say: The Veda is not eternal, because we perceive authors of the Vedas, such as Vyāsa and others. To this we reply: No, because the names of the authors are merely conventional designations (*samākhyā*). Just as the name "Pāṇini" is applied to the grammarian Pāṇini, so too the name "Vyāsa" is applied to the compiler of the Vedas. The Veda itself is eternal. Moreover, the Veda is seen to be without beginning, as there is no memory of its first author. Since there is no recollection of a first author, the Veda is eternal. Furthermore, the Veda is seen to be unchanging across different ages. Since the same mantras and rituals are found in the Vedas of the past, present, and future, the Veda is eternal. Therefore, the Vedic injunction is the means of knowing Dharma. This concludes the third section. Now begins the fourth section. Therein, the author discusses the nature of the Vedic injunction. What is the Vedic injunction? It is a statement that impels one toward a specific action. For example, "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice. This statement impels one to perform the Agnihotra sacrifice for the sake of attaining heaven. Therefore, it is called a Vedic injunction. But how is it known that this statement impels one to act? It is known through the observation of the behavior of those who understand the meaning of the Veda. When people who know the Veda hear the injunction "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra," they proceed to perform that sacrifice. From this observed behavior, we infer that the Vedic injunction has the power to impel one to action. Therefore, the Vedic injunction is the means of knowing Dharma. This concludes the fourth section. Now begins the fifth section. Therein, the author refutes the objection that the Veda is not a source of valid knowledge because it contains contradictions. Some say: The Veda is not a source of valid knowledge, because it contains internal contradictions. For example, the Veda says, "Fire is cold," while elsewhere it says, "Fire is hot. Since such contradictions exist, the Veda cannot be a source of valid knowledge. To this we reply: No, because the apparent contradiction is resolved by the distinction between primary and secondary meanings. The statement "Fire is cold" is a figurative description intended to praise the cooling effect of the fire's heat upon the body, whereas the statement "Fire is hot" describes its actual nature. Thus, there is no true contradiction. Therefore, the Veda is a source of valid knowledge. This concludes the fifth section. Now begins the sixth section. Therein, the author discusses the relationship between words and their meanings. How is the relationship between a word and its meaning established? It is established through convention (*saṃketa*). Just as a father gives a name to his son, so too the ancient sages established conventions for words to denote specific objects. This convention is handed down through tradition. Therefore, the relationship between words and their meanings is eternal. Consequently, the Vedic injunction, being composed of words whose meanings are eternally fixed, is a source of valid knowledge. This concludes the sixth section. Now begins the seventh section. Therein, the author discusses the authority of Smṛti texts. Are Smṛti texts, such as the *Manusmṛti*, a source of valid knowledge regarding Dharma? Yes, they are a source of valid knowledge, provided they are based on the Veda. Since the Smṛtis are consistent with the Veda and do not contradict it, they are authoritative. However, if a Smṛti text contradicts the Veda, it is not authoritative. For example, the Smṛti text that permits the eating of garlic contradicts the Vedic prohibition against eating forbidden food. Therefore, such a Smṛti text is not a source of valid knowledge. But why is it that Smṛtis that are consistent with the Veda are authoritative? Because they are the work of sages who possessed direct knowledge of the Veda. Since these sages knew the Veda, their compositions are trustworthy. Therefore, Smṛtis consistent with the Veda are a source of valid knowledge. This concludes the seventh section. Now begins the eighth section. Therein, the author discusses the authority of local customs (*ācāra*). Are local customs a source of valid knowledge regarding Dharma? Yes, they are a source of valid knowledge, provided they are rooted in the Veda. Local customs that are observed by virtuous people and are consistent with the Veda are authoritative. However, customs that are contrary to the Veda or are practiced by the wicked are not authoritative. Therefore, local customs rooted in the Veda are a source of valid knowledge. This concludes the eighth section. Now begins the ninth section.

It must be accepted that in such a case, how could the status of being a sign (nimittatā) be postulated for the word and its referent?
However, in the Veda, regarding a subject matter not cognizable through other means of knowledge, it is established that "this word is employed in this specific sense."

If it is not understood through such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but the meaning is understood from the mere employment of words alone, then how can the word and its referent (*padapadārtha*) function as a cause (*nimittatā*),
given that there is no apprehension of their causal status? For only when the causal status is apprehended do the word and its referent become the cause.
It must be so for you, and not otherwise; for [the meaning] is not understood from what is heard for the first time, and because it would follow that everything could be understood from everything.
To the question of how the apprehension of the causal status [of words] itself does not exist, he says: "Because the causal status [of a word] is preceded by comprehension."

Having grasped the usage of the elders, one grasps that the word functions as a cause (nimitta) with respect to that object; it cannot be otherwise. Furthermore, the usage of the elders regarding an object not cognizable through other means of knowledge cannot be inferred, because no observation of avoidance or acquisition with respect to such an object is seen. Nor is it possible [to infer] when that [usage] itself is not perceived.
Since avoidance and acquisition are understood only with respect to that [object], there can be no mastery [of a word] regarding what is not cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Since the status of being a cause is preceded by comprehension, he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "But the comprehension of the effect does not arise from the comprehension of the cause alone."
The cognition of the thing signified (*naimittikī*) is preceded by the comprehension of the sign (*nimitta*).
[This] belongs to those who are being instructed (*vyutpādyānām*).

And that process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpoddhāra*) which occurs is restricted to that very object which is apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because for those being instructed, it is understood through the process of avoidance and acquisition, as has been stated regarding the understanding of elders (*vṛddha*).
3. bhāva. ga. [p.

354] Furthermore, comprehension of the meaning of a word is not possible [independently]; rather, it is preceded by comprehension [of the relationship between the word and its object], which serves as the causal basis (nimitta).

Regarding the term "understanding" (*avagama*): from what [is this known]? He says: for when something exists and another comes to be, upon seeing that, the cognition arises that "this is the cause of that"; it does not arise merely from the existence of that [cause] itself.

For the understanding of being a cause arises from its effect, not from its mere essential nature alone. Therefore, the status of being a cause is preceded by comprehension, and the comprehension of meaning from the word itself is preceded by the understanding of that causal status. Thus, when the meaning of the Veda is not understood...

If [the Veda] is the cause for that which cannot be understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be an understanding of the meaning of a sentence from the Veda? To this, he raises an objection: "By whom was it said otherwise?
He states it in a single passage: "Precisely from the understanding of the occasioned [result]."
The comprehension of the occasioning cause (*nimitta*).

It is only when there is comprehension of the meaning of the sentence expressing the occasioned act (*naimittika*) that the status of being an occasioning cause is comprehended. And it is indeed comprehended [in the case of]: "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra."

Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that which is connected with the meanings of the words. Therefore, even in this case, who can deny that the words and their word-meanings serve as the cause?— the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).
He addresses the objection: "How, moreover, is it understood that the meaning of a sentence consists of word-meanings as related [to one another]? [The answer is:
"Related..."
How is it understood that the sentence-meaning here is that in which these word-meanings reside? The objector says:
"Indeed, from this very sentence.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "If [it is understood] from this very sentence..."

If you hold that there is an understanding that "the meaning of the sentence is of such a kind," then you have effectively stated that the understanding of the contingent (naimittika) follows precisely from the understanding of the cause (nimitta); for [you would be saying] that "from the sentence alone this is understood: 'this meaning is the contingent one.'"

1. Not that [is the cause], according to manuscript *ga*. 2. According to manuscript *ga*: "If understanding does not have the meaning as its instrumental cause (*nimitta*), how can there be an understanding of the meaning of the Veda?
3. Omitted: *vākya*, according to manuscript *ga*.
4. He does not conceive [such thoughts]. (ga) 5. "This is divine. (ga) 6. Added: *iti*. (ga)
This is what you have said. But surely this is the case everywhere; so what is this reproach of ours? To this he replies:
"For in the linguistic usage of elders, the status of being indicative (naimittikatva) is understood through [the observation of] rejection, acceptance, and so forth."

For in the world, having observed that immediately after hearing a word there occurs the rejection or acquisition of a specific object, one understands: "This object has been communicated by the word"; yet this does not happen from the word alone. To the objection that "it happens exactly so even here," he says: "In this case..."
Abandonment and acquisition proceed from speech alone; therefore, it is the opposite of that [which you claim].
One must understand the object through speech itself, and then there should be abandonment and acquisition; and by means of abandonment and acquisition, the cause—
The relationship between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*) must be understood; therefore, in this context, the comprehension of the effect arises solely from the cause.

However, in common worldly usage, the status of being a cause is preceded by comprehension. He raises an objection: "But even in the linguistic usage of elders, the comprehender understands the meaning from the sentence itself; it is only the child standing nearby [who perceives] the relationship between word and meaning..."

One understands the relationship through the acts of avoidance and acquisition. Therefore, "the cognizer who is an elder does not, because the comprehension of the word's meaning was previously non-existent, perceive the status of being a cause as preceded by [prior] comprehension."
Thus he thinks. He refutes this:
"True; however, even that person, at a time subsequent to the knowledge of the relationship, cognizes the effect from that cause."
The meaning is that even an elder, by perceiving another elder, understands only the causal status [of the word] like a child,

and only afterwards does he comprehend the object, because the object is not understood upon the first hearing. In the case of the Veda, however, since a person has not yet cognized the relationship between the cause and its effect, what could he know to be the causal status of anything, or what could he know to be the effect?
What is the state of being based on a cause (*naimittikatva*)?

The meaning is that as long as the cognition of the relationship between the cause and its effect has not arisen in the cognizer, it is impossible to comprehend that relationship between the cause and its effect. He then raises another objection.
1. It proceeds (pravartate). Ka. 2. Omitted. Artha. Ga. 3.
And the cognizer (pratipattā). Ga.
4. Omitted. From the sign (*nimitta*). Ga. [p.
356] — Now, inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*) is formulated: in the linguistic usage of elders, between words and their referents—

The state of being a cause (*nimittabhāva*) has been observed; these same word-meanings exist even in the Veda. Therefore, in the Veda as well, the state of being a cause consists in the connection with their own respective meanings.
The meaning of this is: the word-meanings found in the Veda are the causes for the connection with their own respective meanings.

It is established [as follows]: because they are word-meanings (*padārtha*); whatever are word-meanings, those are the causes for their own syntactic connection (*anvaya*), just like those residing in the meaning of a worldly sentence—thus, having their causal status understood through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation), they will cause their own connection to be cognized. He refutes this: if it is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, then in that case, how many...?

Regarding the question of "in what [sentence-meaning] are they related?", we have no means of knowledge; for in the Veda, once the meanings of thousands of word-groups have been understood, it is not known which word-meanings, how many, or in relation to what [other meaning] serve as the cause for the relation. Nor can it be said that, following the usage of elders, expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), proximity (sannidhi), and compatibility (yogyatā) are the restrictive factors.

For, according to that [view], it would follow that there could be no comprehension of the connection between objects not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He raises an objection:
"If it is argued that 'as many [words] as are perceived as connected in a given instance'"; he then refutes it:
In that case, then, the status of being a cause is preceded by comprehension; it is not caused by the inference from common observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).
As many [factors] as are perceived as being concomitant with a particular comprehension, so many are the causes for that comprehension.

If it is maintained that [the relationship] is based on memory, then the status of word-meanings as causes is known precisely from the observation of comprehension itself, not through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).

To the objection, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he replies: "And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such comprehension," as has already been stated. He concludes: "Therefore, in this case, the error arises solely from *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*."
The notion that words and word-meanings are common to both worldly usage and the Veda, and that consequently the meaning of a sentence is understood in the Veda just as it is in the world,
is an illusion. In reality, according to the reasoning already stated, there is no means whatsoever for the comprehension of the Vedic meaning.
Or, the understanding of the unseen [result] is based on convention, preceded by observed usage.
The meaning of this is as follows: 1. [Omitted]. It refutes [the objection]. (ga)

When it is not tenable that the Vedas convey supramundane objects, then the Vedas must be of human origin, having as their object matters within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus, even the relationship between word and meaning [is established by humans].
It is not innate. For why should one postulate an independence of the word that contradicts what is observed, regarding an object for which a convention is possible?
Therefore, the comprehension of the meaning of a word is purely conventional.
But how can it be said that even a convention is possible? For by this person who establishes the convention, [it must necessarily be established...]

It must be admitted that some words possess an eternally established relationship [with their meanings]. Thus, independence [of the word] has already been accepted in certain cases; therefore, what is the use of establishing a convention (*samaya*)? It is replied: the understanding of the unseen [meaning] is preceded by observed usage.

This is what is meant: when people employ words that are already conventional (*sāmāyika*), an understanding of the convention (*samaya*) will arise for those who are proficient; and from that, they will proceed with their linguistic usage. Furthermore, another person becomes proficient through their usage, and in this way, even the proficiency in usage of previous generations arose from convention. Therefore, [the convention] is established.

There is no logical inconsistency in the claim that the Vedas were composed by persons in order to establish for the Vedic tradition a relationship between the means and the goal (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) that was previously unperceived. In this very same way, some have initiated Vedic practice by establishing the relationship between a name and its bearer (*saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandha*) using words whose conventional relationships are already established in the world. And these two—

The two positions—that the relationship is either conventional (*samaya*) or produced (*kṛtaka*)—are indeed subject to the same logic; how they differ has already been demonstrated in the *Sambandhākṣepaparihāra* during the very presentation of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). [The opponent] objects: "But surely, unity of sentence will be based on the unity of the effect (*kārya*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: even in the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda, the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) alone is the cause. For it is thus understood from the usage of elders that words convey their own meanings as being connected to an action (*kārya*). In both the world and the Veda, the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) is one and the same, consisting of an action to be performed.

Therefore, there is no multiplicity of objects for linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Consequently, since as many word-meanings as are connected toward a single purpose constitute a collection of words that expresses those meanings, the status of being a single sentence will be based on the unity of the purpose. Now, [one might object]: "In both the world and the Veda, the meaning consists of a single purpose..."
Why is this so? To this he replies: "And there is identity of effect between the world and the Veda because of the identity of the injunctive word, such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

The meaning is that due to the identity of the signifier, there is identity of the signified. [Objection: But surely, the isolated optative suffix and so forth, being devoid of an *anubandha*, [cannot have a meaning]; having performed [the action], it would be non-Vedic. (ga.)

To the objection that there is no single denoter because of the absence of such a status in both worldly and Vedic usage due to differences in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*), he says: "And the unity of the injunction (*niyoga*) follows from its liberation from the subordinate elements. This has already been stated.

Although the meaning is not understood from the word alone, nevertheless, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), it is indeed possible to understand this: that "it is precisely the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth that convey the sense of what is to be done."

Thus, having resolved this connection, [the author establishes] the identity of the expressive word (*vācaka*) in both worldly usage and the Veda. Now, one might object: "Granted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are one and the same;

nevertheless, since in the world they convey commands (*preṣaṇa*), entreaties (*adhyeṣaṇa*), and the like, whereas in the Veda those [qualities]—which are attributes of a person—are absent, they cannot have a single meaning. To this, he says: "The meaning of the *niyoga* (the mandate) is the meaning of the optative suffix and so forth, both in the world and in the Veda."
That [objection] has also been answered. For instigation (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth have been explained by means of the distinction between what is already established and what is not yet established.

That which was stated by the venerable Pāṇini—that instigation, entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*), and so forth are the meanings of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others—was stated by way of that very distinction between the established and the unestablished.

Even when the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth are employed by equals, inferiors, or superiors, although the "task" (*kārya*) is present in all cases, the "command" (*preṣaṇa*) and other such factors are unestablished and thus serve as limiting conditions (*upādhi*); however, the "task" itself is the meaning in every instance. He concludes:
"Therefore, there is no fault even in the case where [the task] is preceded by a cause."

Although the object is to be understood only after first comprehending the cause, there is nevertheless no fault, because the status of being a cause is already known from the linguistic usage of elders; thus,
inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) is established for the comprehension of the cause.
When the nature of the indicative sign (*nimitta*) is understood, those word-meanings (*padārtha*) that are connected with the action convey their own selves;
and since these are indeed word-meanings, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa-anumāna*) is established. The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) supports this:

This is incorrect. Why? He says: Is it observed in common worldly experience that the meaning of an injunction (*niyoga*) serves as the cause for the comprehension of an object because its referent is not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
The meaning of this is: the injunction is the expressed object (*vācya*).

Regarding that optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, whose meaning is the mandate (*niyoga*): is that optative suffix, whose meaning is not known through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), established in common worldly usage as the cause for the comprehension of an object precisely because its meaning is unknown by any other means of valid cognition, such that you [the opponent] might say this?
1. api. ga.

Does he say this? If it were observed in the world that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers convey an object that is indeed not cognizable by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then in the Veda as well, the optative suffix and others would convey an object that lies beyond the scope of any other means of valid cognition.
The sense is that this is not the case. To the objector, [the author] states the answer with the underlying intention: "We say no. He himself says:
"Does that which is heard for the first time not cause comprehension? This reason is not to be disregarded.

The meaning of this is as follows: if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth have as their object a thing that is not cognizable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] would be impossible, because there can be no apprehension of a relationship when the relatum has not been apprehended. Furthermore, if that which has its relationship unapprehended were to convey a meaning, the unavoidable consequence would follow that it conveys meaning even when heard for the first time. Therefore, [it is not the case that...].

"In common usage, it is perceived that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others have as their object a thing not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) refutes this:
"In that case, another means of valid cognition must be sought even for the distinction among those objects;
[for] there must be another means of valid cognition for the distinction among the objects of the optative suffix and the rest."

Regarding the object to be known—the meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth—in the Veda, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must be sought; for the optative suffix and the like are not its denotator, because the relationship [between word and meaning] has not been apprehended. Now, if it is argued that "that very same meaning of an injunction (*niyoga*) which exists in common worldly usage also exists in the Veda, with the difference being merely due to a distinction in the subordinate elements (*anubandha*)," he replies: "And the subordinate elements follow after those distinctions."

In the world, distinctions are observed among things that are already distinct and serve as the objects of injunctions; however, distinction does not follow from the distinctions in the adjuncts (*anubandha*).

The meaning of this is: even in the world, it is observed that adjuncts are connected only to those things that are already distinct and intended for performance, but distinction does not follow from the adjuncts themselves.

Therefore, the meaning of the *niyoga* (injunction) is distinct precisely by its own nature. Consequently, since the meaning of the *niyoga* differs in the world and in the Veda, and because no apprehension of their relationship has been perceived, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be sought. Precisely because the Vedic meaning of the *niyoga* is distinct, there can be no mutual syntactic connection [between worldly and Vedic meanings] without first ascertaining from another source the delimitation of usage.
It is possible to understand that "this many word-meanings are connected in this comprehension"—
but as long as the delimitation of the specific usage is not known from another source, the mutual connection [of those meanings] cannot be understood.

[It is] not possible to say: "as many [instances] as are seen in the world within that comprehension. If it is argued, "then let the delimitation of usage be known from another source," he says in response: "And that delimitation does not exist.
(The word *na* was omitted in the manuscript *ga*.)
2. Added: *bhinnasya*. Ga. [p. 360]:
Because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it exists in the Veda.

Therefore, another perspective must be sought here regarding the meaning of the Veda for the sake of facilitating the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning]. This is not accepted by those who maintain that the scripture is independent, because its subject matter is cognizable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Since the authority of an independent scripture cannot be established if it is merely an object [of inference], those who advocate for independent scripture do not accept other philosophical systems (*darśana*) as valid regarding the meaning of the Veda; nor has it been stated that there is an intrinsic comprehension [of the relationship] even when the relationship is not grasped due to the absence of other philosophical systems—[as it is said]: "In all cases, our perception is the means of knowledge."

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) concludes: "Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is that which is connected with the meanings of the words as they are perceived, and it does not depend on other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus, it is appropriate [to ask]: how is this profound path of logic to be fathomed?"
[This is] *saṃpradhāraṇā*.

Its meaning is as follows: those word-meanings which are well-established through the linguistic usage of elders and are understood within the sentence-meaning are indeed the invariable concomitants (*anvayinaḥ*); moreover, you have not admitted that they depend upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, this path of reasoning is profound; how can it be fathomed? Is the comprehension of the connected meaning to be abandoned, or is independence from other means of valid cognition [to be abandoned]? It is proper to deliberate on this. In this regard, the sense is that it is better to resort to dependence upon other means of valid cognition in accordance with the observed comprehension of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Now, a proponent of a partial conclusion (*rāddhāntaikadeśin*) [speaks].

Relying precisely upon the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he says: for this very reason that, in the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, the authority of an independent scripture (*svatantrāgama*) is not established,
the knowers of Brahman consider that this one [Brahman] alone is understood through manifold conceptualizations in both the world and the Veda.

The knowers of Brahman, the knowers of the Vedas, and the grammarians maintain that this single word alone, though devoid of actual difference, is perceived in both worldly and Vedic usage as having superimposed differences through the manifold conceptualization of stems and suffixes; for in this view, the sentence is that in which the constituent parts have subsided.

[The word] has a portion [of the object]; nor does it have with its own referent a relationship characterized as that of signifier and signified, but rather one characterized solely by identity; for it is the sentence itself that manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of the sentence-meaning, just as mother-of-pearl manifests in the form of silver. [Otherwise], the capacity to convey meaning would not be established. (Ga.)
2. Added. *pada*. *ga*.

361] by that [means]. In this regard, although the meaning of a Vedic sentence has its relationship [with the word-meanings] ungrasped because it is not accessible through other means of knowledge (*māna*),...

Nevertheless, it is the Vedic sentence itself that will evolve (*vivartate*) in the form of meaning; thus, the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the superimposed roots, suffixes, and words serve merely as a means. Therefore, the knowers of Brahman should understand that this is indeed an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).
Thinking that those who know the Supreme Brahman—the knowers of Vedānta—might not believe him, he says: "by those who know Brahman," which means by those who know the Vedas.
A certain proponent of Mīmāṃsā asks: "But how is this [objection] not applicable under the theory of illusory transformation (vivarta)?"
What is the fault?

It is that which will be stated. He states that very point: first of all, there is no cognition of oneness, for "in common usage, the word 'sound' (śabda) is well-established as referring to an object perceived by the auditory organ."

This has been established by this passage: for the phonemes are indeed perceived as distinct by the auditory organ. [The author] refutes [this objection]: "That very unity does not exist" is wrongly stated;

it is said that [unity is established] because of the contradiction with the effect (*kāryavirodha*), meaning it is said because of the contradiction with the effect characterized by the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence never before heard.
For if unity were absent, the effect would be contradicted; therefore, it is understood that a single sentence consists of a single effect.
A certain follower of the Mīmāṃsā school asks: "Does the effect itself directly perceive its own nature, such that you [claim] it to be one?"
[The opponent] considers [the sentence]: "If indeed perception were to establish itself through its effect, then this might be so;
but this is not the case. He refutes [this objection]: "Let it be that there is no perception; even inference is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By that inference, it is understood that there exists a single sentence. [Objection: "But how [is it known] from inference that [it is] a means of valid cognition..."

Regarding the statement that "the cognition of what has come to be [is derived] from inference," he says: it is indeed logical that the cognition of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) arises even from inference.
The meaning is that there is never any lack of coherence (*anupapatti*). You Mīmāṃsakas yourselves have also stated that in every case, validity is purely inferential.
Here, an objection is raised: how can there be unity of an object understood through inference?
If the sentence is inferred by means of the inference from its effect (*kāryānumāna*), how can it possess unity? Someone says: "Or how could there be diversity?"
1. Added: na. ga. [p.
362] Just as oneness is not established through inference and so forth, how will otherness be established for you either? For the effect...
The cause leads to an inference, but it does not touch upon its being either identical or different. He himself says: "And what is not established without identity?
Therefore, if identity is impossible to comprehend, let it remain so."
"Even though that has been understood, there is no purpose [in further effort]," the opponent objects: "This is not established;
for means do not become conceptualized [as ends]. Moreover, in the absence of oneness, means are not conceptualized."
[They] exist; therefore, oneness must be asserted with effort. Nor has it been argued that the comprehension of oneness is established through inference and so forth.
The meaning of this is: "It is not by me that 'otherness' is comprehended through inference."
Thus it was questioned; however, since it was further questioned, "How is oneness understood?", this is merely a reproach directed at me.
"How can there be otherness?"—this objection does not arise. The follower of Grammar (Vaiyākaraṇa) offers this rebuttal: "This is no fault;

having distinguished the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) through inference, one subsequently perceives its unity with its constituent parts, as in the case of 'the white cloth'."

In such passages as these, the meaning is as follows: having inferred the cause from the effect, one then understands its unity with the constituent parts, because the effect would otherwise be impossible without that unity; for [the effect] cannot exist without [that unity].
This is not tenable; rather, he conceives it thus: this oneness, which is accessible through inference from effects, is understood from scripture—that is, from grammar.
To the question, "What, then, is the meaning of this scriptural passage? he says: "Brahman shines forth of its own accord, with all distinctions of scripture entirely subsided."

The meaning is: that in which all conceptual constructions based on scripture (*āgama*), such as grammatical derivations (*vyākaraṇa-nibandhana*) and those concerning *prakṛti* and so forth, have entirely ceased. As it is said: "In common worldly usage, the word 'word' (*śabda*) is well-known to refer to an object perceived by the sense of hearing."
Thus, that too contradicts scripture;
the meaning is that it contradicts worldly designation. Regarding this, he says: "The word 'cow', the object 'cow', and [the cognition] 'cow'..."
1. Omitted. tasya. ga. 2. tayāpni vinā. ga. 3. karaṇamatānusārī. ga.
4. Furthermore, it is said: "And knowledge... [p. 363] Ga.
Why? Because of the designation by a single name; for it is not possible for distinct things to have a single name simultaneously.
For those distinct objects that are designated by a single word do not [denote their meanings] by that word simultaneously.
They are expressed by words, as in the case of dice and the like; and here there is a simultaneous reference by a single designation.
Therefore, this very single reality manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of the signified (*vācya*), the signifier (*vācaka*), and cognition (*jñāna*). But how is their simultaneity understood?
But how is this simultaneous designation understood? This is the meaning of the question. The answer is:
because the cognition of the essential nature of the signifier, the cognition, and the signified is mutually dependent.
[These are] the signifier, the cognition, and the signified.

To that extent, they appear as mutually dependent; therefore, their simultaneous comprehension occurs at that time, and there is a single designation at that moment. Consequently, it is established that oneness exists because of the occurrence of a single simultaneous designation.
And for this reason, as for what was also said—that there is no apprehension of a universal devoid of the reflective awareness of its own class—[that is refuted].

The meaning of this is as follows: among all words, there is no apprehension of a universal that is devoid of the reflection upon those phonemes which belong to the same class— just as, until the object [itself] is reached, there is only the form of a cow among similar-colored things without abandoning their differences, so too is "word-ness" (śabdatva).
As for what was said—that [the object] is not perceived—that too is incorrect.

Why? Because this reasoning is based on difference; it is a reasoning that holds only if difference were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). For there can be no reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) of something that does not exist.
It exists [in the case of the real], not in the case of the imagined.
Therefore, if difference were ultimate, then this would be tenable—that only difference is perceived, and not the universal; yet difference is not ultimate.
Thus he says: "And the oneness of all words has been stated, because they are designated by the single expression 'word, word.

Therefore, it is established that there is only one word, whose nature is the sentence. Now, with what intention was it asked: "But how is it that this fault does not apply under the theory of transformation (*vivarta*)?"
Thus, he expresses that intention with the words "What follows from that? (tataḥ kim iti).
[Note:
1. The designation of oneness (ekatvavyapadeśa), however, applies at this time. Ga.
2. ...simultaneously indeed...
vyapa. ka, ga. 3. Only as far as the object itself (*yāvadartha eva*), having abandoned the distinctions among similar classes (*savarṇeṣu*) and the form of the cow (*gavākṛti*).
If the distinction is conceptual, how then is there comprehension of the meaning of the Veda? The answer is this:
it follows from that very point that it is by means of conceptualization alone that the usage of elders is said to be the cause;
[the meaning] resides in the conceptualized parts.

Mastery of usage through the elders is merely the instrumental cause, because that which has not been observed in usage is not cognized, whereas even from a sentence concerning the unprecedented (apūrva), that which has been observed in usage is cognized. And this seed of conceptual construction is stated in various ways, beginning with "the first word," and so forth.

The seed of this conceptual construction—the conventional usage of elders which serves as its cause—is described in many ways: that the first word is the sentence, that all words together constitute the sentence, or that the verb alone is the sentence, and so forth. Concluding, he says: "Therefore, [these meanings] are refined by the conceptualization of distinctions through the knowledge of word-meanings."
Conditioned [words], when combined, convey a sentence that is indivisible and non-different; the meaning is that it unfolds in the form of an object.

Now, one might object that in this way, because it is preceded by an imagined distinction, the Veda would lack authority; to this he says: "And the Veda does not lose its authority on this account, because its power with respect to the object of knowledge remains intact," as has been stated.

The Grammarians have stated that even by resorting to means that do not exist [in the ultimate sense], there is the presence of capacity regarding the ultimate object of knowledge; therefore, a conceptual construction that is not based on scripture leads to transgression, whereas one that is Vedic does not.

Although the Vedic meaning is conceptual because it is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word, nevertheless it does not lead to sin, since the Vedic meaning has as its ultimate goal liberation, which is the supreme reality.
Therefore, the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of the relationship between word and meaning is established under this view.

However, it has already been demonstrated that the inherent nature [of words] cannot be established on the view that there is a real distinction [between them]. Precisely because distinction is not ultimate but merely conceptual, those who know the meaning of mantras describe the meanings of the mantras according to their respective applications; for if there were [real] distinction...

For the designation would necessarily be fixed. If indeed there were a distinction [between word-meanings], then the meaning perceived according to the individual power of each word would be that very same [meaning]; however, when the sentence itself is the sentence-meaning, [the meaning is not thus fixed].
In that case, wherever there is the application of a mantra consisting of a sentence, that would be its meaning; not [wherever it is recited]. [ga. p.
365] (Note: "na" and "yatra" are omitted in the source text).
The meaning of a sentence is understood through the linguistic usage of elders; however, whatever meaning is understood from a particular sentence is its meaning.
And because it is to be understood from this [sentence] as having multiple meanings by virtue of its application (*viniyoga*), it possesses multiple meanings within the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Since the non-worldly meaning is indeed unrestricted, therefore [it is said]: "The *uṇādi* suffixes are manifold."
This and so forth would be without scriptural authority (*āgama*).
For when the meaning of a mantra is described in various ways according to its application (*viniyoga*), [the rule] "the *uṇ*-affixes are manifold" (*uṇādayo bahulam*) [is invoked].
This and so forth is applicable [in that context]. However, when denoting a fixed meaning well-established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), it has no utility;
nor is this even desired by you, the Mīmāṃsaka. Furthermore, the instruction regarding the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga-vidyā*) is purposeful.

The instruction of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅgavidyā*), such as phonology (*nigama*), etymology (*nirukta*), and grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), is meaningful only under the view that there is conceptual differentiation (*kālpanika-bheda*).
For if there were actual ontological difference, since differences are already established by worldly convention alone, what else would need to be taught?
In our position, however, conceptual construction follows scripture; and because scripture is infinite, the instruction is purposeful.
Since it is impossible to prevent the occurrence of conceptual construction, the instruction is purposeful. Therefore, this designation of difference [is justified].
[The distinctions apply] to worldly [words], Vedic [words], meters, the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), and the sacred texts (*nigama*).

Furthermore, this distinction exists only on the view that there is a conceptual difference; otherwise, since [all words] are of a single nature by virtue of being composed of phonemes (*varṇa*), the designation of difference would be impossible.
It would not be so. In the traditional grammar (āgama-vyākaraṇa), the various differences in philosophical views (darśana-bheda) become logically consistent.
For instance—some maintain that the root *as* contains the letter *s*, while others read it as *as* in the sense of "to be" (*bhū*); thus, [the diversity] becomes logical.
Under the view that differences are merely conceptual, someone might, by some means, delimit a specific boundary and [regard] that very same entity...

Thus, it is shown that [the sacrifice] consists of a single sentence. Precisely because the difference is conceptual, for that very reason the rites of eleven and twelve potsherds constitute a single action;
otherwise, if the difference were ultimately real, upon the perception of that difference...
1. Thus, it is worldly (laukika).
2. And he says that there is a distinction; likewise, [it consists of] the nature of phonemes (varṇa)—[variant reading *ga*].
If there were a single designation for the eleven and twelve potsherds, it would be mere idle chatter; not only in this case,
but also regarding the single designation for the ritual action, it would be idle chatter even within the context of the verbal expression.
To designate [the Veda] as a single scripture is mere prattle;

for the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that there is a single scripture even across different recensions (*śākhā*). Even that would be prattle if there were actual difference. Moreover, since the status of being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is understood through its effect (*kārya*), and since that effect—the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence—is one—

The designation of various names for a single characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the teaching of various meanings for it are not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because unity and multiplicity are contradictory. Furthermore, although there is a difference in comprehension between a sentence (*vākya*) and a compound (*samāsa*), the statement [in the treatise] serves to prohibit an identical conceptualization; it is meaningful for the purpose of making known the distinctions within the scriptures. Otherwise, the entity itself would be the obstacle.
It might be so; in the sentence "Bring the blue lotus," there is a mutual connection between the two [qualifiers] after they have been connected to the action.

It is understood [as such]; however, in a compound, as in "bring the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam ānaya*), the connection with the action is perceived subsequently between the two [words] which are already mutually related. Thus, even though there is this difference in comprehension, this option (*vā*) was stated by the venerable Pāṇini.

It is for the purpose of establishing what is logically consistent that it is stated: "Let there not be a uniform conception of a compound everywhere"; rather, it is to indicate that a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) proceeds based on that traditional authority (*āgama*), and for the sake of refuting [the former view]. For if no conceptual distinction were to proceed according to the tradition, there would be only the conception of a compound. However, in the ultimate sense (*pāramārthikatva*), [the distinction arises] precisely from the difference in realization through the two means.

It must be so. What is the use of further words? For this very reason, the determination of the power that functions according to the meaning to be expressed belongs to nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles; because when there is a distinction [between them], the difference in their essential nature is ultimate.
In that regard, when recognition occurs, [one says] "he delays."
If [the word] "pralambate" were [identical to] "vipra," there would be no difference [between them].

The meaning of this is as follows: if the word, consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), were recognized [as a single entity], there would be no distinction based on its form as a prefix (*upasarga*) and so forth;
[otherwise] it would not be mere idle chatter (*pralāpa*). (ga.)
2. Even though it is cognizable.
(ga) 3. When conceptual construction operates, it is precisely the conceptual construction of a compound.

But if [the word] were merely conceptual, then due to the absence of unity, it would be logical [that the word does not exist]; thus, for those who maintain that there are only phonemes (*varṇa*) in words such as *bhavati*, [the word] would not exist. [For example: *bhavati*.

Thus, that which is explained regarding the vocative case and the locative case would not apply to one who maintains that [the word] consists merely of phonemes (*varṇa*); for there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the phonemes. Furthermore, there occurs a connection between two words, as in "the king's man's elephant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣasya hastinaḥ*), but not in "the king-man's elephant" (*rājapuruṣasya hastinaḥ*).
Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: for one who maintains that words are merely phonemes (*varṇamātra*), the very same word that occurs in "the king's" (*rājñaḥ*) also occurs in "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*). Consequently, just as there is a connection even in a non-compound (*asamāsa*) by means of two words, [so too is there a connection in the compound].

Regarding the expression "the elephant of the king" (*rājño hastinaḥ*) or "the elephant of the man" (*puruṣasya hastinaḥ*), the same would apply even in a compound, resulting in "the elephant of the king's man" (*rājapuruṣasya hastinaḥ*).
And yet, in this case, the elephant does not belong to the king.

[This concerns] the relationship. In my position, however, in the word *rājapuruṣa*, the word *rāja* does not exist in reality at all; it is merely a conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Thus, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) does not arise. Likewise, in the case of *aupagava*, there is a relationship between the meaning of the word *idam* and two meanings: "this child of Upagu" and "this [belonging to him]. It is not, however, the case that in the word *aupagava*, there is a relationship between the meaning of the word *idam* and the meaning of "Upagu. The same applies to the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of an instrument" (*karaṇena*), there is both the production and the non-production of case endings.
If the case ending is produced after the word *karaṇa*, as in: "Bring water by means of a jar as the instrument" (*ghaṭena karaṇenodakam ānaya*).
Thus, in that case, [the definition] would also apply to the statement "the jar is the instrument (karaṇa) in the bringing of water";

yet if it does not apply to the word "instrument" itself, it would likewise not apply to the phrase "by means of the instrument. However, in my view, because there is a difference between the sentences—
This objection is not valid, because words do not exist within sentences. Likewise, verbal roots with nominal suffixes are "aśvaḥ," "gardabhaḥ," "aśvati," and "gardabhati";
and verbal roots with nominal suffixes are "aśvaḥ" and "gardabhaḥ."
The verbal roots *aśvati* and *gardabhati* are likewise [included]. Thus, the family of the vowel *a* (avarṇakula), divided into eighteen varieties for the sake of conveying meaning,
consists of six types each— short, long, protracted, nasalized, and non-nasalized— and these are further [categorized].

However, in our view, it is logical that [the word], divided into eighteen varieties— such as the threefold division by means of the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth— serves for the comprehension of meaning. Otherwise, if the division into words and phonemes were ultimately real, then because the entity would possess a single uniform nature, there would be the comprehension of all meanings [simultaneously].
It would either always exist, or there would be no cognition at all;

not even a single object would be cognized. For this reason as well, the object consists of the transformation (*vivarta*) of the word: because when an object is already cognized through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the singular apprehension [of it through a word] is false—as in the case of "fragrant..."
"Sandalwood, a cool breeze"—
thus,
fragrance is perceived by the olfactory faculty, [and] sandalwood...

[The substance is perceived] through both sight and touch; likewise, coldness is perceived by the tactile sense organ and the air by inference, according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine. Therefore, smell, touch, and the substance are distinct; and the cognition of non-distinction among these distinct things is false.
It would always be the case that "the sandalwood is fragrant" and "the air is cold."
Therefore, the meaning consists of a transformation (vivarta).

In the case of prefixes and particles, they sometimes serve as qualifiers, as in *prapacati* and similar forms; sometimes they are devoid of meaning, as in *pralambate* and similar forms; and sometimes they possess a contrary meaning, as in *pratiṣṭhate* and similar forms. This occurs when their presence constitutes that very form, or when they maintain a single uniform nature.

This is not tenable; however, it is tenable if [the diversity] is conceptual. Now, if it should be argued that the diversity will arise in accordance with the meaning of the sentence, he says in response:
"And because the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the meanings of its constituent words, a determination based on that [sentence-meaning] alone is difficult to maintain."

If there were no difference in the words, there would be no difference in the meanings of the words, and consequently, in your view, there would be no difference in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning.

Now, if it is argued that in cases such as "pralambate" (he hangs down) and so forth, there is no meaninglessness because this [word] is indeed one and the same when accompanied by the prefix *pra*, he says in response: "And if there were a difference in the words, there would be a destruction of the word-meanings."

If the word *pralambate* is accepted as being distinct from the word *lambate*, then in the case of *pralambate*, there would be no comprehension of the meaning of the word at all for one who has already grasped the relationship [of the word *lambate*] in the context of *lambate*. Therefore, the prefix *pra-* is indeed meaningless; only *lambate* conveys the intended meaning.
In that case, if there is meaninglessness (*ānarthakya*), how can there be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)?

Syntactic unity exists by virtue of being occupied with the comprehension of a single meaning; however, for that which is meaningless, there is no such activity, nor is there the cognition of division. The word "how" is to be supplied [to each]. [This applies to] the phonemes...

For it would indeed be a person [who speaks]. A word becomes distinct by virtue of conveying a distinct meaning. However, if the meaning were not conveyed through division, there would be no division of words; rather, within that very same word, there would be the comprehension of multiple meanings from different phonemes. 1. This is the understanding of a single meaning. (Ga.)
[On page 369] one might think that this has been added as something superfluous; however, on the view that it is a conceptual construction based on scripture, everything is logically consistent.

It is postulated that in the case of derived words (*lambateśabda*), the very process of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, because this is observed to be the case.
If it is asked, "From what does the understanding of the alternatives within the tradition arise?", [the answer is:
"In this manner, through the division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth."
If it is asked, "From what source was it understood by Pāṇini and others that the conceptualized components of speech-sounds are merely means for comprehension?
the answer is: "Precisely from another scripture—from yet another grammatical tradition (vyākaraṇāgama). This has been stated by them:"
“Even the knowledge of the sages is preceded by scripture.
Now, one might object regarding those sages:
To the question "How is this understood?", he says: "And its state of not being 'for the first time' can be understood because of the beginninglessness of saṃsāra.
For if there were some first [being], then a fault would arise—for him, from where [would it come]?"

Regarding the term "knowledge": since saṃsāra is beginningless, there is no such thing as "this is the first [instance]," and thus there is no fault. This very independence is the reason for its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, regarding the position of difference, in that position where there is a distinction between words and phonemes,
all of this would be inconsistent. And the Veda, which primarily consists of knowledge, demonstrates that the Veda possesses the capacity to bring about understanding through delimitation.
For the Vedāntas primarily concern knowledge;

therein, knowledge itself is the object of injunction—namely, "Brahman is to be known. And they, having demarcated [the subject] and postulated an imaginary distinction, establish the Veda's character as a means of comprehension. By which passage? "Now, that which is small..."
"That which is mortal," [and] "Now, that which is the earth— that is immortal."
Now, it has been shown here that what is small is non-abiding by virtue of its mortal nature; what is that "small"?
The answer is: limitation (*avaccheda*). How is it that limitations are non-abiding?
1. This is not so.
Regarding this, [the author of the *Gaṇikā*] says at [page 370]: "A limitation is observed for that which is to be conceptualized, but not for reality (*tattva*)."
Therefore, because their objects are mentally constructed,
these limitations are non-enduring upon the direct realization of reality; as it is said in such passages as, "As far as speech reaches," and so forth.
Everything becomes logically consistent;
that which establishes non-duality (advaita) becomes logically consistent, for otherwise there would be contradiction.

If the injunctions regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*) were to convey mutually distinct meanings, there would be a contradiction between those injunctions and the Vedānta texts which convey distinct meanings; however, in the view that the effect is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the Word (*śabda*), there is no contradiction. And where there is contradiction, there is a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

Because there is a lack of certainty regarding the Vedas, those who know the scriptures explain this entire mass of Brahman— the mass of the Vedas— in a way that is consistent with one [principle], namely, consistent with the single Brahman. This is that very scripture.
Whatever has been declared by Grammar is authoritative; that is the truth. Whatever has been stated in Grammar is indeed the reality.
These grammarians are knowers of Brahman who understand it thus. Therefore, O Mīmāṃsaka, desist from this!
"Because they grasp at distinctions, they follow after cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Now, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) refutes this:
"But even here, the acquisition of proficiency through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) is certainly not helpful.
Why? He says: 'If [the conceptual constructions] arise from scripture (*āgama*...'"
Do they proceed by means of the linguistic usage of elders? If conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are set in motion through scripture (*āgama*),
then comprehension would occur even without the linguistic usage of elders, provided that the comprehension of an object occurs by the power of the conceptual construction based on scripture.

Alternatively, through proficiency gained from the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), those who are initially free from conceptualization (*avikalpita*)—that is, those in whom conceptual construction has not yet arisen—do not engage with the conceptualizations of scripture (*āgama-vikalpa*).

Since grammar alone is incapable of being understood without the conceptualization of the elders' linguistic usage, linguistic usage is also taken into account; this same principle applies equally even to the linguistic usage of differentiation (*bhedavyavahāra*).
The meaning of this is as follows: because it is established even within the conventional usage of difference. (Note: *upapannatvāt* and *nānye* are added in the manuscript *ga*).
3. *ca* added in *ga*.
4. *ttyāvikalpitā na saṃjāta* in *ka*.

If it is argued that "the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) alone is the cause of acquisition of meaning, and this is the same here as well," then this [scriptural authority] is equal to that. Alternatively,

if the acquisition of meaning through the usage of elders is not respected here, and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are accepted solely on the basis of scripture (*āgama*), then what use is there for the comprehension of the cause [of meaning] acquired through the usage of elders?

The meaning of this is as follows: conceptual constructions (vikalpas) proceed solely from grammatical analysis (vyākaraṇa); however, linguistic usage (vyavahāra) is merely a means for attaining that grammatical analysis. This is incorrect;
for what use is there for a grammatical proficiency (vyutpatti) understood through the linguistic usage of elders, which has as its object divisions that do not actually exist? Whatever...
For if that very [word] which has already been mastered is heard once again, then there would be comprehension of the sentence-meaning;

but in its absence, how could there even be an understanding of grammar? Therefore, since this position also depends upon mastery through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), it falls into the very category of the theory of difference (*bheda-pakṣa*); for without difference, neither mastery nor comprehension is possible.

[This objection arises] from the [opponent's] position. [The opponent asks: "But surely this [distinction between the means and the result] will be based on the cognition of difference as imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*).
[Reply: No, because there is no evidence that the cognition of difference is of the nature of ignorance. [The opponent says: "The very effect [of the sentence] is the evidence. [Reply:
No, for the effect—consisting in the cognition of the meaning of the sentence—is established even otherwise. Now, here is another method.
It is rejected: if it is argued that,

just as in the case of a genus and a quality, a relation to a single substance is perceived because they both reside in one and the same substance, so too, when a word denoting a genus and a word denoting a quality are uttered in proximity, their reference to a single object is understood by means of those two.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as there is a relationship characterized by the co-inherence in a single substance between two objects—a genus and a quality—so too will there be a relationship between a word denoting a genus and a word denoting a quality when they are uttered in proximity; and by means of that [relationship],...

[The opponent argues: "The comprehension of a single object consisting of a substance endowed with qualities will be established. [The author] refutes this: "This is not so; for at the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), that is, at the moment of learning the word's meaning, the understanding arises as a mere occasioning cause (*nimittamātra*) through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*), independent of any other distinct category of entity. Thus, it follows that the cognition occurs solely as a mere occasioning cause."
The comprehension of the isolated word-meaning arises from the isolated word alone; [it does not arise] merely through another word.

It might be so, because comprehension arises from that much alone. If it is argued that this results in meaninglessness, [it is not so], because [the meaninglessness applies only] to the mere word-meaning.

If it is argued that because [the meaning] is already understood at the very time the relationship [between word and meaning] is grasped, there is pointlessness (*ānarthakya*) in the words' merely conveying the individual word-meanings, he refutes this: "Pointlessness is not a reason for the understanding of another meaning.
If, by the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is pointlessness—"
Let it be so; however, it is not possible to understand [the relationship] as something other than this. He concludes:

"Therefore, this laborious attempt to describe an innate relationship between word and meaning, based on the linguistic usage of elders, is entirely useless. Consequently, the previously stated fact—that the relationship is either produced (kṛtakatva) or conventional (sāmayikatva)—remains."
This has already been explained previously. Having thus established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he now explains the commentary (*bhāṣya*):
"Even if the word and its relation are innate and eternal, nevertheless..."
He explains the Bhāṣya passage, "Dharma is characterized by injunction," as follows: this is a proposition that the linguistic usage of elders is not the basis for Vedic usage, as has been stated.
Regarding this, another commentary states: “For an injunction (*codanā*) is indeed a sentence,” and so forth; that is untenable. For, as for what cannot be understood from a single word...

The state of being a means of knowledge has been stated; that [objection] is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). As for the assertion that it is understood through three words, [that refers to its] conventional nature (*sāmayikatva*).
[Note: *śodhayitvā* is found in manuscript *ga*.]

This contradicts the opponent's prima facie position; therefore, dispelling these two objections, he says: "For the injunction (*codanā*) is a sentence. And [it is not the case that] 'the Agnihotra'..."
From this single word, "juhoti" (he offers).

"From the *agnihotra* sacrifice, heaven results"—this is understood. However, by the passage stating that [the meaning] is understood when three words have been uttered, it is explained that there is no comprehension from a single word, but rather comprehension from the sentence; this is the statement of the reason.

This is a refutation (*pātanikeyam*). The meaning is that this was stated in order to refute the statement regarding the reason (*hetu*). If it is thus that there is no comprehension from the individual word, but comprehension from the sentence, then what of it? Furthermore, this collection [of words] is not established through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*).
That which is employed in the Veda; therefore, the previously stated lack of causality (*animittatā*) has been described as the meaning of this commentary (*bhāṣya*).
It was precisely this meaning of the commentary that was stated by us previously: [namely] that which belongs to the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*).
The state of being a sign (*nimittatā*): "For these words have been employed [in this way]; their meaning is eternal."

The commentary has been restated. In this regard, there is the following objection: if the linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) of words pertains only to the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*), then the meaning would not be understood from a sentence composed by a newly discovered poet. On the other hand, if—lest this fault occur—the competency does not pertain to the mere word-meaning but rather to the meaning as related (*anvita*), then comprehension would likewise arise from Vedic sentences.
It might be so. To remove that [objection], he says: Even in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of words is established as the cause (*nimitta*);
for it is precisely in that [usage] that the signified object (*naimittika*) is to be apprehended through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But here, however—
1. Regarding the phrase "padāder aprati" (from *ka*, p.

as long as another effect (*naimittika*)—which is not an object of any other means of valid cognition—is not understood, the status of [the preceding word] as a cause (*nimitta*) remains unestablished.
Why? Because the word-complex has not been employed [in this sense].
For if it were known that this Vedic complex had been employed in this specific meaning, then, even though it is beyond the senses, its status as a cause [for understanding] would be established.
From this [Veda], there would indeed be the comprehension of Vedic meaning. This being so, its artificiality has been described.
Furthermore, "the word-meanings alone are not the sentence-meaning; for a word functions with respect to universals (sāmānya)."

Thus [it was argued]. That is untenable; for not every word denotes a universal (sāmānya), since there are exceptions such as "cook" (pācaka) and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he explains [the verse], stating that [the words] lack mutual syntactic connection (ananvaya).
By the term "universal" (sāmānya), that which is mutually unconnected is expressed. To the question "Why is that a universal?", he says: for mutual connection is called a "particular" (viśeṣa).

For the state of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is unique (*asādhāraṇī*), whereas the state of non-concomitance (*ananvita*) is common (*sādhāraṇī*); thus, the universal (*sāmānya*) is non-concomitant. [Objection: Let the word (*pada*) refer to the universal and the sentence (*vākya*) to the particular (*viśeṣa*). Even so, why is this? He says:
"For the word refers to the universal and the sentence to the particular"—by this, the conventional usage of words...
It has been stated that proficiency [in grammar] is useless; and the detailed explanation regarding this has already been given previously.
Its meaning is as follows:
1. *rānvayitām*. (Variant reading: *ka.*)

[Page 375] For, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), a word functions with respect to a meaning that is not yet connected [to others]. Therefore, it has been stated that even in the Veda, there would only be an understanding of the word-meanings from the words, and not an understanding of the sentence-meaning. "Nor is the understanding of the sentence-meaning derived from the word-meanings..."

The commentary states, "Because there is no connection. To this, he raises the following objection: "But surely there is indeed a connection between the word-meanings and the sentence-meaning, since it is precisely the connection among them that constitutes the sentence-meaning."

Regarding this, he states the resolution: "For indeed, a mutual connection cannot be understood if it is devoid of formal application (prayoga); thus, the aforementioned lack of comprehension is based upon this [very] commentary."

What is intended here is the absence of a relationship between the signifier (*nimitta*) and the signified (*naimittika*). Since there is no usage [of words] regarding an object that is not cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is not established that a word-meaning possesses the status of a signifier by conveying a self that is already connected with [other meanings]; therefore, the mutual connection of word-meanings, being devoid of such usage, is non-worldly (*alaukika*).

It was stated that [the meaning] cannot be understood; this is by means of the commentary passage "nor from the word-meanings," which follows the logical principle established by the previously mentioned commentary. "And if there were no connection, regarding some object..."
"If, upon hearing [the word], another meaning were understood, then when one [word] is understood, everything would be understood"—
this is the reason for the sentence-meaning not having the individual word-meanings as its cause.
This is the reason why the meaning of a sentence is not based on the meanings of individual words; this has already been explained:
"Even from a sentence that has never been used before, [the meaning is understood] even in the absence of a [previously established] relationship..."
"The understanding of the meaning arises from the intrinsic nature [of the word]," so says the Bhāṣya; that is untenable, because if it were indicative by its very nature, then— unseen...

To the objection that there would likewise be a cognition of [the Vedic] usage, he says: it has already been explained in this very context that by this [statement], he demonstrates the identity of the effect in the Veda as being free from its adjuncts (*anubandha*). Thus, in both the world and the Veda, there is a single effect that is free from its adjuncts.

This has been demonstrated by this commentary. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how is the subsequent commentary to be understood?", he says: "The word would transcend its own inherent property; and it is not a property of the word that a meaning is cognized from a word that is not employed."
Thus, he demonstrates that the dependence of the subsidiaries [on the primary] persists even when they are separated from their own subsidiaries;
as it has been stated:
