"The purpose is distinct by its very nature, and not merely due to a difference in its subsidiaries. Therefore...

In that case, there is an absence of the apprehension of a relationship for the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth. How then could they convey a distinct meaning of an injunction (*niyoga*)? And if they were to convey it, the word itself would overstep its dependence on the apprehension of a relationship; yet this is not a property of words. For [it is said]: "Not indeed from the first hearing..."
Thinking that this commentary is redundant, he explains: “For no one understands any meaning from a word heard for the first time”;
thus, the previously mentioned contradiction with *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference] is restated.
The contradiction previously mentioned regarding that which was presented as *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* is stated by this commentary: "If [the object were known] even from a word heard for the first time..."

If some were to understand the meaning [from the words alone], then it would be a case of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation). However, since a person understands only that specific object for which they have grasped the relationship [between word and meaning], we consider that the status of being a cause [of cognition] belongs to the word-meanings only in those cases where their causality has been observed in relation to objects cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "That is what is expressed—"

Regarding the Bhāṣya passage: "This is a property of words (*pada*), not a property of sentences (*vākya*); for we are seen to comprehend meaning even from a sentence heard for the first time," he asks therein: "In that case, how is it that there is no comprehension of the meaning?"

If a sentence conveys its meaning even when heard for the first time, why does the very first sentence not cause the child to understand the meaning just as it does an elder? It is not that it does not cause understanding; therefore, we conclude that there must be some specific method [of instruction].

By what does one cause [another] to understand? What is that? The answer is: we know it through comprehension (*avagati*). It was already stated previously in the Bhāṣya that the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), arising solely from the mastery of word-meanings (*padārtha-mātra-vyutpatti*), is the cause for understanding the meaning of the Veda.
The meaning is that once the relationship between word-meanings has been mastered, comprehension occurs even in the case of the Veda. [Objection: "This is not so;
if they were to comprehend from the first hearing, then everyone—both those who know the word-meanings and others—would comprehend it.
However, those who do not know the word-meanings do not comprehend it."
He explains the Bhāṣya as follows: "For it is not the case that what is not used in the world does not cause comprehension.
[p. 378] (Note: The variants indicate that some manuscripts read "does not cause comprehension" while others omit "not.")
The meaning can be understood from the aggregate [of word-meanings],

because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of cognizing any random meaning due to the absence of a specific cause. As for the claim that those who know the meanings of words understand [the sentence-meaning], that is due to the error of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).

It should be understood as being by means of what was stated previously. The meaning is that even when there is no cognition based on the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference], the cognition [that arises] is an error.
[Objection: "But surely, even by those who know the meanings of words, the relation of the sentence-meaning is understood as being indeed uncreated (*akṛtaka*)."
He explains the Bhāṣya passage— "Those whose minds are refined by the cognition of the object will understand that very same object upon hearing it a second time and so forth"—
by asking: "What is the point here of resorting to an error based on *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation)?"
It is better that there be only the causal factor (nimitta) itself, in accordance with the alternatives found in scripture.
Just as, in the Mīmāṃsaka position, the hearing of the accusative case and so forth in the usage of elders is the means [of understanding], so too are the alternatives in scripture.

Thus, this meaning of his has been described previously. We say: "No"; for if the final letter of a sentence, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding letters, [is what conveys the meaning] from the word-meanings—[in the case of non-existence, however, it is not so]. (Ga.)
“If it causes another object to be understood, what benefit could then be derived from the knowledge of the word-meaning?”
The meaning of this is that the aforementioned lack of basis (*animittatva*) of the Veda is the same even in the case of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
"Just as there is a lack of basis for the Veda in the theory of real difference (*bhedavāda*), so too it is in the theory of conceptual construction (*kālpanikavāda*)."

Thus, that which was stated previously is precisely the meaning of this commentary: "But will it not be possible in this way— that a word expressing a general property, such as 'cow' or 'horse', [is qualified] by a word expressing a particular quality, such as 'white' or 'black'?"
1. "That which... is the same. What? When a word falls from the vicinity, then the meaning of the sentence is understood.
Thus he explains the commentary: "That which was stated—
namely, that the cause for the arising of a single cognition with respect to two objects is based on the unity of their effect— that has now been set forth."

The single effect is the comprehension of a qualified object; the basis for this is the capacity of the words "white" and "cow" to produce a single cognition. [Objection: "No; for how could the cognition produced by the hearing of a word denoting a universal—such as 'cow' or 'horse'—which extends toward all cows or all horses, conform to the requirements of a sentence?"
"From some specific [condition], it might deviate.
In the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), because there is an acquisition of the mere cause (*nimitta-mātra*),
and because the mere cause— being independent of other words— is the acquisition of its own meaning, it follows that there would be an apprehension of the mere word-meaning (*padārtha-mātra*).

"That there is no mutual concomitance"—this is what was stated previously, and it is that which has been expressed here. Now, one might object: "Since a quality (guṇa) is concomitant with substance (dravya), it will establish the self's (ātman) concomitance with substance. To this he replies: "But [the concomitance] is for the sake of the meaning; it is based on the referent, not on the word."

That which is the inherence in the substance (*dravyānvayitva*) serves as the cause for that object’s [existence] in the external world; it is not verbal (*śābda*). However, that which is the inherence in specific qualities (*viśeṣānvayitva*) cannot be the cause for the object in the external world, because the object lacks the capacity for inherence in specific qualities. And that which is the verbal inherence in specific qualities is what is being investigated here. In that regard, concerning the word...

The status of being a cause (*nimittatā*) belongs only to that which exists as long as the usage [of the word]; that is, the status of being a cause for its own meaning is stated only insofar as there is usage of this word for the mere object-entity (*padārtha*). Furthermore, in the acquisition of usage, they do not acquire it in every instance where there is usage; rather, let it be so for the sake of the meaning. Ka. 1.1.68.
2. Omitted. Verbal [cognition]... is thus designated. Ga. (p. 384. 5. [p.
381] In the linguistic usage of elders, it is observed that a word serves as the cause for its own meaning by means of the exclusion of other referents, whereby—
Because another word is employed, it can be said that the cognition [of "cow"] is excluded from all non-cows by means of the word.
But if this is so, there would be pointlessness (ānarthakya) regarding the employment of the other word. He provides the rebuttal:

Let there be pointlessness for that whose meaning cannot be determined. For this so-called "pointlessness" is not capable of imagining as a meaningful purpose that which is not the purpose of anything; indeed, it would not even be pointlessness itself.
If it conveys a different meaning, then its meaningfulness is even greater. Therefore, it is established that the relationship [between word and meaning] is artificial;
thus, the lack of dependence [on other means of knowledge] is set aside. This is because the Vedas are artificial, and this reason has already been demonstrated.

Because it consists of sentences, like the *Mahābhārata* and other such works, the Veda is a product of human composition. For this very reason it has been said: "These are indeed collections of words."
Having recited the sūtra: "The collection of words denoting those [entities] is for the sake of action, because the purpose has that as its cause."

He explains: "To this it is said: the Vedic usage might lack the status of a means [for understanding] the meaning of the Vedas if there were a difference in meaning between the world and the Veda; however, there is only a difference in the process of insertion and deletion (āvāpoddhāra). Some..."

Only this much is different: some words are added and others are omitted. But how is there identity of meaning between the worldly and the Vedic? The answer is: because no difference is perceived between the meanings of words in the worldly and the Vedic contexts.

Whatever words exist in the world, those same exist in the Veda as well; and whatever word-meanings exist in the world, those same exist in the Veda as well. Therefore, how can there be a difference in meaning? To this, the opponent objects: Why is this, which has already been answered, being stated again?
How is that which has already been answered stated again? To the question "How is it answered? he says:
"For it has been stated that the meaning of a sentence is the mutual connection of word-meanings;
the mere word-meaning is not the meaning of a sentence."

What then? It is the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Therefore, the recognition of words and word-meanings is not the cause of [the cognition of] the syntactic relation. Let it be granted that the mere word-meanings are understood by the words; what has happened to the syntactic relation? But surely the syntactic relation may be conveyed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for a word, being conventionally established in the mere word-meaning, will convey the mere word-meaning, and that [relation]— [...is conveyed through secondary indication.]
The word-meaning indicates its own concomitance (anvaya); therefore, that concomitance will be verbal. To this, he replies:
"And it has been stated that no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is employed in this case."
For metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs only when the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is known;
and there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the aspect that "this word is employed in the sense of 'conjunction' (*anvaya*). [Objection: But surely, [if it were meaningless]—

If it is argued that because there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) here, the [Vedic statement] must therefore have positive concomitance as its primary meaning, that is incorrect; for there is no evidence that the Veda must necessarily possess a meaningful purpose.
Furthermore, even if a positive concomitance were being indicated, there is no evidence as to what the concomitance is or by which word-meaning it would be indicated.
Therefore, a Vedic positive concomitance devoid of such evidence is baseless.
To this, the proponent replies: "You are a lover of your mother who is ignorant of words and their meanings;
for, out of attachment born of maternal affection, you have not resided for long in the teacher's household. How can you be ignorant?"
He states the answer: first of all, categories of existence are never perceived anywhere as unconnected, at least not with respect to the sense of "being. Connection [is] mutual—

There is a relation; for in all states, things are perceived as being mutually connected. Even where no other object exists, there too they are ultimately intertwined with the sense of "existence. If things are by their very nature interconnected with other entities, what follows from that?

The point is that it does not follow from that much alone that [the objects] must be denoted as being necessarily intermingled with the word. The answer is: this follows from that; they are indeed to be denoted as intermingled.
Thus [it is said]. Why? Because the linguistic usage of words and meanings is for the sake of cognizing that [object].

Since an object must be denoted by a word exactly as it exists, and not otherwise, therefore only those [words] which are already related [to other meanings] are the things to be expressed, by their very nature—

Because of being associated. Now, it is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity that constitutes the expression of association; what then? It is through insertion (*āvāpa*) and deletion (*uddhāra*) in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). And these two are possible only with respect to the mere individual form (*svarūpamātra*), but not with respect to a thing already associated; for if there were a deviation regarding another associated thing, there would follow a deviation regarding that very association. Furthermore, if there were an expression of what is already associated—
1. By this, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is denoted. (Objection:
If that is accepted, there is the burden of postulating a capacity (*śakti*). Furthermore, is it the universal (*sāmānya*) as conjoined with [the particular] that is denoted? Or...
Is it by way of a specific [quality]? In the first case, this statement is redundant, since that [meaning] is established even through the power of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*).

In the second case, however, because specific qualities are infinite, there would be an inability to grasp the relationship [between word and meaning]. Furthermore, if a word were expressive when its relationship [to its meaning] has not been grasped, it would follow that some meaning would be understood even upon the first hearing. Moreover, what is accomplished by that which is expressed?

Is that which is intertwined [with another meaning] denoted specifically, or is it denoted by what has not yet been denoted? In the case of the first position—that it is denoted—there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). Even in the second case, since the second word denotes its own object as intertwined with another denoted object, it depends upon the denotation of the other word; thus, a circularity that is difficult to resolve follows. In the case of the position that it is not denoted, [the role of] the other word...

[Otherwise] the application [of words] would be useless. For this very reason, some maintain that it is the word-meanings themselves, once they have been denoted, that bring about the mutual connection [between them]. They indeed hold the following view: through the processes of insertion and deletion in the linguistic usage of elders, words denote their meanings in their mere formal essence; these meanings, then, are refined by mutual expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency.

They cause the very unperceived mutual connection to be understood. Nor can one raise the objection regarding the inability to grasp the relationship there, for we observe that in the case of sentences composed by contemporary poets, as well as in Vedic sentences, words that convey their own meanings—whose relationships have not been previously grasped—serve to bring about the cognition of the connection between those word-meanings. This is evident with respect to the resulting cognition.
"Because there is no dispute. To this he replies: "And in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), insertion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*) occur exactly according to the interconnection (*vyatiṣaṅga*).

The meaning of this is: in the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), insertion and exclusion occur precisely according to the interconnection—that is, without overstepping the established connection.

For instance, in the command "Bring the cow," there is the insertion of the cow precisely as it is already connected with the act of bringing; whereas in "Bring the buffalo," [the buffalo is inserted].
And the extraction [of the word's meaning] is only that which is already associated with it; therefore, the capacity of the word is determined to reside only in what is so associated.
This occurs in two ways: either through direct denotation (*abhidhāna*), or through the mediation of the intermediate cognition of the individual word-meanings (*padārtha*);
thus it must be deliberated. Since a circuitous route (*praṇāḍī*) is not appropriate when a direct possibility exists, [the word denotes] the associated [meaning].

The denotation itself is now being determined. Nor is there an incapacity to grasp the relationship [between word and meaning], because it is easily accomplished by resorting to specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*). There is nothing inconsistent in adopting the following rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*): words denote their own meanings as connected with other meanings that are fit for syntactic connection, which are brought to mind through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*). As for whoever... [the rest of the sentence follows].

And even for the proponent of the theory of the connection of what has been expressed (*abhihitānvayavādin*), this rule does not fail to apply to word-meanings. Nor is there any excessive burden of postulating a power (*śakti-kalpanā-gaurava*), because the postulation of power is unavoidable even in the case of word-meanings. But surely, this is observed [on page 385]?
The power of things is as follows: one who, by means of the eye, determines the unmanifested specific quality of whiteness,
infers "horseness" through the sound of neighing, and conceives of a "goer" by the sound of footsteps, [cognizes] that "a white horse is going."
Thus it is understood: therein, "whiteness," "horse," and "goer" [are related].

Thus, it is said that these three categories convey their mutual connection. That is untenable; for when "horseness" is inferred from the sound of neighing by means of inference, it is inferred as residing precisely in the object standing before one that is currently neighing, and not independently. For wherever the mark (liṅga) exists, there alone [is the probandum inferred].

It causes one to infer that which possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅgin*). However, for one who has a confusion regarding the location from which the neighing originates, even while perceiving "horseness," they do not ascertain the specific [animal]. Even one who understands the specific through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) understands that specific through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);
thus, there is no instance where the mere word-meaning brings about the cognition of a syntactic relation (*anvaya*).

Moreover, if whiteness and so forth were determined by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and were to convey their mutual connection, then there would be the consequence of [relying on] another means of valid cognition, because that [connection] would not be verbal in nature. Verbal knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the word-meanings presented by words; it is not [verbal] even if it is not preceded by words. Furthermore, regarding the word that first presents itself...

Let such a power be postulated; why then discard it and go so far as to postulate it in the word-meanings? Furthermore, the denotative power of the word is beyond dispute; it is therefore more appropriate to postulate the additional factor in that very [word] rather than postulating a power in the word-meanings, because it is simpler to postulate a property (dharma) than to postulate a substratum possessing that property (dharmī).

As for this objection of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) that has been raised here, it too must be refuted in the following manner: the comprehension of meaning does not arise from a single word alone; rather, having heard as many words as there are in the sentence, one determines a specific mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) according to logical principles, and thereby the meaning is understood. In that process, regarding the words heard first—

Word-meanings are remembered only as already connected, just as a word is [remembered] upon seeing its meaning. For even when the connected meaning is being denoted, the word’s own form does not disappear; therefore, by virtue of that proximity, the word is able to cause the remembrance of its own form alone. In that case, the word denotes its own meaning as connected with the word-meaning present in memory.

There is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For in the case of recollection, since they are independent, the word-meanings, once recollected, themselves bring about the understanding of their mutual connection. As they say: "Even those [word-meanings], when not recollected, do not lead us to understand the sentence-meaning."
"Therefore, it is only when those recollections are combined that they possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
All of this has been stated by us precisely in the *Vākyārthamātṛkā*, because [the meaning] is indeed as follows: the interconnection...

[There is] insertion and extraction; therefore, this word indeed denotes [the two] in mutual connection. But if that were so, would it not follow that there is also a mutual entanglement? Indeed, it would.
And as for this "and like this" (yaccedamiva ca).
3. Thus they are as [stated].
Ga. 4. The basis.
To the question "Why does it not express [the relation]? he replies: "There is no expression of the connection (vyatiṣaṅga), because the connection is understood from that which is connected;
for one who does not perceive the connection cannot perceive that which is connected."

Just as the word "individual" (vyakti) and the word "form" (ākṛti) [are distinct], because their connection is understood through their mutual association, a word does not denote that association itself. Now, if a word denotes what is associated, what will follow from this? It follows that a word is not said to be expressive of something unrelated.

Let it be that [the word] does not denote something unrelated; nevertheless, he asks: "What then? He replies: "And therefore, in common worldly usage, the mandate (niyoga) is understood to denote an action to be accomplished (kārya).
The meaning of this is as follows:

When Devadatta is being prompted by the words of a teacher or others, such as "Devadatta, fetch the fuel," a bystander observes him and determines: "This activity of his is preceded by cognition; that which I have engaged in after cognizing, he too has done."

This is due to a specific kind of intoxication: I do not engage in action merely from the understanding of the act itself, nor from the understanding of the result alone, nor even from the understanding of the act as a means to a result; rather, I engage from the understanding of it as a *kārya* (a duty or task to be accomplished). Even with respect to an act such as suckling at the breast, as long as it was not understood by me as a *kārya*, I did not engage in it; and this is not so...

That which is the state of being a means to the good (*śreyas*) is itself the state of being an effect (*kāryatā*). The nature of being a means toward the good is one thing, whereas the state of being an effect—characterized by being the primary object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*)—is another, namely, the primacy with respect to human effort (*kṛti*), which is to say, human exertion. However, the dull-witted have failed to perceive the distinction that for action, whose essence is affliction, the state of being an effect follows from its being a means to a fruit; and the same applies to pleasure.

There is no comprehension of "taskness" (kāryatā) without the status of being a means to a result; therefore, one infers that Devadatta also acts solely from the comprehension of that [task], thinking, "My activity arises from the cognition of a task distinct from being a means to a result. Since this comprehension of his occurs immediately after the word, it is based on the word alone; thus, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) possesses the denotative power of expressing a task.

It conceives [the injunction]. And since that effect (kārya) is established as being connected with and denotable by [the injunctive suffix], in sentences such as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra," according to the conclusion reached in the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] and elsewhere, the word "one desiring heaven" [denotes] the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

It is established that one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) must perform the offering by means of that [action]. And he who understands the task (*kārya*) is the one to be enjoined (*niyojya*); and the one who desires heaven is connected to that very task by virtue of being its cognizer (*boddhṛ*). This is precisely what [the opponent] was to answer. (ka, ga)
2. The dull-witted [perceive] non-differentiation.
Ka. 3. Where it is established.

It is capable of experiencing its status as the means to that which is desired. Furthermore, an action, being momentary in nature, cannot be the cause of a result that occurs at a later time; therefore, it does not connect with the person to be impelled (niyojya) by way of being something to be accomplished (kārya). However, that which is an effect persisting until a later time is alone capable of entering into such a connection with him; thus, [the object of the injunction] must be something distinct from the action.

The suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) denote an object of action (*kārya*) that is indeed not cognizable through any other means of knowledge. And because it is not previously known by any other means of knowledge, it is called *apūrva* (the "unprecedented").

Now, one might ask: from what is the establishment of that very object of action derived? If you say "from the sacrifice and so forth," then it would follow that the fruit arises immediately [after the act], since that which occurs immediately after an action is the cause of the fruit. To this, it is replied:

Even though it has been produced immediately [after its cause], its fruit will not necessarily follow immediately, because a delay is possible due to dependence upon auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). Nor does dependence on auxiliary factors entail a loss of its status as a cause. If one asks what those auxiliaries are, we reply: they are space, time, and so forth. Furthermore, nothing is impaired by this unless there is a specific cognition of them.

Nor is there a loss of the *apūrva*’s status as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) simply because it is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) due to its producing a fruit, for it assumes a state of being conducive to the fruit in order to obtain a *niyojya* (the person to be impelled) suited to itself; just as a master, while bestowing consciousness upon himself, benefits his slave born in the womb, so too is this case. Consequently, since the theory of the denotation of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is established, the denotation of the task (*kārya*) prevails in common worldly usage.
"It is understood from the injunctive suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth"—thus it connects with what will be stated later: "therefore, there is the denotation of *niyoga*.
By the word *niyoga*, that which is distinct from action (*kriyā*), namely the *apūrva*, is meant; it is that which, as a task (*kārya*), enjoins the person upon themselves.

Nor is it the case that linguistic proficiency arises from the Veda alone; for it is precisely through worldly proficiency that one understands, by following the Vedic sentences, that the meaning of words extends as far as the *apūrva* (the unprecedented transcendental result).
Now, an objection is raised: "In the world, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers do not denote a task to be accomplished (*kārya*"; to this he replies:
"I act because I am impelled by my teacher."
For this has indeed been shown:
one who is impelled, set in motion, or made aware of a task is said to be "instructed"; for otherwise, a conscious being cannot be made to act. But surely—

Furthermore, in common worldly usage, [meanings] such as "sending" and so forth are also understood. Therefore, how can it be said that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others denote only an action to be performed (*kārya*)?
He answers: "For those are merely limiting conditions (*upādhi*); they are not the primary meanings of the word."
In order to explain this very point, he asks: "But by what [means] are these so-called limiting adjuncts (upādhi) defined?
The answer is: "For the limiting adjuncts are extrinsic."
1. Who, then, are these who,
by the mere observation of usage, establish the meaning of a word in a specific instance, such as [the word] "dṛtihari"?
The state of being an animal (*paśutva*).

Its meaning is as follows: those are called *upādhis* (limiting adjuncts) which, while remaining external and not entering into the denotation itself, establish the referents of words in a specific state; for example, that which is denoted by the word *dṛtihari*.

In the case of the word *dṛtihari* ("leather-cord carrier"), "being-an-animal" (*paśutva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). When the act of carrying is related to an animal, then its agent is called a *dṛtihari*. In this same way, this [suffix] such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth, when employed by speakers who are equals, inferiors, or superiors, receives the designations of "command" (*preṣaṇa*) and so on; and the meaning of the optative and other suffixes is likewise employed by equals, inferiors, and superiors.

It is said that *māna* (pride) consists of commands and the like. However, the meaning of the word is "task-ness" (*kāryatva*), which is its capacity to impel action; for this applies universally—whether in the case of equals, inferiors, or superiors—and because it is never abandoned, it is invariable. And that which is invariable is the meaning of the word. Therefore, the term denotes *niyoga* (an authoritative injunction).
This has already been explained previously. Furthermore, when there is the expression of an injunction (*niyoga*), its connection with the means of accomplishment is understood.
And when the injunction—consisting of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) and conjoined with its means—is being expressed, it follows by implication that...

The connection with the means (*sādhana*) is understood. And when the means—such as sacrifice—is denoted as being connected with the end to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the connection with that end is understood by implication. Since this connection is thus understood by implication, it has been said: "of those [words] which have become part of that [sentence], which abide in their own respective meanings, and which denote [their meanings] as interconnected..."
It is logical that [the relationship between word and meaning] has its basis in the cognition of mutual connection. But surely, it is only appropriate to say this when there is actual usage.
The meaning of this is: if usage were observed in words connected with the *apūrva* (the unseen potency), then it would be appropriate to say this; but it is not.

It exists. He refutes [the objection]: "By whom was it said that [this occurs] when there is no usage? For such usage is observed in common worldly (laukika) practice; the Vedic usages are also those very same ones. Therefore, this usage applies only to things of that nature.
1. They are indeed spoken of as "abhi-". 2. And it is stated in the *Prayoga*.
3. For what [is the purpose] regarding the elements (*bhūta*)?

For in the world, words are understood to denote things as connected with an action to be accomplished (*kārya*); therefore, even in the Veda, word-meanings must be expressed by words only as connected with an action to be accomplished. Likewise, by means of the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth, it is an action connected with word-meanings that must be expressed.

Since the syntactic connection (*padānvaya*) is ascertained through semantic competency (*yogyatā*), there is no inconsistency in understanding an effect distinct from the verbal action (*kriyā*). Therefore, it is the *apūrva* itself that is denoted by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like as being syntactically connected. If the comprehension of the connection arises from that which is already connected, then, in that case, the comprehension of the connection of the occasional (*naimittika*) [duty] arises from that which is connected by way of its occasion (*nimitta*). And this is not...
Not perceiving the interconnection, one perceives what is interconnected; how, then, is there an understanding of that interconnection from this?
The answer is: O dull-witted one! Do not speak thus; this is a means of explanation, this is a method of exposition. It is as follows:

It must be said: it is impossible to understand the interconnection (*vyatiṣaṅga*) without first cognizing that which is interconnected. Therefore, in order to show that when that which is interconnected is denoted, the interconnection itself is also understood, the status of the interconnected as the cause (*nimittatva*) is stated. But why is this said? For [one might argue] that [the cognition of the cause] occurs only at a time subsequent to the cognition of the interconnected.
To the question "Why is this not accepted?", he says: "For that which is already connected cannot be understood as being devoid of connection.
Having thus established his own position, he speaks while refuting the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyākaraṇas): "These are the word-meanings as already connected."

The designations for these are "words" (*pada*); thus, this is the *Vākyapadīya*. The aphorism: words denote [their meanings] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāyin*), and not as devoid of the delimitation of meaning; furthermore, a sentence is nothing other than the words themselves.
1. That which is connected with what was previously unconnected is itself connected.
(ga) 2. Without having understood.

Regarding the term *padātireki*: the *Vākyapadīya* was composed concerning sentences (*vākya*) and words (*pada*). The suffix *cha* [forming *-īya*] is applied according to the rule "after *śiśukranda*, *yamasabha*, and *dvandva*. Otherwise, if such word-meanings and words were not accepted, then the division between words and their meanings as it is currently understood would be denied, and that which does not exist would be perceived.

He concludes: Therefore, one’s intellect is not capable of conceiving that the sentence and its meaning—characterized by the comprehension of the sentence-meaning through the effect—are distinct from the words and their word-meanings. It is the words themselves that denote the related [meanings];
the sentence is simply the word-meanings themselves being denoted as related, which constitutes the sentence-meaning. Now, why is there only one sentence and only one [sentence-meaning]?

What is the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*)? It is said: because one object is primary, that very object, as connected with other objects, is what is conveyed; thus, there is a single sentence-meaning. And because it brings about a single cognition, it is a single sentence. Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be unity of sentence in terms of its function (*kāryataḥ*), why does it not exist in terms of direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*)? To this, he says:

However, it has been stated in the section refuting the *sphoṭa* that there can be no such unity, because the distinctions between phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*) are perceived through direct perception. Since the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence is established as valid knowledge, therefore the collection of the Vedas exists for the purpose of [conveying] action (*kriyārtha*).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of action" (*kriyārthena*), [the opponent] objects, thinking that just as in the section on the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*), the word "action" (*kriyā*) refers specifically to the injunction (*niyoga*):
"But surely, in common worldly usage, it is not necessarily only for the sake of action that [words] are handed down;
at least those [words] which have their basis in the Veda..."

As for those words, let it be that they are recorded there for the sake of action (*kriyārtha*); however, those which have as their object matters already known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) do not convey an injunction (*niyoga*), because an injunction cannot be apprehended by any other means of valid cognition. The proponent of a partial view (*ekadeśin*) offers this rebuttal: first of all, the Veda indeed has action as its purpose; this present section (*adhikaraṇa*) will concern that very subject.
The opponent asks: Why is this section not concerned with worldly objects,
such that it is explained in this manner?
A certain partisan says: "What do you think, sir, that you should reproach us? The challenger replies:
"We consider it to apply everywhere, because the formulation of the reasoning is identical."
Since the principle stated—characterized as *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of meanings as already connected)—is the same in both worldly usage and the Veda, this topic applies everywhere;
thus says the proponent of the final conclusion (*paramarāddhāntin*): "Let it be so everywhere."
The challenger says: But surely [it was stated] "for the sake of action" (kriyārthena); [therefore] those which are the roots... [are omitted]. (ga)
[Regarding the term] "pervasive," the proponent says: "This is merely a conventional linguistic usage; considering it to be such an action, please be at ease."
In this context, the word "action" (kriyā) does not denote a mandatory injunction (niyoga); rather, it is intended to mean the form of worldly transaction (vyavahāra).
And since that exists everywhere in the world, it is all-pervasive. He concludes: "Therefore, it is established: [the cognition] of the object has that as its cause..."
"Because of [this]... thus [is established] the fact that the meanings of Vedic words possess a cause (sanimittatva).
For if the meaning, which consists of syntactic connection (anvaya), were not [derived from] the word-meanings...
If words were not themselves the cause [of the sentence meaning], then one would have to postulate that what is called a "sentence" is a single entity to be understood through its effect;

and if such an indivisible [unit] were postulated, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would occur without any cause. However, when it is precisely the related [words] that are the cause of the relation, then the sentence becomes divisible; and since the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) is thus possible, the comprehension of the meaning of Vedic sentences possesses a cause.
He explains the commentary passage, "In those very same word-meanings," as follows: "In those very same word-meanings" [is] followed by...
The meaning is "in those [words]";
regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated: "Words functioning within those very word-meanings cause the sentence-meaning to be understood."
Thus it is said; therein he asks: "Why?
The answer is: "The meaning of a sentence is not perceived independently of the meanings of the individual words."
Since the meaning of a sentence consists precisely of the word-meanings as they are interconnected,
if these are not perceived, of what could the sentence be considered a valid means of knowledge?
Now, [one might object]:

[Page 392] Furthermore, if it is accepted that the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is that which is already connected (*anvita*), then the connection itself is not a word-meaning; rather, it will be the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), the object of cognition for the sentence.

Consequently, by implication, the sentence is also understood to be something other than the individual words. This is what is meant by: "But surely, this is a case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)."
This has been stated by this commentary. He refutes it: "That is not so, because the object is caused by that," meaning that the word-meaning is the related [meaning] through its relation.
By the statement "because it is a cause" (*nimittatvāt*), the meaning of this treatise has been described—namely, that there is no such thing as *arthāpatti* (presumption).
Furthermore, this is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); for indeed, there sometimes occurs this state of an object. (ga.)

Due to a mental lapse, even when these words have been uttered, their meanings are not apprehended. At that time, they do not necessarily comprehend the meaning of the sentence; nor is it the case that they do not comprehend the meaning of the sentence at all.
"They would have understood it as distinct from him, had there been a separate existence for it; however, they do not perceive it as such by necessity.
This is a restatement of the Bhāṣya; [the author] objects: "What has been said here that was not already stated?"

He provides the justification: "Indeed, nothing at all [has been said]. That which was not stated has been stated; for, by means of the words, the meaning of the sentence—the very object of the proposition—is [established].

The non-difference [of the sentence-meaning] is precisely the characteristic of the non-distinction of the referents. However, this reason has been adduced for the sake of establishing that, that is, for the sake of establishing the matter asserted in the proposition. How has it been adduced? It has been adduced as follows: if the sentence-meaning is understood only as the unconnected word-meanings, then the comprehension of word-meanings is merely a matter of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*); why? Because even that which is devoid of the reflection upon linguistic convention [is understood].
Sometimes knowledge does not arise for one who has mastered conventional usage; for example, [people] necessarily understand [fire] from smoke in places such as a kitchen. (ka, ga)
[Page 394] Is the cognition of fire devoid of mental reflection (*marśa*)?
The meaning of this is as follows: those who consider the sentence-meaning to be distinct from the word-meanings.

In response to this, it is said: If [the sentence] has unconnected word-meanings— that is, if the sentence-meaning, which is the injunction (niyoga) that is the primary element, is understood as being devoid of the connection between word-meanings,
and the comprehension of word-meanings is merely a matter of linguistic convention in the form "this is the meaning of this word"— [then the following applies].

This is merely a matter of etymological derivation; why then does the knowledge of the sentence-meaning not arise at times even for one whose usage is firmly established, even when devoid of any reflection upon that derivation and without reflecting upon the derivation, just as [the knowledge of fire arises] from smoke in a place such as a kitchen? [For such a person] has mastered the relationship.

Does the cognition of fire arise even by touching the smoke? Nor is such a form of comprehension observed even for one who has mastered linguistic usage regarding the meaning of a sentence. Therefore, word-meanings are not understood as causes (*nimitta*); rather, they are understood solely as effects (*naimittika*).

Here, an objection is raised: What is the reason that, in the case of conventional usage (*nirūḍhavyavahāra*), the comprehension of the signified (*naimittikāvagati*) does not depend on the cause consisting of the recollection of the relationship? For in all cases, comprehension ought to occur only by depending upon that [recollection]. He replies: For one whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been accumulated does not necessarily [require] a cause...
It requires an operation.
He shows this as follows: "Like a blind man who has traversed a path by habit, he does not require the seeing of it."
For one whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have not been accumulated, the mere recollection of the relationship is the sole cause; for one whose [impressions] have been accumulated...

For a *saṃskāra* (mental impression), however, the cause is twofold: the accumulation of impressions and the recollection of the relationship [between word and meaning]; this is said to be established upon experience (*anubhava*). In this case, since the meaning of the sentence always depends upon that [recollection] and requires the consideration of the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), that very collection of word-meanings is called the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If the sentence-meaning were merely the word-meanings themselves, then [the sentence-meaning would be] from the word-meanings...

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, “the cognition of the sentence-meaning,” how is this demonstration of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) to be understood? He provides the answer: such is this negative concomitance—that from words already associated [with meanings] arises the cognition of the association [of those meanings].

Having intended the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha) as the logical connection (anvaya), the distinction (vyatireka) was stated by means of the proposition that "the sentence-meaning is understood from the word-meanings. Furthermore, even without the utterance of words, one who perceives whiteness necessarily perceives the substance possessing the quality of whiteness.
Having restated the commentary, he asks: "Is this merely a supplement to the commentary on positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)?
A proponent of a partial conclusion (rāddhāntaikadeśin) replies:
It is said: "Om.

He himself says: For in that commentary (*bhāṣya*), the exclusion of the word-meaning was shown, stating that when the word-meaning is excluded, the sentence-meaning is excluded; whereas here, the inclusion of the word-meaning is shown—in the word-meaning...
"The sentence-meaning arises when there is [the word-meaning]," says the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*). "That is true; however, it is not merely this much.
It is not only the connection of word-meanings that is shown here. The partial proponent (*ekadeśin*) asks: "What is added?"

The proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*) says: This is excessive. For if the linguistic mastery (*vyutpatti*) regarding words were restricted solely to the word-meanings themselves, then upon seeing unconnected word-meanings, their recollection would be impossible; yet they are indeed recollected.
And; therefore, the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) is established.
Its meaning is as follows: for if, indeed, during the process of linguistic acquisition... [omitted] ...ga.

If, at the time of linguistic convention (*samaya*), there were an acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) regarding the mere referent of a word (*padārtha*) alone, without its being connected [to others], then,
when that unconnected referent is perceived through perception and other means, there would arise a recollection of that connected referent permeated by the words.

It would not be so; yet it is remembered. The meaning as connected [with others] is remembered by virtue of being denotable by a word, as in: "The quality white is connected with the possessor of the quality; this is what is denoted by the word 'white'.
Therefore, the theory of the denotation of the connected (anvitābhidhāna) is established. "Not of this word..."
Having restated the Bhāṣya passage, "The connection is with the aggregate," he explains: "There is no validity for those things that constitute an aggregate."

The meaning of a sentence is not understood through [words] that have become a mere aggregate or whose division into denotative elements has vanished; rather, it is understood precisely through those words whose own meanings are engaged in function, as established by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

The primary meaning of words is understood solely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); it is precisely when words function as denoters of that [meaning] that they possess authority (*prāmāṇya*). As for the claim that the directly expressed word-meaning ought not to be set aside for some particular reason in deference to the sentence—this is incorrect.
Having restated the commentary, he explains it: the intention is [to ask], "How, moreover, can it be asserted that comprehension occurs even for those devoid of linguistic proficiency?
As long as there is comprehension of the mere meaning from a word that has been uttered—
How could that [cognition] be devoid of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*)? And yet it is so. Therefore, the sense is that there is no expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*).
The resolution here is: "This is indeed true. For usage has as its purpose practical activity (*vyavahāra*), and because of the specific nature [of that activity]—
1. endowed with qualities (guṇānvitaḥ) ga. 2. therefore, not endowed [with qualities] (ato’nanvitaḥ) ga.

Furthermore, since linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is established, the comprehension of the related meaning alone is the purpose of those words; there is no recollection of another related meaning, because that is not a constituent part of linguistic usage.
The meaning of this is as follows: a word is employed for the sake of linguistic usage, and linguistic usage consists of [the cognition of] a related [meaning].

The object of words is that which is related [to others]; therefore, by the force of their application (*prayoga*), words possess the capacity to convey a meaning that is already connected [with others]. As for this cognition of an unrelated meaning, it is merely a recollection (*smaraṇa*); it is not produced by the denotation of the word, because it is not a factor in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
Indeed, no linguistic usage whatsoever is carried out with something unrelated. This is what is meant: immediately after hearing a word...

When, from a given object accompanied by a linguistic item, another object—the mere essential nature of the word-meaning—resides in the intellect, that is indeed memory (*smṛti*), just as the recollection of a word arises from the perception of its referent. And in that case, there is no denotative function (*abhidhāna-vyāpāra*) of the word, because [the recollection] occurs even without it;
just as the referent is not the denoter of the word, yet the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) exists by virtue of their mutual relationship.
Just as the word produces a recollection by way of being a signifier, so too does the word [signify] the object.

In this regard, the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* and *siddhānta* commentaries is as follows: since the comprehension of the unconnected meaning occurs immediately after hearing the words, the word-meaning is directly denoted (*śrauta*) as something unconnected; therefore, it cannot be established as a specific connected meaning merely in accordance with the sentence—this is the *pūrvapakṣa*.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: although a word-meaning is first cognized as unrelated (*ananvita*), nevertheless, because there is no linguistic usage based on a mere isolated word-meaning during the process of learning through the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), the acquisition of meaning for words occurs only in relation to a related meaning (*anvita*).

The cognition of the unrelated meaning, moreover, is merely a matter of recollection (*smaraṇa*). Thus it has been said: "And that meaning which [is derived] from the meaning [of another], that is not..."
"the meaning of the injunction.
That recollection of an unrelated object which does not depend upon the function of denotation is not that [meaning].

Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the word": [The opponent objects]—"If the unconnected meaning, being remembered, is not intended to be expressed, then how can the connected meaning be intended? To this he replies: It is not merely because that memory of an unrelated meaning is not intended to be expressed due to its lack of utility in linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*), that the connected meaning—which is indeed perceived from the word—is likewise not intended.
1. Omitted. Because it is not a constituent part of legal procedure (*vyavahārānaṅgatvāt*). (Ga) 2.
Because it has not been understood (*navagatatvāt*). (Ga) 3. The insertion [of the word] "manifesting" (*dhānaṃ vyā-*)—(Ga)

[Page 398] It may be argued that even those things useful for conventional usage can be said not to be intended for expression. To this, an objection is raised: "A thing is understood from a word as its cause, yet it is not the word's meaning; what does this mean?"

"Whatever is understood from a word is the meaning of that word"—thus, it would be logical for even that which is remembered to be the meaning of the word. He refutes this: because [the object] is remembered as being denotable by another word, and because memory lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*); therefore, even the claim that it is caused by the word has been stated only by those who are mistaken.
Just as in the case of perception and other means of knowledge regarding an object to be remembered,
a subsequent word [is not understood] from the preceding sentence consisting of words in conjunction,
because that preceding sentence is remembered only as the denotatum of that [subsequent] word; for it is not [remembered] solely as the denotatum of the words contained within the preceding sentence.

It is expressed by a word occurring within another sentence. Furthermore, how can a word, which is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), produce a memory that is not a means of valid cognition? Therefore, even the claim that [memory] is caused by a word has been asserted only by those who are deluded.
In ultimate reality, however:
In this case, the word is not the cause; rather, it is the mental impression (saṃskāra) awakened by the hearing of the word that produces this recollection.
Just as perception and other means of knowledge do not function as causes regarding an object already remembered, so too is it with the word.
And thus, the negation of other qualities is not the meaning of the word.
Having restated the commentary thus, he explains: "It is avoided by avoiding the imagined cause;
[it is] that which has a cause constructed by conceptualization."
"The meaning of a word (*padārtha*) is indeed [the exclusion of others]," so the Buddhists believe; in their view, scripture (*śruti*) is restricted solely to the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Consequently, the meaning of the word "white" is the negation of other qualities (*guṇāntara-pratiṣedha*); this very point has been refuted by the statement "imagined... (*kalpita-*).
1. By that very [means], Ga.
2. Thus being so, the qualities—Ga.
In the *Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā*, it says: "The sign does not exist. Furthermore: "The second case-ending and so forth, which are uttered following a nominal stem..."

Thus the commentary has been restated. He explains: they remember the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as having its meaning already connected [with other words], because of which the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā vibhakti*) arises from a nominal stem denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*).

They perform [the function]; and an instrument (*karaṇa*) is that which is related to an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, it is stated that a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expresses its own meaning as being related to an action. Furthermore, the case-endings (*vibhakti*) express through direct hearing (*śruti*) the state of being a correlate (*anvayitā*) for a meaning that was previously remembered from another usage—namely, a meaning that was understood in one context and is now recalled in another context—thereby conveying their mutual syntactic connection.

Therefore, it is precisely that which is already connected [with the meaning] that is denoted by the word; thus, the case-endings themselves are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard. Consequently, this is a supporting argument for the [position that words denote] the connected [meaning]. As for the claim that there is no intention to express what is unconnected, the inference based on "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) has already been refuted.

As for the inference that "the Veda is also a product because it consists of a collection of words," that has been refuted by the demonstration that the linguistic usage of elders can serve as its causal basis. "Moreover," [it continues:]

By this passage, he demonstrates the aforementioned incapacity for establishing a relationship: there is no power to establish a relationship with respect to supersensible effects or with respect to those things that are connected to an effect.
1. Omitted. *bhavati...sambandhi-ga.* [p.
400] Now, if the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote a supersensible effect, do they not then denote their own meanings as conjoined with that [effect]?

And as for words, how then is the use of words in the world possible apart from those [categories]? To this he says: "In the world, however, it is indeed appropriate because they have as their object that which is cognized by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since linguistic usage is preceded by those [other means of knowledge]."

For whatever is established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), that alone is what people intend to express. Therefore, setting aside a supersensible effect, people employ the verbal suffixes (śabda) in a figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) solely for the sake of the effect of action; for the status of being an "unseen" (apūrva) effect is invariably concomitant with the status of being an effect of action. Consequently, with that as their primary referent, people employ the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth, as do other words as well.
Since words are employed precisely as being connected with an action (*kāryānvitatayā*), there is no contradiction with worldly usage. Therefore,
"from the words alone arises the cognition of word-meanings, and from the word-meanings arises the cognition of the sentence-meaning."
[The opponent says: "This is the commentary [of Śabara]; that is untenable, because it has been shown that 'the meaning of a sentence is simply the meanings of the words'.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "It has been explained."
That this refers to the intention of mutual interconnection has already been explained. He concludes: "Therefore, it is established.

The eternality (*autpattikatva*) of the relationship [between word and meaning] is established for the sake of the linguistic usage of the elders, as well as its being the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of Vedic sentences; this is logically consistent for it. As for [objections] such as "it lags behind" (*vilambate*), they have been refuted by the mere fact of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the word.
For that fault occurs in the case of denotation,
as in the words ‘vilambate’ and ‘pralambate’.

Thus, what was stated by the grammarians—that the status of *vi* and *pra* as prefixes is incompatible with their being names (*nāman*) in the word *vipra* because there is no difference in their essential form (*svarūpa*)—is refuted; for even when there is no difference in essential form, their nature as denotative expressions (*abhidhānarūpatā*) is indeed distinct. Therefore, in certain cases, having a different meaning is not a fault. This applies to compounds (*samāsa*) and so forth.
However, in each such case, a rebuttal is stated.

As for what was said— that in a compound there is no connection between two words, as in "rājapuruṣasya hastinaḥ" (the king's elephant) and so forth— a rebuttal to that is also stated in each respective instance.
Therefore, that too is not a fault.

Regarding the [sūtra] "And some [say that] the Vedas are of human origin because of their proximity [to human authors]," the Bhāṣya states: "The objection based on words and sentences has been refuted."
Thus [it is said]. Here, this doubt arises: "But what is this thing called a 'word' (pada) and what is a 'sentence' (vākya)?

For there is no such thing as a sentence apart from words; therefore, how can they be presented separately? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The distinction [between them] is due to the mention of their division and because their functions are not distinct."

The designation "word" (*pada*) is applied because words function as denoters through their division; and since the single, undivided effect of all words is the comprehension of a specific, unified meaning, that [comprehension] is the basis for it.

The usage of "sentence" (vākya) applies precisely to those very words. Therefore, by virtue of function, there is the usage of "word" (pada) for phonemes, and by virtue of function, there is the status of "sentence" for words; thus, the distinction between sentence and word is logical. As it has been said:
"Because no author is remembered, the Veda is uncreated."

Thus, this is contradicted by the designation (*samākhyā*). That designation, such as "Kāṭhaka" and so forth, demonstrates the produced nature of the Veda. Here, he asks: Is the designation based solely on the fact of being a product?

The intention is this: if the designation were based solely on the effect, then by virtue of that designation, there would be the quality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*); however, since the designation is indeed possible even through the teaching (*pravacana*), [the objection does not hold].
The reply is: "Certainly."
The designation is based specifically on the instrument (karaṇa). Why?
Because a designation occurs by means of that which is unique (asādhāraṇa);
for the instrument is indeed unique, [whereas the agent is not].
For it is possible that what was done by one might be performed by another; moreover, the status of being a speaker is common to all.
There are indeed many who are expounders. If the designation "expounder" were not applicable,
how then could there be the [Pāṇinian rules] "kṛte granthe" (when a work is composed) and "tena proktam" (proclaimed by him)?
And as for these two sūtras of the Blessed One,
the response is: the statement [of yours] that "only those which are semantically capable" is incorrect.
Because of this contradiction [with the rule] "samarthānāṃ prathamādvā" (Pāṇini 2.1.57).

Thus, a taddhita suffix occurs only when there is semantic competency (*sāmarthya*). Now, the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) "proclaimed by Kaṭha" is not understood from the word *kāthaka*; therefore, due to the absence of semantic competency, a taddhita suffix does not arise at all in that sense. Consequently, this statement is incorrect. Therefore, [it is] a designation (*samākhyā*)—
From its very appearance, it is understood that the Veda possesses the nature of an effect.
Here he raises an objection: What is this "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) in the case of words, given that words are eternal and the relationship [between word and meaning] is innate?
For words are certainly not produced, because they are eternal; nor is their relationship with meanings produced.
It is produced precisely because it is eternal. Therefore, what is this "state of being an effect"? He answers: "dependence upon another means of knowledge.
The meaning of this is: "This object has been apprehended by this [person] through another means of knowledge."
Thus, this dependence upon other means of valid cognition is the state of being produced; and accordingly, a Vedic statement consistent with the state of being produced is observed:
“Babara Prāvāhaṇi,” and so forth. In the Veda, the descendant of Pravāhaṇa is mentioned;
therefore, it is understood that this text did not exist prior to the birth of Prāvāhaṇi. To this, it is replied: this might indeed be so.

If it were the case that a designation as "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) could not be established without some modification [of the word], then we reply: even on account of excellence (prakarṣa), a designation as "uncommon" is observed in common usage.
That which is the excellence residing in the word itself is what is called "uncommon."

A designation based on that [connection] is indeed possible; for example, the authority of the Veda is proclaimed by Bādarāyaṇa. Precisely because a designation is possible even on the basis of excellence, the Blessed Pāṇini composed two sūtras.
Regarding the rules "when a work is composed" and "that which was proclaimed by him."
And there is no contradiction with the phrase "of those that are capable," because capability is possible even when there is an excellence of expression.
Regarding what was stated, namely "Babara Prāvāhaṇi," it is said in response: since the authority [of the Veda] is established...
He will state that this is a figurative description (*guṇavāda*).

The meaning is that it should be explained according to that principle. Now, for what purpose has this which is about to be stated been mentioned here? To this he says: "And that which is about to be stated has already been explained by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) in this context."
He raises an objection: For what reason was it not stated, "we shall explain"?
He refutes [the objection] for the purpose of showing that it is an irrelevant statement:
"Now, how is this not like the speech of a madman?"— this [is the response to] the irrelevance.

[Page 406] This has been explained here by way of praise of its qualities (*guṇavāda*) in order to introduce it. He removes the charge of its being irrelevant: "That cannot be postulated in the injunctive statements (*vidhyuddeśa*) regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices, because of their syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*)."
And there is no lack of connection in such [passages] as "The trees performed a sacrificial session" (vanaspatayaḥ satram āsata).
Moreover, the instruction of a friend is not subject to contradiction.
Thus he explains the Bhāṣya: "He shows that [the meaning] is universally accepted and free from error. The meaning is that there is no error regarding the meaning of the Veda for anyone. Therefore—
Thus, it is established that injunction alone is the means of valid cognition for dharma; this is the proven meaning of the proposition.
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Ṛjuvimalā* commentary composed by Śālika-nātha Miśra.
Concluded.
1. Added. Śrī. Ka.
